explanation: WA cost = Total Value / Total Units = (50×₹20 + 100×₹25) / (50+100) = (1,000 + 2,500) / 150 = ₹3,500 / 150 = ₹23.33/unit. Closing stock = (150 − 80) × ₹23.33 = 70 × ₹23.33 = ₹1,633.33. Note: Option A had a calculation variance — correct answer is ₹1,633.33.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Net Realisable Value (NRV) of inventory is best defined as:

options.option_text: Estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business less estimated costs of completion and selling
The original purchase price of goods at the time of acquisition
The replacement cost of buying the same goods in the current market
The auction value if the business were to be wound up immediately

explanation: NRV = Expected Selling Price − Costs to Complete − Estimated Selling Costs. It represents what the firm will actually net from the inventory. If NRV < Cost, write down to NRV (impairment). Replacement cost is different — NRV looks at what you'll REALISE on sale, not what you'd pay to REPLACE.

subject: Finance & Accounts
topic: FIFO vs WA in Rising Prices
stem: In a period of RISING prices, which statement is CORRECT?

options.option_text: FIFO gives higher closing stock, lower COGS, and higher profit than Weighted Average
FIFO gives lower closing stock and higher COGS than Weighted Average
Weighted Average gives higher closing stock and higher profit than FIFO
Both methods give identical profit in the long run and differ only in timing

explanation: Rising prices: FIFO assumes cheapest (oldest) units are sold first. COGS = cheapest cost → lower COGS. Closing stock = latest (most expensive) units → higher value. Result: FIFO profit > WA profit in rising prices. (Also: FIFO profit > LIFO profit; that's why LIFO was used in US for tax savings when prices rose.)

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the Perpetual Inventory System:

options.option_text: Stock records are updated continuously after every purchase and sale transaction
Physical stock-taking is done once a year and closing stock is then determined
Closing stock is estimated from the Gross Profit ratio without physical verification
Stock is revalued at market price at the end of every quarter

explanation: Perpetual system: real-time stock tracking after each transaction (computerised POS systems, large retailers). Periodic system: no continuous tracking; closing stock counted physically at year-end. Perpetual gives better control but requires more effort.

subject: Finance & Accounts
topic: Effect of Inventory Error on Two Years
stem: Closing stock of Year 1 was UNDERSTATED by ₹8,000. What is the combined effect on profits of Year 1 and Year 2?

options.option_text: Year 1 profit understated by ₹8,000; Year 2 profit overstated by ₹8,000; combined error = NIL
Both Year 1 and Year 2 profits are understated by ₹8,000 each
Year 1 profit overstated ₹8,000; Year 2 profit understated ₹8,000; combined = NIL
Year 1 profit understated ₹8,000; Year 2 profit also understated ₹8,000 (error compounds)

explanation: Year 1: Closing stock understated → COGS overstated → GP/NP understated by ₹8,000. Year 1 closing stock = Year 2 opening stock → Year 2 COGS understated → GP/NP overstated by ₹8,000. Self-correcting over two years — combined two-year profit is correct.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Asset cost ₹1,05,000; scrap ₹5,000; useful life 4 years. Under SYD method, depreciation for Year 1 is:
explanation: SYD: Sum of digits = 1+2+3+4 = 10. Year 1 fraction = 4/10 (highest, since most depreciation in early years). Depreciable amount = Cost − Scrap = 1,05,000 − 5,000 = ₹1,00,000. Year 1 depreciation = 4/10 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹40,000. Year 2 = 3/10 × 1,00,000 = ₹30,000, etc.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a Not-for-Profit Organisation (NPO), the Income and Expenditure Account is analogous to which account of a profit-seeking firm?

options.option_text: Profit & Loss Account — both are nominal accounts on accrual basis showing surplus/deficit
Trading Account — both show the gross earnings from core activities
Receipts and Payments Account — both are cash-based summaries
Balance Sheet — both show the financial position at a point in time

explanation: I&E Account ≈ P&L Account. Both: prepared on accrual basis, cover a period, show revenue items only, result in surplus/deficit (NPO) or profit/loss (business). The key difference: I&E shows surplus/deficit not profit; no Trading Account in NPOs.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Receipts and Payments Account of an NPO is prepared on which basis?

options.option_text: Cash basis — records all actual cash and bank receipts and payments regardless of period
Accrual basis — like the Income and Expenditure Account
Hybrid basis — cash for receipts, accrual for payments
Fund basis — each fund tracked separately in one consolidated statement

explanation: R&P Account is a cash-basis summary of all receipts (Dr side) and payments (Cr side) — both capital and revenue, current and previous year. It resembles a cash book summary. I&E Account is accrual-based and covers only the current period's revenue items.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In an NPO's Balance Sheet, the Capital Fund (Accumulated Fund) represents:

options.option_text: The excess of assets over liabilities, built up from surpluses and capital receipts over the years
Cash raised from members as one-time subscription fees for the current year
A specific fund set aside for purchase of fixed assets in the next year
Borrowed funds from banks used to finance the NPO's capital projects

explanation: Capital Fund (= General Fund / Accumulated Fund) is the NPO equivalent of capital in a business. It accumulates over years: Opening Capital Fund + Surplus (from I&E) + Capital Receipts (life membership, specific donations capitalised) − Deficit. It's on the liability side of the Balance Sheet.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Life Membership fees received by an NPO are generally treated as:

options.option_text: Capital receipt — credited to a Life Membership Fund (shown on liability side of Balance Sheet)
Revenue receipt — credited to Income and Expenditure Account as subscription income
Specific fund to be used only for providing services to life members exclusively
Temporary liability until the member avails services worth the full fee

explanation: Life membership fees are received once for lifetime benefit → Capital receipt. Credited to Life Membership Fund on the liability side of BS. NOT credited to I&E Account. Some institutes transfer a portion to I&E each year, but the default treatment is as a capital receipt.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Subscription received during 2024–25: ₹60,000. Subscription outstanding at 31 March 2025: ₹5,000. Subscription received in advance for 2025–26 as on 31 March 2025: ₹3,000. Subscription outstanding from 2023–24 (not received in 2024–25): ₹2,000. What is the subscription income for 2024–25 in the I&E Account?

options.option_text: ₹60,000 (only cash basis — accruals ignored in NPO accounts)
₹65,000 (received + outstanding)
₹58,000 (received − advance received)

explanation: Subscription for 2024–25 = Received (₹60,000) + Outstanding for 2024–25 (₹5,000) − Advance for 2025–26 (₹3,000) − Outstanding from prior year collected (₹2,000) = 60,000 + 5,000 − 3,000 − 2,000 = ₹60,000. Short Trick: Income = Current-year entitlement = received in period + closing OS − opening OS − closing advance + opening advance.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club receives a specific donation of ₹1,00,000 for construction of a new library. This should be:

options.option_text: Credited to a Library Fund (specific fund on liability side) — used only for library construction
Credited to Income and Expenditure Account as donation income for the year
Added to the Capital Fund since all donations eventually strengthen the fund
Split equally between I&E Account and the Capital Fund

explanation: Specific donations must be used for the stated purpose only → credited to a specific fund (Library Fund). When the library is built, the cost is debited to Library Fund. If unspent at year end, Library Fund balance remains on the liability side of the Balance Sheet.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Entrance fees received by an NPO from new members are:

options.option_text: Generally treated as a capital receipt and credited to Capital Fund (unless constitution says otherwise)
Always treated as revenue income in the Income and Expenditure Account
Divided: 50% capital, 50% revenue as per standard NPO practice
Refundable deposits shown under liabilities until the member leaves the organisation

explanation: Entrance fees: received once on joining, non-recurring → usually Capital Receipt → credited to Capital Fund. However, if small and regular (like a registration charge), they may be treated as revenue. The NPO's constitution or exam question usually specifies the treatment.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Self-Balancing Ledger system is designed to:

options.option_text: Allow each subsidiary ledger (Debtors, Creditors) to be independently balanced without reference to the full ledger
Automatically close all accounts at year end without manual posting
Replace the journal by recording all transactions directly in the ledger
Electronically cross-check all entries for mathematical accuracy in real time

explanation: Self-Balancing Ledgers: each subsidiary ledger (Debtors Ledger, Creditors Ledger) has an 'Adjustment Account' (control account) that mirrors the General Ledger entry. Both ledgers can be independently checked for balance, localising errors quickly.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a self-balancing system, credit sales are recorded in the Debtors Ledger Adjustment Account (in the General Ledger) as:

options.option_text: Debit — mirroring the debit entry in individual debtors' accounts in the Debtors Ledger
Credit — to reduce the General Ledger's debtors total
No entry — credit sales only appear in the Debtors Ledger, not in the General Ledger
Credit in Debtors Ledger Adjustment Account and Debit in Creditors Ledger Adjustment Account

explanation: Self-balancing: For credit sales, individual debtor accounts in the Debtors Ledger are Debited. The Debtors Ledger Adjustment Account (in General Ledger) is also Debited. The General Ledger Adjustment Account (in Debtors Ledger) is Credited — making both ledgers self-balancing.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India is established under which Article of the Constitution?

options.option_text: Article 148
Article 280
Article 324
Article 315

explanation: Article 148: CAG of India. Article 280: Finance Commission. Article 324: Election Commission. Article 315: Union/State Public Service Commissions. The CAG is the Supreme Audit Institution of India.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG of India is appointed by the President and holds office for a term of:

options.option_text: 6 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
5 years or until 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
6 years without any age limit for superannuation
During the pleasure of the President, renewable every 3 years

explanation: CAG tenure: 6 years OR 65 years of age — whichever is earlier. This mirrors the tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner and members of the UPSC. The CAG is NOT eligible for further office under the Union or State Government after retirement.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG of India can be removed from office:

options.option_text: By the President on an address by both Houses of Parliament on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity
By the President alone on the advice of the Council of Ministers at any time
By the Supreme Court through a special bench set up for the purpose
By a two-thirds majority of the Lok Sabha only, without Rajya Sabha involvement

explanation: CAG removal procedure mirrors that of a Supreme Court judge: President's order following an Address by BOTH Houses of Parliament (not just Lok Sabha), adopted by special majority, on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity (not just inefficiency or political disagreement).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the CAG of India?

options.option_text: Controlling the release of funds from the Consolidated Fund of India (Comptroller function)
Auditing the accounts of the Union Government and State Governments
Certifying government accounts for submission to Parliament/Legislature
Conducting performance audits to evaluate efficiency of government programmes

explanation: After the Constitutional amendment in 1976, the CAG lost the Comptroller function — the pre-audit control over government expenditure was removed. The CAG now only AUDITS (post-audit) — it does not control or sanction expenditure before it happens. Options B, C, D are genuine CAG functions.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: CAG's 'Performance Audit' evaluates government programmes on which three criteria?

options.option_text: Economy, Efficiency, and Effectiveness (the 3E framework)
Legality, Propriety, and Compliance with Rules and Regulations
Revenue, Expenditure, and Asset Management performance
Input, Process, and Output measurement of government spending

explanation: Performance Audit (also called Value-for-Money Audit): Economy (minimum inputs), Efficiency (maximising output per unit of input), Effectiveness (achieving objectives). Compliance Audit checks rules/regulations. Propriety Audit checks financial prudence and judgement of expenditure.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG's report on Union Government accounts is submitted to:

options.option_text: The President, who causes it to be laid before both Houses of Parliament
The Prime Minister, who tables it in the Lok Sabha during budget session
The Finance Minister for review before submission to Parliament
The Public Accounts Committee directly for immediate scrutiny

explanation: Under Article 151: CAG's report on Union accounts → President → Parliament (both Houses). CAG's report on State accounts → respective Governor → State Legislature. The reports are then examined by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament/Legislature.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which provision ensures the financial independence of the CAG from executive interference?

options.option_text: The salary and service conditions of the CAG are charged to the Consolidated Fund of India — not subject to vote
The CAG is appointed by Parliament, not the executive, ensuring legislative control
The CAG has unlimited power to reject government budgets that are not balanced
The CAG can directly withhold funds from any ministry found to be overspending

explanation: Financial independence: CAG's salary, pension, and service conditions are charged to CFI — Parliament cannot reduce them through the appropriation process. This prevents government from using financial control to pressure the CAG. Similar protection exists for Supreme Court judges and Election Commissioners.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG of India is often described as the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the:

options.option_text: Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament
Finance Commission of India
Estimates Committee of Parliament
Standing Committee on Finance in the Rajya Sabha

explanation: PAC examines the CAG's reports to hold the executive accountable. The CAG provides technical expertise to the PAC — hence 'friend, philosopher and guide'. Without the CAG's audit findings, the PAC would have no basis to question executive expenditure decisions.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Finance Commission of India is constituted under Article:

options.option_text: 280 of the Constitution
148 of the Constitution
266 of the Constitution
324 of the Constitution

explanation: Article 280: Finance Commission. Article 148: CAG. Article 266: Consolidated Fund and Public Account. Article 324: Election Commission. The Finance Commission is a quasi-judicial body appointed by the President to recommend Centre-State financial relations.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Finance Commission of India consists of:

options.option_text: A Chairman and four other members appointed by the President
A Chairman and six members — three from Centre and three from States
The Finance Minister as ex-officio Chairman and five expert economists
A five-member body headed by the RBI Governor as ex-officio Chairman

explanation: Finance Commission: 1 Chairman + 4 Members = 5 total, all appointed by the President. Parliament decides qualifications for membership. It is NOT a permanent body — constituted every 5 years (or earlier if needed). The Finance Minister is NOT a member.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 14th Finance Commission (2015–20), chaired by Y.V. Reddy, recommended tax devolution to States at:

options.option_text: 42% of the divisible pool — a significant jump from the 13th FC's 32%
41% of the divisible pool, matching the 15th FC recommendation
35% of the divisible pool as a compromise between Centre and States
32% of the divisible pool — same as the 13th FC

explanation: 14th FC (Y.V. Reddy): 42% devolution — biggest single jump in Centre-State tax sharing. 13th FC (Vijay Kelkar): 32%. 15th FC (N.K. Singh): 41% (slightly reduced from 14th). The 14th FC also abolished many tied grants, giving States greater financial autonomy.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following correctly matches Finance Commission chairmen with their terms?

options.option_text: 15th FC (2021–26): N.K. Singh; 16th FC (2026–31): Arvind Panagariya
15th FC (2021–26): Y.V. Reddy; 16th FC (2026–31): N.K. Singh
15th FC (2020–25): Vijay Kelkar; 16th FC (2025–30): Arvind Panagariya
15th FC (2021–26): Arvind Panagariya; 16th FC (2026–31): N.K. Singh

explanation: 15th Finance Commission (2021–26): N.K. Singh — 41% devolution, used 2011 Census data. 16th Finance Commission (2026–31): Arvind Panagariya — submitted recommendations in October 2025. The 14th FC (2015–20) was chaired by Y.V. Reddy with 42% devolution.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the Finance Commission?

options.option_text: Recommending the GST rate structure and slabs to the GST Council
Recommending the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Centre and States
Recommending grants-in-aid to States from the Consolidated Fund
Recommending measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of States

explanation: The Finance Commission (Art 280) recommends: (1) vertical tax devolution between Centre and States, (2) horizontal distribution among States, (3) grants-in-aid, (4) measures for augmenting State finances. GST rate-setting is the domain of the GST Council (Art 279A), NOT the Finance Commission.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The recommendations of the Finance Commission are:

options.option_text: Advisory — the Union Government is not legally bound to implement them
Binding — the President must implement them within 90 days of the report
Binding for tax devolution but advisory for grants-in-aid
Subject to approval by both Houses of Parliament before implementation

explanation: Finance Commission recommendations are advisory (quasi-judicial body). The Union Government can accept, modify, or reject them. In practice, most recommendations on tax devolution are accepted. However, the government has discretion on grants-in-aid patterns and special purpose grants.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Horizontal devolution by the Finance Commission refers to:

options.option_text: Distribution of the States' share of central taxes among individual States based on criteria like population, income distance, area
Distribution of tax revenue between the Central Government and all States combined
Sharing of tax revenues between different departments of the Central Government
The transfer of grants-in-aid from Centre to local bodies within States

explanation: Vertical devolution: Centre → States combined (e.g., 42% of divisible pool). Horizontal devolution: inter-State distribution using criteria such as population, income distance (poorer States get more), area, forest cover, demographic performance. The 15th FC used 2011 Census data for population.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG audits Government Companies under which provision?

options.option_text: Section 139(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 — CAG appoints or re-appoints statutory auditors of government companies
Article 148 of the Constitution — CAG's authority extends to all incorporated entities
SEBI regulations for listed government companies — CAG replaces internal auditors
RBI Act provisions for nationalised banks where government holds majority stake

explanation: For Government Companies (≥51% government shareholding), the CAG appoints the statutory auditor under Section 139(5) of Companies Act 2013, and conducts a supplementary audit under Section 143(6). This gives CAG oversight over public-sector commercial enterprises.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which fund holds amounts received by the government in its capacity as a trustee or custodian, such as provident fund deposits?

options.option_text: Public Account of India (Article 266(2)) — holds funds held in trust
Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266(1)) — all government revenues
Contingency Fund of India (Article 267) — for unforeseen emergencies
National Investment Fund — established by notification, not the Constitution

explanation: Public Account (Art 266(2)): government receives certain funds as custodian/trustee — small savings, PF deposits, State insurance funds. Parliamentary appropriation is NOT needed to withdraw from Public Account. Consolidated Fund (Art 266(1)): all regular revenue receipts and expenditure — requires Parliamentary vote.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Appropriation Accounts prepared by the CAG show:

options.option_text: The actual expenditure against each grant voted by Parliament, highlighting savings or excesses
The tax collection for the year against budgetary estimates across all heads
The overall surplus or deficit of the government for the financial year
Department-wise performance targets and actual outcomes for the year

explanation: Appropriation Accounts: prepared by each ministry, certified by CAG. They show how each grant voted by Parliament was actually spent — savings (under-spend) or excesses (overspend without re-appropriation). Finance Accounts show the overall receipts and expenditure of the government.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which correctly distinguishes the Finance Commission from the Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog)?

options.option_text: Finance Commission is a constitutional body dealing with statutory transfers; Planning Commission was a non-statutory body managing plan grants at executive discretion
Finance Commission handles only non-plan grants; Planning Commission handled only plan revenue grants
Finance Commission transfers are voluntary; Planning Commission transfers were constitutionally mandated
Both are constitutional bodies — Finance Commission under Art 280 and Planning Commission under Art 39

explanation: Finance Commission: constitutional body (Art 280), transfers are statutory devolution (mandatory). Planning Commission: established by Cabinet resolution (1950), non-statutory — discretionary plan grants. This created a 'dual transfer system' which was criticised. NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission in 2015 but also has no statutory grant-making power.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which economist defined Economics as 'the science of wealth'?

options.option_text: Adam Smith in 'The Wealth of Nations' (1776)
Alfred Marshall in 'Principles of Economics' (1890)
Lionel Robbins in 'An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science' (1932)
Paul Samuelson in 'Economics' (1948)

explanation: Adam Smith (1776): wealth-based definition. Alfred Marshall (1890): welfare-based ('study of mankind in the ordinary business of life'). Lionel Robbins (1932): scarcity-based ('study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means'). Samuelson: growth-based (dynamic, includes both micro and macro).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Robbins' definition of Economics focuses on:

options.option_text: Scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants — the problem of choice among alternative uses
The material welfare of human beings and measurement of national income
Dynamic growth of national output over time through capital accumulation
Wealth creation and distribution mechanisms in a market economy

explanation: Robbins (1932): 'Economics is the science which studies human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.' Key elements: unlimited wants, scarce resources, alternative uses → choice → opportunity cost. This is considered the most scientific and universal definition.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is a statement of Normative Economics?

options.option_text: 'India should increase the minimum wage to reduce income inequality'
'A 10% rise in petrol prices leads to a 5% fall in petrol consumption'
'India's GDP grew at 7.2% in FY 2023–24'
'When interest rates rise, investment spending tends to fall'

explanation: Normative Economics: value judgements about what 'ought to be' — subjective and policy-prescriptive (should, ought, must). Positive Economics: objective, factual, testable statements about what 'is' — can be verified with data. Options B, C, D are all positive statements.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An economy produces only wheat and steel. It is currently at a point inside the Production Possibility Curve (PPC). This indicates:

options.option_text: Underutilisation of resources — the economy can produce more of both goods
Optimal allocation of resources between the two goods
The economy is at the maximum achievable output given technology
An impossible combination — all points inside PPC are unattainable

explanation: PPC interpretation: On the curve = efficient/fully employed. Inside the curve = inefficient (unemployment or underutilisation). Outside the curve = currently unattainable (requires better technology or more resources). An inside-curve point means both goods can be increased simultaneously.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The slope of the Production Possibility Curve represents:

options.option_text: The Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT) — the opportunity cost of producing one more unit of a good
The price ratio between the two goods in the market
The income elasticity of demand for the two goods
The tax rate imposed on production in a mixed economy

explanation: The PPC slopes downward because increasing production of one good means sacrificing the other. The slope = MRT = opportunity cost. The PPC is concave to the origin due to the Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost (resources are not perfectly substitutable between uses).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The central economic problem 'How to produce?' relates to:

options.option_text: Choice of production technique — labour-intensive vs capital-intensive methods
Determining the quantity and type of goods to be produced by the economy
Deciding who in society receives what share of the total output produced
Setting the price at which produced goods will be sold in the market

explanation: Three central problems: (1) WHAT to produce (which goods, in what quantities), (2) HOW to produce (technique — labour vs capital intensive), (3) FOR WHOM to produce (income distribution — who gets what). All economies face these regardless of their economic system.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In a Socialist economy, the central economic problems are solved by:

options.option_text: Central planning by the government — the state decides what, how, and for whom to produce
Price mechanism — market forces of demand and supply determine resource allocation
A combination of market forces and government intervention
Custom and tradition — production decisions follow historical patterns

explanation: Capitalist economy: price mechanism (invisible hand — Adam Smith). Socialist economy: central planning. Mixed economy: both market and planning (India is a mixed economy). Traditional economy: custom and tradition (primitive tribes).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The study of how individual firms determine output and pricing is an example of:

options.option_text: Microeconomics — analysis of individual decision-making units
Macroeconomics — analysis of economy-wide aggregates
Econometrics — mathematical modelling of economic systems
Development Economics — study of economic growth strategies

explanation: Micro (coined by Ragnar Frisch): individual households, firms, markets, price theory. Macro (coined by Ragnar Frisch also): national income, inflation, unemployment, monetary policy. Keynes is the 'father of modern macroeconomics' with his General Theory (1936).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is the FOURTH factor of production?

options.option_text: Entrepreneurship — the organiser who combines land, labour, and capital and bears risk
Money — the medium of exchange that facilitates production
Technology — the knowledge used to combine inputs in production
Management — the process of coordinating employees within a firm

explanation: Four factors of production: Land (natural resources, reward = rent), Labour (human effort, reward = wages), Capital (man-made aids, reward = interest), Entrepreneurship (risk-bearing organisation, reward = profit). Money is NOT a factor — it's only a medium. Technology is embedded in capital and entrepreneurship.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In economics, 'Capital' as a factor of production refers to:

options.option_text: Man-made physical assets used in production (machinery, tools, buildings) — not money
Money invested by shareholders in the company's equity
The total wealth owned by households in the economy
Financial capital raised through bonds and debentures from the market

explanation: Economic capital = produced means of production (machines, tools, factories, equipment). NOT money or financial assets. Money facilitates exchange but doesn't directly produce goods. Capital's reward = interest. Capital is reproducible (unlike land) and depreciates (unlike land).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A student can either join a ₹6,00,000/year job or pursue an MBA costing ₹4,00,000/year (fees). The opportunity cost of pursuing the MBA is:

options.option_text: ₹6,00,000 (the salary foregone — the best alternative given up)
₹4,00,000 (only the actual money paid as fees)
₹10,00,000 (fees + salary foregone)
Zero — the MBA is an investment that will give higher returns in future

explanation: Opportunity cost = value of the BEST FOREGONE alternative. The student gives up ₹6,00,000 salary. The fees (₹4,00,000) are an explicit cost, not opportunity cost. Total economic cost = explicit cost (₹4,00,000) + opportunity cost (₹6,00,000) = ₹10,00,000. But opportunity cost alone = ₹6,00,000.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A criticism of Alfred Marshall's welfare definition of Economics is that it:

options.option_text: Limits Economics to material welfare only — ignoring services and non-material goods
Focuses too much on scarce resources without considering unlimited wants
Excludes the role of government in economic activity
Applies only to developed economies with high levels of material wealth

explanation: Criticism of Marshall's definition: (1) Ignores non-material (mental, spiritual) welfare; (2) 'Ordinary business of life' is vague; (3) Narrow focus on 'material welfare' excludes services like teaching, medicine. Robbins corrected this by focusing on scarcity and choice regardless of materiality.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Law of Demand states that, other things remaining equal:

options.option_text: Quantity demanded increases as price falls, and decreases as price rises
Quantity demanded increases as price rises due to income effects
Price and quantity demanded move in the same direction always
Demand is constant regardless of price changes in the short run

explanation: Law of Demand: inverse (negative) relationship between price and quantity demanded, ceteris paribus (all else held constant). Demand curve slopes downward. Exceptions exist (Giffen goods, Veblen goods, speculative demand, necessities of life).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Giffen goods are an exception to the Law of Demand because:

options.option_text: They are strongly inferior goods where a price rise increases real income sufficiently to buy more substitutes, reducing demand for the Giffen good — but rising price actually increases quantity demanded due to a dominant income effect
They are luxury goods where consumers buy more as prices rise to signal status
They are perfectly inelastic goods that people must buy regardless of price
They are speculative goods whose demand rises with expected future price increases

explanation: Giffen goods (Robert Giffen, 19th century): inferior goods where income effect dominates and is negative — when price of bread rises, people can afford less meat (inferior income effect), and must buy more bread to survive. Classic example: bread for poor workers. Demand curve is upward-sloping.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Veblen goods exhibit an upward-sloping demand curve because:

options.option_text: Higher price signals higher status or prestige — consumers buy more as a conspicuous consumption signal
They are essential goods with no substitutes so consumers pay any price
The substitution effect of price rise is stronger than the income effect
They are inferior goods where rising price reduces real income and demand falls

explanation: Veblen goods (Thorstein Veblen, 'Theory of the Leisure Class', 1899): luxury goods (designer handbags, luxury cars, diamonds) where demand RISES with price. Mechanism: conspicuous consumption — the high price itself is the signal of exclusivity. Different from Giffen (which involves inferior goods and income effect).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When the income of consumers increases and they buy more of a normal good at the SAME price, this is described as:

options.option_text: An increase in demand — the demand curve shifts rightward
An extension of demand — movement along the existing demand curve
A contraction of demand — movement up the existing demand curve
A change in quantity supplied — since more goods are now produced

explanation: Movement along the curve = change in quantity demanded due to price change (extension/contraction). Shift of the curve = change in demand due to non-price factors (income, tastes, price of related goods, expectations, population). Income rise for normal goods → rightward shift = 'increase in demand'.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of demand that causes the demand curve to shift?

options.option_text: A change in the price of the good itself
A change in consumers' income levels
A change in the price of a related good (substitute or complement)
A change in consumer tastes and preferences

explanation: Change in a good's own price causes MOVEMENT along the demand curve (not a shift). Shift factors (determinants of demand) include: income, prices of related goods, tastes/preferences, expectations about future prices, population size, and distribution of income.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Price of a good rises from ₹100 to ₹120 (20% rise), and quantity demanded falls from 500 to 400 units (20% fall). The Price Elasticity of Demand (Ed) is:

options.option_text: −1 (unitary elastic demand)
−2 (elastic demand)
−0.5 (inelastic demand)
+1 (positive elastic demand — Giffen good)

explanation: Ed = % change in Qd / % change in P = −20% / +20% = −1. |Ed| = 1 → Unitary elastic. |Ed| > 1 → Elastic. |Ed| < 1 → Inelastic. |Ed| = 0 → Perfectly inelastic. |Ed| = ∞ → Perfectly elastic. The negative sign confirms inverse relationship (Law of Demand).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If demand is ELASTIC (Ed > 1), what happens to Total Revenue when price falls?

options.option_text: Total Revenue INCREASES — percentage rise in quantity > percentage fall in price
Total Revenue DECREASES — price fall always reduces revenue
Total Revenue remains unchanged since elasticity = 1 at all times
Total Revenue INCREASES — consumers buy less when price falls

explanation: PED–TR relationship: Elastic demand (Ed > 1): price ↓ → TR ↑ (% rise in Q exceeds % fall in P). Inelastic (Ed < 1): price ↓ → TR ↓. Unitary (Ed = 1): price ↓ → TR unchanged. Short trick: when demand is elastic, price and TR move in OPPOSITE directions. When inelastic, they move in the SAME direction.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which type of goods has a NEGATIVE income elasticity of demand?

options.option_text: Inferior goods — as income rises, consumers switch to superior alternatives
Normal goods — demand falls when income rises due to saturation
Luxury goods — consumers avoid status goods as they become wealthier
Giffen goods — their price and income effects cancel each other out

explanation: Income elasticity (Ey) = % ΔQd / % ΔY. Ey > 0: Normal goods. Ey > 1: Luxury goods (elastic). 0 < Ey < 1: Necessities (inelastic). Ey < 0: Inferior goods (demand falls as income rises). Ey = 0: Independent goods (income has no effect — e.g., salt).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Cross Elasticity of Demand between Tea and Coffee is positive. This implies Tea and Coffee are:

options.option_text: Substitute goods — when coffee price rises, demand for tea increases
Complementary goods — they are consumed jointly by consumers
Inferior goods — consumers switch to cheaper alternatives when income falls
Independent goods — price changes in one do not affect demand for the other

explanation: Cross Elasticity (Exy) = % ΔQx / % ΔPy. Positive: substitutes (Tea-Coffee, Butter-Margarine). Negative: complements (Car-Petrol, Pen-Ink). Zero: independent goods. Higher the Exy between substitutes, closer the substitutes are (competing brands may have high cross-elasticity).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility states that as a consumer consumes more units of a good:

options.option_text: The marginal utility from each additional unit decreases, though total utility may still rise
Total utility decreases with each additional unit consumed
Marginal utility remains constant since total utility increases steadily
Both marginal utility and total utility decrease after the first unit

explanation: LDMU (Gossen's First Law): MU falls as consumption increases. TU = sum of all MUs → still rises as long as MU > 0. TU is maximum when MU = 0. TU starts falling when MU < 0 (disutility). Key: MU falls but TU can still rise — a common exam trap.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Why are indifference curves convex to the origin?

options.option_text: Diminishing Marginal Rate of Substitution — the consumer gives up less and less of one good to get an additional unit of the other
Because goods are perfect substitutes and can be exchanged at a constant rate
Because the budget line is a straight line tangent to the convex IC
Because income is limited — higher IC levels require more spending

explanation: IC is convex because MRS declines as we move down the IC. MRS = marginal utility of X / marginal utility of Y. As you have more X and less Y, Y becomes more valuable relative to X → you give up less X to get one more Y. Constant MRS → straight-line IC (perfect substitutes). L-shaped IC → perfect complements.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Two indifference curves CANNOT intersect because:

options.option_text: Intersection would imply a point is on two different utility levels simultaneously — a contradiction since utility is transitive
The budget constraint limits consumers to one indifference curve at a time
Indifference curves can intersect only in the case of perfect substitutes
Mathematically, two convex curves cannot intersect in two-dimensional space

explanation: Proof: If IC1 and IC2 intersect at point A, then all points on IC1 are indifferent to A, and all points on IC2 are also indifferent to A. By transitivity, IC1 ≡ IC2 — contradiction (IC1 and IC2 represent different utility levels). Hence intersection violates transitivity of preferences.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Consumer equilibrium under the Indifference Curve approach is achieved when:

options.option_text: MRS = Px/Py (the slope of the indifference curve equals the slope of the budget line)
MU of good X = MU of good Y at the chosen consumption bundle
Total expenditure on X and Y equals the entire budget available
Marginal utility per rupee spent on X = marginal utility per rupee spent on Y

explanation: Ordinal (Hicks-Allen) equilibrium: IC must be tangent to budget line → MRS_xy = Px/Py. Option D is the CARDINAL (Marshallian) equilibrium condition (MU of last rupee spent is equal for both goods — equi-marginal principle). Both arrive at the same point, but use different frameworks.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following would cause the supply curve to shift RIGHTWARD (increase in supply)?

options.option_text: A technological improvement that reduces production costs
An increase in the price of the good itself
An increase in input prices (wages, raw material cost)
Expectation of lower future prices by producers

explanation: Shift factors of supply: technology improvement (rightward shift), input price fall (rightward), number of sellers increase (rightward), subsidies (rightward), favourable weather (agriculture). Own price change → movement along the supply curve (extension/contraction). Option D would cause supply to increase now (sell before price drops) — but in the future, supply would decrease.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If market price is BELOW the equilibrium price:

options.option_text: A shortage (excess demand) emerges and price is pressured upward toward equilibrium
A surplus (excess supply) emerges and price is pressured downward
Both demand and supply shift rightward to restore equilibrium
Price remains below equilibrium — markets are 'sticky downward'

explanation: Below equilibrium price: Qd > Qs → Shortage. Producers raise price; buyers compete. Price rises toward equilibrium. Above equilibrium: Qs > Qd → Surplus. Sellers cut price; price falls toward equilibrium. At equilibrium: Qd = Qs → no pressure to change.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A government imposes a Price Ceiling (maximum price) BELOW the equilibrium price. The immediate effect is:

options.option_text: A persistent shortage — quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the legal maximum price
A persistent surplus — producers supply more at the guaranteed minimum price
No market effect — price ceiling above equilibrium is ineffective
The market price rises above equilibrium as sellers avoid the ceiling

explanation: Price Ceiling (below equilibrium): shortage. Example: rent control, essential commodity price caps. Binding = below equilibrium → distortion. Non-binding = above equilibrium → no effect. Price Floor (above equilibrium): surplus. Example: minimum wage, MSP for farmers. Non-binding = below equilibrium → no effect.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: People buy more gold when its price is rising, expecting further price rises. This is an example of which exception to the Law of Demand?

options.option_text: Speculative demand — buyers expect higher future prices and purchase now
Giffen good exception — gold is an inferior good in rising price conditions
Veblen good — buyers purchase more to signal wealth through conspicuous consumption
Emergency demand — buyers stock up in fear of further price increases

explanation: Speculative demand: buyers purchase more when price rises, expecting prices to rise further (commodity speculation, stock market bubbles). This is different from Veblen (status signalling) and Giffen (inferior good income effect). Common during commodity price spikes — hoarding behaviour.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which factor makes demand MORE ELASTIC for a good?

options.option_text: Availability of close substitutes — consumers can switch easily when price rises
The good is a necessity with no alternative — like insulin for diabetics
The good forms a very small proportion of consumer income
The time period is very short — consumers haven't adjusted behaviour yet

explanation: Elasticity is higher when: (1) Many close substitutes exist, (2) Good is a luxury, (3) Good forms a large share of income, (4) Longer time period (more adjustment possible). Elasticity is lower: necessities, no substitutes, small budget share, very short run. Insulin example: perfectly inelastic (Ed ≈ 0).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In which stage of the Law of Variable Proportions does Total Product increase but at a decreasing rate while Marginal Product is positive but falling?

options.option_text: Stage II — the rational stage of production (TP increases but MP falls from its maximum)
Stage I — TP increases at an increasing rate, MP is rising
Stage III — TP starts falling and MP becomes negative
Stage IV — TP is constant at its maximum level for an extended period

explanation: Law of Variable Proportions (Short-run): Stage I: TP rises at increasing rate, MP rises (increasing returns). Stage II: TP rises at decreasing rate, MP positive but falling (diminishing returns) — RATIONAL stage. Stage III: TP falls, MP negative (total disuse of labour beyond optimum). Producers should operate in Stage II.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The relationship between Marginal Product (MP) and Average Product (AP) is:

options.option_text: When MP > AP, AP is rising; when MP < AP, AP is falling; when MP = AP, AP is at its maximum
When MP > AP, AP is falling; AP reaches maximum when MP = 0
AP always rises when MP is positive and falls when MP is negative
MP and AP are always equal in the short run since they measure the same output

explanation: This is the 'marginal-average rule': marginal pulls the average. When MP > AP → AP rises (like a student scoring above class average raises the average). When MP < AP → AP falls. MP curve intersects AP curve at AP's maximum. Same rule applies to MC-AC relationship.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If a firm doubles all inputs (labour and capital) and output MORE than doubles, the firm experiences:

options.option_text: Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS) — economies of scale in the long run
Constant Returns to Scale (CRS) — proportional increase in output
Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) — output increases by less than input increase
Diminishing Returns to a Variable Factor — short-run phenomenon

explanation: Returns to Scale (long run, ALL factors variable): IRS: output rises more than proportionately (2× inputs → >2× output). CRS: proportionate (2× inputs → 2× output). DRS: less than proportionate (2× inputs → <2× output). Distinguish from Law of Variable Proportions which is short-run (one variable factor).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Total Fixed Cost (TFC) at zero output is ₹50,000. Total Variable Cost (TVC) at 100 units output is ₹1,00,000. What is Average Total Cost at 100 units?

options.option_text: ₹1,000 per unit (only TVC / units)
₹500 per unit (only TFC / units)
₹2,500 per unit (sum of AFC and AVC as separate rates)

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Average Fixed Cost (AFC) curve is a rectangular hyperbola because:

options.option_text: AFC × Q = TFC (constant) — so as Q rises, AFC falls proportionately, tracing a rectangular hyperbola
Fixed costs fall over time as machinery depreciates
AFC equals zero at the break-even output level of the firm
Fixed costs are shared equally among all units produced

explanation: TFC is constant = AFC × Q. Since TFC is a constant value, AFC and Q have an inverse proportional relationship → rectangular hyperbola (product of two variables is constant). AFC never reaches zero (TFC never = 0). AFC falls continuously but never touches the horizontal axis.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Marginal Cost (MC) curve cuts the Average Cost (AC) curve at:

options.option_text: The minimum point of the AC curve
The maximum point of the AC curve
Any point on the AC curve depending on the cost function
The point where AC = AFC (when variable costs equal zero)

explanation: Marginal-average rule: MC cuts AVC at its minimum and MC cuts AC at its minimum. When MC < AC → AC falls. When MC > AC → AC rises. When MC = AC → AC is at minimum. Same logic applies for MC cutting AVC at its minimum. MC curve is typically U-shaped and lies below AC and AVC initially.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A firm spent ₹10,00,000 on market research for a new product that turned out to be unviable. This ₹10,00,000 is a sunk cost. For future decision-making, this cost should be:

options.option_text: Ignored — sunk costs are irrelevant to forward-looking decisions
Included in the calculation of future breakeven requirements
Recovered by producing the unviable product anyway to justify the spending
Written off from equity capital to maintain the accounting equation

explanation: Sunk cost fallacy: past unrecoverable costs should not influence rational future decisions. What matters for future decisions is future (marginal) costs and revenues. Continuing a bad project to 'recover sunk costs' is irrational. Economic decision-making ignores sunk costs entirely.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In the short run, a firm should shut down production when:

options.option_text: Price falls below Average Variable Cost (P < AVC) — it cannot even cover variable costs
Price falls below Average Total Cost (P < ATC) — it is making a loss
Price falls below Marginal Cost (P < MC) — marginal production is unprofitable
Price falls below Average Fixed Cost (P < AFC) — fixed costs cannot be recovered

explanation: Short-run shut-down decision: If P ≥ AVC → continue producing (even if loss, since fixed costs are sunk). If P < AVC → shut down immediately (losses exceed fixed costs — better to produce nothing). If AVC ≤ P < ATC → produce and minimise losses. The point P = AVC is the 'shut-down point'.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A sole proprietor runs a shop earning ₹8,00,000/year. His best alternative employment would pay ₹5,00,000/year. His accounting profit is ₹3,00,000 (after explicit costs). His economic profit is:

options.option_text: −₹2,00,000 (accounting profit ₹3,00,000 − implicit cost/opportunity cost ₹5,00,000)
₹3,00,000 (same as accounting profit — implicit costs are not real costs)
₹8,00,000 (total revenue before any costs are deducted)
₹5,00,000 (the salary foregone = economic profit in this context)

explanation: Economic profit = Accounting profit − Implicit costs (opportunity cost). Accounting profit = ₹3,00,000 (revenue − explicit costs). Implicit cost = ₹5,00,000 (forgone salary). Economic profit = 3,00,000 − 5,00,000 = −₹2,00,000 (economic loss). He earns less than his best alternative — the business is not economically viable, even if accountably profitable.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is a characteristic of Perfect Competition?

options.option_text: Homogeneous products — all firms sell identical goods with no differentiation
A few large sellers with significant market power over pricing
High barriers to entry preventing new firms from entering the market
Different products sold under different brand names and advertising

explanation: Perfect Competition: (1) Large number of buyers and sellers, (2) Homogeneous product, (3) Free entry and exit, (4) Perfect knowledge, (5) No transport costs. Firms are price takers (not price makers). Examples: wheat market, foreign exchange market, commodity futures.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In Perfect Competition, the firm's Average Revenue (AR) and Marginal Revenue (MR) curves are:

options.option_text: Both equal and horizontal at the ruling market price (AR = MR = P = Demand)
Both downward-sloping, with MR below AR at every output level
AR is constant but MR is upward-sloping due to economies of scale
AR is downward-sloping but MR is horizontal at the equilibrium price

explanation: Under Perfect Competition: firm is a price taker. Price (= AR = MR) is fixed by market. AR = MR = P = horizontal line. Under Monopoly/Monopolistic/Oligopoly: AR is downward-sloping demand curve; MR is below AR and steeper (MR = 0 at midpoint of elastic portion).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of Monopoly?

options.option_text: Free entry and exit of firms in the long run
Single seller with no close substitutes
Price maker — can set price or output but not both simultaneously
High barriers to entry preventing competition

explanation: Free entry and exit is a feature of Perfect Competition (not Monopoly). Monopoly has BARRIERS to entry: patents, licences, economies of scale (natural monopoly), control over resources, government franchise. Barriers prevent long-run entry of competitors, allowing monopoly to earn supernormal profits permanently.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm earns _____ profit, while a monopolist can earn _____ profit.

options.option_text: Normal profit (zero economic profit); Supernormal (abnormal) profit
Supernormal profit; Normal profit due to regulation
Zero accounting profit; Supernormal economic profit
Normal profit; Normal profit — competition among buyers limits monopoly profit

explanation: Perfect Competition: Long-run → free entry attracts firms when supernormal profit exists → price falls → economic profit = 0 (normal profit). Monopoly: barriers to entry → no new entrants → supernormal profit can persist in long run. Normal profit = TR covers all opportunity costs (including implicit).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An airline charges ₹5,000 for economy class and ₹20,000 for business class on the same flight. This is an example of which degree of price discrimination?

options.option_text: Third-degree price discrimination — different prices to different consumer groups
First-degree (perfect) discrimination — each consumer charged their maximum willingness to pay
Second-degree discrimination — bulk pricing, charging less per unit for larger quantity
No price discrimination — different seats are different products

explanation: Price Discrimination: 1st degree: different price per unit for each consumer (theoretical, e.g., personalised pricing). 2nd degree: different prices for different quantities (block pricing, electricity tariffs). 3rd degree: different prices to different market segments (airlines, cinema hall, student discounts). Airline: business vs economy is 3rd degree.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Kinked Demand Curve theory (Sweezy, 1939) explains price rigidity in oligopoly by arguing:

options.option_text: Rivals match price cuts but ignore price rises — making demand highly elastic above and inelastic below the current price
Rivals match both price cuts and price increases — so no firm has incentive to change price
The demand curve has a kink because oligopolists collude secretly to maintain prices
Product differentiation creates a kink in demand as some loyal customers never switch

explanation: Sweezy's kinked demand: If one firm raises price, rivals don't follow (they gain customers) → demand is elastic above kink. If it cuts price, rivals follow to avoid losing share → demand is inelastic below kink. This creates a kink, discontinuous MR, and MC can shift without changing optimal P/Q → Price Rigidity.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Excess Capacity is a feature of Monopolistic Competition. It means that in long-run equilibrium:

options.option_text: Firms produce below the output level where AC is minimum — there is unutilised productive capacity
Firms produce above their optimal capacity, causing higher per-unit costs
Firms earn supernormal profits due to underproduction
All firms in the industry collectively have more capacity than the market needs

explanation: Chamberlin's Excess Capacity theorem: In LR equilibrium under monopolistic competition, tangency of downward-sloping demand curve with AC curve occurs at a point to the LEFT of AC minimum. The gap between actual output and output at AC minimum = excess capacity = the 'cost of monopolistic competition' (variety but not efficiency).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A Natural Monopoly arises when:

options.option_text: Average costs fall continuously over the entire relevant range of demand — one firm can serve the market most efficiently
A government grants an exclusive licence to one firm to produce a good
A firm controls a unique natural resource essential for production
A firm achieves monopoly through superior innovation and patents

explanation: Natural Monopoly: economies of scale so large that LRAC falls throughout, making it cheaper for one large firm to serve the market than multiple competing firms (electricity, water, railways). Government typically regulates natural monopolies to prevent monopoly pricing while allowing their efficiency benefits.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under monopoly, compared to perfect competition, social welfare is reduced because:

options.option_text: Monopolist produces less at a higher price — the deadweight loss represents consumer and producer surplus that is lost to society
Monopolist earns supernormal profit — all income transfers from consumers to the monopolist
Monopolist charges higher prices only to rich consumers and lower prices to poor — reducing overall surplus
There is no welfare loss — monopoly profits are reinvested creating future innovation

explanation: Monopoly deadweight loss (Harberger triangle): Monopolist restricts output below competitive level and charges P > MC. The unrealised transactions that would have been mutually beneficial under competition are lost. The profit transfer (consumer surplus → monopolist) is NOT deadweight loss — it's redistribution. Only the unrealised gains are DWL.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A Cartel in oligopoly is:

options.option_text: An agreement among oligopolists to fix prices and output to maximise collective profits like a monopoly
A government-mandated minimum price coordination among competing firms
A pricing rule where the dominant firm sets price and others follow
An industry association that lobbies for tariff protection from imports

explanation: Cartel: explicit collusion — firms agree to act as a joint monopolist (fix price, limit output, share markets). OPEC is the classic example (oil cartel). Cartels are generally illegal under competition laws (Competition Act 2002 in India, Sherman Act in USA). Cartels are unstable due to 'prisoner's dilemma' — each member has incentive to cheat.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Monopsony refers to a market situation where:

options.option_text: There is a single buyer (buyer has market power) — example: a single employer in a company town
There is a single seller facing many buyers (typical monopoly scenario)
There are two large competing buyers in the market
There is both one buyer and one seller (bilateral monopoly)

explanation: Monopsony: single buyer, many sellers (buyer's monopoly). Example: Walmart as a monopsonist in supplier markets; a coal mine being the only employer in a small town (labour monopsony). Monopsonist pays LESS than competitive wage (analogous to monopolist charging more than competitive price). Bilateral monopoly = one buyer + one seller.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GDP at Factor Cost = GDP at Market Price − _____ + _____

options.option_text: Indirect Taxes + Subsidies
Subsidies + Indirect Taxes
Depreciation + NFIA
NFIA − Depreciation

explanation: GDP at FC = GDP at MP − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies. Rationale: Market price includes indirect taxes (GST, excise) and excludes subsidies. To get factor cost (what factors of production earn), remove taxes and add back subsidies. Short Trick: FC = MP − IT + Sub.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GNP at Market Price = GDP at Market Price + _____

options.option_text: Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)
Net Indirect Taxes (NIT = Indirect taxes − Subsidies)
Capital Consumption Allowance (Depreciation)
Net Current Transfers from Abroad (Remittances)

explanation: GNP = GDP + NFIA. NFIA = Factor income earned by residents abroad − Factor income earned by non-residents in India. If NFIA is positive, GNP > GDP (India's residents earn more abroad than foreigners earn in India). NFIA includes wages, interest, dividends earned abroad.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The correct chain from GDP to National Income (NNP at FC) is:

options.option_text: GDP(MP) → GNP(MP) → NNP(MP) → NNP(FC) = National Income
GDP(MP) → NNP(MP) → GNP(MP) → NNP(FC) = National Income
GDP(FC) → GNP(FC) → NNP(FC) = National Income (skipping MP step)
GNP(MP) → GDP(MP) → NNP(FC) = National Income

explanation: GDP(MP) + NFIA = GNP(MP). GNP(MP) − Depreciation = NNP(MP). NNP(MP) − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies = NNP(FC) = National Income. Mnemonic: G-G-N-N: GDP → GNP (add NFIA) → NNP (subtract depreciation) → then FC adjustment (subtract net indirect taxes).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Income Method of National Income calculation sums up:

options.option_text: Compensation of employees + Operating surplus + Mixed income + Depreciation
Value added by all productive sectors (agriculture, industry, services)
Private consumption + Government spending + Investment + Net exports
Total revenue of firms minus cost of intermediate goods purchased

explanation: Three methods of NI: (1) Production/Output/Value-Added Method: sum of value added by all sectors. (2) Income Method: sum of incomes earned = wages + rent + interest + profit + mixed income + depreciation (= GNP at FC before adjustments). (3) Expenditure Method: C + G + I + (X−M). All three give the same result.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The National Statistical Office (NSO), which is the apex body for economic data in India, was formed by merging:

options.option_text: Central Statistical Office (CSO) and National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) in 2019
Planning Commission and Central Statistics Ministry in 2015
NITI Aayog's data wing and the Finance Ministry's statistics division in 2017
RBI statistical division and Ministry of Statistics in 2019

explanation: NSO was formed in May 2019 by merging CSO (which prepared National Accounts Statistics) and NSSO (which conducted household surveys). NSO functions under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI). Base year for current GDP series: 2011-12.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If Nominal GDP = ₹200 lakh crore and Real GDP = ₹160 lakh crore, the GDP Deflator is:

options.option_text: 125 (Nominal GDP / Real GDP × 100 = 200/160 × 100)
80 (Real GDP / Nominal GDP × 100)
40 (Nominal GDP − Real GDP)
160 (Real GDP represents the deflated base-year GDP)

explanation: GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP / Real GDP) × 100 = (200/160) × 100 = 125. This means the price level has risen by 25% since the base year. GDP Deflator is a broader inflation measure than CPI (covers all goods/services in GDP) and is used to convert nominal to real GDP.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which sector contributes the LARGEST share to India's GDP but employs the SMALLEST share of the workforce?

options.option_text: Services sector — approximately 55% of GDP but employs ~30% of workforce
Agriculture sector — primary employer but small GDP share
Manufacturing sector — backbone of industrial economy
Mining sector — high GDP contribution due to resource extraction

explanation: India's structural paradox: Services ≈ 55% of GDP, employs only ~30% of workers (high productivity). Agriculture ≈ 17-18% of GDP but employs ≈ 45% of workers (disguised unemployment, low productivity). Manufacturing ≈ 25-28% of GDP. This is the 'missing middle' problem in India's industrialisation.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which committee's poverty estimates, based on caloric intake and non-food expenditure, replaced the Lakdawala formula in 2009?

options.option_text: Tendulkar Committee (2009) — poverty based on consumption expenditure norms
Rangarajan Committee (2014) — higher estimates using enhanced consumption norms
Alagh Committee (1979) — first scientific poverty line in India
Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee — caloric method for rural poverty

explanation: Poverty line evolution: Alagh (1979) → Lakdawala (1993) → Tendulkar (2009) → Rangarajan (2014). Tendulkar linked poverty to consumption expenditure (not just calories), recommended monthly per capita ₹447 rural/₹579 urban (2004-05 prices). Rangarajan (2014) gave higher estimates: ₹972 rural/₹1,407 urban.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When a farmer in rural India works only during the sowing and harvesting seasons and remains idle for most of the year, this is called:

options.option_text: Seasonal unemployment — occurs due to seasonal nature of agricultural activity
Disguised unemployment — marginal product of the farmer is zero
Structural unemployment — mismatch between skills and available jobs
Cyclical unemployment — caused by economic downturn reducing demand

explanation: Seasonal unemployment: demand for labour varies by season (farmers idle in non-harvest periods, tourism workers in off-season). Disguised unemployment: more workers engaged than productively required (MP of extra worker = 0 but they appear employed). Structural: skills mismatch. Cyclical: Keynesian, demand-deficient, occurs in recessions.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Disguised unemployment means:

options.option_text: More workers are employed in a job than are productively required — marginal product of the extra workers is near zero
Workers are employed part-time while wanting full-time jobs
Workers are employed in jobs below their skill level
Unemployment that is hidden in government employment figures

explanation: Disguised unemployment (hidden unemployment) is prevalent in Indian agriculture. If 10 workers are cultivating land that only needs 6, the extra 4 add nothing (MP ≈ 0) but appear 'employed'. Removing them wouldn't reduce output. Solution: structural transformation, shifting labour to manufacturing/services.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: MGNREGA (Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act) guarantees how many days of employment per year to rural households?

options.option_text: 100 days per household per year (extended to 150 days in some drought-affected areas)
150 days per household per year as a flat national standard
200 days per household per year since its revision in 2012
50 days per individual adult member per rural household

explanation: MGNREGA (2005, enacted 2006): guarantees 100 days of unskilled manual work per household per year in rural areas. If employment is not provided within 15 days, the applicant is entitled to unemployment allowance. Aim: reduce rural-urban migration, create rural assets, improve livelihoods.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Green Revolution in India (1960s–70s) is associated with:

options.option_text: Introduction of high-yielding varieties (HYV) of wheat and rice — associated with Norman Borlaug and M.S. Swaminathan
Massive expansion of dairy production through Operation Flood
Rapid growth of horticulture and export of fresh fruits and vegetables
Introduction of bio-gas plants and solar energy in rural agriculture

explanation: Green Revolution: HYV seeds (dwarf wheat varieties), fertilisers, irrigation — India went from food shortage to self-sufficiency in wheat/rice. Norman Borlaug (Nobel 1970): developed HYV wheat globally. M.S. Swaminathan: 'Father of Green Revolution in India'. White Revolution (Operation Flood): dairy — Verghese Kurien.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on:

options.option_text: 1 January 2015 — established by Cabinet Resolution (not an Act of Parliament)
1 April 2015 — the start of the new financial year for clean administrative transition
26 January 2015 — Republic Day announcement by Prime Minister Modi
1 January 2014 — during the UPA Government's last year

explanation: Planning Commission (1950–2014): statutory plan-making and grant allocation. NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India): established 1 January 2015 by Cabinet Resolution — think-tank role, advisory, no power to allocate plan funds. The 12th Five-Year Plan (2012–17) was the last; NITI Aayog works on 3-year Action Plans and 7-year strategies instead.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite of which three dimensions?

options.option_text: Long and healthy life (health), knowledge (education), and decent standard of living (income)
Economic growth, political freedom, and environmental sustainability
Per capita income, poverty reduction, and employment rates
Life expectancy, literacy rate, and industrial output

explanation: HDI (UNDP, 1990, Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen): Health = Life Expectancy at Birth; Education = Mean years of schooling + Expected years of schooling; Income = GNI per capita (PPP). India's HDI rank is in medium human development category. HDI values range 0 to 1.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A Gini Coefficient of 0 would mean:

options.option_text: Perfect equality — every person in the economy has the same income
Perfect inequality — one person has all income and others have nothing
The income distribution is identical to the national average
The Lorenz Curve is bowed maximally away from the line of equality

explanation: Gini Coefficient: 0 = perfect equality (Lorenz Curve = diagonal line of perfect equality). 1 = perfect inequality (Lorenz Curve = right-angle). The Gini measures the area between the Lorenz Curve and the diagonal as a fraction of total area under diagonal. Higher Gini = more inequality.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: What triggered India's 1991 Balance of Payments crisis, prompting LPG reforms?

options.option_text: Forex reserves dropping to just 2–3 weeks of import cover, forcing India to pledge gold to IMF for emergency credit
Massive government budget deficit leading to hyperinflation above 50%
Complete collapse of the banking sector due to NPAs exceeding 80% of loans
Trade embargo by USA following the Gulf War, cutting off Indian exports

explanation: 1991 crisis: Gulf War (1990) raised oil prices, NRI withdrawals post-Ayodhya, fiscal deficit at 8% of GDP. Forex reserves fell to ~$1 billion (2 weeks' imports). India pledged 67 tonnes of gold to IMF/BoE for emergency credit. PM Narasimha Rao + FM Manmohan Singh launched LPG reforms.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: LPG in the context of India's 1991 economic reforms stands for:

options.option_text: Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation
Labour, Production, and Growth policies
Licensing, Planning, and Government control
Land, People, and Governance reforms

explanation: LPG: Liberalisation = removing industrial licensing (License Raj abolished), reducing government controls. Privatisation = selling government stakes in PSUs (disinvestment) to improve efficiency. Globalisation = opening economy to FDI, reducing tariffs, joining WTO (1995). Together they shifted India toward a market-oriented mixed economy.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) 1973 was replaced by which Act in 1999?

options.option_text: Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) 1999 — shifted forex violations from criminal to civil offence
Foreign Investment Promotion Act 1999 — encouraged foreign capital inflows
Foreign Exchange Control Act 1999 — maintained RBI's control over forex
Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act 1992 — regulated imports and exports

explanation: FERA (1973): strict forex control, violations = criminal offence, presumption of guilt. FEMA (1999): replaced FERA post-liberalisation. Violations = civil offence (penalty, not jail). RBI manages forex under FEMA. The shift reflected India's move from forex scarcity to relative abundance post-1991 reforms.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act 1969 was replaced by the Competition Act in:

options.option_text: 2002 — establishing the Competition Commission of India (CCI) to regulate anti-competitive behaviour
1999 — as part of the same set of reforms that replaced FERA
2005 — after India joined the WTO and needed a market-based competition framework
2010 — MRTP was retained till CCI became fully operational

explanation: MRTP Act (1969): controlled monopolies and market concentration pre-liberalisation. Competition Act (2002): modern competition law focussed on anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominance, and mergers — replaced monopoly regulation with market-conduct regulation. CCI established under Competition Act 2002.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: SEBI (Securities and Exchange Board of India) was established as a statutory body under the SEBI Act in:

options.option_text: 1992 (statutory; set up initially as non-statutory body in 1988)
1991 (along with other LPG reforms)
1996 (when stock market regulation became critical after NSE launch)
2000 (post dot-com boom requiring stronger stock market oversight)

explanation: SEBI timeline: 1988 — set up as non-statutory administrative body. 1992 — SEBI Act gave it statutory powers to regulate securities markets, protect investors, and promote market development. The 1992 Harshad Mehta scam accelerated SEBI's statutory empowerment.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) came into existence on:

options.option_text: 1 January 1995 — replacing GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, 1947)
1 January 1992 — as part of the post-Cold War new world order
15 April 1994 — when the Marrakesh Agreement was signed
1 September 1999 — after India ratified all WTO obligations

explanation: WTO: established 1 January 1995 (HQ Geneva). The Marrakesh Agreement establishing the WTO was SIGNED on 15 April 1994 (end of Uruguay Round). WTO is permanent, with legal personality, dispute settlement mechanism — unlike GATT (1947) which was a provisional treaty. India is an original member.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 was enacted primarily to:

options.option_text: Create a time-bound (180+90 day) insolvency resolution process, replacing fragmented laws (SICA, RDDBFI, etc.)
Allow banks to write off all NPAs over ₹1 crore without court approval
Regulate the securitisation of non-performing assets by commercial banks
Provide a voluntary restructuring mechanism for viable but stressed companies

explanation: IBC 2016: consolidated insolvency and bankruptcy law. Time-bound CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) — 180 days + 90 days extension. SARFAESI Act 2002: allows banks to enforce security without court intervention for NPA recovery. Different from IBC (which is a full insolvency framework).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: DIPAM, which manages disinvestment of government stakes in public sector enterprises, stands for:

options.option_text: Department of Investment and Public Asset Management
Department of Industrial Privatisation and Asset Management
Directorate of Investment Policy and Asset Monetisation
Division of Infrastructure Projects and Asset Management

explanation: DIPAM (under Ministry of Finance) manages strategic disinvestment (sale of majority stakes with management transfer) and minority disinvestment (public offering of shares while government retains majority). Previously called DISE/DIPAM after multiple renaming. Separate from FDI policy (DPIIT's domain).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which are the PRIMARY functions of money?

options.option_text: Medium of Exchange and Unit of Account (Standard of Value)
Store of Value and Standard of Deferred Payment
Transfer of Value and Distribution of National Income
Store of Value and Medium of Exchange only

explanation: Functions of money: Primary: (1) Medium of Exchange (eliminates double coincidence of wants), (2) Unit of Account (standard measure of value). Secondary: (3) Store of Value, (4) Standard of Deferred Payment. Contingent (Seligman): Transfer of Value, Distribution of Income, Basis of Credit, Guarantor of Solvency.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: M3 (Broad Money) in India = M1 + _____

options.option_text: Net Time Deposits of commercial banks
Savings deposits with Post Offices
Total deposits with Post Office Savings Bank (excluding NSC, etc.)
Government securities held by the public

explanation: M1 = Currency (notes + coins) with public + Demand deposits + OD with RBI. M2 = M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office. M3 = M1 + Net Time Deposits of banks (Broad Money — most widely tracked by RBI). M4 = M3 + Total deposits with Post Office Savings Bank. M3 is the primary monetary aggregate for policy.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established on 1 April 1935 under:

options.option_text: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881
The Companies Act, 1956

explanation: RBI: established 1 April 1935 under RBI Act 1934. Nationalised: 1 January 1949. HQ: Mint Street, Mumbai (initially Calcutta). First Governor: Sir Osborne Smith (British). First Indian Governor: C.D. Deshmukh (1943). Current Governor: Sanjay Malhotra (from December 2024).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Repo Rate is the rate at which:

options.option_text: Commercial banks borrow short-term funds from RBI against government securities as collateral
RBI borrows funds from commercial banks against government securities
Commercial banks lend to each other overnight in the call money market
RBI charges penalty interest on banks that default on CRR requirements

explanation: Repo = Repurchase Agreement. Banks sell securities to RBI with agreement to repurchase next day. Repo rate = cost of overnight borrowing from RBI. Higher repo → borrowing costly → less lending → less money supply → controls inflation. Reverse Repo (now SDF) = RBI borrows from banks.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: What is the difference between CRR and SLR?

options.option_text: CRR is maintained as cash with RBI; SLR is maintained in approved liquid assets (G-secs, cash, gold) in the bank itself
CRR is maintained in government bonds; SLR is maintained as cash with RBI
Both CRR and SLR are identical — together called the reserve ratio
CRR applies to commercial banks only; SLR applies to cooperative banks only

explanation: CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio): % of NDTL banks must keep as cash with RBI. No interest earned by banks on CRR. SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio): % of NDTL banks must maintain in liquid assets (government securities, gold, cash) — in their own vault. SLR compliance supports government borrowing. Both are quantitative tools of RBI monetary policy.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the RBI consists of how many members, and what is the inflation target?

options.option_text: 6 members (3 from RBI + 3 from Government); CPI inflation target of 4% ± 2% (band 2–6%)
5 members (RBI Governor + 4 economists); WPI target of 4%
