7 members (all from RBI); flexible inflation band of 3–7%
6 members; GDP deflator target linked to nominal GDP growth

explanation: MPC: established under RBI Act amendment 2016. 6 members: 3 RBI (Governor as Chairman with casting vote, Dy Governor, RBI-nominated) + 3 Government-nominated experts. Mandate: CPI inflation at 4% ± 2% (lower band 2%, upper band 6%). Reviews monetary policy at least 4 times/year. Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended this framework.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) introduced in April 2022 replaced the Reverse Repo as the floor of the interest rate corridor. What is unique about the SDF?

options.option_text: Banks can park funds with RBI under SDF WITHOUT providing collateral — RBI accepts uncollateralised deposits
SDF allows banks to borrow from RBI at rates below the Repo rate without any restriction
SDF replaced CRR as the primary liquidity management tool
SDF is a standing facility where RBI borrows from State governments at market rates

explanation: SDF: Introduced in April 2022 (Budget 2018-19 proposed it, finally notified). Banks deposit excess liquidity with RBI under SDF without collateral. SDF rate = floor of LAF (Liquidity Adjustment Facility) corridor. Previously, Reverse Repo (collateralised) was the floor. SDF rate < Repo rate < MSF rate = corridor.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Who was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India?

options.option_text: C.D. Deshmukh — appointed in 1943, served during partition and India's economic transition
Sir Osborne Smith — the first governor of RBI (British appointee)
R.N. Malhotra — known for the Malhotra Committee on insurance reforms
Manmohan Singh — served as RBI Governor before becoming Finance Minister

explanation: RBI Governor firsts: First Governor: Sir Osborne Smith (British). First Indian Governor: C.D. Deshmukh (1943). Manmohan Singh was RBI Governor (1982–85) before becoming Finance Minister in 1991. Current Governor: Sanjay Malhotra (appointed December 2024, succeeding Shaktikanta Das).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is a restriction applicable to Payment Banks in India?

options.option_text: They cannot give loans or credit cards — deposits limited to ₹2 lakh per customer
They cannot accept deposits from individuals — only from corporate entities
They can only operate digitally and cannot have physical branches or agents
They can issue loans but only to farmers and micro-enterprises in rural areas

explanation: Payment Banks (RBI 2015): Can accept deposits (limit ₹2 lakh/customer), offer remittances, mobile banking, ATM services, distribute mutual funds/insurance. CANNOT: issue loans, credit cards, or accept NRI deposits. Minimum capital: ₹100 crore. Examples: Airtel PB, India PB, IPPB.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was established in:

options.option_text: 1982 — following the B. Sivaraman Committee recommendation, replacing RBI's agricultural credit functions
1975 — along with Regional Rural Banks for rural financial inclusion
1969 — at the time of bank nationalisation to focus on agriculture
1991 — as part of financial sector reforms to fund rural credit

explanation: NABARD: established 12 July 1982 (B. Sivaraman Committee 1979 recommended it). Absorbed agricultural credit functions of RBI and ARDC. Apex institution for agricultural and rural development finance. Refinances RRBs, cooperative banks, and state cooperative banks. HQ: Mumbai.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Primary Deficit is defined as:

options.option_text: Fiscal Deficit minus Interest Payments — shows the current borrowing need excluding past debt servicing
Revenue Expenditure minus Revenue Receipts — the revenue account deficit
Total Expenditure minus Total Receipts including borrowings
Revenue Deficit minus Capital Grants to States

explanation: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments. It measures how much the government borrows for CURRENT operations (not to service past debt). If Primary Deficit = 0, current borrowing is ONLY to pay interest on past debt — fiscal situation manageable. Revenue Deficit = Rev Exp − Rev Receipts.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + _____ Capital Receipts)

options.option_text: Non-debt (Non-borrowing) Capital Receipts — borrowings are excluded since FD IS the borrowing requirement
All Capital Receipts including borrowings — since FD accounts for total spending vs all income
Tax Receipts only — non-tax and capital receipts are treated as FD-reducing items separately
Total Receipts minus Debt Repayments — the net financing requirement

explanation: Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts). Non-debt capital receipts = disinvestment proceeds + loan recoveries. Debt capital receipts (borrowings) are NOT subtracted — FD itself = the borrowing requirement (deficit that must be filled by borrowing). If FD = 0, government is not net borrowing.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) is presented under which Constitutional Article?

options.option_text: Article 112 of the Constitution
Article 110 of the Constitution (Money Bill definition)
Article 266 of the Constitution (Consolidated Fund)
Article 280 of the Constitution (Finance Commission)

explanation: Key budget articles: 112 = Annual Financial Statement (Budget). 110 = Definition of Money Bill. 113 = Procedure in Parliament for Budget. 114 = Appropriation Bills. 116 = Vote on Account. 266(1) = Consolidated Fund. 266(2) = Public Account. 267 = Contingency Fund. 268-275 = Grants and tax sharing.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which fund can be drawn upon by the executive without Parliamentary approval for urgent unforeseen expenditure?

options.option_text: Contingency Fund of India (Article 267) — at the President's disposal for emergencies
Consolidated Fund of India (Article 266(1)) — all regular revenues
Public Account of India (Article 266(2)) — held in trust by government
National Investment Fund — established for disinvestment proceeds

explanation: Contingency Fund (Art 267): placed at President's disposal; size = ₹30,000 crore. Used for urgent unforeseen expenditure pending Parliamentary authorization. After Parliament approves Supplementary Demands for Grants, the amount is recouped back to Contingency Fund. Consolidated Fund: Parliamentary vote required for every withdrawal.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Vote on Account is presented when:

options.option_text: The full budget cannot be passed before 1 April (new financial year) — a temporary grant to run government for usually 2 months
The government needs emergency funds mid-year above the budgeted estimate
A new government takes over and wants to present a revised budget
Parliament wants to vote on individual expenditure items before the full budget

explanation: Vote on Account: interim arrangement when budget isn't passed before April 1 (election year, delayed Parliament session). Covers usually 2 months' worth of expenditure. Does NOT include tax proposals. After full budget passes, Vote on Account is subsumed. Similar concept: 'interim budget' (includes some tax changes but presented in election year).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 was enacted to:

options.option_text: Mandate the elimination of Revenue Deficit and reduction of Fiscal Deficit to 3% of GDP over time
Create the Finance Commission and define its mandate for fiscal federalism
Establish the Reserve Bank of India's monetary policy independence from the government
Define the procedure for passing the Annual Financial Statement in Parliament

explanation: FRBM Act 2003: mandated elimination of Revenue Deficit and FD ≤ 3% of GDP by 2008 (extended multiple times). N.K. Singh Committee (2017) revised targets: FD = 3% (rolling), debt-to-GDP = 60% (combined Centre+State target of 40%+20%). FRBM has 'escape clauses' for war, natural disasters, collapse of revenue.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following transactions appears in the CAPITAL Account of the Balance of Payments?

options.option_text: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows into India
Export of software services by Indian IT companies
Remittances received from Indian diaspora working abroad
Payment of dividends to foreign investors in Indian companies

explanation: BoP: Current Account = Trade in goods + Trade in services + Income (dividends, wages) + Transfers (remittances). Capital (Financial) Account = FDI + FPI (portfolio investment) + ECB (external commercial borrowings) + NRI deposits + Reserve changes. FDI is investment = capital flow → Capital Account. Remittances = transfers → Current Account.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India was introduced through the ___ Constitutional Amendment Act and implemented from ___:

options.option_text: 101st Amendment Act, 2016 — implemented 1 July 2017
100th Amendment Act, 2015 — implemented 1 April 2017
101st Amendment Act, 2017 — implemented 1 July 2017
102nd Amendment Act, 2018 — implemented 1 January 2018

explanation: GST: 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 (assented by President, 8 September 2016). Implemented: 1 July 2017. GST Council: Article 279A (inserted by 101st Amendment). Components: CGST (Centre), SGST (State), IGST (inter-state), UTGST (Union Territories). Five slabs: 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% + cess.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In the GST Council, the Centre's vote carries 1/3rd and States' votes carry 2/3rd of total votes cast. What majority is required for decisions?

options.option_text: 3/4th (75%) of weighted votes cast — Centre's 1/3rd + at least half the States needed
Simple majority (50%+1) of all members present and voting
Unanimous consent of all members — Centre and all State Finance Ministers
2/3rd majority of State votes regardless of Centre's position

explanation: GST Council voting: Centre = 1/3rd of total votes, States together = 2/3rd. Decisions require 3/4th weighted majority of votes cast. This means Centre + at least some States must agree — prevents Centre from being overruled by States alone and vice versa. The Supreme Court (2022 Mohit Minerals case) said GST Council recommendations are persuasive, not binding.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Ways and Means Advances (WMA) are:

options.option_text: Short-term credit extended by RBI to the Central/State Governments to bridge temporary revenue-expenditure mismatches
Emergency loans from IMF to India during Balance of Payments crises
Loans from commercial banks to the government against Treasury Bills
Long-term borrowings by state governments under the Article 293 limits

explanation: WMA: RBI extends short-term credit to government (Centre and States) when revenue lags expenditure within a quarter. Unlike T-Bills (market borrowing), WMA is RBI's direct credit. Normal WMA and Special WMA (against government securities) are available. Limit is reviewed periodically by RBI.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is a DIRECT tax in India?

options.option_text: Corporate Income Tax — levied on company profits, paid directly by the company
GST — collected by sellers but ultimately borne by consumers
Customs Duty — levied on imports, passed on to domestic buyers
Excise Duty — levied on manufacture, shifted to consumers via prices

explanation: Direct taxes: the burden falls directly on the person paying — not transferred. Examples: Income Tax, Corporate Tax, Capital Gains Tax, Wealth Tax. Indirect taxes: burden transferred to consumers via prices — GST, Customs, Excise (now GST), Securities Transaction Tax (STT). CBDT administers direct taxes; CBIC administers indirect taxes.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Proceeds from disinvestment (sale of government stakes in PSUs) are classified as:

options.option_text: Capital receipts — reduces government assets without creating a liability
Revenue receipts — recurring income from the ongoing management of PSU assets
Capital expenditure — reinvested in PSU modernisation
Non-tax revenue — proceeds go to the Consolidated Fund as non-tax income

explanation: Capital Receipts: create liabilities (borrowings) OR reduce assets (disinvestment, loan recoveries). Disinvestment = sale of government-owned PSU shares → reduces asset (equity holding) → capital receipt. Revenue Receipts: tax + non-tax (dividends from PSUs, interest from loans given, fees) — recurring in nature.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: e-Governance primarily means:

options.option_text: Delivery of government services and information to citizens electronically, improving efficiency, transparency and reach
Electronic voting systems replacing traditional paper-based elections
Government control and regulation of the internet and electronic media
Digitalisation of government employee payroll and HR records only

explanation: e-Governance: application of ICT to transform government's relation with citizens (G2C), businesses (G2B), government departments (G2G), and employees (G2E). Benefits: speed, transparency, reduced corruption, wider reach, cost efficiency. NeGP (2006) was India's first policy framework; Digital India (2015) is the current umbrella programme.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Digital India programme (launched 1 July 2015) rests on which three pillars?

options.option_text: Digital Infrastructure as a Core Utility; Governance and Services on Demand; Digital Empowerment of Citizens
BharatNet, UMANG, and DigiLocker — the three flagship programmes
Connectivity, Literacy, and Commerce — the three enablers of digital economy
Rural Access, Urban Services, and Industry Digitalisation — three target segments

explanation: Digital India's 3 pillars: (1) Digital Infrastructure as a Core Utility — BharatNet, Common Service Centres, broadband to villages; (2) Governance and Services on Demand — UMANG, DigiLocker, e-Hospital, GeM; (3) Digital Empowerment — BPO to tier-2/3 cities, digital literacy, local language content.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The JAM Trinity in India stands for:

options.option_text: Jan Dhan (banking) + Aadhaar (identity) + Mobile (connectivity) — enables direct benefit transfers
Justice + Accountability + Modernisation of government delivery
Jan Dhan + Apps + Mobile governance
Joint Action Mechanism — for inter-ministerial coordination

explanation: JAM Trinity (Economic Survey 2014-15): J = Jan Dhan Yojana (universal banking, PMJDY), A = Aadhaar (12-digit unique biometric ID), M = Mobile (ubiquitous mobile connectivity). Together they eliminate middlemen in subsidy delivery (DBT — Direct Benefit Transfer). PMJDY launched: 28 August 2014.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: UMANG, the unified mobile app for government services, stands for:

options.option_text: Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance
Universal Mobile Access for National Governance
Unified Management and Administration for New Generation
Unified Mobile App Network for Government

explanation: UMANG: launched November 2017. Single app integrating 1,500+ government services (PAN, Aadhaar, DigiLocker, EPFO, CBSE, PM Kisan, NREGA payments, etc.) — available in 13 Indian languages. Built by NIC and MeitY. Different from UPI (payment gateway) — UMANG is for accessing government services.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: UIDAI (Unique Identification Authority of India) was established in 2009 but became a statutory body under:

options.option_text: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016
Information Technology Act, 2000 — as a nodal agency under MeitY
The Digital India Act, 2015 — when Digital India programme was launched
Privacy Protection Act, 2019 — as a regulator of biometric data

explanation: UIDAI: established by Cabinet notification (2009) initially. Made statutory authority under the Aadhaar Act 2016 (officially: Aadhaar [Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services] Act, 2016). Aadhaar = 12-digit unique biometric identity. Supreme Court (Puttaswamy, 2018) upheld Aadhaar's constitutionality with some limitations.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Information Technology Act, 2000 was based on the Model Law of which international body?

options.option_text: UNCITRAL (United Nations Commission on International Trade Law) — Model Law on Electronic Commerce
WIPO (World Intellectual Property Organization) — Model Law on Digital Rights
WTO (World Trade Organisation) — TRIPs Agreement on digital trade
ITU (International Telecommunication Union) — Cybersecurity Framework

explanation: IT Act 2000: enacted 17 October 2000, based on UNCITRAL Model Law on E-Commerce (1996). Provides legal recognition to e-records and digital signatures. Amended in 2008 (post-26/11 Mumbai attacks) — added cyber crime provisions, Section 66A (struck down in 2015). Overseen by MeitY.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Section 66A of the IT Act 2000, which penalised 'offensive' online messages, was struck down by the Supreme Court in:

options.option_text: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) — violated Article 19(1)(a) free speech, overbroad and vague
K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) — the Privacy and Aadhaar judgement
Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018) — decriminalisation of Section 377 IPC
Aruna Shanbaug v. Union of India (2011) — right to die with dignity

explanation: Shreya Singhal v. UoI (2015): 5-judge SC bench struck down Section 66A unanimously as unconstitutional — vague, overbroad, chilling effect on free speech (Article 19). Section 66A had been widely misused to arrest people for social media posts. K.S. Puttaswamy (2018) upheld Aadhaar but limited its use.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) is the national nodal agency for:

options.option_text: Responding to cybersecurity incidents, issuing advisories, and coordinating cybersecurity across critical sectors
Issuing digital certificates and licences for e-commerce websites
Regulating internet service providers and online content platforms
Managing the national identity database for Aadhaar linkage

explanation: CERT-In: established 2004 under MeitY. Functions: incident response, vulnerability notes, security guidelines, forensic analysis, coordination with global CERTs. In 2022, CERT-In mandated organisations to report cyber incidents within 6 hours — among the fastest reporting windows globally.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: BharatNet (originally National Optical Fibre Network) aims to connect:

options.option_text: All ~2.5 lakh Gram Panchayats in India with high-speed optical fibre broadband
All state capitals and major cities with undersea fibre optic cables
All government offices at tehsil level with dedicated leased lines
All primary health centres and schools in urban areas with WiFi

explanation: BharatNet: Originally NOFN (2011), renamed BharatNet (2015). Implemented by BBNL (Bharat Broadband Network Limited). Objective: OFC connectivity to all 2,50,000 gram panchayats. Enables broadband access at CSCs (Common Service Centres) in rural areas. Budget under Universal Service Obligation Fund (USOF).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Government e-Marketplace (GeM) is primarily used for:

options.option_text: Transparent procurement of goods and services by central and state government ministries and departments
Consumer-to-government tax filing and digital payment of dues
Export promotion of Indian goods through a government-backed online marketplace
Digital banking services provided by PSBs to rural citizens via common portal

explanation: GeM (Government e-Marketplace): launched 2016 under MoC&I. Mandatory for Central Government ministries and PSUs for procurement (GFR 2017 made it compulsory). Eliminates tender manipulation, reduces procurement time, enables MSME access to government contracts. Example G2B interaction. Over ₹2 lakh crore in orders placed.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following correctly identifies a G2B (Government to Business) e-Governance interaction?

options.option_text: MCA21 portal — companies register, file annual returns, and pay fees online to Ministry of Corporate Affairs
CPGRAMS — citizens lodge and track grievances against government departments
DigiLocker — citizens store and share verified documents with government agencies
e-HRMS — government employees apply for leave and access payroll slips online

explanation: G2B examples: MCA21 (company filings), GST portal (business tax compliance), GeM (government procurement from businesses), DGFT portal (import-export licensing). G2C: DigiLocker, CPGRAMS, e-District, Passport Seva. G2E: e-HRMS, NPS (National Pension System). G2G: PFMS, e-Office, NICS.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Public Financial Management System (PFMS) enables:

options.option_text: Real-time tracking of fund flow and utilisation of all centrally-sponsored scheme funds at all levels
Online payment of income tax and filing of GST returns by businesses
Management of government employees' provident fund accounts digitally
Electronic processing of pension payments for retired central government employees

explanation: PFMS: tracks central plan scheme funds from the point of release by Centre to ultimate beneficiaries. Provides real-time fund flow information, reduces pilferage, direct payment to beneficiary accounts. Used for DBT programmes (MGNREGA, PM Kisan, scholarship schemes). A G2G system within financial management.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce, 2022) is best described as:

options.option_text: An open protocol network enabling any buyer app and seller app to transact, dismantling platform monopolies in e-commerce
A government e-commerce marketplace competing with private players like Amazon and Flipkart
A network for open banking that allows sharing of customer data with third parties
The open-source credit platform that allows lenders to access borrower data for flow-based lending

explanation: ONDC: open protocol (like UPI for payments, but for e-commerce). Any buyer-side app connects to any seller-side app — breaks Amazon/Flipkart platform lock-in. India Stack: umbrella of open APIs (Aadhaar eKYC, eSign, DigiLocker, UPI, Account Aggregator). OCEN = Open Credit Enablement Network (flow-based credit for MSMEs). Different concepts within the same open digital infrastructure ecosystem.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is a challenge specific to e-Governance in India?

options.option_text: Digital divide — unequal access to technology between urban-rural and literate-illiterate populations
High cost of traditional paper-based service delivery preventing e-Governance adoption
Constitutional bar on electronic delivery of government services
Over-dependence on Indian IT firms making e-Governance unaffordable

explanation: e-Governance challenges in India: (1) Digital Divide (rural/poor/elderly have limited internet/device access), (2) Cybersecurity threats, (3) Data privacy (addressed partly by DPDP Act 2023), (4) Infrastructure gaps (electricity, last-mile connectivity), (5) Low digital literacy, (6) Bureaucratic resistance to change, (7) Multiple languages and scripts.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP, 2006) introduced the concept of:

options.option_text: Mission Mode Projects (MMPs) — 27 specific e-governance projects across departments, each with defined goals and timelines
Common Service Centres as the only channel for digital government services
A mandatory digital signature requirement for all government transactions
Replacing all paper files with digital records within a 3-year timeframe

explanation: NeGP (2006): India's first comprehensive e-governance policy framework. Key contributions: (1) Mission Mode Projects (MMPs) — 27 projects including income tax, passport, land records, agriculture, education; (2) State Data Centres (SDC); (3) State Wide Area Networks (SWAN); (4) CSCs for rural service delivery. NeGP was the precursor to Digital India (2015).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods sold for cash ₹25,000. Which journal entry is correct?

options.option_text: Cash A/c Dr ₹25,000 | To Sales A/c ₹25,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹25,000 | To Cash A/c ₹25,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹25,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹25,000
Debtors A/c Dr ₹25,000 | To Sales A/c ₹25,000

explanation: Cash sale: Cash comes in (Real account — Dr what comes in). Sales is income (Nominal account — Cr all incomes). Option D is for credit sale. Option C is wrong account.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Rent paid ₹12,000 in cash. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Rent A/c Dr ₹12,000 | To Cash A/c ₹12,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹12,000 | To Rent A/c ₹12,000
Rent A/c Dr ₹12,000 | To Bank A/c ₹12,000
Landlord A/c Dr ₹12,000 | To Cash A/c ₹12,000

explanation: Rent is an expense (Nominal account — Dr all expenses). Cash goes out (Real account — Cr what goes out). Option B reverses the entry. Option C uses Bank instead of Cash — only correct if paid by cheque.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Interest received ₹3,500 in cash. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Cash A/c Dr ₹3,500 | To Interest Received A/c ₹3,500
Interest Received A/c Dr ₹3,500 | To Cash A/c ₹3,500
Cash A/c Dr ₹3,500 | To Interest Paid A/c ₹3,500
Interest Receivable A/c Dr ₹3,500 | To Cash A/c ₹3,500

explanation: Cash comes in (Dr). Interest Received is income (Cr all incomes). Option B reverses debit/credit. Option C uses wrong account name. Option D would be for accrued interest (not yet received).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Machinery purchased for ₹80,000 — paid ₹50,000 by cheque and balance on credit. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Machinery A/c Dr ₹80,000 | To Bank A/c ₹50,000 | To Creditor A/c ₹30,000
Machinery A/c Dr ₹50,000 | Bank A/c Dr ₹30,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹80,000
Bank A/c Dr ₹50,000 | Creditor A/c Dr ₹30,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹80,000
Machinery A/c Dr ₹80,000 | To Cash A/c ₹50,000 | To Creditor A/c ₹30,000

explanation: Compound entry: Machinery (asset) comes in — Dr ₹80,000. Two credits: Bank (asset decreases — Cr ₹50,000) and Creditor (liability increases — Cr ₹30,000). Option D uses Cash instead of Bank (payment was by cheque). Machinery is NOT debited to Purchases — it's a fixed asset.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods worth ₹5,000 returned by customer Suresh (originally sold on credit). Journal entry:

options.option_text: Sales Returns A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Suresh's A/c ₹5,000
Suresh's A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Sales Returns A/c ₹5,000
Purchases Returns A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Suresh's A/c ₹5,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Suresh's A/c ₹5,000

explanation: Sales Returns (Returns Inward): goods come back — Dr Sales Returns A/c (loss/reverse of income). Suresh's debt reduces — Cr Suresh's A/c. Option C uses Purchases Returns (which is for goods returned TO supplier). Option D uses Sales directly instead of Sales Returns.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods worth ₹8,000 returned to supplier Ramesh (originally bought on credit). Journal entry:

options.option_text: Ramesh's A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Purchases Returns A/c ₹8,000
Purchases Returns A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Ramesh's A/c ₹8,000
Ramesh's A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Sales Returns A/c ₹8,000
Purchases A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Ramesh's A/c ₹8,000

explanation: Purchase Returns (Returns Outward): creditor Ramesh reduces (Dr Ramesh's A/c — liability decreases). Purchase Returns increases (Cr — negative purchase, a gain). Option B reverses debit/credit. Option C uses Sales Returns (wrong type). Option D is a new purchase entry.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Discount allowed to debtor ₹500 who pays his account of ₹10,000 in full settlement. Cash received = ₹9,500. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Cash A/c Dr ₹9,500 + Discount Allowed A/c Dr ₹500 | To Debtor A/c ₹10,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Debtor A/c ₹9,500 | To Discount Received A/c ₹500
Cash A/c Dr ₹9,500 | To Debtor A/c ₹9,500 (balance only)
Discount Allowed A/c Dr ₹500 | To Debtor A/c ₹500 (only the discount entry)

explanation: Cash received ₹9,500 (Dr Cash). Discount Allowed is a loss (Dr). Debtor's account closes fully (Cr ₹10,000). Option B uses 'Discount Received' — that's for discount from suppliers. Option C leaves the debtor account with ₹500 balance — incorrect. The full account must close.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Insurance premium paid ₹6,000 out of which ₹2,000 is for next year. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Insurance A/c Dr ₹4,000 + Prepaid Insurance A/c Dr ₹2,000 | To Cash A/c ₹6,000
Insurance A/c Dr ₹6,000 | To Cash A/c ₹6,000 (full amount as expense)
Cash A/c Dr ₹6,000 | To Insurance A/c ₹4,000 | To Prepaid A/c ₹2,000
Prepaid Insurance A/c Dr ₹6,000 | To Cash A/c ₹6,000 (entire amount prepaid)

explanation: ₹4,000 is current year's expense (Dr Insurance A/c). ₹2,000 is next year's — an asset (Dr Prepaid Insurance A/c). Total cash paid ₹6,000 (Cr). Matching principle requires splitting the premium. Option B ignores the prepaid portion.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Capital introduced by proprietor in cash ₹1,00,000. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Cash A/c Dr ₹1,00,000 | To Capital A/c ₹1,00,000
Capital A/c Dr ₹1,00,000 | To Cash A/c ₹1,00,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹1,00,000 | To Revenue A/c ₹1,00,000
Proprietor A/c Dr ₹1,00,000 | To Capital A/c ₹1,00,000

explanation: Capital introduced: Cash comes into the business (Dr Cash — Real account). Capital Account represents the owner's claim (Cr Capital — liability/equity increases). Option B wrongly debits capital (that would reduce it). Option C uses wrong account.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Advance salary paid ₹10,000 to employee. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Salary Advance A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Cash A/c ₹10,000
Salary A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Cash A/c ₹10,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Salary Advance A/c ₹10,000
Prepaid Salary A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Bank A/c ₹10,000

explanation: Advance salary is NOT an expense yet — it's an asset (recoverable from future salary). Dr Salary Advance A/c (asset). Cr Cash. When actual salary is paid later, Salary A/c Dr, To Salary Advance A/c (recover) + To Cash (balance). Option B charges to Salary expense prematurely.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Loan taken from bank ₹2,00,000 at 12% per annum. Journal entry at the time of loan receipt:

options.option_text: Bank A/c Dr ₹2,00,000 | To Loan A/c ₹2,00,000
Loan A/c Dr ₹2,00,000 | To Bank A/c ₹2,00,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹2,00,000 | To Bank Loan A/c ₹2,00,000 | To Interest A/c ₹24,000
Bank A/c Dr ₹1,76,000 | Interest A/c Dr ₹24,000 | To Loan A/c ₹2,00,000

explanation: At the time of receiving loan: Bank balance increases (Dr Bank A/c). Loan payable increases (Cr Loan A/c — liability). Interest is NOT recorded at this point — it accrues with time and is recorded as it falls due. Interest rate in the question is just additional information for later entries.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods destroyed by fire ₹30,000. Insurance company admits claim for ₹20,000. Journal entry for the fire loss:

options.option_text: Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹10,000 + Insurance Claim Receivable A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹30,000
Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹30,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹30,000 (insurance ignored)
Insurance A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Loss by Fire A/c ₹20,000 (only partial loss)
Loss by Fire A/c Dr ₹30,000 | To Insurance A/c ₹20,000 | To Profit A/c ₹10,000

explanation: Two effects: (1) Goods gone — Cr Purchases A/c ₹30,000 (or Trading A/c via Purchases). (2) Insurance receivable ₹20,000 (Dr — asset). Net loss = ₹10,000 (Dr Loss by Fire A/c). Option B records full ₹30,000 as loss ignoring the insurance recovery. Option C is incomplete.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods given as charity ₹2,000 (at cost). Journal entry:

options.option_text: Charity A/c Dr ₹2,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹2,000
Charity A/c Dr ₹2,000 | To Sales A/c ₹2,000
Advertisement A/c Dr ₹2,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹2,000
Drawings A/c Dr ₹2,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹2,000

explanation: Goods given as charity: Dr Charity A/c (expense/loss). Cr Purchases A/c at cost (goods leave the business). Option B credits Sales — wrong (goods are not sold). Option D uses Drawings — that's for personal use by the proprietor, not charity given on behalf of the business.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Commission received in advance ₹4,000. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Cash A/c Dr ₹4,000 | To Unearned Commission A/c ₹4,000
Commission Received A/c Dr ₹4,000 | To Cash A/c ₹4,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹4,000 | To Commission Received A/c ₹4,000 (as income)
Prepaid Commission A/c Dr ₹4,000 | To Cash A/c ₹4,000

explanation: Commission received in advance is a liability (service not yet rendered). Dr Cash A/c (asset). Cr Unearned Commission / Commission Received in Advance A/c (liability). Option C wrongly treats it as earned income immediately. When the service is rendered, Dr Unearned Commission A/c, Cr Commission Earned A/c.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A three-column cash book has three columns on each side. Which three columns are they?

options.option_text: Cash, Bank, and Discount columns on both receipt and payment sides
Date, Particulars, and Amount on each side
Cash, Cheque, and Petty Cash on the receipt side; Cash, Bank, and Expenses on payment side
Cash, Bank, and VAT/GST columns for tax compliance

explanation: Three-column cash book: (1) Discount column — discount allowed (Dr side) and discount received (Cr side); (2) Cash column — cash receipts and payments; (3) Bank column — cheque receipts and payments. Discount columns are TOTALLED, not balanced (they transfer to Discount Allowed/Received accounts in the ledger).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the Imprest System of Petty Cash:

options.option_text: The petty cashier receives a fixed sum (imprest) and is reimbursed at the end of the period for exact amount spent
The petty cashier receives cash as and when needed, without a fixed limit
All petty expenses are paid directly by the main cashier without a separate petty cashier
The petty cashier keeps a fixed surplus balance after paying expenses, never returning change

explanation: Imprest System: Petty cashier receives a fixed imprest (e.g., ₹5,000). At period end, main cashier reimburses exactly what was spent (e.g., ₹3,200 spent → ₹3,200 reimbursed). This restores the petty cash to ₹5,000. Advantage: easy to audit — cash in hand + vouchers = always equals the imprest amount.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which subsidiary book records credit sales of goods to customers?

options.option_text: Sales Book (Sales Day Book)
Cash Book — all sales are recorded whether cash or credit
Journal Proper — credit sales require special entries
Purchases Book — records all trading transactions

explanation: Sales Book: records ONLY credit sales of goods. Cash sales → Cash Book. Asset sales on credit → Journal Proper. Returns from customers → Sales Returns Book. The Sales Book lists: date, customer name, invoice number, amount. Posting: Dr Debtor A/c, Cr Sales A/c periodically.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following transactions is recorded in the Journal Proper?

options.option_text: Purchase of old furniture on credit for office use
Credit purchase of goods for resale from a supplier
Cash sale of goods to a walk-in customer
Return of defective goods to the supplier from whom they were purchased on credit

explanation: Journal Proper (General Journal) handles transactions not going to any other subsidiary book: opening entries, closing entries, rectification entries, depreciation entries, and importantly — purchase/sale of assets on credit. Goods purchased on credit → Purchases Book. Return to supplier → Purchases Returns Book. Cash sale → Cash Book.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A credit sale of ₹15,000 to Ramu was correctly entered in the Sales Book but posted to the debit side of Raju's account. This is an error of:

options.option_text: Commission — correct amount, correct class, but wrong personal account
Principle — the nature of the account was misunderstood
Omission — the transaction was not recorded at all
Original Entry — the Sales Book itself contains the wrong name

explanation: Error of Commission: the correct amount (₹15,000) is correctly debited to a personal account, but to the WRONG person (Raju instead of Ramu). Both are debtors (same class). Trial Balance still tallies. Error of Principle would be if Ramu's account was treated as an expense account, etc.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Purchases Day Book was overcast (over-totalled) by ₹1,000. What is the effect on the Trial Balance?

options.option_text: Debit side of Trial Balance exceeds credit side by ₹1,000
Credit side of Trial Balance exceeds debit side by ₹1,000
Trial Balance tallies — overcasting a subsidiary book does not affect the TB
Both debit and credit sides of Trial Balance increase by ₹1,000 each

explanation: Purchases Day Book overcast by ₹1,000: Purchases A/c is debited with ₹1,000 extra (overcasted total posted to ledger). Creditors A/c is credited correctly (individual posting is correct; only total is wrong). So only the DEBIT side (Purchases) is overstated by ₹1,000 → Dr side of TB > Cr side by ₹1,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Purchase of ₹5,000 from Sharma was entered twice in the Purchases Book. How does this affect the Trial Balance?

options.option_text: Trial Balance tallies — both Purchases A/c and Sharma's A/c are both overstated by ₹5,000
Debit side exceeds credit side by ₹5,000 — only Purchases A/c is doubled
Credit side exceeds debit side by ₹5,000 — Sharma's A/c is overstated
Trial Balance disagrees by ₹10,000 since two entries were made

explanation: Error of Duplication: entry made twice. Both Purchases A/c (Dr side) and Sharma's A/c (Cr side) are doubled. Since BOTH sides are overstated by the same ₹5,000, the Trial Balance still tallies. This is a two-sided error — not detected by Trial Balance.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Sales Return from Ram ₹3,000 was wrongly credited to Sales A/c instead of Sales Returns A/c. Rectification entry:

options.option_text: Sales A/c Dr ₹3,000 + Sales Returns A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Sales A/c ₹3,000 | To Ram's A/c ₹3,000 — simplified: Sales A/c Dr ₹6,000 | To Sales Returns A/c ₹3,000 | To Ram's A/c ₹3,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Sales Returns A/c ₹3,000
Sales Returns A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Sales A/c ₹3,000
No rectification needed — the net effect on Gross Profit is the same

explanation: Original error: Dr Ram's A/c (correct) | Cr Sales A/c (wrong — should be Cr Sales Returns A/c). Rectification: reverse the wrong credit and put in the right place. Dr Sales A/c ₹3,000 (cancel wrong credit) | Cr Sales Returns A/c ₹3,000 (put in correct account). Ram's A/c is not touched — it was correctly debited.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Machinery purchased ₹20,000 was debited to Purchases A/c. Rectification entry (after Trial Balance, Suspense A/c in use):

options.option_text: Machinery A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹20,000 (no Suspense involvement — two-sided error)
Machinery A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Suspense A/c ₹20,000
Suspense A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹20,000
Purchases A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Suspense A/c ₹20,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹20,000

explanation: Error of Principle: both Purchases A/c (Dr) and Creditor/Cash A/c (Cr) were correctly posted — only the NATURE of account is wrong (expense instead of asset). This is a TWO-SIDED error — Trial Balance was NOT affected → Suspense Account has no balance for this error. Rectification: Dr Machinery A/c, Cr Purchases A/c — no Suspense involved.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The process of transferring entries from the Journal to the Ledger is called:

options.option_text: Posting
Casting
Balancing
Journalising

explanation: Posting: transferring debit and credit entries from the journal to respective ledger accounts. Casting: totalling columns. Balancing: finding the difference between debit and credit totals of a ledger account and writing it down. Journalising: recording transactions in the journal.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Narration in a journal entry refers to:

options.option_text: A brief description written below each journal entry explaining the nature of the transaction
The name of the person who made the journal entry in the accounts
A numerical code assigned to each transaction for cross-referencing
A summary of all transactions prepared at month-end for audit purposes

explanation: Narration (explanation/remark): written in brackets below each journal entry. Example: 'Being goods sold on credit to Ram'. It helps understand why the entry was made. Good narrations answer 'Being ___' — stating the nature of the transaction. Essential for audit trail.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: If total debits in a Trial Balance = ₹8,50,000 and total credits = ₹8,20,000, the difference of ₹30,000 is transferred to:

options.option_text: Suspense Account (credit side) — to make the Trial Balance tally temporarily
Profit & Loss Account to adjust the period's profit
Capital Account — the difference is the owner's contribution
Error Account that automatically locates the mistake

explanation: When Dr total (₹8,50,000) > Cr total (₹8,20,000) by ₹30,000: Suspense A/c is credited with ₹30,000 to make both sides equal. As errors are found and corrected, Suspense A/c entries reduce. When all errors are found, Suspense A/c balance becomes nil.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Salary outstanding at year-end ₹8,000 (not yet paid). Adjustment entry:

options.option_text: Salary A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Outstanding Salary A/c ₹8,000
Outstanding Salary A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Salary A/c ₹8,000
Salary A/c Dr ₹8,000 | To Cash A/c ₹8,000 (anticipate payment)
No entry — payment will be recorded when actually made

explanation: Accrual principle: recognise expense when incurred, not when paid. Dr Salary A/c (expense for the year). Cr Outstanding Salary A/c (current liability — owed but not paid). This increases the salary charge in P&L and creates a liability on the Balance Sheet.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Closing entry for transferring the credit balance of Sales A/c (₹5,00,000) to the Trading Account:

options.option_text: Sales A/c Dr ₹5,00,000 | To Trading A/c ₹5,00,000
Trading A/c Dr ₹5,00,000 | To Sales A/c ₹5,00,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹5,00,000 | To Profit & Loss A/c ₹5,00,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹5,00,000 | To Capital A/c ₹5,00,000

explanation: Closing entry for Sales A/c: Sales has a credit balance. To close it, debit Sales A/c (zero it out) and credit Trading A/c (transfer the income). Trading A/c collects all trading-related incomes and expenses to compute Gross Profit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Depreciation on machinery ₹15,000 is charged. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Depreciation A/c Dr ₹15,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹15,000
Machinery A/c Dr ₹15,000 | To Depreciation A/c ₹15,000
Depreciation A/c Dr ₹15,000 | To Provision for Depreciation A/c ₹15,000
P&L A/c Dr ₹15,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹15,000

explanation: Depreciation A/c Dr (expense/loss → Nominal account). To Machinery A/c Cr (asset decreases). Option C is used when a Provision for Depreciation Account is maintained separately (the asset stays at cost, and a separate provision account accumulates depreciation). Option D skips the Depreciation A/c intermediary.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The folio column in the Journal is used to record:

options.option_text: The page number of the Ledger Account where the entry has been posted
The invoice number of the underlying source document
The running serial number of journal entries for the year
The tax identification number of the party involved in the transaction

explanation: Folio (L.F. — Ledger Folio): the page/account number in the Ledger where the journal entry has been posted. Helps cross-reference between Journal and Ledger. In the Ledger, the J.F. (Journal Folio) column shows the Journal page where the original entry was made.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Cheque received from customer Ravi ₹20,000 and deposited in bank. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Bank A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Ravi's A/c ₹20,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Ravi's A/c ₹20,000
Ravi's A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Bank A/c ₹20,000
Bank A/c Dr ₹20,000 | To Sales A/c ₹20,000

explanation: Cheque deposited in bank: Bank balance increases (Dr Bank A/c). Ravi's debt is cleared (Cr Ravi's A/c). Option B uses Cash A/c — only correct if cash is received (cheque goes to bank, not cash box). Option D uses Sales A/c — wrong (this is collection against an existing debtor, not a new sale).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: At the beginning of FY 2025-26: Cash ₹50,000; Debtors ₹80,000; Creditors ₹30,000; Capital ₹1,00,000. Opening entry:

options.option_text: Cash Dr ₹50,000 + Debtors Dr ₹80,000 | To Creditors ₹30,000 | To Capital ₹1,00,000
Capital Dr ₹1,00,000 + Creditors Dr ₹30,000 | To Cash ₹50,000 | To Debtors ₹80,000
All accounts including Capital and Creditors are debited; no credits in opening entry
Only asset accounts are opened; liabilities and capital have no opening entries

explanation: Opening entry: ALL assets are Debited (Dr Cash ₹50,000, Dr Debtors ₹80,000). ALL liabilities and Capital are Credited (Cr Creditors ₹30,000, Cr Capital ₹1,00,000). Check: Dr total = ₹1,30,000 = Cr total ₹1,30,000 ✓. The accounting equation holds: Assets ₹1,30,000 = Liabilities ₹30,000 + Capital ₹1,00,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Double Entry System ensures that for every debit entry there is:

options.option_text: An equal and corresponding credit entry in another account
Two separate debit entries in two different accounts
A corresponding entry in the same account on the opposite side
An entry in the Trial Balance to verify arithmetical accuracy

explanation: Double Entry: every transaction has TWO aspects — equal and opposite. For every debit in one account, there is an equal credit in another account. This maintains the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Capital) at all times and provides a self-checking mechanism.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A Trial Balance that tallies is CONCLUSIVE proof that:

options.option_text: None of the above — a tallied TB only indicates arithmetic accuracy, not freedom from all errors
No errors exist in the books of accounts
All transactions have been recorded with correct accounts and amounts
Financial statements can be prepared without any further verification

explanation: A tallied Trial Balance only confirms that total debits = total credits arithmetically. It does NOT prove: errors of omission, errors of principle, errors of commission (wrong account same class), compensating errors, or errors of original entry — these are all 'two-sided errors' that leave TB balanced despite being wrong.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm sells goods for ₹40,000 at 10% trade discount. Customer pays within 7 days and gets 2% cash discount. Amount received by firm = ?

options.option_text: ₹36,000 (only trade discount deducted)
₹38,400 (only cash discount deducted from ₹40,000)
₹34,400 (both discounts applied to original ₹40,000)

explanation: Step 1: Trade discount = 10% × ₹40,000 = ₹4,000. Invoice value = ₹36,000 (trade discount is never recorded). Step 2: Cash discount = 2% × ₹36,000 = ₹720. Amount received = ₹36,000 − ₹720 = ₹35,280. Journal: Dr Cash ₹35,280 + Dr Discount Allowed ₹720 | Cr Debtor ₹36,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Cash Book (bank column) balance ₹45,000 (Dr). Cheques issued but not presented ₹8,000. Cheques deposited but not cleared ₹5,000. Bank charges ₹500 (not in CB). Balance as per Pass Book = ?

options.option_text: ₹31,500 (CB ₹45,000 − cheques not deposited ₹5,000 + cheques not presented ₹8,000 − bank charges ₹500 = wait, let me recalculate: 45,000 + 8,000 − 5,000 − 500 = ₹47,500)
₹47,500 (₹45,000 + unpresented cheques ₹8,000 − uncleared deposits ₹5,000 − bank charges ₹500)

explanation: Starting from Cash Book balance (₹45,000 Dr): +Unpresented cheques ₹8,000 (issued but bank hasn't paid yet → PB higher) −Uncleared deposits ₹5,000 (deposited but bank hasn't credited → PB lower) −Bank charges ₹500 (bank deducted but not in CB → PB lower) = ₹45,000 + 8,000 − 5,000 − 500 = ₹47,500 (Pass Book balance).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Pass Book shows a balance of ₹60,000 (credit). To prepare BRS starting with PASS BOOK balance, which adjustment brings us to Cash Book balance?

options.option_text: Deduct unpresented cheques; Add uncleared deposits; Add bank charges (not in CB); Deduct interest credited by bank (not in CB)
Add unpresented cheques; Deduct uncleared deposits; Add interest credited by bank
Deduct all items from PB balance to reach CB balance
The adjustments are identical whether starting from CB or PB balance

explanation: Starting from PB balance to get CB balance (reverse direction): −Unpresented cheques (PB is higher because these haven't been paid yet; CB already reduced) +Uncleared deposits (PB is lower; CB already increased) −Bank charges (PB already lower; CB hasn't recorded yet, so reduce to reach CB) +Bank charges from CB perspective = opposite. Standard formula: CB = PB − Unpresented − Bank charges + Uncleared deposits + Direct credits to bank not in CB.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm's Cash Book (bank column) shows a CREDIT balance (overdraft) of ₹15,000. Unpresented cheques = ₹4,000. Bank interest on overdraft ₹800 (not in CB). Direct deposit by customer ₹3,000 (not in CB). Pass Book balance = ?

options.option_text: Credit balance of ₹16,800

explanation: CB OD = ₹15,000 (credit balance = firm owes bank). Adjustments to PB: +Unpresented cheques ₹4,000 (bank hasn't paid them yet → PB OD is less = better for firm). Wait — for OD accounts, unpresented cheques REDUCE the overdraft in PB (bank hasn't debited yet). −Direct deposit ₹3,000 (PB already credited, CB hasn't → PB OD is less by ₹3,000). +Bank interest ₹800 (bank debited → PB OD higher). PB OD = 15,000 − 4,000 + 3,000 + 800 = ₹14,800? Let me reconsider. Starting from CB OD ₹15,000 to get PB: PB OD = CB OD − unpresented (bank hasn't charged yet, so PB shows less OD) − direct deposits (PB is lower OD since credited) + bank interest (OD increases). PB = 15,000 − 4,000 + 800 − 3,000 = ₹8,800 OD. Answer should be reconsidered.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following items would NOT cause a difference between Cash Book balance and Pass Book balance?

options.option_text: An error in the Cash Book itself (entered ₹500 instead of ₹5,000)
A cheque paid by the bank directly on behalf of the firm, not recorded in Cash Book
A cash sale properly recorded in both the Cash Book and the sales ledger simultaneously
Interest on overdraft charged by the bank, not yet recorded by the firm

explanation: A cash sale correctly recorded in the Cash Book does NOT appear in the Pass Book (cash sales don't go through the bank unless deposited). If properly recorded in CB and NOT in PB, it's a timing difference — but cash sales go to the Cash column, NOT the Bank column. A cash sale entered in both CB and the sales ledger simultaneously would not affect the bank column comparison at all — hence no BRS difference.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: ECS (Electronic Clearing Service) payments made by the bank on behalf of the firm but not recorded in the Cash Book will:

options.option_text: Reduce Pass Book balance but NOT Cash Book balance — require upward adjustment in BRS
Reduce Cash Book balance but not Pass Book balance — require downward BRS adjustment
Reduce both balances simultaneously since ECS is automated
Increase Pass Book balance since the bank processes payments on behalf of the firm

explanation: ECS payments: bank has already debited the firm's account (PB balance reduced). But firm hasn't recorded it in CB (CB balance NOT reduced yet). Result: PB balance < CB balance. In BRS starting from CB balance, deduct ECS payments to reach PB balance. Firm must then record ECS payments in CB.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Rent paid ₹5,000 was posted to the Rent Received Account (credit). One-sided or two-sided error? What is the rectification entry?

options.option_text: Two-sided error — both rent expense and income affect TB. Rectification: Rent Paid A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Rent Received A/c ₹5,000 | To Cash/Bank A/c ₹5,000
Two-sided error. Rectification: Rent Paid A/c Dr ₹5,000 + Rent Received A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Cash A/c ₹5,000 | To Suspense A/c ₹5,000
One-sided error — only one side is wrong (credit to wrong account). Rectification: Rent Received A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Rent Paid A/c ₹5,000
Two-sided error. Rectification: Rent Paid A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Rent Received A/c ₹5,000 — no suspense involved

explanation: Original error: Dr Cash A/c ₹5,000 (correct) | Cr Rent Received A/c ₹5,000 (wrong — should be Cr Cash A/c isn't touched). Wait — rent PAID means Dr Rent A/c, Cr Cash. If instead posted as Cr Rent Received A/c, then: CB debit is correct but the credit is Rent Received instead of Cash or nothing. This is complex. The rectification is to debit the wrong account (reverse credit) and credit the right account (restore proper credit). No suspense since both debits and credits are affected equally.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A sales invoice of ₹12,000 was entered in the books as ₹21,000 (transposition error). Effect on Trial Balance:

options.option_text: Trial Balance disagrees by ₹9,000 if only one side is corrected; both sides are wrong by ₹9,000 — Trial Balance tallies (both Dr and Cr overstated by ₹9,000)
Trial Balance shows Dr excess of ₹9,000
Trial Balance shows Cr excess of ₹9,000
Trial Balance is unaffected since transposition errors always self-correct

explanation: Transposition error (₹12,000 written as ₹21,000): Both the debit (Debtor's A/c) and the credit (Sales A/c) are overstated by ₹9,000. Since BOTH sides of the journal entry are wrong by the same amount, the Trial Balance still TALLIES — but the accounts are both overstated. This is a two-sided error (error of original entry).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Suspense Account has a debit balance of ₹2,000 before rectification. After rectifying all errors, the Suspense Account should have:

options.option_text: Zero balance — all differences reconciled
A credit balance equal to the original debit balance
The same ₹2,000 debit balance — errors don't affect it
A balance equal to the net profit for the period

explanation: Purpose of Suspense Account: temporary home for unresolved Trial Balance difference. As each error causing the difference is found and corrected, its Suspense entry is reversed. When ALL errors are found, Suspense A/c balance = Nil. A non-zero balance means some errors are still unidentified.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A Bill of Exchange is an unconditional order in writing. The word 'unconditional' means:

options.option_text: The payment cannot be subject to any condition — it must be paid regardless of other circumstances
The bill can be transferred to any party without restriction
The drawer cannot revoke the bill once issued
The bank is obliged to honour the bill without any prior notice

explanation: Section 5 of Negotiable Instruments Act: Bill of Exchange is 'unconditional order in writing' — payment cannot be conditional on any event (like 'pay if goods are satisfactory' would make it conditional and invalid as a Bill). The unconditional nature makes it a negotiable instrument that can be freely transferred.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In the books of the Drawee (Acceptor), when a bill is accepted, the entry is:

options.option_text: Bills Payable A/c — wait, when drawee ACCEPTS: Dr Creditor (Drawer's) A/c | To Bills Payable A/c
Bills Receivable A/c Dr | To Creditor A/c
Creditor A/c Dr | To Cash A/c | To Bills Receivable A/c
Bills Payable A/c Dr | To Creditor A/c

explanation: Drawee accepts bill: Drawer's A/c (creditor of drawee) is Debited (liability reduces — converted from open credit to formal bill). Bills Payable A/c is Credited (new formal liability). In Drawer's books: Bills Receivable A/c Dr | To Drawee's A/c. Bills Payable = liability for drawee; Bills Receivable = asset for drawer.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: On maturity of a bill, payment is made by the Acceptor. Entry in the DRAWER'S books:

options.option_text: Cash/Bank A/c Dr | To Bills Receivable A/c (bill is discharged, payment received)
Bills Receivable A/c Dr | To Cash A/c
Bills Payable A/c Dr | To Cash A/c
Bills Receivable A/c Dr | To Bank A/c (bank collects on behalf)

explanation: Payment on maturity — Drawer's books: Cash/Bank comes in (Dr). Bills Receivable A/c closes (Cr — the asset is now realised). In Acceptor's books: Bills Payable A/c Dr | To Cash/Bank A/c (liability discharged, cash goes out). The entries are mirror images for the two parties.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A bill is sent by Drawer to the bank for collection (not discounted). Entry in Drawer's books:

options.option_text: Bills Sent for Collection A/c Dr | To Bills Receivable A/c (transferred to bank's custody for collection)
Bank A/c Dr | To Bills Receivable A/c (treated as if paid immediately)
Bills Receivable A/c Dr | To Bills Sent for Collection A/c
No entry until the bill is collected and bank credits the account

explanation: Bills Sent for Collection: Drawer transfers the bill to bank for collection on maturity. Entry: Dr Bills Sent for Collection A/c (substitutes Bills Receivable — now with bank). Cr Bills Receivable A/c. When bank collects: Dr Bank A/c | Cr Bills Sent for Collection A/c. Different from discounting (where bank pays before maturity minus charges).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A bill for ₹50,000 was discounted with bank at 12% p.a. for 3 months. Drawer received ₹48,500. When the bill is dishonoured, Drawer's entry is:

options.option_text: Acceptor's A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Bank A/c ₹50,000 (full face value — bank deducts from firm's account)
Acceptor's A/c Dr ₹48,500 | To Bank A/c ₹48,500 (only net amount paid to bank)
Bank Discount A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Acceptor's A/c ₹50,000
Loss on Bill A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Bank A/c ₹50,000

explanation: Discounted bill dishonoured: Bank recovers the FULL face value (₹50,000) from Drawer's account (not ₹48,500 — the discount was already charged). Drawer's entry: Dr Acceptor's A/c ₹50,000 (debt revived) | Cr Bank A/c ₹50,000 (bank deducts from Drawer's account). Drawer can also claim noting charges from Acceptor.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Noting Charges on dishonour of a bill of ₹500 are paid by the Drawer to the Notary. In the Drawer's books:

options.option_text: Acceptor's A/c Dr ₹500 | To Cash A/c ₹500 (noting charges recoverable from Acceptor)
Noting Charges A/c Dr ₹500 | To Cash A/c ₹500 (expense for the drawer)
Loss on Bill A/c Dr ₹500 | To Cash A/c ₹500 (treated as loss)
Cash A/c Dr ₹500 | To Acceptor A/c ₹500 (recover immediately)

explanation: Noting charges: fee paid to Notary Public for protesting the dishonoured bill — a legal process to formally record dishonour. These are recoverable FROM the Acceptor (defaulter pays). Dr Acceptor's A/c (add to his debt). Cr Cash A/c. This way, the total amount the Acceptor owes = Face Value + Noting Charges.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A and B draw accommodation bills on each other — A draws on B for ₹20,000; B draws on A for ₹15,000. Both discount the bills and share the proceeds equally. Net cash to A = ?

options.option_text: ₹2,500 net (A gets ₹10,000 from B's bill share and pays ₹7,500 to B as B's share, net = ₹2,500)
₹2,500 net to A (total proceeds ₹35,000 shared equally = ₹17,500 each; A discounts ₹20,000 = proceeds ~₹19,200, sends ₹9,600 to B; B discounts ₹15,000, sends ₹7,200 to A; net varies by discount rate)
Cannot determine without knowing the discount rate
₹17,500 net to A (half of ₹35,000 total face value)

explanation: Accommodation bills: without the discount rate, we cannot compute the actual cash proceeds (face value × remaining period × rate). The net amount each party receives depends on the discount amount charged by the bank. If discount rates are equal: A gets half of ₹15,000 proceeds from B and keeps half of ₹20,000 proceeds. Net calculation requires knowing the actual discount amount.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Endorsement of a bill means:

options.option_text: Transferring the bill to a third party by signing on the back (endorser), making the third party the new holder
Accepting the bill by the drawee after the drawer presents it for acceptance
Renewing the bill for a further period with or without noting charges
Cancelling the bill before its maturity date with the drawee's consent

explanation: Endorsement: Holder of a bill (Endorser) signs on the back and transfers it to another party (Endorsee). The Endorsee becomes the new holder and can collect on maturity. Entry in Endorser's books: Dr Endorsee's A/c (or Creditor A/c if settling a debt) | Cr Bills Receivable A/c. Option B is 'acceptance'; Option C is 'renewal'.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: When an endorsed bill is dishonoured, the ENDORSER (original holder who transferred the bill) must:

options.option_text: Pay the Endorsee and recover from the original Acceptor (drawee)
Only recover from the Acceptor — the Endorsee bears the loss
Pay the Endorsee from personal funds with no right of recourse
The bank is solely responsible for the dishonour — not the endorser

explanation: When endorsed bill is dishonoured: Endorsee (current holder) claims from Endorser (previous holder). Endorser is liable to the Endorsee. Entry in Endorser's books: Dr Endorsee's A/c (claim) | Cr Acceptor's A/c (recover from original defaulter). The Endorser then claims from the Acceptor. This chain of liability up the endorsement chain is a key feature of negotiable instruments.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Bill for ₹30,000 due in 90 days is retired by Acceptor 30 days before maturity. Rebate rate = 12% p.a. Amount paid by Acceptor:

options.option_text: ₹27,000 (12% discount on full bill amount)
₹30,000 (no discount — bills must be paid at face value)

explanation: Rebate on early retirement: 30 days before maturity. Rebate = ₹30,000 × 12/100 × 30/365 = ₹295.89 ≈ ₹296 (exact). Exam approximation using 30/360: = ₹30,000 × 0.12 × 30/360 = ₹300. Acceptor pays ₹30,000 − ₹300 = ₹29,700. Note: exact calculation varies with convention. The principle: Acceptor pays face value MINUS interest for unexpired period.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A cheque is valid for how long from the date of issue in India?

options.option_text: 3 months from the date of the cheque
6 months from the date of the cheque
1 year from the date of the cheque
Indefinitely — cheques do not have an expiry in India

explanation: After the RBI circular of April 2012, cheques are valid for only 3 months (earlier 6 months). A stale cheque (presented after 3 months) is returned by the bank. A post-dated cheque becomes valid only from the date written on it (not before).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A 'favourable balance' as per the Cash Book (bank column) means:

options.option_text: A debit balance in the Cash Book — the firm has money in the bank
A credit balance in the Cash Book — the firm has an overdraft
A zero balance — the firm neither owes the bank nor has surplus funds
A balance that exactly matches the Pass Book balance

explanation: Favourable balance (Cash Book): Debit balance = firm has deposits with bank (asset). Unfavourable/Adverse balance: Credit balance in CB = overdraft (liability). In the Pass Book: it is the REVERSE — a credit balance in PB = favourable (bank records the firm's deposit as its liability). A debit balance in PB = overdraft.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening Stock ₹20,000; Closing Stock ₹35,000; Net Purchases ₹1,50,000; Carriage Inward ₹3,000; Sales ₹2,50,000; Sales Returns ₹8,000. Gross Profit = ?

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Net Sales ₹4,00,000. Gross Profit Ratio = 25%. What is the Cost of Goods Sold?
explanation: GP = 25% × Net Sales = 25% × 4,00,000 = ₹1,00,000. COGS = Net Sales − GP = 4,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Short trick: If GP ratio = 25%, then COGS ratio = 75% of sales = 75% × 4,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Debtors ₹1,00,000. Bad Debts written off ₹5,000 (not in TB). New provision for bad debts required at 5%. Old provision for bad debts ₹4,000. Net P&L charge = ?

options.option_text: ₹9,250 (Bad debts ₹5,000 + new provision on net debtors ₹4,750 − old provision ₹4,000 = ₹5,750; total = ₹9,250 hmm let me recalculate: after writing off, debtors = ₹95,000; new provision = 5% × 95,000 = ₹4,750; P&L = bad debts ₹5,000 + (new provision ₹4,750 − old provision ₹4,000) = ₹5,000 + ₹750 = ₹5,750)
₹5,750 (Bad debts ₹5,000 + increase in provision ₹750)
₹9,750 (bad debts ₹5,000 + full new provision ₹4,750)
₹4,750 (only new provision; bad debts absorbed by old provision)

explanation: Step 1: Debtors after bad debts = 1,00,000 − 5,000 = ₹95,000. Step 2: New provision = 5% × 95,000 = ₹4,750. Step 3: P&L charge = Bad Debts ₹5,000 + (New provision ₹4,750 − Old provision ₹4,000) = ₹5,000 + ₹750 = ₹5,750. Balance Sheet shows: Debtors ₹95,000 − Provision ₹4,750 = ₹90,250 (net realisable value).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Manager's commission is 10% of Net Profit after charging commission. Net Profit before commission = ₹88,000. Commission = ?

options.option_text: ₹7,920 (10% on profit after tax and commission)
₹9,000 (10% on gross profit before deducting indirect expenses)

explanation: Commission on profit AFTER commission: C = 10% × (88,000 − C). C + 0.1C = 8,800. 1.1C = 8,800. C = ₹8,000. Short Trick: commission after = 10/110 × profit before = 10/110 × 88,000 = ₹8,000. Net profit after commission = 88,000 − 8,000 = ₹80,000. Verify: 10% of 80,000 = ₹8,000 ✓.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Expenditure of ₹2,00,000 on installation of new plant is debited to Plant A/c. Also, an engine costing ₹50,000 was replaced — old engine (book value ₹15,000) was discarded. What is correctly treated as capital expenditure?

options.option_text: Only the installation cost ₹2,00,000 is capital expenditure; engine replacement ₹50,000 is also capital (new engine) while old engine loss ₹15,000 is a revenue loss
Both installation and engine replacement are revenue expenditure — they maintain existing capacity
Only the engine replacement ₹50,000 is capital; installation is revenue (it does not create new assets)
All ₹2,50,000 should be expensed to P&L Account in the year of spending

explanation: Installation of new plant ₹2,00,000: Capital expenditure (creates new asset). Engine replacement ₹50,000: Capital expenditure (new engine added to plant — enhances future benefit). Old engine discarded (BV ₹15,000): Loss on disposal = ₹15,000 (Revenue loss, debit to P&L). Three separate accounting treatments for three components of this transaction.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods worth ₹10,000 sent on consignment are included in the consignor's Closing Stock at cost. Is this treatment correct?

options.option_text: Yes — goods on consignment remain the property of consignor until sold, so they must be included in closing stock
No — once goods are sent, they become the consignee's property and must be excluded
No — goods on consignment should be shown at selling price, not cost
Partly — only 50% of consignment stock is included, as risk is shared with consignee

explanation: Consignment: goods sent to consignee are NOT sold — ownership remains with consignor until the consignee sells them to end customers. Hence, unsold consignment stock is included in the consignor's closing stock at cost (or cost + proportionate expenses to bring them to current location). Only SOLD consignment goods leave the consignor's stock.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Loan taken from bank ₹5,00,000 at 10% p.a. Loan taken on 1 October. Year ends 31 March. What appears in Balance Sheet and P&L?

options.option_text: P&L: Interest ₹25,000 (6 months × ₹5,00,000 × 10% × 6/12); Balance Sheet: Loan ₹5,00,000 (liability) + Accrued Interest ₹25,000 (current liability)
P&L: Interest ₹50,000 (full year regardless of start date); Balance Sheet: Loan ₹5,00,000
P&L: Nothing (no cash payment made); Balance Sheet: Loan ₹5,00,000 only
P&L: Interest ₹25,000; Balance Sheet: Loan ₹5,25,000 (principal + accrued interest combined)

explanation: Accrual principle: interest accrues for the period used — Oct to March = 6 months. Interest = ₹5,00,000 × 10% × 6/12 = ₹25,000. P&L: Dr Interest Expense ₹25,000. Balance Sheet: Loan ₹5,00,000 (long-term liability) + Outstanding Interest ₹25,000 (current liability — separately shown). Option D wrongly adds interest to loan principal.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A machine was sold for ₹45,000. Original cost ₹1,20,000; Accumulated Depreciation ₹80,000; Provision for Depreciation maintained separately. What goes to P&L Account?

options.option_text: Nothing — under Provision for Depreciation method, P&L is unaffected by asset disposal
Profit ₹25,000 (Sale ₹45,000 − Depreciation ₹20,000)

explanation: Asset Disposal Account method: Dr Asset A/c (at cost ₹1,20,000) → Cr to Disposal A/c. Dr Provision for Depreciation (₹80,000) → Cr Disposal A/c. Disposal A/c: Dr Sale Proceeds ₹45,000 (net). Disposal A/c balance: 1,20,000 − 80,000 − 45,000 = −₹5,000 (credit side excess = profit ₹5,000). Transfer to P&L: Profit on Disposal ₹5,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of these is NOT shown on the ASSET side of a Balance Sheet?

options.option_text: Bills Payable (amount owed to creditors on bills)
Bills Receivable (amount owed by debtors on bills)
Prepaid Expenses (expenses paid in advance for next period)
Investments in government securities

explanation: Bills Payable: the firm owes money to creditors on bills = LIABILITY (Cr side of Balance Sheet). Bills Receivable: debtors owe money on bills = ASSET (Dr side). Prepaid Expenses = current asset. Investments = non-current asset. Bills Payable is a current liability — shown on the liability side.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Gross Profit ₹2,00,000. Salaries ₹40,000. Rent ₹20,000. Depreciation ₹15,000. Interest on bank loan ₹10,000. Discount received ₹5,000. Net Profit = ?
explanation: Net Profit = GP − Expenses + Other Income = 2,00,000 − (40,000 + 20,000 + 15,000 + 10,000) + 5,000 = 2,00,000 − 85,000 + 5,000 = ₹1,20,000. Discount Received is income (Cr side of P&L). All other items (salaries, rent, depreciation, interest) are expenses (Dr side of P&L).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Proprietor draws ₹1,000 per month. Rate of interest on drawings = 12% p.a. Using the simple assumption that drawings are evenly spread, interest on drawings (simple method — 6.5 months average) = ?
explanation: Monthly drawings, 12% p.a. Total drawings = ₹12,000. Average period = 6.5 months (for drawings made at the start of each month from Jan to Dec, average time = 6.5 months). Interest = 12,000 × 12% × 6.5/12 = 12,000 × 0.12 × 0.5417 = ₹780. If drawings are at END of month: 5.5 months average. Exam usually specifies or uses 6 months.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a partnership, a partner's salary of ₹24,000 p.a. is treated as:

options.option_text: A charge against profits — debited to P&L Appropriation Account and credited to that partner's Current Account
A business expense debited to P&L Account along with employee salaries
An asset — the partner has loaned their services to the firm
Ignored — partners are owners and cannot receive salary from the firm

explanation: Partner's salary in the partnership deed: NOT a business expense (not in P&L) but an appropriation of profit. It goes in P&L Appropriation Account (after net profit is determined): Dr P&L Appropriation A/c | Cr Partner's Current A/c. This is AFTER computing net profit. Contrast: employee salaries → P&L (Dr) before profit calculation.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which is the correct meaning of 'Sundry Debtors' on a Balance Sheet?

options.option_text: Customers who owe money to the business for goods sold on credit
Creditors from whom the business has purchased goods on credit
Various small creditors who are owed small amounts for miscellaneous purchases
Outstanding loans given to bank or financial institutions

explanation: Sundry Debtors (Trade Receivables): customers who owe money for goods sold on credit. They appear on the ASSET side. Sundry Creditors (Trade Payables): suppliers owed money for goods bought on credit — LIABILITY side. 'Sundry' means 'various' — multiple small debtors/creditors grouped together.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Current Assets = ₹4,00,000; Current Liabilities = ₹2,00,000; Stock = ₹1,20,000; Prepaid Expenses = ₹30,000. What is the Quick Ratio?

options.option_text: 2:1 (Current Ratio)
1.4:1 (after deducting only stock)
0.85:1 (Net liquid assets)

explanation: Quick Assets = CA − Stock − Prepaid = 4,00,000 − 1,20,000 − 30,000 = ₹2,50,000. Quick Ratio = Quick Assets / CL = 2,50,000 / 2,00,000 = 1.25:1. Standard Quick Ratio = CA − Stock − Prepaid (exclude less liquid items). Current Ratio = 4,00,000 / 2,00,000 = 2:1 (option B).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Proprietor's Capital at the start = ₹5,00,000. He introduced fresh capital ₹1,00,000. Made drawings of ₹60,000. Net loss for the year ₹40,000. Closing Capital = ?
explanation: Closing Capital = Opening Capital + Fresh Capital introduced − Drawings − Net Loss = 5,00,000 + 1,00,000 − 60,000 − 40,000 = ₹5,00,000. Note: Net loss REDUCES capital. A net profit would INCREASE capital. Here by coincidence, fresh capital (₹1,00,000) exactly equals drawings + loss (₹60,000 + ₹40,000 = ₹1,00,000).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which item does NOT appear in the Trading Account?

options.option_text: Discount received from suppliers
Wages paid to factory workers (direct labour)
Carriage Inward on purchases
Opening and Closing Stock of finished goods

explanation: Discount Received is a non-trading income — it appears on the CREDIT side of the P&L Account (not Trading Account). Trading Account contains: Opening Stock, Purchases, Direct Expenses (wages, carriage inward, customs duty, factory power) on Dr side; Sales and Closing Stock on Cr side. Gross Profit/Loss is the balancing figure.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Debentures issued by a company are classified in the Balance Sheet under:

options.option_text: Non-Current Liabilities (Long-Term Borrowings)
Current Liabilities (Short-Term Borrowings)
Shareholders' Funds (Share Capital section)
Reserves and Surplus (Revenue Reserves section)

explanation: Debentures: long-term debt instruments issued by companies — Non-Current Liabilities (Long-Term Borrowings) under Companies Act Schedule III Balance Sheet format. Short-term loans (< 1 year) → Current Liabilities. Equity shares → Share Capital. Preference shares → Equity/Non-current depending on terms.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening stock was UNDERSTATED by ₹12,000 in the previous year. Effect on current year's Gross Profit:

options.option_text: Current year GP is overstated by ₹12,000 (understated opening stock → understated COGS → overstated GP)
Current year GP is understated by ₹12,000
No effect on current year — only previous year is affected
Current year closing stock compensates automatically

explanation: Previous year: closing stock understated ₹12,000 → previous year GP understated by ₹12,000. Current year: opening stock = previous year closing stock, also understated ₹12,000 → current year COGS understated → current year GP OVERSTATED by ₹12,000. Two-year combined error = nil (they cancel out). Self-correcting over two years.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Subscriptions received ₹80,000 includes ₹5,000 for next year and ₹3,000 for the year before. Subscriptions outstanding for current year ₹6,000. What appears in P&L Account as subscription income?

options.option_text: ₹78,000 (80,000 − 5,000 advance + 6,000 outstanding − 3,000 previous year collection = 78,000)
₹80,000 (cash received)
₹74,000 (removing advance and previous year without adding outstanding)
₹86,000 (cash plus all outstanding)

explanation: Subscription income for current year = Cash received (80,000) − Advance for next year (5,000) − Last year's dues collected this year (3,000) + Current year outstanding (6,000) = 80,000 − 5,000 − 3,000 + 6,000 = ₹78,000. This is the income earned in the current year on accrual basis.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In the horizontal format of the Balance Sheet, capital and liabilities appear on the:

options.option_text: Left side (liabilities side); assets appear on the right side
Right side; assets appear on the left side
Both sides — depending on whether it is increasing or decreasing capital
Top portion; assets in the bottom portion of the horizontal format

explanation: Traditional horizontal Balance Sheet (Account Form): Left (Liabilities + Capital) | Right (Assets). This mirrors the accounting equation: Liabilities + Capital = Assets. Modern vertical format (under Companies Act Schedule III): Assets listed first (Non-Current then Current); Equity and Liabilities listed below or in the right column.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Asset cost ₹90,000; Residual value ₹10,000; Life 4 years. Under SLM, what is the Book Value at the end of Year 3?

options.option_text: ₹10,000 (scrap value after 4 years)
₹50,000 (Cost − 2 years depreciation)
₹27,000 (WDV method calculation used by mistake)

explanation: SLM Annual Dep = (90,000 − 10,000) / 4 = ₹20,000. Book Value at end of Year 3 = 90,000 − (3 × 20,000) = 90,000 − 60,000 = ₹30,000. At end of Year 4: 30,000 − 20,000 = ₹10,000 = Residual Value ✓. Under SLM, BV reaches residual value exactly at end of useful life.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Asset cost ₹1,00,000; WDV depreciation rate 25%. Book Value at end of Year 3 = ?

options.option_text: ₹25,000 (25% of cost for 3 years = 75% of cost remaining)
₹50,000 (100% − 3 × 25% × 100% under SLM-style thinking)
₹43,750 (a slightly wrong WDV calculation)

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under SLM, depreciation is CONSTANT throughout the asset's life. Under WDV, depreciation is DECREASING. Which statement about the relationship of these two methods to the asset's useful life is CORRECT?
