options.option_text: Under SLM, the asset reaches residual value exactly at the end of useful life; under WDV, it never theoretically reaches zero (asymptotic approach)
Under WDV, the asset reaches residual value before the end of useful life; under SLM it reaches zero
Both methods result in the same total depreciation over the asset's useful life
WDV gives higher total depreciation than SLM over the same period

explanation: SLM: (Cost − Salvage)/n per year → exactly reaches salvage at year n. WDV: each year charges a % on reducing balance → mathematically never reaches zero (but reaches a very small amount). Both charge the SAME total depreciation (Cost − Salvage) over the asset life — only the distribution differs (front-loaded vs constant). Option C is TRUE — total depreciation is the same.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Machine Hour Rate method of depreciation is most suitable for:

options.option_text: Plant and machinery where actual usage (hours run) is the key factor in depreciation
Natural resources like oil wells where output quantity drives depletion
Buildings and furniture where time passage is the primary cause of depreciation
Intangible assets like patents and trademarks with fixed legal life

explanation: Machine Hour Rate: depreciation per hour = (Cost − Salvage) / Total estimated hours. Annual dep = Actual hours used × Rate per hour. Best for machinery that depreciates based on USE rather than time. Depletion method: output-based (mines). Time-based (SLM/WDV): buildings, furniture. Intangibles: SLM over legal life.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: When an asset is sold mid-year, how is depreciation charged for that year under SLM?

options.option_text: Depreciation is charged for the period the asset was used (pro-rata basis until date of sale)
No depreciation in year of sale — only full-year depreciation in year of purchase
Full year depreciation is always charged regardless of sale date
Depreciation and gain/loss are netted out at book value without pro-rata adjustment

explanation: Pro-rata depreciation: Asset used Jan–June (6 months) → 6/12 of annual depreciation. Then disposal account is prepared with: Cost Dr, Accumulated Dep Cr, Sale proceeds Cr, and the balance = profit or loss. In examination problems, unless stated otherwise, charge depreciation for the period the asset was owned in the year of sale.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening stock: 100 units @ ₹15. Purchased: 200 units @ ₹18 on 5th; 150 units @ ₹20 on 15th. Sold: 250 units on 20th (FIFO). Closing stock value = ?

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening: 100 units @ ₹10. Purchase: 200 units @ ₹13. Sold 180 units. Weighted Average cost per unit and closing stock value = ?

options.option_text: WA cost ₹12/unit; Closing stock = 120 units × ₹12 = ₹1,440
WA cost ₹11.50/unit; Closing stock = ₹1,380
Closing stock = 120 units × ₹13 = ₹1,560 (latest price)
WA cost ₹12.50/unit; Closing stock = ₹1,500

explanation: WA cost = Total Cost / Total Units = (100×10 + 200×13) / 300 = (1,000 + 2,600) / 300 = 3,600 / 300 = ₹12/unit. Units sold = 180; Closing stock = 300 − 180 = 120 units. Closing stock value = 120 × ₹12 = ₹1,440.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Item A: Cost ₹500; NRV ₹450. Item B: Cost ₹300; NRV ₹380. Item C: Cost ₹200; NRV ₹200. Total inventory under Lower of Cost or NRV (item-by-item basis) = ?

options.option_text: ₹1,000 (all at cost)
₹930 (using aggregate comparison: total cost ₹1,000 vs total NRV ₹1,030 — take lower = ₹1,000)
₹1,030 (all at NRV)

explanation: Lower of Cost or NRV applied ITEM BY ITEM (per AS 2): A: min(500, 450) = ₹450. B: min(300, 380) = ₹300. C: min(200, 200) = ₹200. Total = ₹950. Note: aggregate comparison (total cost vs total NRV) would give ₹1,000 — but AS 2 requires item-by-item basis. Item-by-item always gives equal or lower valuation.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: When a firm maintains a separate 'Provision for Depreciation Account', the asset account is shown in the Balance Sheet at:

options.option_text: Historical cost (original cost), with the Provision for Depreciation shown as a deduction to arrive at net book value
Net book value (cost minus accumulated depreciation in the asset account)
Current market value, since the provision accounts for the difference
Only the current year's depreciation — prior year provision is transferred to P&L

explanation: Provision for Depreciation method: Asset A/c maintained at COST always (not reduced). Separate Provision for Dep A/c accumulates annual depreciation. Balance Sheet shows: Asset at cost ₹X, Less: Provision for Depreciation ₹Y, Net Book Value ₹(X−Y). Advantage: asset cost is always visible; useful for insurance valuation.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Revaluation Method of depreciation is most appropriate for:

options.option_text: Loose tools and small items that are valued physically at the end of each year
Land and buildings that appreciate over time
Machinery whose output can be accurately measured each year
Patents and copyrights with a fixed legal life

explanation: Revaluation Method: physical stock of loose tools/small items counted at year-end, valued at current price. Depreciation = Opening value − Closing value (+ purchases during year). Used when items are too numerous to track individually (spanners, chisels, small tools). Annual depreciation = Fall in value of the stock of tools.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Closing stock was OVERVALUED by ₹15,000. How does this affect the next year's Net Profit?

options.option_text: Next year's Net Profit is UNDERSTATED by ₹15,000 (opening stock in next year is overstated → COGS overstated → GP/NP understated)
Next year's Net Profit is OVERSTATED by ₹15,000
No effect on next year — the error only affects the current year
Effect depends on whether FIFO or Weighted Average is used

explanation: Current year: closing stock overstated ₹15,000 → COGS understated → GP/NP OVERSTATED ₹15,000. Next year: opening stock = current closing stock = OVERSTATED ₹15,000 → COGS overstated → GP/NP UNDERSTATED ₹15,000. Self-correcting: 2-year combined profit is CORRECT. This is why inventory accuracy matters — errors cascade into subsequent year.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: AS 10 (Revised) relates to which accounting aspect?

options.option_text: Property, Plant and Equipment (PPE) — accounting for fixed assets including depreciation
Accounting for Inventories under cost and NRV rules
Revenue Recognition and timing of income in financial statements
Accounting for foreign exchange transactions and translations

explanation: Key Accounting Standards: AS 2 = Inventories. AS 9 = Revenue Recognition. AS 10 (Revised, 2016) = PPE (Property, Plant and Equipment) — replaced old AS 10 on Fixed Assets. AS 11 = Foreign Exchange. AS 6 (Depreciation Accounting) was withdrawn and merged into AS 10 (revised). Ind AS 16 = PPE (converged with IFRS).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under AS 2, which of the following costs are EXCLUDED from inventory valuation?

options.option_text: Selling and distribution costs (these are period costs, not product costs)
Raw material cost directly attributable to the product
Manufacturing overhead allocated on a systematic basis
Import duty paid on raw materials imported for production

explanation: AS 2 costs included in inventory: purchase cost (raw materials + import duty + freight inward), conversion costs (direct labour + manufacturing overhead). Excluded: selling/distribution costs, abnormal wastage costs, storage costs for finished goods, administrative overhead unrelated to production. Selling costs are 'period costs' expensed in the year incurred.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm changes its depreciation method from WDV to SLM. Under which accounting standard must this change be disclosed?

options.option_text: AS 5 — Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies
AS 10 — Property, Plant and Equipment
AS 2 — Valuation of Inventories (inventory policy changes)
AS 1 — Disclosure of Accounting Policies (initial disclosure only)

explanation: AS 5: governs changes in accounting policies, estimates, and prior period items. A change in depreciation method (WDV → SLM) is a change in accounting policy — must be disclosed under AS 5 with effect of change on profit. AS 1 requires disclosure of policies adopted; AS 5 governs changes to those policies. The change must be made only if required by statute, or for better presentation.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening Stock ₹40,000; Closing Stock ₹60,000; COGS ₹2,00,000. Stock Turnover Ratio = ?

options.option_text: 4 times (COGS ₹2,00,000 / Average Stock ₹50,000)
5 times (COGS / Opening Stock)
3.33 times (COGS / Closing Stock)
4.44 times (Net Sales / Average Stock)

explanation: Stock Turnover Ratio = COGS / Average Stock. Average Stock = (Opening + Closing) / 2 = (40,000 + 60,000) / 2 = ₹50,000. STR = 2,00,000 / 50,000 = 4 times. Interpretation: inventory is completely sold and replaced 4 times in the year. Higher STR = more efficient inventory management.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: From the following, compute Subscription Income for the year: Subscription received in cash ₹90,000; Opening subscription receivable ₹8,000; Closing subscription receivable ₹12,000; Opening subscription received in advance ₹4,000; Closing subscription received in advance ₹6,000.
explanation: Subscription Income = Cash received + Closing OS − Opening OS − Closing Advance + Opening Advance = 90,000 + 12,000 − 8,000 − 6,000 + 4,000 = ₹92,000. Logic: add what's owed (closing OS), subtract what was already earned last year (opening OS already recognised then), subtract advance (next year's), add back advance recognised this year (opening advance).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A sports club received a legacy of ₹2,00,000 from a deceased life member. This should be treated as:

options.option_text: Capital Receipt — credited to Capital Fund (not I&E Account)
Revenue Receipt — credited to I&E Account as non-recurring income
Specific Donation — must be kept in a separate Legacy Fund and used for stated purpose
Liability — returnable to legal heirs if challenged within 3 years

explanation: Legacy: a gift under a will (bequest). Since it is non-recurring and non-specific (no specific purpose stated), it is treated as a Capital Receipt → credited to Capital Fund on the liability side of the Balance Sheet. Only if legacy is specifically directed to a purpose (e.g., 'for building a gymnasium') should it go to a specific fund.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Income and Expenditure Account of an NPO differs from Receipts and Payments Account in that I&E:

options.option_text: Covers only REVENUE items for the CURRENT period, on accrual basis; R&P covers all CASH flows regardless of period
Is prepared on cash basis; R&P is prepared on accrual basis
Includes capital receipts and payments; R&P excludes capital items
I&E is prepared quarterly while R&P is prepared annually only

explanation: Key distinction: I&E Account = revenue items only, current period, accrual basis (like P&L). R&P Account = ALL cash and bank flows (both capital and revenue, all periods), cash basis (like Cash Book summary). R&P opens with opening cash/bank and closes with ending cash/bank. I&E shows surplus or deficit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club received ₹50,000 as government grant specifically for purchasing sports equipment. Journal entry:

options.option_text: Cash A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Government Grant (Sports Fund) A/c ₹50,000 — shown as liability till equipment is purchased
Cash A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Income A/c ₹50,000 — recognised as income immediately
Equipment A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Cash A/c ₹50,000 — treat as if equipment already bought
Capital Fund A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Cash A/c ₹50,000 — merged with general funds

explanation: Specific government grant: until the specified purpose is fulfilled (equipment purchased), the grant remains a LIABILITY (deferred income). Entry: Dr Cash, Cr Specific Fund A/c. When equipment is bought: Dr Equipment A/c, Cr Cash. The grant offsets the asset purchase — net effect on fund position is nil. This follows the deferral (capital approach) method.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club's Opening Capital Fund = ₹3,00,000. Surplus from I&E Account = ₹40,000. Life Membership Fees received = ₹20,000. Legacy received = ₹30,000. Closing Capital Fund = ?
explanation: Closing Capital Fund = Opening CF + Surplus + Life Membership (capital receipt) + Legacy (capital receipt) = 3,00,000 + 40,000 + 20,000 + 30,000 = ₹3,90,000. All three additions increase the Capital Fund. Capital receipts (life membership, legacy) go directly to Capital Fund, bypassing I&E Account.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following is shown on the EXPENDITURE side of the Income and Expenditure Account?

options.option_text: Depreciation on fixed assets of the NPO
Life membership fees received from new members
Opening balance of cash and bank in the Receipts and Payments Account
Capital Fund at the beginning of the year

explanation: Expenditure side of I&E Account: all revenue expenses for the current period = salaries, rent, telephone, depreciation on NPO assets, repairs, audit fees, etc. Income side: subscriptions, entrance fees (if treated as revenue), interest on investments, donations (general). Life membership, legacy → Capital Fund (not I&E).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a self-balancing system, when cash is paid to a creditor ₹5,000, the entry in the CREDITORS LEDGER Adjustment Account (maintained in the General Ledger) is:

options.option_text: Creditors Ledger Adjustment A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Cash A/c (internal — this mirrors the creditor's individual payment in the Creditors Ledger)
Cash A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Creditors Ledger Adjustment A/c ₹5,000
No entry in the General Ledger — only individual creditor accounts in Creditors Ledger are updated
Debtors Ledger Adjustment A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Creditors Ledger Adjustment A/c ₹5,000

explanation: Self-balancing: Payment to creditor. In individual Creditors Ledger: Dr Individual Creditor A/c ₹5,000 (liability decreases). To keep Creditors Ledger self-balancing, a General Ledger Adjustment A/c (in CL) is credited ₹5,000. In General Ledger: Dr Creditors Ledger Adjustment A/c ₹5,000 (mirrors the payment). Cr Cash A/c ₹5,000 (cash paid).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A match fund of ₹15,000 exists in a sports club. During the year, ₹12,000 was spent on organising matches. How should the balance ₹3,000 be treated?

options.option_text: Carried forward in the Match Fund on the liability side of Balance Sheet for next year's matches
Transferred to Income side of I&E Account as surplus from match fund
Transferred to Capital Fund since the match season is over
Written off to Expenditure side as unspent money cannot be held

explanation: Specific Fund (Match Fund): created for a specific purpose. Unspent balance remains in the fund on the liability side — it cannot be transferred to I&E or Capital Fund unless the specific purpose is permanently abandoned. If a match is to be organised next year, the balance ₹3,000 continues in Match Fund.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a hospital (NPO), medical fees received from patients are:

options.option_text: Revenue income — credited to I&E Account (core service income for the NPO)
Capital receipt — credited to Capital Fund since fees build long-term capacity
Deferred income — spread over 5 years since treatment continues
Contra entry — offset against medical expenses directly

explanation: For a charitable hospital (NPO), medical fees are the primary income source from its core activities → Revenue Income → I&E Account (credit side). Despite being an NPO, fees from services rendered are current period revenue. Only non-recurring, non-trading amounts like donations and grants may be capital receipts.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The advantages of the Self-Balancing Ledger system include:

options.option_text: Errors can be localised to a specific subsidiary ledger and trial balance can be prepared for each ledger separately
It eliminates the need for a Trial Balance altogether
Reduces the number of entries required since each transaction is posted only once
Allows the firm to operate without a General Ledger for smaller transactions

explanation: Self-Balancing advantages: (1) Errors localised — if Debtors Ledger doesn't balance, error is within that ledger only. (2) Independent trial balance for each subsidiary ledger. (3) Division of work — different clerks can maintain different ledgers. (4) Better internal control. Disadvantage: more work (double posting — both adjustment accounts).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG's audit of the accounts of the Union Government covers which of the following under Article 149?

options.option_text: Accounts of all receipts and expenditures of the Union — including railway and defence accounts
Only accounts of ministries under the Prime Minister's Office
Only plan expenditure and centrally sponsored scheme funds
Only accounts of PSUs where government holds more than 75% shares

explanation: Article 149: Parliament may prescribe the CAG's duties and powers by law. The Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers, and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 empowers the CAG to audit ALL government accounts including Railways (separate P&L), Defence, Posts and Telecommunications, and all departments. The threshold for PSU audit is ≥51%, not 75%.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG's Audit Report on State Government accounts is submitted to the Governor of the State, who then:

options.option_text: Causes it to be laid before the State Legislature (Article 151(2))
Sends it to the Prime Minister's office for review
Forwards it to the President of India for final approval
Transmits it directly to the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament

explanation: Article 151: (1) Union accounts report → President → Parliament. (2) State accounts report → Governor → State Legislature (Vidhan Sabha or Vidhan Parishad). After laying, the report is examined by the State Public Accounts Committee (PAC) which works similarly to Parliament's PAC.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: What changed in CAG's role after the amendment to the Comptroller and Auditor General's Act in 1971?

options.option_text: The Comptroller function (pre-audit control over government expenditure) was removed — CAG now only does post-audit
CAG was given additional powers to sanction expenditure for emergency projects
CAG was merged with the Finance Commission to improve coordination
CAG was made a constitutional body with enhanced powers over RBI audit

explanation: Pre-1976 (effective date of change): CAG functioned as BOTH Comptroller (pre-audit — approving withdrawals from Consolidated Fund) AND Auditor General (post-audit). Post 1971 Act amendment: CAG's Comptroller function was separated — the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) under Finance Ministry now does pre-audit/accounting. CAG does only post-audit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Propriety Audit by the CAG evaluates:

options.option_text: Whether public money was spent with financial prudence and that it served legitimate public interest
Whether the expenditure was within the legal limits prescribed by Parliament
Whether the government achieved its programme objectives efficiently
Whether digital records were properly maintained per IT Act 2000

explanation: Types of CAG audit: (1) Regularity/Compliance Audit: check rules followed, authorisation obtained. (2) Propriety Audit: was money spent wisely? Is the expenditure necessary, justified, and in public interest? Goes beyond mere legality. (3) Performance/Value-for-Money Audit: Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness. Option C describes Performance Audit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Finance Commission recommends tax devolution from which pool?

options.option_text: The Divisible Pool — comprising all central taxes EXCEPT cesses and surcharges levied for specific purposes
All central taxes including cesses and surcharges
Only income tax and corporation tax (direct taxes)
GST collections minus States' own SGST share

explanation: Divisible Pool: net proceeds of all central taxes excluding cesses and surcharges (these flow to Consolidated Fund but are not shared). Includes: Income Tax, Corporation Tax, Customs, Union Excise duties (post-GST adjustment), CGST share, service tax (residue). 14th FC: 42%; 15th FC: 41%. Cesses (Swachh Bharat, education) are NOT shared.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which Finance Commission is known for the biggest single jump in devolution to States?

options.option_text: 14th Finance Commission (2015-20) under Y.V. Reddy — raised devolution from 32% to 42%
13th Finance Commission under Vijay Kelkar — 32% devolution
15th Finance Commission under N.K. Singh — 41% devolution
12th Finance Commission under C. Rangarajan — 30.5% devolution

explanation: The 14th Finance Commission (Y.V. Reddy) raised States' share from 32% (13th FC) to 42% — a 10 percentage point jump, the largest single increase in the history of Finance Commissions. The 15th FC (N.K. Singh) slightly reduced it to 41% due to the newly created Jammu & Kashmir Union Territory (whose share reduced from States' pool).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The criteria used by Finance Commissions for horizontal devolution among States typically include:

options.option_text: Population, Income Distance (poorer States get more), Area, Forest/Ecology, Demographic Performance
GDP of State, number of PSUs, tax collection efficiency only
Per capita income alone — states with lower per capita get higher share
Population and area only — the two most objective measures

explanation: 15th FC horizontal devolution criteria: Population (15%, using 2011 Census), Area (15%), Forest and Ecology (10%), Income Distance (45% — States with lower per capita income get more), Demographic Performance (12.5% — States that reduced fertility rates rewarded). The multi-criteria approach balances equity, efficiency, and environmental concerns.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India WITHOUT a vote in Parliament?

options.option_text: Charged expenditure — including CAG salary, President's salary, SC/HC judges' salaries, and debt servicing
Defence expenditure — since it is strategic and cannot be voted on openly
All expenditure — Parliament only oversees plan expenditure
Revenue expenditure only — capital expenditure requires voting

explanation: Charged expenditure (Article 112(3)): NOT subject to Parliamentary vote — presented for information only. Includes: President's salary, CAG salary, SC/HC judges, Speaker/Deputy Speaker salaries, Lok Sabha Secretariat, interest on national debt (debt charges), sums required to satisfy court judgements. Everything else is 'voted expenditure'.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Controller General of Accounts (CGA) differs from the CAG in that the CGA:

options.option_text: Manages accounting and pre-audit (cash management) while CAG conducts post-audit of completed accounts
Is a constitutional authority while CAG is a statutory creation of Parliament
Audits State accounts while CAG audits only Union accounts
Reports to Parliament directly; CAG reports to the President

explanation: CGA (under Ministry of Finance): maintains government accounts, prepares monthly accounts, manages PFMS, oversees the accounting machinery. Statutory body under Civil Accounts. CAG (Constitutional body under Art 148): independent auditor that audits accounts maintained by CGA and departments. CGA = accountant; CAG = auditor. Both serve Parliament but independently.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under Article 280(3)(bb) added by the 73rd/74th Constitutional Amendments, the Finance Commission must also recommend:

options.option_text: Measures to augment Consolidated Fund of States to supplement Panchayats and Municipalities
Special economic zones for States to enhance revenue generation
Minimum guaranteed income for farmers in all States
Revision of salary scales for State government employees

explanation: Art 280(3)(bb): Added by 73rd/74th Amendments (local self-government). Finance Commission must recommend measures to augment CFI of States to supplement resources of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies. The 15th FC made significant recommendations for local bodies (urban and rural), totalling ₹4.36 lakh crore over 2021-26.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A firm raises price of its product from ₹100 to ₹110. Quantity demanded falls from 1,000 to 900 units. Using the Mid-Point (Arc) Elasticity formula, |Ed| = ?

options.option_text: 1.0 exactly (using simple point elasticity method)
1.1 (using arc elasticity: |ΔQ/avg Q| ÷ |ΔP/avg P|)
0.91 (inverse of 1.1)

explanation: Arc (Mid-point) elasticity: Ed = [(Q2-Q1)/((Q1+Q2)/2)] / [(P2-P1)/((P1+P2)/2)] = [(900-1000)/950] / [(110-100)/105] = (-100/950) / (10/105) = (-0.1053) / (0.0952) ≈ −1.105. |Ed| ≈ 1.1. Elastic demand. Simple point Ed = (100/1000) / (10/100) = 0.1 / 0.1 = 1.0 exactly. Arc method gives slightly different result due to averaging.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Consumer Surplus is defined as:

options.option_text: The difference between what a consumer is willing to pay (maximum price) and what they actually pay (market price)
The excess of producer revenue over cost of production
The total satisfaction gained by consuming a good, measured in money terms
The amount a consumer saves when buying in bulk at a discount

explanation: Consumer Surplus (Alfred Marshall): CS = (Willingness to Pay) − (Price Actually Paid). Graphically: area below demand curve and above the market price (triangular area). When price falls, CS increases. CS is redistributed (not destroyed) when a monopolist engages in perfect price discrimination (extracts all CS as revenue).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When income rises by 10% and demand for a good rises by 20%, the Income Elasticity of Demand is:

options.option_text: 2 — this is a LUXURY good (Ey > 1)
0.5 — this is a necessity (0 < Ey < 1)
−2 — this is an inferior good (Ey < 0)
1 — this is a normal good with unitary elasticity

explanation: Ey = %ΔQd / %ΔY = +20% / +10% = +2. Positive Ey: normal good. Ey > 1: luxury good (demand rises proportionately more than income). Examples: branded goods, holidays, automobiles. Ey = 0: independent (necessities like salt). 0 < Ey < 1: necessities. Ey < 0: inferior goods.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Engel Curve shows the relationship between:

options.option_text: Consumer income and quantity demanded at a given price — shows how demand varies with income
Price and quantity demanded — same as the demand curve
Two goods' relative quantities in the consumer's optimal bundle
Total expenditure on a good and the consumer's income level

explanation: Engel Curve (Ernst Engel, 19th century German statistician): plots income on X-axis and quantity demanded on Y-axis. Normal good: upward-sloping Engel curve. Inferior good: backward-bending (demand falls as income rises). Engel's Law: as income rises, proportion spent on food falls (food is a necessity with Ey < 1).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Price Elasticity of Supply (PES) > 1 means supply is:

options.option_text: Elastic — quantity supplied rises proportionately MORE than price rises
Inelastic — quantity supplied rises proportionately LESS than price rises
Perfectly inelastic — supply doesn't change with price
Negative — quantity supplied falls when price rises

explanation: PES = %ΔQs / %ΔP. PES > 1: elastic. PES < 1: inelastic. PES = 0: perfectly inelastic (vertical supply curve, e.g., land). PES = ∞: perfectly elastic (horizontal supply). Supply is generally more elastic in the long run (firms can adjust capacity). Agricultural supply is inelastic in the short run (harvest takes time).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under the Quantitative Theory of Money (Fisher's Equation), MV = PT. If money supply (M) doubles and velocity (V) and volume of transactions (T) remain constant, what happens to Price Level (P)?

options.option_text: P doubles — price level rises proportionately with money supply
P remains unchanged — velocity adjusts to absorb the money increase
P halves — increased money supply improves purchasing power
T doubles — more money stimulates more transactions, not inflation

explanation: Fisher's Equation of Exchange: MV = PT. If M doubles, V and T constant → P must double. This is the Quantity Theory of Money (QTM): money supply and price level are proportional in the long run. Critics (Keynes): velocity is not constant; money also held for speculation. But QTM remains foundational.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Credit Multiplier (Money Multiplier) in the banking system is the inverse of:

options.option_text: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) — money multiplier = 1/CRR in a simple model
Repo Rate — higher repo creates more credit in the economy
SLR — statutory liquidity ratio determines the multiplier
Bank Rate — the discount rate determines lending capacity

explanation: Simple money multiplier = 1/CRR. If CRR = 10%, multiplier = 1/0.1 = 10. ₹100 of base money creates ₹1,000 in deposits. Real multiplier is lower due to cash leakage and excess reserves. Higher CRR → lower multiplier → less credit. Lower CRR → more credit creation → potentially inflationary.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Selective credit controls (as a qualitative monetary policy tool) are used to:

options.option_text: Regulate credit flow to specific sectors — e.g., restrict lending to speculators in commodity markets
Uniformly reduce credit across all sectors by raising the Repo Rate
Increase the money supply to stimulate growth in all industries equally
Regulate foreign exchange outflows through currency controls

explanation: Monetary policy tools: Quantitative (general) = Repo, Reverse Repo, CRR, SLR, OMO. Qualitative (selective) = Selective Credit Controls (direct RBI guidelines on which sectors to lend/avoid, margin requirements, credit rationing). Used to control credit to specific sectors (e.g., restrict loans against hoarded food stocks to fight inflation without affecting overall investment).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) are loans where the borrower has not made interest or principal payment for:

options.option_text: 90 days or more — classified as NPA by RBI (special mention accounts before that)
60 days or more under Basel III norms
180 days or more under the older RBI definition
30 days — any delay is classified as NPA immediately

explanation: RBI NPA definition: an asset becomes NPA if interest/principal is overdue for >90 days (for term loans). Special Mention Accounts (SMA-0: 1-30 days; SMA-1: 31-60 days; SMA-2: 61-90 days) are early warning signals. NPA categories: Sub-standard (< 12 months as NPA), Doubtful (12+ months), Loss assets (unrecoverable). SARFAESI Act 2002 helps recover NPAs.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is operated by:

options.option_text: NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) — the retail payments and settlement systems organisation
RBI directly — as part of the payment and settlement infrastructure
SEBI — regulates all financial market instruments including digital payments
UIDAI — Aadhaar-based payment authentication requires UIDAI oversight

explanation: NPCI (set up by RBI and banking sector, 2009): operates UPI (2016), IMPS, NACH, RuPay card network, FASTag, Cheque Truncation System (CTS). UPI allows real-time interbank transfers via mobile — over 10 billion transactions/month as of 2025. RBI regulates NPCI; NPCI operates the infrastructure.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Revenue Deficit = ₹80,000 crore. Grants for creation of capital assets = ₹15,000 crore. Effective Revenue Deficit = ?

options.option_text: ₹65,000 crore (RD − Grants for capital assets)
₹95,000 crore (RD + Grants)
₹80,000 crore (same as revenue deficit — grants don't affect it)
₹15,000 crore (only grants are relevant)

explanation: Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD) = Revenue Deficit − Grants for creation of capital assets. Logic: some grants transferred to States/others are used for capital creation even though they appear as revenue expenditure in the Centre's books. Subtracting these gives a 'true' revenue deficit. ERD = 80,000 − 15,000 = ₹65,000 crore.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Treasury Bills in India are short-term government securities issued for maturities of:

options.option_text: 91 days, 182 days, and 364 days — issued at a discount to face value
30 days, 90 days, and 180 days
1 year, 2 years, and 3 years (short-term bonds)
91 days only — other maturities use dated government securities

explanation: Treasury Bills (T-Bills): short-term money market instruments issued by Government of India through RBI. Maturities: 91-day T-Bill (most liquid), 182-day, 364-day. Issued at DISCOUNT to face value (e.g., ₹98 for ₹100 face value) — difference is interest. Used for short-term government cash management. No interest coupon.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If Fiscal Deficit = ₹15,00,000 crore and Interest Payments = ₹11,00,000 crore, Primary Deficit as a percentage of FD = ?

options.option_text: 26.67% (Primary Deficit ₹4,00,000 crore / FD ₹15,00,000 crore)
73.33% (Interest Payments as % of FD)
100% (PD cannot exceed FD)
26.67% is wrong — PD = FD so it's 100%

explanation: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit − Interest Payments = 15,00,000 − 11,00,000 = ₹4,00,000 crore. PD as % of FD = 4,00,000 / 15,00,000 × 100 = 26.67%. The high ratio of interest to FD (73.33%) means most of the FD is for servicing past debt — not for current operational needs. A zero PD means current borrowing only covers interest.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: IGST (Integrated GST) is levied on:

options.option_text: Inter-state supply of goods and services and on imports — collected by Centre and shared with destination State
Intra-state supply of goods — collected and retained by the Centre
Intra-state supply of services — collected and retained by the State
Both intra and inter-state supplies, replacing both CGST and SGST

explanation: GST Types: CGST = Centre's share on intra-state supply. SGST = State's share on intra-state supply. IGST = inter-state supply + imports (collected by Centre; IGST on imports acts as customs substitute for domestic supply). IGST shared: portion going to destination State based on consumption = SGST equivalent; Centre retains CGST equivalent. UTGST replaces SGST in Union Territories.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's Current Account shows a deficit when:

options.option_text: Import payments exceed export receipts + invisibles (services, remittances, income) combined
Foreign investment outflows exceed foreign investment inflows into India
Government spending exceeds tax revenue — fiscal deficit translates to CA deficit
RBI's foreign exchange reserves fall below 3 months of import cover

explanation: Current Account Deficit (CAD): Debit side (imports of goods and services + income payments + transfers paid) > Credit side (exports of goods and services + income receipts + remittances received). India typically has a TRADE deficit (goods imports > goods exports) partly offset by SURPLUS in invisibles (software exports, remittances). Net result is usually a modest CAD.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Paul Samuelson's definition of Economics is considered modern because it:

options.option_text: Incorporates both micro and macro dimensions and emphasises growth over time, not just allocation
Focuses exclusively on scarce resources and individual choice like Robbins
Restricts the scope to material welfare as studied by Marshall
Treats Economics as a natural science similar to Physics or Chemistry

explanation: Samuelson (1948): 'Economics is the study of how people and society choose to employ scarce productive resources... to produce various commodities and to distribute them for consumption, now or in the future.' Key additions over Robbins: dynamic (over time), includes growth not just allocation, covers both micro and macro. Hence 'modern' or 'growth-based' definition.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An economy producing INSIDE the Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) can move to a point ON the PPF by:

options.option_text: Better utilising existing resources — removing unemployment or underemployment without new technology
Discovering new natural resources or improving technology (shifts the curve outward)
Increasing population size to add more labour without any other change
Reducing the production of one good to zero so all resources go to the other

explanation: Inside the PPF = inefficiency (unemployment, underutilisation). Moving TO the PPF requires better utilisation of existing resources — no new resources needed. Moving BEYOND the PPF (outward shift) requires: new technology, discovery of resources, better institutions, or population growth. The two movements are distinct in their requirements.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Invisible Hand' metaphor used by Adam Smith refers to:

options.option_text: The price mechanism in a free market that coordinates individual decisions to achieve social good without central direction
Government's hidden role in regulating markets through taxation and subsidies
The monopolist's ability to set prices without consumer awareness
The role of technology in automating production decisions

explanation: Adam Smith (Wealth of Nations, 1776): individuals pursuing self-interest are led by an 'invisible hand' to promote society's welfare — even though this was not their intention. The price system (market mechanism) coordinates millions of decentralised decisions efficiently. Basis for laissez-faire (free market) economics. Contrasts with socialist central planning.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is a Macroeconomic question?

options.option_text: What causes India's overall price level to rise (inflation)?
Why does Maruti charge a higher price for the Swift than the Alto?
How does a consumer maximise satisfaction given their budget?
Why do monopolies restrict output compared to perfect competition?

explanation: Macroeconomics (Ragnar Frisch coined the term, 1933): aggregate economy — national income, inflation, unemployment, balance of payments, fiscal and monetary policy. Options B, C, D are Microeconomic questions (individual firm pricing, consumer theory, market structure). The boundary is not always sharp — macro builds on microeconomic foundations.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The slope of the Production Possibility Curve is CONCAVE (bowed outward) rather than straight, because of:

options.option_text: The Law of Increasing Opportunity Cost — as more of one good is produced, the opportunity cost (in terms of the other good) increases
The Law of Diminishing Returns — adding more inputs reduces output per unit
Economies of scale — larger production reduces unit cost
The Law of Supply — producers supply more at higher prices

explanation: PPC is concave (bowed outward): resources are not perfectly substitutable between industries. As we shift resources from wheat to steel production, the resources transferred (e.g., unskilled agricultural workers) are progressively less suited to steel production — each unit of steel requires giving up more and more wheat. This increasing opportunity cost makes the curve concave.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following best illustrates the concept of a 'merit good'?

options.option_text: Education — society benefits more from widespread education than individuals would voluntarily consume
A luxury car — high price ensures only affluent buyers consume it
Salt — consumed by everyone regardless of income
A concert — private good consumed only by ticket-holders

explanation: Merit goods (Richard Musgrave): goods whose benefits society judges to be greater than individuals recognise. Individuals may underconsume them (due to information failure or short-sightedness). Government subsidises or mandates consumption (compulsory schooling, vaccines). Contrast: demerit goods (tobacco, alcohol) — individuals overconsume.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Total Product (TP), Average Product (AP), and Marginal Product (MP) relationships: when AP is MAXIMUM, MP is:

options.option_text: Equal to AP (MP crosses AP from above at AP's maximum)
Greater than AP
Zero (MP = 0 when TP is maximum, not when AP is maximum)
Negative (negative MP is Stage III, well beyond AP maximum)

explanation: The Marginal-Average rule: MP = AP at AP's maximum. When MP > AP → AP is rising. When MP < AP → AP is falling. At the intersection: MP = AP = AP maximum. Similarly, MC = AVC at AVC's minimum. This is the law of averages applied to production theory.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which stage of production is considered 'irrational' for the producer?

options.option_text: Stage III — Total Product is declining and Marginal Product is negative; adding more labour reduces output
Stage I — increasing returns, TP rises at increasing rate
Stage II — TP rises at decreasing rate; MP positive but falling
All stages before maximum TP are irrational

explanation: Stage III: TP falls, MP < 0. Adding another worker REDUCES total output — that worker destroys value. No rational producer operates here (you'd have to pay the worker and get LESS output — doubly irrational). Stage I: irrational to STOP (AP still rising, fixed factor underutilised). Stage II: rational zone (both MP and AP positive but diminishing).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When output is ZERO, Total Variable Cost (TVC) is:

options.option_text: Zero — variable costs only arise when production occurs
Equal to Total Fixed Cost — since all costs are fixed when nothing is produced
Equal to Total Cost — since no revenue is generated to offset costs
Negative — the firm recovers some costs by not producing

explanation: At zero output: TVC = 0 (no raw materials used, no variable labour employed). TFC remains constant at some positive amount (rent, loan EMI, salary of permanent staff). TC = TFC + TVC = TFC + 0 = TFC. This is why the TC curve starts from the TFC level (not from zero) on the cost-output graph.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Long-Run Average Cost (LRAC) curve is U-shaped due to:

options.option_text: Economies of scale (falling portion) and Diseconomies of scale (rising portion)
Fixed costs in the short run and variable costs in the long run
The Law of Variable Proportions operating in the long run
Rising input prices as the firm buys more raw materials at scale

explanation: LRAC is U-shaped (or L-shaped in some modern theories): Left side falls due to ECONOMIES OF SCALE (specialisation, technical efficiency, bulk buying, managerial economies). Right side rises due to DISECONOMIES OF SCALE (managerial inefficiency, coordination problems as firm grows too large). The minimum point = Most Efficient Scale (MES). Law of Variable Proportions is a SHORT-RUN concept.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Output increases from 10 to 11 units. TC rises from ₹500 to ₹530. What is the Marginal Cost of the 11th unit?

options.option_text: ₹50 (AC at 10 units)
₹530 (TC at 11 units)

explanation: MC = Change in TC / Change in output = (530 − 500) / (11 − 10) = ₹30 / 1 = ₹30. MC is the cost of producing ONE MORE unit. It equals the change in TOTAL cost (TVC also changes by ₹30 since TFC is constant). AC at 11 units = 530/11 = ₹48.18 — different from MC.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Internal Economies of Scale arise from:

options.option_text: Advantages specific to the firm as it grows larger — technical, managerial, financial, marketing economies
Benefits that arise from the growth of the entire industry, not individual firms
Government subsidies granted to large-scale producers
Lower input prices due to reduced raw material quality at higher volumes

explanation: Internal Economies of Scale: firm-specific advantages as it grows. Types: Technical (indivisible machinery used more fully), Managerial (specialised managers), Financial (easier/cheaper credit), Marketing (bulk buying, advertising spread over more units), Risk-bearing (diversification). External Economies: industry-wide benefits (specialised suppliers, skilled labour pool, knowledge spillovers).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A price discriminating monopolist charges ₹100 to Group A (PED = 2) and ₹150 to Group B (PED = 0.5). Which group has more elastic demand?

options.option_text: Group A (PED = 2) — they get the lower price because they are more price-sensitive
Group B (PED = 0.5) — higher price means they are less sensitive
Both groups are equally elastic since they buy the same product
Elasticity cannot be determined from price information alone

explanation: Price discrimination rule (Pigou): charge higher price to segment with less elastic demand (less responsive = will pay more). Group B: PED = 0.5 (inelastic) → higher price ₹150. Group A: PED = 2 (elastic) → lower price ₹100. Examples: first-class rail vs economy; elderly/student discounts (more elastic). This is third-degree price discrimination.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which market structure has the MOST efficient allocation of resources?

options.option_text: Perfect Competition — P = MC (price equals marginal cost at long-run equilibrium)
Monopoly — single firm produces optimal output for the market
Monopolistic Competition — product differentiation maximises consumer welfare
Oligopoly — large firms have resources to invest in efficient technology

explanation: Allocative efficiency: P = MC (price = social marginal cost = social marginal benefit from last unit). Achieved only in Perfect Competition (long-run equilibrium). Under monopoly: P > MC → underproduction and deadweight loss. Monopolistic competition: excess capacity (P > minimum AC). Oligopoly: collusion keeps P > MC.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Features that distinguish Monopolistic Competition from both Perfect Competition and Monopoly include:

options.option_text: Product differentiation and relatively free entry/exit; many firms, each with some pricing power
Only one seller with complete market control over price and quantity
Identical products and no individual firm's pricing power
A few large interdependent firms with kinked demand curves

explanation: Monopolistic Competition (Chamberlin, 1933): many sellers, differentiated products (brand, quality, packaging), free entry/exit, each firm faces downward-sloping demand (limited pricing power). Short run: supernormal profit possible. Long run: entry erodes profit → normal profit + excess capacity. Examples: toothpastes, soaps, restaurants.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Lerner Index of Monopoly Power = (P − MC) / P. A Lerner Index of 0 indicates:

options.option_text: Perfect competition — P = MC, no pricing power at all
Perfect monopoly — firm controls the entire market
Maximum monopoly power — all producer surplus captured
The market is in long-run equilibrium regardless of structure

explanation: Lerner Index ranges 0 to 1. LI = 0: P = MC (perfect competition — no market power). LI = 1: MC = 0 with positive price (maximum monopoly power, hypothetical). Higher LI = more monopoly power. Also equals 1/|Ed| — firms with more elastic demand have lower Lerner Index (less monopoly power). Used to measure market power in competition law cases.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Net National Product (NNP) differs from Gross National Product (GNP) by:

options.option_text: Capital Consumption Allowance (Depreciation) — NNP = GNP − Depreciation
Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) — NNP = GNP − NFIA
Indirect Taxes minus Subsidies — NNP = GNP − NIT
Transfer Payments — NNP = GNP − Transfer Payments

explanation: GNP = GDP + NFIA. NNP = GNP − Depreciation. NNP represents the NET addition to the economy's capital stock — what's produced after accounting for the wear of existing assets. NNP at Factor Cost = National Income. The 'Gross' vs 'Net' distinction ALWAYS refers to depreciation (capital consumption allowance).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's current GDP measurement series uses which base year?

options.option_text: 2011-12 — adopted by NSO (MoSPI) when the new national accounts series was released in 2015
2004-05 — the older series used before 2015
2019-20 — updated after COVID to reflect structural changes
1999-2000 — the last census-aligned base year

explanation: India's GDP base year: Until 2014, base year was 2004-05. In January 2015, MoSPI (then MOS&PI) released a new series with base year 2011-12. This series also changed methodology — GVA at basic prices replaced GDP at factor cost as the headline. GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + product taxes − subsidies.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The multiplier effect in Keynesian economics states that:

options.option_text: An initial increase in investment creates a larger final increase in national income through successive rounds of spending
Savings automatically equal investment in the long run, stabilising income
Prices multiply proportionately with the money supply
Government spending has a multiplying negative effect on private investment (crowding out)

explanation: Keynesian Multiplier (k) = 1/(1−MPC) = 1/MPS. If MPC = 0.8, k = 5. An injection of ₹100 crore in investment leads to ₹500 crore rise in national income. Mechanism: ₹100 spent → ₹80 re-spent → ₹64 re-spent → ... until sum converges. Higher MPC = higher multiplier = more potent fiscal stimulus.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Lorenz Curve measures income distribution. A Lorenz Curve that coincides with the diagonal line of perfect equality implies:

options.option_text: Gini Coefficient = 0 — perfect equality where every person has identical income
Gini Coefficient = 1 — one person owns all income
The economy has no poverty — all incomes are above the poverty line
The median income equals the mean income in the economy

explanation: Lorenz Curve: x-axis = cumulative % of population; y-axis = cumulative % of income. Perfect equality: diagonal (bottom 10% own 10%, bottom 50% own 50%). Perfect inequality: right angle (one person owns 100%). Gini = area between Lorenz Curve and diagonal / total area below diagonal. Gini = 0 when Lorenz = diagonal.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which body replaced the Planning Commission in India from 1 January 2015?

options.option_text: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India)
Economic Advisory Council to Prime Minister (EAC-PM)
National Development Council (NDC)
Finance Commission of India

explanation: NITI Aayog: established 1 January 2015 by Cabinet Resolution (not by statute). PM Modi as Chairperson. Key differences from Planning Commission: (1) No power to allocate funds, (2) Cooperative/competitive federalism focus, (3) Think-tank/advisory role, (4) States are partners not just recipients. The 12th Five-Year Plan (2012-17) was the last plan; NITI Aayog works with 3-year Action Plans.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Structural Unemployment arises due to:

options.option_text: A mismatch between workers' skills and available job requirements — often caused by technological change or industrial shift
Workers voluntarily between jobs while searching for better opportunities
Seasonal fluctuations in demand for labour (agriculture in lean season)
Insufficient aggregate demand in the economy (Keynesian unemployment)

explanation: Structural unemployment: long-term mismatch. Example: coal miners unemployed after coal industry declines; traditional weavers displaced by power looms. Hard to solve with demand stimulus — requires retraining. Option B = Frictional (short-term, voluntary search). Option C = Seasonal. Option D = Cyclical/Demand-deficient (Keynesian — solved by fiscal stimulus).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The base year for the new Consumer Price Index (CPI) in India (launched 2012) is:

options.option_text: 2012 (January 2012 = 100; released by MoSPI, used by MPC for inflation targeting)
2004-05 (same as older WPI and national accounts base)
2011-12 (same as GDP base year)
2010 (aligned with global CPI measurement conventions)

explanation: CPI (Combined): base year 2012 (Jan 2012 = 100). Covers rural + urban. Published by MoSPI. Used by MPC as the headline inflation target (4% ±2%). WPI (Wholesale Price Index): base year 2011-12; published by DPIIT (Commerce Ministry). CPI is consumer-facing; WPI is producer-facing. RBI shifted from WPI to CPI for inflation targeting in 2014-15.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'License Raj' abolished as part of 1991 liberalisation refers to:

options.option_text: The system under the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 requiring government licences to set up or expand industrial units
Import licences required before 1991 for all foreign goods
Licences required by street vendors and small traders for operating businesses
Environmental clearances required for industrial projects

explanation: Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 (IDRA): required industrial licence for setting up, expanding, or relocating any industrial unit. Created 'Licence Raj' — excessive bureaucratic control, delays, corruption, inefficiency. New Industrial Policy 1991: abolished licensing for most industries (except reserved: defence, atomic energy, railways, a few others). Liberalisation's first major step.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) differs from FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment) in that FDI:

options.option_text: Involves long-term investment with management control; FPI is short-term financial investment in securities without management control
Can only occur in manufacturing; FPI applies to services and financial markets
Is subject to government approval always; FPI is automatic
Cannot be repatriated; FPI can be withdrawn at any time by the investor

explanation: FDI: investment ≥10% equity stake (OECD definition) — involves control/management, long-term commitment, technology transfer. Stable capital inflow. FPI (Hot Money): <10% stake, investment in listed securities (stocks, bonds) — short-term, volatile, can be withdrawn rapidly. India's Current Account includes both under Capital Account. FDI subject to sectoral caps (DPIIT policy); automatic vs approval route.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Narasimham Committee Report-I (1991) on banking sector reforms recommended:

options.option_text: Reduction in CRR and SLR to release funds for productive lending, and setting up Asset Reconstruction Companies for NPAs
Nationalisation of all remaining private sector banks for better public control
Introduction of GST to replace multiple indirect taxes
Merger of RBI with the Finance Ministry for better coordination

explanation: Narasimham Committee I (1991, M. Narasimham): Banking sector reform. Key recommendations: (1) Reduce SLR from 38.5% to 25% and CRR substantially; (2) Phase out directed credit (priority sector lending ratios); (3) Deregulate interest rates; (4) Capital adequacy norms (Basel); (5) Asset Reconstruction Company/Fund for NPAs. Narasimham II (1998): focused on bank mergers and further NPA resolution.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The full form of TRAI is:

options.option_text: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India — established under TRAI Act 1997
Trade Regulation and Administration of India
Technology Research and Analytics Institute
Tariff Regulation Authority of India

explanation: TRAI: established 1997 under TRAI Act to regulate telecom sector post-liberalisation. Functions: recommend telecom licences, set tariffs, ensure quality of service, resolve disputes. Supreme Court cases (2G spectrum, 2012) involved TRAI and spectrum allocation. Similarly: IRDA (insurance, 1999), SEBI (securities, 1992), CCI (competition, 2002) — all sector regulators created post-LPG.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's current foreign exchange management framework classifies current account transactions as:

options.option_text: Fully convertible — any resident or non-resident can freely transact for current account purposes without RBI approval
Partially convertible — only exporters can convert freely; importers need RBI permission
Restricted — all transactions require advance approval from the Finance Ministry
Banned for individuals — only corporations can make current account transactions

explanation: India's convertibility position: Current Account = FULLY convertible (since 1994 — India accepted Article VIII of IMF). Capital Account = PARTIALLY convertible (FDI, FPI allowed; full capital account convertibility not yet achieved). This means: trade payments, services, remittances — no RBI permission needed. Overseas investments, borrowings — limits and permissions apply under FEMA.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) in India were established under the SEZ Act:

options.option_text: 2005 — providing a dedicated legal framework after earlier zones under EXIM Policy
1991 — as the first major reform during LPG liberalisation
2000 — introduced in the EXIM Policy without a separate act
2010 — after China's SEZ success model was studied

explanation: SEZ Act 2005: provided statutory backing for SEZs (export-oriented units in designated zones with tax concessions, simplified regulations, world-class infrastructure). Earlier: Export Processing Zones (EPZs) existed under EXIM policy. SEZ concept introduced in India's EXIM policy 2000, but the formal Act came in 2005. Benefits: 100% FDI, tax holidays, no customs for imports.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on:

options.option_text: 28 August 2014 — financial inclusion scheme for universal banking access
1 January 2015 — same day as NITI Aayog
2 October 2014 — Gandhi Jayanti launch for symbolic significance
15 August 2014 — Independence Day announcement

explanation: PMJDY (28 August 2014): universal financial inclusion — zero-balance savings accounts, ₹1 lakh accidental insurance, ₹30,000 life insurance, overdraft facility (₹10,000 after 6 months). The 'J' in JAM Trinity. By 2025: over 53 crore accounts opened. Enabled DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) for LPG, MGNREGA wages, scholarships, etc.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The production function Q = f(L, K) in the SHORT RUN is best described as:

options.option_text: Q = f(L | K̄) — only labour varies; capital is fixed at K̄ (given a bar)
Q = f(L, K) — both labour and capital can be varied freely
Q = constant — output cannot change in the short run
Q = f(K | L̄) — only capital varies; labour is the fixed factor

explanation: Short run: at least one factor is fixed (typically capital — machines, factory size). Only variable factors (typically labour) can be changed. Long run: ALL factors are variable. Ultra-short run: even labour is fixed. The distinction short run vs long run in economics is not about calendar time but about factor variability.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Number of workers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Total Product: 10, 22, 30, 35, 35. Marginal Product of the 4th worker = ?

options.option_text: 5 (TP at 4 workers is 35; TP at 3 workers is 30; MP = 35 − 30 = 5)
8.75 (AP at 4 workers = 35/4)
0 (5th worker adds nothing — TP stays at 35)
12 (MP of 2nd worker = 22 − 10 = 12)

explanation: MP of nth worker = TP(n) − TP(n−1). MP of 4th worker = TP(4) − TP(3) = 35 − 30 = 5. Full MP schedule: 1st=10, 2nd=12, 3rd=8, 4th=5, 5th=0. MP is rising then falling (Law of Variable Proportions). 5th worker's MP = 35 − 35 = 0 (start of Stage III boundary). Stage III begins when MP < 0.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: At output Q = 50 units: TVC = ₹5,000; TFC = ₹2,000. A firm produces one more unit (Q = 51) and TVC rises to ₹5,080. What is MC of 51st unit and AVC at Q = 51?

options.option_text: MC = ₹80; AVC at 51 = ₹5,080/51 ≈ ₹99.6 (which is less than current AVC of ₹100 → MC < AVC pulls AVC down)
MC = ₹80; AVC at 51 = ₹100 (unchanged)
MC = ₹80; AVC at 51 = ₹101 (AVC rises since MC is positive)

explanation: MC of 51st unit = ΔTVC/ΔQ = (5,080 − 5,000)/1 = ₹80. AVC at Q=50 = 5,000/50 = ₹100. AVC at Q=51 = 5,080/51 ≈ ₹99.61. MC (₹80) < AVC (₹100) → AVC is FALLING. This confirms the marginal-average rule: when MC < AVC, AVC falls; when MC > AVC, AVC rises; MC = AVC at AVC minimum.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Economies of scale differ from returns to scale in that:

options.option_text: Returns to scale refers to the production function; economies of scale refers to cost — both may point in the same direction but are conceptually distinct
Economies of scale is a short-run concept; returns to scale is long-run
Returns to scale measures efficiency; economies of scale measures profitability
They are interchangeable terms meaning the same thing

explanation: Returns to Scale: physical concept — what happens to OUTPUT when ALL inputs are scaled up proportionately (IRS, CRS, DRS). Economies of Scale: cost concept — what happens to AVERAGE COST as output increases. IRS → falling LRAC (economies of scale). CRS → constant LRAC. DRS → rising LRAC (diseconomies). IRS implies economies of scale but the measurement unit differs (physical vs monetary).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Envelope Theorem in cost theory explains why the Long-Run Average Cost (LRAC) curve is:

options.option_text: The lower envelope of all possible Short-Run Average Cost (SRAC) curves — each SRAC is optimal for a specific plant size
Always U-shaped because fixed costs are always present in the long run too
Identical to the SRAC curve for the optimal plant size
A horizontal line at the minimum SRAC when all scales are available

explanation: LRAC = envelope of SRACs: In the long run, a firm can choose any plant size (any SRAC curve). The LRAC traces the MINIMUM cost achievable at each output level across all possible plant sizes. Graphically, LRAC is tangent to (touches but stays below) each SRAC curve. The LRAC curve is smoother and flatter than any individual SRAC curve.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following correctly describes CONSTANT Returns to Scale?

options.option_text: Doubling all inputs exactly doubles output — production is homogeneous of degree 1
Doubling all inputs more than doubles output — increasing returns
Doubling all inputs less than doubles output — decreasing returns
Output remains constant regardless of input changes in the short run

explanation: CRS: output changes proportionately with inputs (scale factor = 1). IRS: more than proportionate (scale factor > 1). DRS: less than proportionate (scale factor < 1). Mathematical: if Q = f(L,K) and f(λL, λK) = λQ → CRS (homogeneous degree 1). f(λL,λK) > λQ → IRS. Examples: many manufacturing processes exhibit CRS over a wide range.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Normal Profit is included in which cost concept?

options.option_text: Economic Cost (implicit cost) — normal profit is the entrepreneur's opportunity cost of using their own capital and skills
Accounting Cost (explicit cost) — paid to the entrepreneur as salary
Fixed Cost — since it is fixed regardless of output level
Neither cost — normal profit is a residual after paying all costs

explanation: Normal Profit = minimum return needed to keep entrepreneur in the business = opportunity cost of entrepreneurship. It IS an economic cost (implicit). When economists say a firm earns 'zero economic profit,' it means the firm earns exactly normal profit. Accounting profit includes normal profit (it doesn't subtract it). Economic profit = Accounting profit − Normal profit (implicit cost).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: At what level of output does a firm achieve PRODUCTIVE efficiency?

options.option_text: At the output where Average Cost (AC) is at its minimum — lowest cost per unit of output
Where Marginal Cost equals Marginal Revenue (profit-maximising output)
Where Total Revenue equals Total Cost (break-even point)
Where Average Fixed Cost is minimised (as output approaches infinity)

explanation: Productive efficiency: producing at minimum AC (using resources in the cheapest way). This occurs at the bottom of the U-shaped AC curve, where AC = MC. Allocative efficiency: P = MC (resources allocated to highest-value uses). Perfect competition achieves both in the long run. Monopoly achieves neither. Break-even = normal profit point where TR = TC (P = AC).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A monopolist faces demand curve: P = 100 − Q. Marginal Cost = ₹20 (constant). Profit-maximising output and price are:

options.option_text: Q = 80, P = ₹20 (competitive equilibrium where P = MC)
Q = 50, P = ₹50 (midpoint of demand)
Q = 40, P = ₹20 (wrong — substituting Q=40 into wrong equation)

explanation: Monopolist maximises profit where MR = MC. MR = dTR/dQ = d(PQ)/dQ = d((100−Q)Q)/dQ = 100 − 2Q. Set MR = MC: 100 − 2Q = 20 → 80 = 2Q → Q = 40. Price from demand: P = 100 − 40 = ₹60. Profit per unit = P − MC = 60 − 20 = ₹40. Total profit = 40 × 40 = ₹1,600. Under competition (P=MC): Q = 80, P = 20 — deadweight loss triangle at Q=40-80.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Collusive Oligopoly (Cartel) behaves like a:

options.option_text: Monopolist — the cartel collectively maximises joint profit as if they were a single seller
Perfect competitor — cartel members compete vigorously with each other
Price-taker — cartel members have too little market power individually
Monopsonist — cartel controls buying price from suppliers

explanation: Cartel = collective monopoly: member firms agree to act as a single monopolist (fix joint output at MR = MC level, share market, set common price). Joint profit > sum of individual competitive profits. BUT: cartel is inherently unstable (each member gains by cheating — producing more than quota at the fixed price). Prisoner's dilemma: rational to defect individually, irrational collectively.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In the kinked demand curve model (Sweezy), the demand curve has a kink at the existing price. Above the kink, demand is elastic. Below the kink, demand is inelastic. As a result:

options.option_text: MR has a DISCONTINUITY (gap) at the kink — MC can shift within this gap without changing the profit-maximising price and output (price rigidity)
Firms always undercut each other on price, leading to a race to the bottom
Demand becomes perfectly elastic at the kink price — firms cannot raise price at all
Firms collude formally to maintain the kink price through binding agreements

explanation: Kinked demand → kinked MR: at the kink, MR has a vertical discontinuity (gap). Elastic portion: MR₁ above. Inelastic portion: MR₂ below. Gap = MR₁ to MR₂ at the kink quantity. As long as MC passes through this gap, profit-maximising output (MR=MC) stays at the kink quantity regardless of cost changes. This explains why oligopoly prices are 'sticky' despite cost fluctuations.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which market structure is characterised by 'non-price competition' as the primary competitive strategy?

options.option_text: Monopolistic Competition — firms compete on product quality, advertising, branding, packaging rather than price
Perfect Competition — uniform price, no product differentiation
Pure Monopoly — no competition at all, only pricing decisions
Duopoly — two firms compete primarily on price (Bertrand model)

explanation: Non-price competition (Monopolistic Competition): firms cannot lower price easily (risk of price war) but can compete by: product differentiation (features, quality), advertising (brand building), packaging, customer service, after-sales support, location. This is how soaps, toothpaste, restaurants, clothing brands, and fast food chains compete. Also present in oligopoly — price changes are avoided due to kinked demand.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Second Degree Price Discrimination' means:

options.option_text: Charging different prices for different quantities — consumers self-select into cheaper bulk rates (block pricing)
Charging each consumer their exact maximum willingness to pay
Charging different prices to different market segments (students vs adults)
Offering a lower price to buyers in markets where competition is intense

explanation: Degrees of price discrimination: 1st: perfect — different price for each unit to each consumer (extracts ALL consumer surplus). 2nd: block/quantity pricing — different prices for different quantities bought (slab pricing, electricity tariffs, airline seat classes). Consumer self-selects. 3rd: market segmentation — different markets, different prices (student discounts, geographic pricing). Examples of 2nd: BSNL data plans, electricity slabs.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under Perfect Competition, the long-run equilibrium condition is P = MC = AC = minimum AC. This means:

options.option_text: Firms earn only normal profit (zero economic profit) and operate at the most efficient scale
Firms earn maximum profit at the lowest cost possible
Price equals zero as competition drives down all profits
No firm has any incentive to enter or exit the market regardless of profits

explanation: Perfect Competition long-run equilibrium: P = MR = MC (profit maximisation) = AC (zero economic profit — no incentive to enter/exit) = minimum AC (productive efficiency). This triple equality is unique to perfect competition. Under monopoly: P > MC (allocative inefficiency). Under monopolistic competition LR: P = AC but P > MC (some allocative inefficiency).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Limit Pricing is a strategy used by incumbent firms in which they:

options.option_text: Set price BELOW the profit-maximising level to deter new entrants by making entry unprofitable
Set a maximum (limit) price above which they will not go, regardless of demand
Use price caps imposed by the government to control natural monopoly pricing
Collude with other firms to set a common price limit across the industry

explanation: Limit Pricing (Bain, 1956): incumbent prices low enough that new entrants cannot profitably enter. Entry-deterring price < short-run profit-maximising price. Mechanism: if incumbents' costs are lower (due to scale/experience), they can price above their AC but below entrant's AC → entrant cannot break even. Trade-off: lower current profit vs protection of future market position.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Transfer payments like old-age pensions, unemployment benefits, and student scholarships are NOT included in National Income because:

options.option_text: They do not correspond to any productive activity — they are redistribution of income, not new output
They are paid in cash and cannot be measured in national accounts
They are included only in the fiscal deficit, not in national income
They are too small to be statistically significant in a large economy

explanation: National Income measures the VALUE OF PRODUCTION (goods and services produced). Transfer payments represent redistribution of existing income (government gives to recipient without receiving any service back). Including them would double-count — the taxed income of workers is already counted; redistribution to pensioners would count it twice. Hence excluded from NI calculations.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GDP at MP = ₹200 lakh crore. Indirect taxes = ₹30 lakh crore. Subsidies = ₹5 lakh crore. Depreciation = ₹15 lakh crore. NFIA = ₹2 lakh crore. National Income (NNP at FC) = ?

options.option_text: ₹162 lakh crore
₹157 lakh crore
₹177 lakh crore
₹185 lakh crore

explanation: GDP(MP) = 200. GNP(MP) = GDP + NFIA = 200 + 2 = 202. NNP(MP) = GNP − Dep = 202 − 15 = 187. NNP(FC) = NNP(MP) − IT + Sub = 187 − 30 + 5 = 162. National Income = ₹162 lakh crore. Short trick: NI = GDP(MP) + NFIA − Dep − (IT − Sub) = 200 + 2 − 15 − 25 = 162.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Personal Income differs from National Income in that Personal Income:

options.option_text: Adds transfer payments and subtracts undistributed profits, corporate taxes, and social security contributions from National Income
Is exactly equal to National Income in a closed economy
Excludes wages and salaries and includes only property income
Is always higher than National Income due to informal sector inclusion

explanation: Personal Income = National Income − Corporate taxes − Undistributed profits − Social Security contributions + Transfer payments (pensions, unemployment benefits). Personal Disposable Income = Personal Income − Personal Direct Taxes. These distinctions are tested especially in theory papers — know the chain: NI → Personal Income → Disposable Income.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Operation Flood, the world's largest dairy development programme, was spearheaded by:

options.option_text: Verghese Kurien — 'Father of the White Revolution in India', founded AMUL model
Norman Borlaug — Nobel laureate who led the Green Revolution
M.S. Swaminathan — Father of Green Revolution in India
Hiralal Chaudhuri — associated with fisheries development

explanation: Verghese Kurien: 'Milkman of India', Father of the White Revolution. Founded AMUL (Anand Milk Union Limited), led Operation Flood (1970-1996) — transformed India from a milk-deficient country to the world's largest milk producer. The Cooperative model of AMUL is studied globally. Norman Borlaug = Green Revolution globally. Swaminathan = Green Revolution India.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Human Development Index (HDI) was first published by UNDP in:

options.option_text: 1990 — conceptualised by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen
1980 — as part of Brundtland Commission on sustainable development
2000 — alongside the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs)
1995 — after Beijing Women's Conference broadened development metrics

explanation: HDI first published in UNDP Human Development Report 1990. Mahbub ul Haq (Pakistan economist) and Amartya Sen (Indian Nobel laureate) are the intellectual architects. HDI challenged the GDP-only approach to measuring development by adding health (life expectancy) and education (literacy/schooling years) dimensions. India's HDI rank has improved but remains 'medium development'.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Frictional unemployment is best described as:

options.option_text: Short-term unemployment arising from the time taken to match job-seekers with vacancies
Unemployment caused by automation and technological displacement of workers
Unemployment caused by a recession or fall in aggregate demand
Unemployment that exists due to seasonal fluctuations in agriculture

explanation: Frictional unemployment: 'search unemployment' — workers between jobs or new entrants searching for suitable employment. Always exists even in a healthy economy (natural rate of unemployment). Caused by information imperfections, not deficient demand. Solution: better job market information (job portals). Structural (technology), Cyclical (recession), Seasonal (agriculture) are distinct types.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 2011 Census recorded India's population as approximately:

options.option_text: 121 crore (1.21 billion) — making India the second most populous country after China
100 crore (1 billion) — crossed in 2000 according to Census 2001
140 crore (1.4 billion) — this was the 2021 estimate, not 2011 Census
84 crore — the 1991 Census figure

explanation: Census 2011: India's population = 121.09 crore (1.21 billion). Decadal growth rate = 17.7% (declined from 21.5% in 2001). Sex ratio = 940 females per 1000 males. Literacy = 74%. Next Census was delayed post-2021 due to COVID. As of 2023, India overtook China to become the world's most populous country (~143 crore).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which is the CORRECT statement about India's economic sectors?

options.option_text: Services sector contributes ~55% to GDP but employs fewer people than agriculture, which contributes ~17% but employs ~45% of workforce
Agriculture contributes the most to GDP since it employs the most people
Manufacturing sector contributes ~55% of GDP making India a manufacturing-led economy
Services, manufacturing, and agriculture each contribute approximately one-third of GDP

explanation: India's structural paradox: Services (IT, finance, trade, transport, real estate) ≈ 55% of GDP but employs ~30% workers (high productivity). Agriculture ≈ 17-18% of GDP but employs ~45% workers (low productivity per worker, disguised unemployment). Manufacturing/Industry ≈ 28%. This dualism — high-productivity services vs low-productivity agriculture — is the central challenge.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Expenditure Method of calculating National Income uses the formula:

options.option_text: NI = C + I + G + (X − M) − Depreciation − Net Indirect Taxes + NFIA (adjusted to factor cost)
NI = Wages + Rent + Interest + Profit (incomes of all factors)
NI = Value of output − Value of intermediate goods (value-added approach)
NI = Total Sales − Raw Material Costs − Depreciation

explanation: Expenditure Method (GDP at MP): C + I + G + (X−M). To get National Income: add NFIA (→ GNP at MP), subtract Depreciation (→ NNP at MP), subtract Net Indirect Taxes (→ NNP at FC = NI). Option B = Income Method. Option C = Production/Value-Added Method. All three give same NI — consistency check in national accounts.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) method of comparing GDPs between countries adjusts for:

options.option_text: Differences in price levels across countries — a dollar buys more in India than in USA
Differences in population — per capita GDP is divided by population
Exchange rate fluctuations over the comparison period
Informal economy and black market activities not captured in official data

explanation: PPP adjusts for price level differences. $1 buys 1 burger in USA but the same dollar (₹84) buys several items in India where prices are lower. PPP method inflates Indian (and other developing countries') GDP relative to market exchange rate method. At PPP, India is the 3rd largest economy (after USA, China). At nominal exchange rates, India ranks lower (~5th).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Blue Revolution in India relates to:

options.option_text: Development of fisheries sector — both marine and inland fish production
Development of water conservation and irrigation infrastructure
Expansion of blue-collar manufacturing employment in India
Clean energy revolution replacing thermal power with hydropower

explanation: Revolution naming in India's agricultural development: Green Revolution = food grains (wheat/rice). White Revolution = dairy (Operation Flood). Blue Revolution = fisheries. Yellow Revolution = oilseeds. Pink Revolution = poultry/meat. Silver Revolution = eggs. Golden Revolution = fruits/overall horticulture. Golden Fibre Revolution = jute.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Keynesian multiplier works through the concept of Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC). If MPC = 0.75, the multiplier is:

options.option_text: 0.75 (equals MPC itself)

explanation: Multiplier (k) = 1/(1−MPC) = 1/MPS. MPC = 0.75, MPS = 0.25. k = 1/0.25 = 4. Meaning: an initial investment of ₹100 crore generates ₹400 crore of national income through successive spending rounds. Higher MPC → higher multiplier → more potent stimulus.
