Open economy multiplier is smaller (import leakage reduces it).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Gross Capital Formation (GCF) in national accounts represents:

options.option_text: Investment in fixed assets (machinery, buildings, infrastructure) plus changes in inventories
Total savings of all households in the economy during the year
Foreign capital inflows including FDI and FPI
Government expenditure on capital projects funded through the budget

explanation: Gross Capital Formation = Gross Fixed Capital Formation (GFCF: factories, equipment, buildings) + Change in Inventories. GCF includes both private and public sector investment. Net Capital Formation = GCF − Depreciation. India's GCF as % of GDP (Investment rate) has varied between 30-35%. Higher GCF → higher economic growth (capital deepening).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which committee recommended the 'Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana' (PMGSY)?

options.option_text: PMGSY was not from a committee — it was launched directly by PM Vajpayee on 25 December 2000 under Bharat Nirman
Tendulkar Committee recommendation for rural connectivity with poverty alleviation
Narasimham Committee recommendation for rural infrastructure financing
Rangarajan Committee for linking rural roads to job creation

explanation: PMGSY: launched 25 December 2000 by PM Atal Bihari Vajpayee. Aimed to connect all unconnected habitations (>500 population in plains; >250 in hills/tribal) with all-weather roads. Implemented by NRRDA (National Rural Roads Development Agency) under Ministry of Rural Development. Later included under Bharat Nirman scheme (2005).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Baumol-Tobin model explains which component of money demand?

options.option_text: Transactions demand — how much cash individuals hold for day-to-day transactions, balancing interest income lost vs transaction costs
Speculative demand — how investors allocate between bonds and money based on expected interest rates
Precautionary demand — buffer stock of money held for unexpected contingencies
Portfolio demand — optimal allocation across all assets for risk-return optimization

explanation: Baumol (1952) and Tobin (1956) independently developed the inventory-theoretic transactions demand model: optimal cash balance = √(2bT/r) where b = transaction cost, T = total transactions, r = interest rate. Higher interest → hold less cash (more trips to bank). Counter-intuitive insight: transactions demand is ALSO interest-elastic (not just income-elastic). Keynes's speculative demand relates to bond vs money choice.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Lender of Last Resort' function of RBI means:

options.option_text: RBI provides emergency liquidity to banks facing sudden cash shortages to prevent bank runs and systemic failure
RBI gives loans to businesses when commercial banks refuse to lend
RBI provides final credit to government when all other financing options are exhausted
RBI guarantees all deposits in commercial banks up to ₹5 lakh per depositor

explanation: Lender of Last Resort (Bagehot's dictum, 1873): Central bank must lend freely, at a PENALTY rate, against good collateral, to solvent but illiquid banks during a crisis. Purpose: prevent bank runs from becoming bank failures and systemic crises. RBI lends via MSF (Marginal Standing Facility) in India. Deposit insurance: DICGC guarantees ₹5 lakh per depositor (enhanced from ₹1 lakh in 2020).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which monetary policy tool involves the RBI buying government securities from commercial banks?

options.option_text: Open Market Operations (OMO) — buying securities injects liquidity into the banking system
Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) reduction — frees up deposits for lending
Repo Rate cut — reduces cost of borrowing from RBI
Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) cut — reduces mandatory security holdings

explanation: OMO: RBI buys government securities from banks → banks receive cash → credit expansion (liquidity injection). Reverse: RBI sells securities → banks pay cash → credit contraction (liquidity absorption). Used to manage day-to-day liquidity in the banking system. Unlike CRR/SLR (which change ratios), OMO directly changes money supply through market transactions.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The difference between Repo Rate and Bank Rate is:

options.option_text: Repo involves repurchase of securities (short-term, collateralised); Bank Rate is the rate at which RBI provides long-term credit to banks (uncollateralised)
Bank Rate is set by commercial banks; Repo Rate is set by RBI only
Repo Rate is always higher than Bank Rate by 25 basis points
Bank Rate applies to depositors; Repo Rate applies to borrowers

explanation: Bank Rate (Section 49, RBI Act): rate at which RBI extends credit to commercial banks for a longer period, without collateral (discounting eligible bills). Currently Bank Rate = MSF rate = Repo + 0.25%. Repo Rate: overnight/short-term, with collateral (repurchase agreement). In practice, banks use Repo (cheaper, shorter), not Bank Rate. Bank Rate = penal rate for maintaining minimum CRR.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: DICGC (Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation) provides deposit insurance up to:

options.option_text: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank — enhanced from ₹1 lakh after PMC Bank crisis (2020)
₹1 lakh per depositor per bank — original limit since 1961
₹10 lakh per depositor — enhanced after YES Bank crisis
Full deposit amount — no limit since India implemented FSAP recommendations

explanation: DICGC (subsidiary of RBI, est. 1978): insures deposits in commercial banks, RRBs, cooperative banks. Limit raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank in February 2020 (after PMC Bank crisis exposed inadequacy of ₹1 lakh limit). Covers savings, fixed, current, recurring deposits. Premium paid by banks (not depositors).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were established in India in:

options.option_text: 1975 — under the Regional Rural Banks Act 1976, based on Narasimham Working Group (1975) recommendation
1969 — along with the first wave of bank nationalisation
1982 — same year as NABARD, to strengthen agricultural credit
1991 — as part of financial sector liberalisation reforms

explanation: First RRB (Prathama Grameen Bank) established 2 October 1975 in Moradabad, UP. Set up under RRB Act 1976 on Narasimham Working Group recommendation. Joint ownership: Central Government (50%), State Government (15%), Sponsor Bank (35%). Serve rural areas with small loans to farmers, artisans, agricultural labourers. Consolidated into fewer, larger RRBs over time (from 196 to ~43 after mergers).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Basel III norms (implemented in India as 'Basel III Capital Regulations') require banks to maintain minimum capital as a percentage of Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA). The minimum Total Capital Ratio under Basel III is:

options.option_text: 10.5% (Minimum Capital Ratio 8% + Capital Conservation Buffer 2.5%)
8% (the original Basel I requirement)
12% including D-SIB surcharge for all banks
6% Tier 1 only — Tier 2 capital is optional

explanation: Basel III (post-2008 GFC reforms): Minimum Capital = 8% of RWA. Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) = 2.5%. Total = 10.5%. India requires additional: Counter-cyclical buffer (0-2.5% when needed) and D-SIB surcharge (0.2-0.8% for SBI, HDFC, ICICI). Tier 1 (loss-absorbing going-concern) > Tier 2 (gone-concern). India implements via RBI circular.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) was established to:

options.option_text: Provide refinance and financial support to small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and micro-finance institutions
Finance agricultural operations and rural development schemes
Provide home loans and housing finance to urban and rural households
Facilitate import-export financing for small manufacturing exporters

explanation: SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India): established 2 April 1990. Principal financial institution for promoting, financing and developing MSMEs. Functions: refinancing MSME loans of commercial banks/SFCs, direct lending, MFI refinancing, venture capital. NHB = housing. NABARD = agriculture. EXIM Bank = export-import. Mudra Bank = micro loans (under SIDBI umbrella).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The first bank nationalisation in India (1969) covered banks with deposits exceeding:

options.option_text: ₹50 crore — 14 major private banks were nationalised by PM Indira Gandhi
₹100 crore — only the very large banks were nationalised initially
₹10 crore — to include medium-sized banks in public sector
All banks without any deposit criterion were nationalised at once

explanation: First nationalisation: 19 July 1969 — 14 banks with deposits > ₹50 crore (SBI was already nationalised in 1955). Banks included: Punjab National Bank, Bank of Baroda, Canara Bank, Allahabad Bank, etc. Second nationalisation: 1980 — 6 more banks with deposits > ₹200 crore. Total 20 banks nationalised (plus SBI). Rationale: social banking, credit to priority sectors.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Monetary Policy transmission mechanism works through which channels (select all that are standard channels)?

options.option_text: Interest rate channel, Exchange rate channel, Credit channel, and Asset price channel — all are standard transmission channels
Only the interest rate channel — other channels are secondary and less important
Tax rate channel and fiscal multiplier — these determine monetary effectiveness
Only the credit channel — bank lending rates determine investment and consumption

explanation: Monetary Policy Transmission Channels: (1) Interest Rate: Repo ↓ → lending rates ↓ → investment/consumption ↑. (2) Exchange Rate: lower rates → capital outflow → depreciation → exports ↑. (3) Credit Channel: banks have more lendable funds → credit availability ↑. (4) Asset Price: lower rates → equity/property prices ↑ → wealth effect → consumption ↑. All four operate simultaneously.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) targets for domestic commercial banks require lending at least __% of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sectors:

options.option_text: 40% overall — with sub-targets for agriculture (18%), micro-enterprises, weaker sections, etc.
25% overall — with no sub-targets for individual sectors
60% overall — since 1980 nationalisation extended priority sector definition
50% overall — half of all bank credit must go to priority sectors

explanation: PSL targets (RBI Master Directions): 40% of ANBC for domestic banks. Sub-targets: Agriculture 18% (of which 8% to small/marginal farmers), Micro Enterprises 7.5%, Weaker Sections 12%. Foreign banks (with <20 branches): 40% of ANBC under priority sector guidelines but with different sub-targets. Shortfall → RIDF/SEDF contribution to NABARD/NHB.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: What is 'Inflation Targeting' as adopted by India in 2016?

options.option_text: A monetary policy framework where the RBI's primary mandate is to maintain CPI inflation at 4% ±2%, with MPC making decisions to achieve this
The government's fiscal policy of capping fuel price inflation through price controls
RBI's policy of pegging the exchange rate to contain imported inflation
A banking regulation requiring banks to price loans below the inflation rate

explanation: Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT): adopted 2016 via amendment to RBI Act. MPC sets policy rate with primary objective of 4% CPI ±2% (2-6% band). If inflation stays outside band for 3 consecutive quarters → RBI must report to government explaining failure and remedial action. Based on Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommendation. India was the first major emerging market to adopt FIT formally.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT) system settles transactions:

options.option_text: On a deferred net settlement basis in hourly batches — 48 half-hourly batches available 24×7 since December 2019
In real-time gross settlement (RTGS) — each transaction settled individually as it arrives
Only during banking hours — not available on weekends or public holidays
Instantly like UPI — same-day settlement within seconds

explanation: NEFT: Net settlement in batches. Since December 2019, NEFT is available 24×7 (48 half-hourly batches per day). Minimum transfer: ₹1. No upper limit. Settlement within 2 hours typically. RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement): each transaction settled immediately, individually. Minimum ₹2 lakh. Used for large-value transfers. UPI: instant (seconds), limit ₹1 lakh per transaction.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) in India are those:

options.option_text: Listed in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934 — satisfying criteria of paid-up capital and reserves ≥ ₹5 lakh
Listed on the NSE or BSE stock exchanges with >50% public shareholding
Operating in at least 3 states with branches in rural and urban areas
Nationalized banks plus State Bank of India — private banks are non-scheduled

explanation: Scheduled Banks (Section 42(6) RBI Act): listed in Second Schedule of RBI Act. Criteria: paid-up capital and reserves ≥ ₹5 lakh; must not be prejudicial to depositors' interest; satisfactory financial position. Benefit: eligible for RBI refinance/credit. Non-scheduled banks: smaller cooperative banks not in Second Schedule. SBI, PSBs, private banks, foreign banks, RRBs, SFBs, Payment Banks — all are scheduled.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The National Housing Bank (NHB) was established to:

options.option_text: Promote, finance, and regulate housing finance institutions in India — refinances home loans of HFCs and banks
Provide home loans directly to individuals at subsidised rates
Regulate real estate developers and enforce building codes nationally
Manage government housing schemes like PMAY centrally

explanation: NHB (National Housing Bank): established July 1988, subsidiary of RBI (till 2019, now under government). Apex institution for housing finance. Functions: refinance housing finance companies (HFCs), regulate HFCs (after NHB Amendment 2019 — earlier RBI regulated HFCs). HDFC (before its bank merger), LIC Housing Finance, PNB Housing — all regulated/refinanced by NHB.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework of RBI is triggered when a bank:

options.option_text: Breaches certain risk thresholds in Capital Adequacy, Asset Quality (NPA ratio), or Profitability (Return on Assets)
Fails to meet its PSL targets for two consecutive years
Has more than 30% of its deposits in foreign currencies
Reports losses for one quarter (any single quarter)

explanation: PCA Framework (RBI): triggers when bank breaches: (1) Capital Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) falls below 10.25%, (2) Net NPA exceeds 6%, (3) Return on Assets (RoA) negative for two consecutive years. Restrictions imposed: dividend payments, branch expansion, new lending. Banks in PCA: directed to raise capital, reduce NPAs. Dena Bank, Corporation Bank were under PCA before being merged.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A Progressive Tax system means:

options.option_text: The tax rate INCREASES as taxable income increases — higher income earners pay a larger percentage
The tax rate is the same (flat) for all income levels regardless of earnings
The tax rate DECREASES as income increases — regressive on higher earners
Tax is levied only on income above a minimum threshold, with all below-threshold income untaxed

explanation: Progressive tax: tax rate rises with income (India's income tax slabs: 5%, 20%, 30% at different levels). Promotes equity — higher burden on higher earners. Proportional (flat) tax: same rate for all (e.g., some countries' flat tax proposals). Regressive tax: rate falls as income rises (e.g., a fixed-amount tax is regressive since it's a larger % of lower incomes). Indirect taxes are often regressive.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Finance Bill, presented along with the Annual Budget, deals with:

options.option_text: Proposals for taxation changes — imposing new taxes, modifying rates, or abolishing existing taxes
All government expenditure proposals for the upcoming year
Grants to States and Union Territories under Article 275
Constitutional amendments required for implementing budget proposals

explanation: Budget documents: (1) Annual Financial Statement (Art. 112) — statement of estimated receipts and expenditure. (2) Demands for Grants — department-wise expenditure. (3) Appropriation Bill — authorises withdrawal from CFI. (4) Finance Bill — proposes tax changes (levying, continuing, altering taxes). Finance Bill is a Money Bill (Art. 110) if it deals only with taxes.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Total Expenditure = ₹45,00,000 crore. Revenue Receipts = ₹25,00,000 crore. Non-debt Capital Receipts = ₹80,000 crore. Interest Payments = ₹11,00,000 crore. What is Primary Deficit?

options.option_text: ₹19,20,000 crore (Fiscal Deficit only, not Primary)
₹11,00,000 crore (equals interest payments)

explanation: Step 1: Fiscal Deficit = Total Exp − (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Cap Receipts) = 45,00,000 − (25,00,000 + 80,000) = 45,00,000 − 25,80,000 = ₹19,20,000 crore. Step 2: Primary Deficit = FD − Interest Payments = 19,20,000 − 11,00,000 = ₹8,20,000 crore. Revenue Deficit = Rev Exp − Rev Receipts (not calculable here without Rev Exp split).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'Crowding Out' in fiscal policy means:

options.option_text: Increased government borrowing pushes up interest rates, reducing private investment
Government spending directly substitutes for private spending in the same sectors
Fiscal expansion crowds out exports by causing currency appreciation
High taxation reduces savings, limiting funds available for investment

explanation: Crowding Out: Government deficit → borrows more from market → higher demand for loanable funds → interest rates rise → private investment falls (expensive to borrow). Complete crowding out: every rupee of government spending displaces one rupee of private investment (net GDP effect = 0). Keynesian view: crowding out is partial, especially in recession (savings pool is large, rates don't rise much).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which Constitutional article defines a 'Money Bill' in the Indian context?

options.option_text: Article 110 — a bill dealing ONLY with taxation, borrowing, Consolidated Fund, custody of CFI, or appropriation is a Money Bill
Article 112 — the Annual Financial Statement is a Money Bill
Article 266 — bills relating to Consolidated Fund are Money Bills
Article 109 — procedure for ordinary bills vs money bills

explanation: Article 110: Money Bill definition — deals ONLY with: (a) imposition/abolition/remission/alteration/regulation of any tax, (b) regulation of government borrowing, (c) custody of Consolidated Fund, (d) appropriation, (e) declaring expenditure charged on CFI, (f) audit of accounts. Certified by Lok Sabha Speaker. Rajya Sabha can only delay 14 days, cannot reject.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Automatic stabilisers in fiscal policy refer to:

options.option_text: Built-in features (progressive taxes, unemployment benefits) that automatically reduce fiscal surplus in booms and deficits in recessions without new policy action
RBI's automatic interest rate response to inflation and deflation signals
Constitutional limits on deficit that automatically cap government spending
Market mechanisms that automatically return the economy to full employment

explanation: Automatic Stabilisers: Boom → incomes rise → progressive taxes collect more automatically → private spending power reduced (stabilises overheating). Recession → incomes fall → taxes fall → unemployment benefits rise → disposable income partially maintained (stabilises contraction). No new legislation needed — they work automatically. Discretionary policy requires deliberate new action (stimulus package, tax cuts).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Supplementary Demands for Grants are presented when:

options.option_text: The amount authorised in the original budget is found insufficient OR new services arise during the year
The original budget is rejected by Rajya Sabha and must be re-presented
The Finance Minister changes during the year requiring a fresh budget
Actual revenue collections exceed original estimates by more than 10%

explanation: Supplementary Demands for Grants (Article 115): when original grants are insufficient for the year, or when new services/policies require spending not anticipated in the original budget. Presented mid-year. Must be voted by Lok Sabha like the original grants. Examples: flood relief, defence emergency spending, new welfare schemes launched mid-year.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Non-tax Revenue of the Central Government includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options.option_text: Corporate income tax collected from companies (this is tax revenue)
Dividends received from PSUs and RBI
Interest received on loans given to States
Fees, fines, and administrative charges collected by departments

explanation: Revenue Receipts: Tax Revenue (income tax, corporate tax, GST, customs) + Non-Tax Revenue (dividends from PSUs/RBI, interest on state loans, fees/fines, spectrum charges, economic services). Corporate income tax = Tax Revenue. PSU dividends, RBI surplus transfer, interest on state loans = Non-Tax Revenue. This distinction is frequently tested in budget-related questions.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Speculative attack on a currency typically occurs when:

options.option_text: Traders expect currency devaluation — they short-sell the currency, accelerating the fall they expect
Foreign central banks purchase the currency to support its value artificially
Domestic interest rates rise sharply, attracting capital inflows and currency appreciation
The government runs a budget surplus, reducing currency in circulation

explanation: Speculative Attack (currency crisis): occurs in fixed exchange rate regimes. Speculators expect devaluation → sell domestic currency massively → central bank loses forex reserves defending the peg → eventually forced to devalue. Self-fulfilling prophecy. India's 1991 crisis had elements of this. Thailand 1997 Asian Crisis = classic case. Fixed rates are vulnerable; floating rates adjust automatically.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The GST Compensation Cess charged over and above the 28% slab is levied on:

options.option_text: Demerit and luxury goods like tobacco, pan masala, aerated drinks, large cars — cess proceeds compensate States for revenue loss
All goods in the 28% slab uniformly as part of the standard rate
Essential goods in the 0% slab to ensure States still get revenue
Imports only — domestic production is not subject to compensation cess

explanation: GST Compensation Cess: levied on select demerit/luxury goods (tobacco products, pan masala, aerated drinks, coal, large/luxury cars) over the 28% rate. Proceeds → Compensation Fund → paid to States for 5-year revenue loss guarantee from GST switchover (2017-2022). The cess period was extended to 2026 to repay loans taken during COVID for State compensation. Rate varies by product.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The NK Singh Committee (2017) on FRBM review recommended the following as the new fiscal consolidation roadmap:

options.option_text: Fiscal Deficit at 3% of GDP and total public debt (Centre + States) at 60% of GDP as medium-term targets
Eliminate Revenue Deficit by 2019 and bring FD to 2.5% of GDP
Abolish FRBM and replace with automatic fiscal stabiliser mechanism
Increase FD target to 5% to fund infrastructure expansion

explanation: NK Singh Committee (2017): recommended Fiscal Responsibility Review. Key: (1) FD at 3% of GDP as rolling target. (2) Total public debt: Centre 40% + States 20% = 60% of GDP. (3) Revenue Deficit = 0.8% of GDP. (4) Fiscal Council (independent body to monitor). (5) Escape clauses: FD can exceed 3% by 0.5% in specific conditions (structural reform year, agriculture crisis, security threat).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India is consistently among the top recipients of remittances globally. These remittances appear in the Balance of Payments under:

options.option_text: Current Account — specifically under Private Transfers (Secondary Income)
Capital Account — as NRI deposit flows into Indian banks
Financial Account — as portfolio investment from NRIs
Capital Account — as NRI direct investment in Indian businesses

explanation: Remittances (money sent by Indian diaspora to family in India) = Private Transfers under Current Account (Secondary Income). They help offset India's trade deficit. ~$110 billion annually (2023 — largest globally). NRI Bank Deposits (NRE/NRO/FCNR accounts) = Financial Account. NRI direct investment in businesses = Financial Account. The distinction between remittances vs NRI investments is exam-critical.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which type of budget presents estimated receipts and expenditures for the NEXT fiscal year?

options.option_text: Budget Estimate (BE) — presented in February for the next financial year beginning April 1
Revised Estimate (RE) — presented mid-year to revise the original estimates
Actual (Final Accounts) — the definitive figures after the year ends
Rolling Budget — 3-year forward projection updated annually

explanation: Indian budget cycle: (1) Budget Estimate (BE): original estimates presented in February for April-March year. (2) Revised Estimate (RE): mid-year revision (presented with next year's BE or in a separate session). (3) Actual: CAG-audited final figures 2-3 years later. Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement: 3-year projections. FRBM requires presenting these statements.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The GST Council is chaired by:

options.option_text: Union Finance Minister — with State Finance Ministers as members
RBI Governor — as the monetary authority overseeing indirect taxes
Prime Minister — who chairs all major policy councils
CAG — since GST receipts flow to the Consolidated Fund

explanation: GST Council (Article 279A): Chairperson = Union Finance Minister. Members = Union MoS (Finance) + State Finance Ministers (or equivalent). Decisions by 3/4 weighted majority. Centre has 1/3 vote; all States combined have 2/3 vote. The Council recommends GST rates, exemptions, thresholds, and administration. Supreme Court (2022): recommendations are persuasive but not legally binding.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: External Commercial Borrowings (ECBs) by Indian companies appear in the Balance of Payments under:

options.option_text: Financial Account (Capital and Financial Account) — as debt capital inflows from overseas lenders
Current Account — as interest payments on external debt
Current Account — as income receipts from foreign investments
Capital Account — as one-time capital transfers from foreign entities

explanation: ECBs: loans raised by Indian corporates from international banks/bond markets. ECB principal receipts → Financial Account (capital inflow). ECB interest payments → Current Account (income outflow, under Primary Income). Repayment of principal → Financial Account (capital outflow). This cross-account treatment of debt (principal = capital; interest = current) is a common exam trap.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A company switches from SLM to WDV method from the current year. WDV rate = 20%. The existing asset had cost ₹1,00,000, is 2 years old, and SLM rate was 10% (salvage ₹10,000). WDV of asset (for WDV going forward) = ?

options.option_text: ₹80,000 — net book value at end of Year 2 under SLM is used as opening WDV for the new method
₹1,00,000 — restart depreciation from original cost under WDV
₹64,000 — apply WDV retrospectively for 2 years
₹90,000 — only one year of SLM depreciation recognised on switch

explanation: SLM depreciation per year = (1,00,000 − 10,000)/10 = ₹9,000. After Year 2: NBV = 1,00,000 − 2 × 9,000 = ₹82,000 (not 80,000 — let me verify: 1,00,000 × 10% = 10,000 per year if rate is 10%; or ₹9,000 if formula used with salvage). Under typical exam approach: when switching, the current book value (SLM NBV = ₹82,000) becomes the opening WDV. Year 3 WDV dep = 20% × 82,000 = ₹16,400.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the SYD (Sum of Years Digits) method, for an asset with useful life of 5 years, the depreciation fraction for Year 4 is:

options.option_text: 2/15 (remaining life at START of year 4 = 2 years; SYD = 1+2+3+4+5 = 15; fraction = 2/15)
4/15 (using year number directly)
3/15 (middle year gets middle fraction)
1/15 (last fraction)

explanation: SYD fractions: SYD = n(n+1)/2 = 5×6/2 = 15. Year 1: 5/15, Year 2: 4/15, Year 3: 3/15, Year 4: 2/15, Year 5: 1/15. Pattern: Year k fraction = (n−k+1)/SYD = remaining life at START of year k divided by SYD. Year 4 remaining life = 5−4+1 = 2. Fraction = 2/15. Total = 15/15 = 100% of depreciable amount.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm values inventory at FIFO during inflation. Compared to WA method, FIFO will show:

options.option_text: Higher closing stock, lower COGS, higher gross profit, and higher tax in an inflationary period
Lower closing stock and higher COGS — old (cheaper) stock remains unsold
Same values as WA — both methods give identical results under GAAP
Higher COGS and lower gross profit — FIFO uses most recent (expensive) costs first

explanation: Inflation effect comparison: FIFO sells cheaper (older) units first → COGS = cheaper costs → LOWER COGS → HIGHER Gross Profit → HIGHER Tax. Closing stock = latest (expensive) units → HIGHER closing stock value. WA uses average cost → intermediate values. LIFO (not allowed under AS 2/IAS 2): most expensive units sold first → HIGHEST COGS → LOWEST Profit → LOWEST Tax. This is the core of LIFO prohibition rationale in IAS 2.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Annuity Method of depreciation charges higher depreciation in early years or later years?

options.option_text: LATER years — annual depreciation is calculated to provide a return on investment, with interest element reducing each year as asset value falls; net depreciation charge rises each year
EARLIER years — like WDV, more depreciation at start
Equal every year — like SLM, constant charge throughout
Only in years of actual use — like Machine Hour Rate

explanation: Annuity Method: the asset is treated as an investment. Annual charge = annuity amount (constant) which covers both interest on the asset's opening book value AND depreciation. As book value falls, the interest component falls, so more of the annuity goes toward depreciation → net depreciation charge increases each year. Used in long-term leases and some regulated asset bases.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: ABC analysis of inventory classifies items into A, B, and C categories. 'A' items are:

options.option_text: High-value, low-volume items requiring tight control and frequent ordering — typically 10-20% of items but 70-80% of total inventory value
Low-value, high-volume items with no need for close monitoring
All items above the reorder level requiring immediate procurement
Items alphabetically starting with A in the inventory list

explanation: ABC Analysis (Pareto Principle — 80/20 rule): A items: 10-20% of items, 70-80% of value → strict control, frequent review, accurate records. B items: 15-25% of items, 15-25% of value → moderate control. C items: 60-70% of items, 5-10% of value → loose control, bulk ordering. Management focuses resources on A items since they have the biggest financial impact.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG of India submits how many types of Audit Reports to Parliament?

options.option_text: Three main types — Civil Audit Report, Commercial Audit Report (PSUs), and Defence/Railways Audit Report
One consolidated report — all audits compiled into a single annual report
Two reports — a compliance report and a performance report only
Seven reports — one for each major ministry

explanation: CAG submits multiple Audit Reports to Parliament: (1) Report on Union Government Finance Accounts. (2) Report on Union Government Appropriation Accounts. (3) Report on Commercial (PSU) audits. (4) Report on Defence. (5) Railway audit report. Each is laid before Parliament separately and examined by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) or Estimates Committee.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Fiscal Federalism' principle underlying Finance Commission recommendations requires balancing:

options.option_text: Vertical balance (Centre vs States) and Horizontal balance (equity among States), while respecting efficiency and macroeconomic stability
Only horizontal equity — all states should receive equal per-capita transfers
Only vertical balance — Centre should retain maximum resources for national priorities
Political representation — states with more Lok Sabha seats get higher devolution

explanation: Fiscal Federalism (Musgrave, Oates): Vertical fiscal imbalance: Centre collects most taxes but States have larger expenditure responsibilities → need transfers. Horizontal fiscal disparities: rich States (Maharashtra, Karnataka) vs poor States (Bihar, UP) → equity requires poorer States getting larger per-capita transfers. The Finance Commission balances these while ensuring macroeconomic stability (FRBM compliance) and efficiency (performance-based incentives).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Social Audit differs from CAG audit in that Social Audit involves:

options.option_text: Direct participation of beneficiaries and local community in reviewing scheme implementation — gram sabhas scrutinise MGNREGA expenditure through social audit
CAG's audit of social welfare schemes with special focus on outcomes
Audit by civil society organisations appointed by the Supreme Court
RBI's audit of banks' compliance with social banking mandates

explanation: Social Audit: Community-based review of public programme implementation. Mandated for MGNREGA under Section 17 of MGNREGA Act — gram sabhas must hold social audits. Workers verify: were all registered? Were actual wages paid? Were assets created real? Social Audit Units (SAUs) at State level facilitate this. Different from CAG audit (institutional) — Social Audit is participatory and bottom-up.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Grants-in-Aid recommended by Finance Commission under Article 275 are of which type?

options.option_text: Statutory grants to States that cannot cover administrative expenses from assigned revenues — based on assessed needs
Discretionary grants from Planning Commission (now NITI Aayog) for plan projects
Emergency grants during natural disasters — released from Contingency Fund
Matching grants requiring States to spend equal amounts from their own resources

explanation: Article 275: Grants-in-Aid from Consolidated Fund of India to States that are in need of financial assistance. Finance Commission recommends the amounts. These are statutory (Parliament must pass), unlike discretionary grants by the executive. The 15th FC made significant Article 275 grants for health, education, local bodies, and disaster management.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG's Appropriation Accounts show:

options.option_text: Actual expenditure against each grant voted by Parliament — revealing savings (under-spend) or excess (overspend)
The proposed budget estimates before Parliamentary approval
Tax collection performance vs target for each revenue head
Consolidated balance sheet of the Government of India

explanation: Appropriation Accounts (prepared by each ministry, certified by CAG): Prescribed Form 19 — show demand-wise comparison of (a) amount voted by Parliament and (b) actual expenditure. Savings: voted > actual (money not spent). Excess: actual > voted (needs Parliament's post-facto sanction under Article 115). PAC examines appropriation accounts to question under-utilisation or unauthorised excess.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The India Stack is a set of open APIs. Which of the following is NOT part of India Stack?

options.option_text: UPI (Unified Payments Interface) — real-time interbank payment system (UPI is part of India Stack's payment layer)
BHIM (Bharat Interface for Money) — UPI-based app, not an API/layer itself
Account Aggregator — consent-based financial data sharing framework
BHIM is the correct answer — it's a consumer app built ON India Stack, not a layer of India Stack itself

explanation: India Stack layers: (1) Presence-less: Aadhaar biometric eKYC. (2) Paperless: eSign, DigiLocker. (3) Cashless: UPI (payments). (4) Consent: Account Aggregator (AA) — financial data sharing with user consent. BHIM is a mobile app that USES UPI — it's a product built on India Stack, not a layer of the stack. OCEN (Open Credit Enablement Network) is another layer being added.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act was passed in India in:

options.option_text: 2023 — providing a comprehensive framework for processing personal data with consent
2022 — along with the Telecommunications Act 2023
2019 — the Personal Data Protection Bill lapsed; DPDP came later
2020 — prompted by the Supreme Court's Puttaswamy privacy judgement of 2017

explanation: DPDP Act 2023: India's first comprehensive data protection law. Applies to processing of digital personal data in India. Key concepts: Data Principal (individual), Data Fiduciary (entity processing data), consent requirement, data minimisation, purpose limitation, Data Protection Board of India (adjudication). Based on the K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) right to privacy judgement. Rules still being framed (2024-25).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: CPGRAMS stands for:

options.option_text: Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System — portal for citizens to lodge complaints against government departments
Central Public Government Revenue and Management System
Comprehensive Procurement and Grant Regulation Management System
Citizen Portal for Government Revenue and Administration Management

explanation: CPGRAMS: online grievance portal under Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG). Citizens can lodge complaints about any central government ministry/department. Complaint tracks through system. Time-bound resolution mandated. Integrated with UMANG. Example of C2G (Citizen to Government) e-Governance interaction. Also linked to state portals in some cases.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: MCA21 portal serves as the point of interaction between:

options.option_text: Ministry of Corporate Affairs and companies/businesses — for registration, filings, compliance under Companies Act 2013
Ministry of Commerce and 21 major export-oriented industries
Ministry of Civil Aviation and airline operators
Ministry of Consumer Affairs and consumer courts across 21 states

explanation: MCA21: Ministry of Corporate Affairs' e-Governance portal. Services: company registration (SPICe+ form), director KYC, annual return filing, charge registration, insolvency filings. First government service to use Digital Signature Certificates (DSC) mandatorily. Version 3.0 (MCA21 V3) upgraded to improve user experience. Classic G2B interaction example.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA) under the IT Act 2000 is responsible for:

options.option_text: Licensing and regulating Certifying Authorities (CAs) that issue Digital Signature Certificates (DSCs)
Managing Aadhaar-based e-KYC systems on behalf of UIDAI
Controlling all government websites and their SSL/TLS certificates
Regulating internet service providers under the IT Act 2000

explanation: CCA (under MeitY): apex authority for digital signature infrastructure in India. Functions: licenses CAs (like eMudhra, (n)Code Solutions, NSDL e-Gov), issues Root Certificate, maintains Root Certifying Authority of India (RCAI). Digital Signatures are legally recognised under IT Act 2000 for e-contracts, tax filings, ROC filings. CCA ≠ CERT-In (which handles cybersecurity incidents).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Aarogya Setu was launched in 2020 primarily as:

options.option_text: A COVID-19 contact tracing app that tracks proximity to COVID-positive persons using Bluetooth and GPS
A health insurance portal for Ayushman Bharat scheme beneficiaries
A telemedicine platform for connecting rural patients with doctors
A digital prescription and pharmacy management system

explanation: Aarogya Setu: launched April 2020 (COVID-19 pandemic). Contact tracing app using Bluetooth (proximity detection) and location data. 'Aarogya Setu' = 'Bridge to Health' in Sanskrit. Open-sourced (April 2020). Helped track potential COVID exposure. Became one of the fastest-adopted apps globally (~150 million downloads). Developed by National Informatics Centre (NIC) and MEITy.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The demand for a commodity is said to be perfectly inelastic when:

options.option_text: A change in price has NO effect on quantity demanded — the demand curve is vertical
A small change in price leads to an infinite change in quantity demanded
The percentage change in quantity equals the percentage change in price
Consumers buy more only when the price falls significantly

explanation: Perfectly inelastic demand (Ed = 0): vertical demand curve. Quantity demanded is fixed regardless of price. Example: insulin for a diabetic — they need the exact dose whether it costs ₹10 or ₹1000. No substitutes, no way to reduce consumption. Graphically: a vertical straight line at the fixed quantity.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If price falls by 5% and quantity demanded rises by 5%, Total Revenue will:

options.option_text: Remain unchanged — unitary elastic demand (Ed = 1), TR = P × Q stays constant
Rise — price fall always increases total revenue for sellers
Fall — quantity increase cannot compensate for price fall
Double — both effects multiply rather than cancel

explanation: Unitary elastic demand (Ed = 1): %ΔP = %ΔQ → TR is constant. If price falls 5% but quantity rises 5%, new TR = (0.95P)(1.05Q) = 0.9975PQ ≈ PQ (constant). TR-Elasticity rule: Ed = 1 → TR unchanged; Ed > 1 → TR rises when P falls; Ed < 1 → TR falls when P falls.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Price elasticity of demand = −1.5. A firm raises price by 10%. What happens to Total Revenue?

options.option_text: TR falls — demand is elastic (|Ed| > 1), so price rise reduces revenue
TR rises — higher price always increases revenue
TR is unchanged — elasticity of 1.5 means proportional change
TR falls by exactly 15% (1.5 × 10%)

explanation: |Ed| = 1.5 > 1 → elastic demand. When price rises 10%, quantity falls by 15% (1.5 × 10%). Net effect on TR: %ΔTR ≈ %ΔP + %ΔQ = +10% + (−15%) = −5%. TR falls. Rule: elastic demand → price and TR move in OPPOSITE directions. The firm should LOWER price to increase revenue.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which good is most likely to have the HIGHEST price elasticity of demand?

options.option_text: A specific brand of bottled water (many substitutes — other brands and tap water)
Petrol for a vehicle (very few short-run alternatives)
Rice for a rural household (staple food, necessity)
Life-saving medicine with no alternatives

explanation: Factors making demand MORE elastic: (1) Many close substitutes — easiest to switch. (2) Luxury goods. (3) Large share of income. (4) Longer time period. A specific brand of water has many close substitutes (other brands, tap water) → very elastic. Petrol, rice, life-saving medicine have few/no alternatives → inelastic.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following will cause the demand curve for petrol to SHIFT LEFT (decrease in demand)?

options.option_text: A significant increase in the number of electric vehicles on the road
A fall in the price of petrol itself
An increase in consumer incomes (petrol is a normal good)
An increase in the price of diesel (a substitute for petrol)

explanation: The demand curve SHIFTS when non-price factors change. EVs substitute for petrol-powered vehicles → reduces demand for petrol at every price → leftward shift. Option B (price fall) causes movement ALONG the curve (extension), not a shift. Option C (income rise) → rightward shift. Option D (diesel price rise) → more people switch to petrol → rightward shift.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A 20% rise in the price of tea causes a 15% rise in the demand for coffee. Cross Elasticity of Demand between coffee and tea = ?

options.option_text: +0.75 — positive, confirming they are substitutes
−0.75 — negative, confirming they are complements
+1.33 — elastic cross-demand relationship
0 — cross elasticity is always zero for unrelated goods

explanation: Cross Elasticity (Exy) = %ΔQx / %ΔPy = +15% / +20% = +0.75. Positive → substitutes (tea and coffee). When tea price rises, some consumers switch to coffee → coffee demand rises. Negative Exy → complements (car and petrol — when petrol price rises, fewer cars sold). Zero → independent goods.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The demand schedule shows: At ₹10 → 100 units; At ₹8 → 120 units. Using POINT elasticity at ₹10:

options.option_text: Ed = −0.83 (using midpoint formula)
Ed = −2 (percentage change method: 20% / 20% = 1, but sign is wrong)
Ed = +1 (sign not considered in point elasticity)

explanation: Point elasticity at (P=10, Q=100): Ed = (dQ/dP) × (P/Q). ΔQ/ΔP = (120−100)/(8−10) = 20/(−2) = −10. Ed = −10 × (10/100) = −10 × 0.1 = −1. Unitary elastic at this point. The negative sign reflects inverse relationship. |Ed| = 1 means a 1% price change causes a 1% quantity change.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Substitution Effect of a price change states that when the price of good X rises:

options.option_text: Consumers substitute X with relatively cheaper alternatives Y, reducing demand for X
Real income increases, allowing consumers to buy more of X
The supply of X automatically increases to stabilise the market
The government intervenes to provide X at the old price

explanation: Substitution Effect: when P(X) rises, X becomes more expensive RELATIVE to substitutes → consumers switch to Y (which is now relatively cheaper). Always negative (for normal substitutes). Income Effect: higher P(X) reduces real purchasing power → for normal goods, buy less X; for inferior goods, buy MORE X. Giffen paradox: income effect overwhelms substitution effect.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An Indifference Curve for perfect COMPLEMENTS (e.g., left shoe and right shoe) has the shape of:

options.option_text: An 'L' shape (right angle) — both goods must be consumed in fixed proportion
A downward-sloping straight line — constant rate of substitution
A convex curve bowed toward the origin — diminishing MRS
A horizontal line — one good adds no utility regardless of quantity

explanation: Perfect complements (left/right shoe, pen/ink cartridge): must be consumed in fixed ratio. IC is L-shaped (right angle at the optimal ratio point). MRS = 0 on horizontal segment (extra right shoes add nothing without matching lefts) and undefined on vertical segment. Consumer equilibrium at the corner of the L.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An Indifference Curve for perfect SUBSTITUTES (e.g., two identical brands of water) has the shape of:

options.option_text: A downward-sloping straight line — constant Marginal Rate of Substitution
An L-shape at a right angle
A convex curve bowed toward the origin
A horizontal straight line — consumer is indifferent about both goods

explanation: Perfect substitutes: can replace each other at a constant rate. IC is a straight line with constant slope (constant MRS). Consumer is willing to give up exactly 1 unit of Good Y for 1 unit of Good X always. Consumer equilibrium: typically a corner solution (buy only the cheaper good). Normal convex ICs occur because MRS diminishes (goods are imperfect substitutes).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When both demand and supply increase simultaneously, what happens to equilibrium price?

options.option_text: Equilibrium price may rise, fall, or stay the same — it depends on the relative magnitudes of the shifts
Equilibrium price always rises — increased demand always dominates
Equilibrium price always falls — increased supply always reduces price
Equilibrium price is unchanged but equilibrium quantity always doubles

explanation: Simultaneous demand and supply increase: Equilibrium quantity always RISES (both shifts push quantity up). But price is ambiguous: if demand rises MORE than supply → price rises. If supply rises MORE than demand → price falls. If equal shifts → price unchanged. Equilibrium quantity rises regardless. This 'ambiguous' case is a frequent exam favourite.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Market equilibrium is disturbed when government imposes a Price Floor ABOVE the equilibrium price. The immediate result is:

options.option_text: A persistent SURPLUS — Qs > Qd at the artificially high price floor
A persistent SHORTAGE — Qd > Qs at the high floor price
No effect — price floors above equilibrium are non-binding
The equilibrium price rises to match the floor — market self-corrects

explanation: Price Floor (minimum price) set ABOVE equilibrium: producers want to supply more at the higher price (Qs ↑) but consumers demand less (Qd ↓) → SURPLUS. Example: Minimum Support Price (MSP) for wheat — government must buy surplus grain. Price Ceiling below equilibrium → SHORTAGE. Non-binding: floor below equilibrium or ceiling above equilibrium → no market effect.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Inferior goods differ from Giffen goods in that:

options.option_text: All Giffen goods are inferior, but not all inferior goods are Giffen — Giffen goods have an upward-sloping demand curve; many inferior goods still have downward-sloping demand curves
Inferior goods have negative income elasticity; Giffen goods have positive income elasticity
Giffen goods are luxury goods at high incomes; inferior goods are necessities
Inferior goods are consumed less as price rises; Giffen goods are consumed more as price rises

explanation: Both are inferior goods (Ey < 0). The difference: for most inferior goods, the substitution effect still dominates → demand still falls when price rises (downward-sloping curve). For Giffen goods, the negative income effect of a price rise is so STRONG that it overwhelms the substitution effect → demand rises when price rises (upward-sloping curve). Giffen = subset of inferior goods.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'Consumer's Surplus' was first introduced by:

options.option_text: Alfred Marshall — defined as the excess of total utility over total market price paid
Adam Smith — in 'Wealth of Nations' as surplus production value
John Hicks — as part of ordinal utility theory
Leon Walras — in the general equilibrium framework

explanation: Consumer Surplus (CS): introduced by Jules Dupuit (1844) but popularised by Alfred Marshall in 'Principles of Economics' (1890). Marshall defined CS as the amount a consumer is willing to pay MINUS what they actually pay. Graphically: area below demand curve and above market price (triangular area). Hicks later refined it using compensating variation and equivalent variation.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Demand for a commodity increases when the price of its COMPLEMENT rises. This statement is:

options.option_text: FALSE — when complement price rises, demand for the commodity FALLS
TRUE — complementary goods move in the same direction in demand
TRUE — higher complement prices boost demand through substitution
Neither — complements are independent goods with no cross-demand effect

explanation: Complementary goods (consumed together): Car & Petrol, Pen & Ink, Bread & Butter. When petrol price rises → fewer people drive → demand for cars FALLS. Cross elasticity for complements is NEGATIVE. Opposite to substitutes (where rising price of one increases demand for the other — positive cross elasticity).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following would DECREASE the supply of wheat in India?

options.option_text: A severe drought destroying standing crops
A rise in the market price of wheat
Improvement in harvesting technology reducing costs
A government subsidy on fertilisers used by farmers

explanation: Decrease in supply (leftward shift of supply curve): natural disasters (drought, floods), rise in input prices (fuel, fertiliser), unfavourable government policies (export restrictions). A rise in wheat price → movement ALONG the supply curve (extension), not a shift. Technology improvement and fertiliser subsidies → increase supply (rightward shift).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Marshallian demand analysis uses CARDINAL utility. Hicksian (Indifference Curve) demand analysis uses ORDINAL utility. The key difference is:

options.option_text: Cardinal utility assigns numerical values to satisfaction; Ordinal utility only ranks bundles without measuring magnitude
Cardinal utility applies only to luxury goods; Ordinal utility applies to necessities
Ordinal utility requires knowledge of exact income levels; Cardinal utility does not
Both approaches yield identical demand curves and are mathematically equivalent in all cases

explanation: Cardinal utility (Marshall): utility measured in utils (1, 2, 3...). Assumes: measurable utility, constant marginal utility of money, diminishing MU. Demand derived from MU = Price condition. Ordinal utility (Hicks-Allen): only requires ranking (A preferred to B, or indifferent). No measurement needed. Demand derived from IC tangency with budget line. Ordinal approach is theoretically stronger (weaker assumptions).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The budget line shows all combinations of two goods a consumer CAN buy given their income. The slope of the budget line equals:

options.option_text: −Px/Py (negative ratio of prices of the two goods)
The Marginal Rate of Substitution at consumer equilibrium
The consumer's income divided by the total utility obtained
The ratio of quantities of the two goods consumed

explanation: Budget line: Px·X + Py·Y = M. Rearranging: Y = M/Py − (Px/Py)·X. Slope = −Px/Py. The slope is the market rate of exchange — how many units of Y must be given up to buy one more unit of X at market prices. At consumer equilibrium (IC tangency): MRS = Px/Py. The slope tells us what the market requires; MRS tells us what the consumer is willing to trade.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Minimum Support Price (MSP) for agricultural products is an example of:

options.option_text: Price floor — a legally mandated minimum price above the market equilibrium
Price ceiling — a maximum price set by the government to protect consumers
Market equilibrium price — determined by demand and supply forces
Procurement price — set by farmers' cooperatives, not the government

explanation: MSP = Price Floor: government guarantees farmers receive at least the MSP — a minimum price. If market price falls below MSP, government (via FCI/NAFED) procures at MSP. This creates: (1) Assured income for farmers, (2) Potential surplus with government (excess supply at MSP). CCEA (Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs) sets MSP for 23 kharif and rabi crops.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Market demand curve is derived by:

options.option_text: Horizontal summation of all individual demand curves at each price level
Vertical summation of individual demands weighted by income share
Taking the average of individual demand curves across consumers
Multiplying individual demand by the number of consumers in the market

explanation: Market demand = HORIZONTAL summation: at each price, add up the quantities demanded by all individual consumers. If consumer A demands 10 units and consumer B demands 15 units at ₹100 → market demand = 25 units at ₹100. Horizontal summation (adding quantities at each price). Vertical summation is used for public goods (adding willingness to pay at each quantity level).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Price Consumption Curve (PCC) traces consumer equilibrium as the price of one good changes (income constant). When PCC is horizontal, it implies:

options.option_text: Demand for the good whose price changed is unit elastic (consumer spends same total amount)
Demand is perfectly inelastic — quantity does not change with price
Demand is perfectly elastic — quantity changes proportionately more than price
The consumer is in equilibrium regardless of price change

explanation: PCC and elasticity relationship: Horizontal PCC → Ed = 1 (unitary elastic, total expenditure on good X constant). Negative-sloped PCC (PCC falling to right) → Ed > 1 (elastic, expenditure on X rises as price falls). Positive-sloped PCC (PCC rising to right) → Ed < 1 (inelastic, expenditure on X falls as price falls). An advanced but frequently tested connection.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When consumers expect the price of a good to RISE in the future, their current demand will:

options.option_text: Increase NOW — consumers buy more today to avoid higher future prices (speculative demand)
Decrease NOW — consumers wait to see if expectations materialise first
Remain unchanged — future expectations don't affect current demand
Become perfectly inelastic until the price rise occurs

explanation: Future price expectations shift current demand. If consumers expect price to rise → buy more NOW (before price rises) → current demand increases (rightward shift). This explains hoarding behaviour during inflationary expectations, commodity price spikes, and speculative bubbles. Conversely, expectation of price FALL → buy less now (wait) → demand decreases.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Demand function: Qd = 100 − 2P. Supply function: Qs = 20 + 3P. Equilibrium price and quantity are:
explanation: Equilibrium: Qd = Qs. 100 − 2P = 20 + 3P. 100 − 20 = 3P + 2P. 80 = 5P. P = 16. Q = 100 − 2(16) = 100 − 32 = 68. Verify with supply: Q = 20 + 3(16) = 20 + 48 = 68 ✓. Short trick: collect P terms on right, constants on left → solve for P, then substitute back.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The supply of land is said to be perfectly inelastic because:

options.option_text: The total quantity of land in existence cannot be increased regardless of how high the price rises
Land is a free good available to everyone and has no market price
The government controls all land and sets supply by policy
Land depreciates rapidly, reducing effective supply each year

explanation: Classical economics: supply of land = perfectly inelastic (PES = 0). Natural resource in fixed supply — no matter how high the rent, you cannot produce more land. Graphically: vertical supply curve. Rent = pure economic surplus (transfer earnings = 0 for land in classical view). However, supply of 'usable' or 'developed' land can change (land reclamation, construction).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Revealed Preference Theory (Paul Samuelson, 1938) derives demand curves from:

options.option_text: Actual observed purchasing behaviour — if a consumer buys bundle A when B is also affordable, A is 'revealed preferred' to B
Consumer surveys about willingness to pay at various prices
Cardinal utility functions derived from experimental economics
Indifference curves drawn by consumers ranking hypothetical bundles

explanation: Revealed Preference (Samuelson, 1938): avoids unobservable utility concepts entirely. Uses ACTUAL choices. Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP): if A is chosen when B is affordable, then B is never chosen when A is affordable (consistency). Derives the downward-sloping demand curve from observable market behaviour without assuming utility maximisation explicitly.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Labour = 5 workers; Total Product = 100 units. Average Product = ? When a 6th worker is added, TP rises to 108. Marginal Product of the 6th worker = ?

options.option_text: AP = 20 units per worker; MP of 6th worker = 8 units
AP = 25; MP = 8

explanation: AP = TP/L = 100/5 = 20 units per worker. MP of 6th worker = TP(6) − TP(5) = 108 − 100 = 8 units. Note: AP at 6 workers = 108/6 = 18. Since MP (8) < AP (18 or 20), AP is falling — consistent with stage II of variable proportions where AP is declining.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: At output Q=10: AVC = ₹30; TFC = ₹200. A firm produces Q=11 units. If MC of the 11th unit = ₹35, what is ATC at Q=11?

options.option_text: ₹35 (ATC equals MC at Q=11)
₹50 (rounded estimate)

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following correctly describes an ISOQUANT?

options.option_text: A curve showing all combinations of Labour and Capital that produce the SAME level of output
A curve showing all combinations of two goods a consumer can afford given their income
A curve showing the minimum cost of producing each level of output
A curve showing the total output achievable from a single variable input

explanation: Isoquant (Equal Product Curve): production theory equivalent of an Indifference Curve. Shows all (L, K) combinations giving the same output level Q. Properties: Downward-sloping (MRTS is positive), Convex to origin (MRTS diminishes), Higher isoquant = more output, Two isoquants don't intersect. MRTS_{LK} = dK/dL = MP_L/MP_K. Isocost = cost constraint (analogous to budget line). Producer equilibrium: isoquant tangent to isocost.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Explicit Costs include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.option_text: Opportunity cost of the owner's own capital invested in the business
Wages paid to hired labour
Rent paid for factory premises
Raw material purchases from suppliers

explanation: Explicit Costs: actual cash payments to external factors — wages, rent, material costs, interest on borrowed funds. Implicit Costs: opportunity cost of self-owned/self-employed resources — interest forgone on own capital, salary of owner, rent of own building used in business. Economic Cost = Explicit + Implicit. Accounting Profit = Revenue − Explicit. Economic Profit = Revenue − (Explicit + Implicit).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS) between Labour and Capital measures:

options.option_text: How much Capital can be reduced when one more unit of Labour is added while keeping output constant (= MP_L / MP_K)
The rate at which output changes when labour is substituted for capital
The relative wage rate of labour vs the rental cost of capital
The efficiency ratio between labour productivity and capital productivity

explanation: MRTS_{LK} = −dK/dL (holding output constant) = MP_L / MP_K. Diminishing MRTS: as L increases and K decreases along an isoquant, each additional worker adds less to output (MP_L falls) and each unit of K forgone becomes more valuable (MP_K rises). Hence MRTS diminishes → isoquant is convex. Special cases: Perfect substitutes → constant MRTS (straight isoquant); Perfect complements → MRTS undefined (L-shaped isoquant).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A firm produces 100 units with TC = ₹10,000. At zero output, TC = ₹2,000. Calculate AFC and AVC at Q = 100.

options.option_text: AFC = ₹80; AVC = ₹20

explanation: At Q=0, TC = TFC = ₹2,000 (variable costs = 0 when nothing produced). At Q=100, TC = ₹10,000. TVC at Q=100 = TC − TFC = 10,000 − 2,000 = ₹8,000. AFC = TFC/Q = 2,000/100 = ₹20. AVC = TVC/Q = 8,000/100 = ₹80. ATC = TC/Q = 10,000/100 = ₹100. Check: AFC + AVC = 20 + 80 = 100 = ATC ✓.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: External Economies of Scale arise when:

options.option_text: Growth of the entire INDUSTRY benefits all firms — skilled labour pool, specialised suppliers, infrastructure, knowledge spillovers
A single firm grows large enough to exploit specialisation and technical advantages
A firm exports goods and benefits from foreign exchange earnings
An economy achieves economies in government sector through privatisation

explanation: External Economies of Scale: benefits that accrue to ALL firms in an industry as the INDUSTRY grows. Examples: Silicon Valley (tech cluster — shared talent pool, VC ecosystem); Tiruppur textile cluster (shared dyeing units, transport infrastructure); industrial districts. All firms benefit whether they themselves are large or small. Contrast: Internal Economies = specific to the individual firm's growth.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A firm's total cost function is TC = 500 + 2Q + 0.5Q². MC = ?

options.option_text: MC = 2 + Q (differentiating TC with respect to Q)
MC = 2 (constant — the coefficient of Q)
MC = Q (ignoring the constant coefficient)
MC = 2Q + 0.5Q² (the variable cost portion only)

explanation: TC = 500 + 2Q + 0.5Q². MC = dTC/dQ = 0 + 2 + 0.5 × 2Q = 2 + Q. TFC = 500 (constant when Q=0). TVC = 2Q + 0.5Q². At Q=10: MC = 2 + 10 = ₹12. AVC = TVC/Q = (2Q + 0.5Q²)/Q = 2 + 0.5Q = 2 + 5 = ₹7 at Q=10. MC > AVC → AVC is rising. ATC = 500/10 + 7 = 50 + 7 = ₹57 at Q=10.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Diseconomies of Scale in the long run are primarily caused by:

options.option_text: Managerial diseconomies — coordination becomes harder as the firm grows; bureaucracy, communication breakdown, loss of control
Fixed costs becoming variable as the firm expands
Diminishing returns to variable factors in the short run
Government regulations that restrict firm size beyond a threshold

explanation: Diseconomies of Scale (LRAC rising): (1) Managerial diseconomies: span of control too wide, bureaucracy slows decisions, coordination costs rise. (2) Labour diseconomies: workers feel alienated in large firms, productivity falls. (3) Marketing diseconomies: serving diverse distant markets raises distribution costs. (4) Financial diseconomies: very large debt increases risk premium. Note: Diminishing returns = SHORT-RUN concept (not scale).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If a production function exhibits Constant Returns to Scale (CRS), doubling all inputs:

options.option_text: Exactly doubles output — no advantage or disadvantage from size
More than doubles output — firm benefits from expansion
Less than doubles output — firm is too large for its resources
Has no predictable effect on output — CRS is a special case that rarely exists

explanation: CRS (homogeneous of degree 1): f(λL, λK) = λ × f(L,K). If λ=2, output exactly doubles. LRAC is constant under CRS (no economies or diseconomies of scale). Many industries exhibit CRS over a wide range of output. Cobb-Douglas Q = AL^α × K^β: CRS when α+β=1; IRS when α+β>1; DRS when α+β<1.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under Perfect Competition, each firm's demand curve is horizontal (perfectly elastic) because:

options.option_text: Each firm is a price taker — it can sell any quantity at the ruling market price but cannot influence the price
The firm produces a differentiated product that has no substitutes
Government regulations fix the price at a level acceptable to all firms
All consumers are identical and willing to pay the same price only

explanation: Perfect Competition: many tiny firms, homogeneous product → each firm is a price TAKER. The firm's output is such a tiny fraction of market supply that changing it has zero effect on market price. Hence the firm faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve at the ruling market price. AR = MR = P = Demand curve. Slope of market demand curve is downward; but individual firm's demand is horizontal.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In a monopoly, if AR = 100 − 2Q (demand curve), then MR = ?

options.option_text: MR = 100 − 4Q (MR has twice the slope of the linear demand curve)
MR = 100 − 2Q (same as AR)
MR = 50 − Q (half the demand curve)
MR = 100 − Q (same intercept, half the slope)

explanation: For a linear inverse demand P = a − bQ: MR = a − 2bQ. MR has the same y-intercept as AR but TWICE the slope. Here AR = P = 100 − 2Q, so MR = 100 − 2(2)Q = 100 − 4Q. MR = 0 when Q = 25 (elastic portion ends). MR < 0 for Q > 25 (inelastic portion). Monopolist NEVER operates in the inelastic portion (MR < 0 → increasing price raises TR).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Oligopoly is best characterised by:

options.option_text: Mutual interdependence — each firm's pricing/output decision considers rivals' expected reactions
Complete independence — firms make decisions without considering competitor behaviour
Perfect collusion — all firms coordinate to maximise joint profit at all times
Price-taking behaviour — each firm accepts the industry price as given

explanation: Oligopoly's distinguishing feature: strategic interdependence. Since few firms dominate, each must consider how rivals will react to its price/output changes. This is why game theory (Nash Equilibrium, Prisoner's Dilemma) is used to analyse oligopoly. Models: Cournot (quantity competition), Bertrand (price competition), Kinked Demand (Sweezy), and Cartel (collusive).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Prisoner's Dilemma in oligopoly shows that:

options.option_text: Individually rational behaviour (cheat on cartel) leads to collectively worse outcomes (competitive pricing with lower profits for all)
Cooperation always leads to lower profits than competition in oligopoly markets
Firms always end up colluding because they can communicate easily
Government intervention is always needed to prevent monopoly pricing in oligopoly

explanation: Prisoner's Dilemma: Each oligopolist has an incentive to defect from a cartel (undercut others to gain sales). But if ALL defect → competitive equilibrium → all earn lower profits than cartel outcome. Nash Equilibrium = both defect (dominant strategy). Solution in repeated games: cooperation can be sustained if firms interact repeatedly (tit-for-tat strategy, grim trigger). Real-world cartels are unstable for this reason.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Contestable Market Theory (Baumol, 1982) suggests that even a monopoly will price competitively if:

options.option_text: Entry and exit are FREE (no sunk costs) — the threat of potential competition disciplines the incumbent's pricing
The government regulates the monopoly's pricing through a price commission
The monopoly faces a perfectly elastic demand curve at the competitive price
The number of actual competitors is at least three in the market

explanation: Contestable Markets (Baumol-Panzar-Willig): if there are no sunk costs (all costs recoverable on exit), potential entrants can 'hit and run' — enter when incumbent earns supernormal profit, undercut, take profit, exit before incumbent responds. Threat of entry alone disciplines pricing → incumbent prices at AC level. Policy implication: competition policy should focus on reducing sunk costs/barriers, not number of firms.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The VALUE-ADDED method of calculating GDP means:

options.option_text: Summing Gross Value Added (GVA) by each producing unit = output minus intermediate consumption, then adding product taxes and subtracting subsidies
Adding up all final sales values in the economy to avoid double counting
Summing factor incomes (wages, rent, interest, profit) earned in production
Valuing the economy's output at import prices to account for international competition

explanation: Value Added method: GVA = Output − Intermediate Consumption (raw materials, energy, services bought from other firms). Summing all GVAs avoids double-counting (wheat farmer's output, flour miller's output would both count wheat twice if using gross output). GDP(MP) = Sum of all GVAs + Product Taxes − Product Subsidies. India's new national accounts (2015) use GVA at basic prices as the primary aggregate.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru adopted a development strategy centred on:

options.option_text: Nehru-Mahalanobis model — emphasis on heavy industry and public sector in a mixed economy with Five-Year Plans
Export-led growth through free trade and FDI liberalisation from the start
Agriculture-first strategy with land reforms and rural development as the primary focus
Monetarist approach with tight fiscal discipline and free markets

explanation: Nehru-Mahalanobis model (1956, 2nd Five-Year Plan): P.C. Mahalanobis designed a two-sector model prioritising capital goods (heavy industry — steel, cement, power) over consumer goods. Rationale: build capital goods sector → produce more machines → produce more consumer goods later. Mixed economy: large PSUs in 'commanding heights' + private sector. Soviet-influenced central planning.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Hindu Rate of Growth' refers to:

options.option_text: The low GDP growth rate of approximately 3.5% per year that India achieved during 1950-1980 — a term coined by economist Raj Krishna
The growth rate prescribed by Hindu philosophers for sustainable development
The GDP growth rate for states with majority Hindu population
A religious concept linking economic growth to cultural values

explanation: Hindu Rate of Growth (Raj Krishna, economist): India's historically low and steady ~3.5% GDP growth rate pre-1980. Post-1991 reforms, India's growth accelerated to 6-8% — breaking out of the 'Hindu rate.' The term was somewhat pejorative, implying Indian economy was inherently slow — later scholars debated the causation (not Hinduism but policy mix of high protection, low private investment, bureaucratic controls).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Public Distribution System (PDS) in India is managed through:

options.option_text: FCI (Food Corporation of India) for procurement and storage; state governments manage fair price shops for last-mile distribution
Directly by Ministry of Agriculture through district collectors only
NABARD for rural areas and SBI for urban distribution centres
Private retail chains that are contracted by the government annually

explanation: PDS: FCI (established 1965) procures wheat and rice at MSP, stores in warehouses. Central government → State governments → District → Block → Fair Price Shops (ration shops). National Food Security Act 2013: legal entitlement to subsidised food grains (5 kg/person/month for 75% rural, 50% urban population). One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) allows portability across states.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1000 notes was announced by PM Modi on:

options.option_text: 8 November 2016 — with immediate effect; old notes ceased to be legal tender at midnight
1 April 2016 — start of financial year for clean transition
15 August 2016 — Independence Day announcement
1 January 2017 — new year initiative to curb black money

explanation: Demonetisation: 8 November 2016 (Note Bandi). ₹500 and ₹1000 notes (86% of currency in circulation) demonetised. New ₹500 and ₹2000 notes introduced. Objectives: curb black money, counterfeit notes, terrorism financing, promote digital payments. Controversial economic impact: short-term contraction in informal economy; GDP slipped from ~7.5% to ~6.5% in FY 2016-17.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Make in India' initiative was launched in:

options.option_text: September 2014 — to promote India as a global manufacturing hub and attract FDI
January 2015 — along with NITI Aayog on Republic Day
July 2017 — coinciding with GST launch to boost manufacturing
August 2013 — by PM Manmohan Singh for the manufacturing sector

explanation: Make in India: launched 25 September 2014 by PM Modi. Focus: 25 priority sectors (automobiles, aviation, defence, pharmaceuticals, IT, textiles). Goals: increase manufacturing's share in GDP to 25% (from ~16%), create 100 million new manufacturing jobs by 2022. Later complemented by: Aatmanirbhar Bharat, PLI (Production Linked Incentive) schemes.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The formula GDP(MP) = C + I + G + (X − M) is the EXPENDITURE method. In this, 'I' represents:

options.option_text: Gross Domestic Investment = GFCF + Change in Inventories (includes both fixed investment and stock building)
Income earned by all residents of the country
Imports only — to adjust for goods produced abroad
Interest payments on government debt included in GDP measurement

explanation: Expenditure approach: C = Private Final Consumption Expenditure. I = Gross Domestic Investment = GFCF (Gross Fixed Capital Formation: machinery, equipment, buildings) + ΔInventories (change in stock). G = Government Final Consumption Expenditure (not transfer payments). X = Exports. M = Imports. (X−M) = Net Exports. Sum = GDP at Market Prices.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: According to the Kuznets curve hypothesis, as per capita income rises in a developing country, income inequality:

options.option_text: First INCREASES then DECREASES — forming an inverted U-shape on a graph of inequality vs income
Continuously decreases as more people benefit from economic growth
Continuously increases as capital owners capture disproportionate gains
Remains constant — income distribution is unaffected by economic growth

explanation: Kuznets Curve (Simon Kuznets, 1955): As countries industrialise, workers shift from low-productivity agriculture to high-productivity industry. Initially: urban-rural gap and wage inequality RISE (inverted U going up). Later: more workers in formal sector, stronger institutions, redistribution → inequality FALLS. Environmental Kuznets Curve: similar inverted U for pollution vs income. Debated empirically — some countries don't follow this pattern.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is related to:

options.option_text: Crop insurance for farmers — providing financial support against crop losses due to natural calamities, pests, or diseases
Rural housing scheme for Below Poverty Line farmers
Irrigation infrastructure building at village level
Free seed distribution scheme for small and marginal farmers

explanation: PMFBY (launched 2016): replaced existing NAIS and MNAIS schemes. Key features: uniform premium for farmers (2% for kharif, 1.5% for rabi, 5% for commercial/horticultural crops) — government pays the balance to insurance companies. Technology: Crop cutting experiments for yield assessment, remote sensing/drones for loss assessment. Implemented by selected insurance companies including public sector AIC (Agriculture Insurance Company).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's Economic Survey is released:

options.option_text: A day before the Union Budget — by the Ministry of Finance, provides comprehensive economic review
By the RBI annually in April — as part of monetary policy statement
By NITI Aayog every 3 years — to coincide with action plan reviews
By CAG after completing audit of the Annual Financial Statement

explanation: Economic Survey: prepared by Ministry of Finance (Chief Economic Adviser's office). Released a day before the Union Budget. Reviews economic performance of the year, analyses key sectors, provides economic data and policy recommendations. Not a statutory document — but highly influential and widely cited.
