Chief Economic Adviser (CEA) is the principal author (Arvind Subramanian, K.V. Subramanian, V. Anantha Nageswaran held this role).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which sector does NOT contribute to GDP calculation in India?

options.option_text: Services of housewives doing domestic work (unpaid, non-market activities are excluded)
Financial services provided by banks and insurance companies
Imputed rent of owner-occupied houses (even without actual payment)
Services of government employees (included at cost of employment)

explanation: GDP excludes non-market activities: housewives' domestic services, subsistence farming (partially), volunteer work. Included (even without market transaction): Imputed rent of owner-occupied houses (treated as if owner pays rent to self), government services (at cost), informal sector (estimated). Exclusion of domestic work from GDP is a major feminist criticism of national income accounting.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Atal Pension Yojana (APY) targets:

options.option_text: Unorganised sector workers — provides a guaranteed minimum pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 per month on retirement at age 60
Government employees already covered under NPS
Senior citizens above 65 years for immediate pension support
Widows and physically challenged individuals only

explanation: APY (launched June 2015, replaced Swavalamban): targets unorganised sector workers (aged 18-40). Monthly pension = ₹1,000/₹2,000/₹3,000/₹4,000/₹5,000 based on contribution. Administered by PFRDA (Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority). Government co-contributes 50% of subscriber's contribution (upto ₹1,000/year) for 5 years (2015-20). Account through banks.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'Privatisation' in India specifically refers to:

options.option_text: Strategic disinvestment — transfer of management control AND majority equity of a PSU to a private buyer
Any sale of government shares in a PSU, including minority stake sale through stock exchange
Allowing private sector to compete in areas previously monopolised by government
Converting PSUs into companies listed on the stock exchange

explanation: Distinctions in public sector reform: Disinvestment = any sale of government equity (minority or majority). Privatisation (Narrow definition) = Strategic Disinvestment: government sells majority stake + transfers management control. Examples: Air India (sold to Tata Group, 2022), HPCL (stake sold to ONGC), BPCL (in process). Pure equity dilution without management change = disinvestment, not privatisation.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Washington Consensus' (John Williamson, 1989) prescriptions for developing countries included:

options.option_text: Fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, and securing property rights — standard IMF/World Bank reform agenda
Central planning, state ownership, and import substitution industrialisation
Currency devaluation, high tariffs, and capital controls to protect domestic industry
Universal basic income and increased government spending on welfare

explanation: Washington Consensus (Williamson, 1989): 10 policy reforms believed necessary for Latin American and developing countries: (1) Fiscal discipline, (2) Reordering public expenditure priorities, (3) Tax reform, (4) Interest rate liberalisation, (5) Competitive exchange rate, (6) Trade liberalisation, (7) FDI liberalisation, (8) Privatisation, (9) Deregulation, (10) Property rights. India's 1991 reforms partly followed this model, though with selective adoption.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Competition Commission of India (CCI) was established under the Competition Act 2002 with jurisdiction to investigate:

options.option_text: Anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant position, and regulation of combinations (mergers/acquisitions)
Price gouging by consumers and unfair trade practices in retail
Labour market cartelisation and wage fixing by employers
Only foreign companies entering India through FDI for monopolistic practices

explanation: CCI (became fully operational 2009): investigates three domains. (1) Section 3 — Anti-competitive agreements (price fixing, market sharing, bid rigging) — per se illegal. (2) Section 4 — Abuse of dominant position (predatory pricing, tying, refusal to deal). (3) Sections 5-6 — Combinations (mergers above threshold requiring CCI approval). CCI replaced the MRTP Commission (Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Commission).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme provides incentives based on:

options.option_text: Incremental sales from units manufactured in India — a fixed % of additional turnover above the base year threshold
Number of workers employed in the manufacturing unit
Capital investment made in new plant and machinery
Export earnings above a specified minimum threshold

explanation: PLI Scheme (launched 2020): incentive = % of incremental sales (sales above base year) from eligible domestic manufacturing. Sectors include mobile phones, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, textiles, automobiles, specialty steel, solar PV modules, etc. Disbursed over 4-6 years. Aims to attract large investments, create economies of scale, and boost exports. ₹1.97 lakh crore committed across 14 sectors.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The IRDAI (Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India) was set up under:

options.option_text: IRDA Act 1999 — regulates insurance sector following LIC and GIC Act amendments
Companies Act 2013 — insurance companies are regulated as companies
RBI Act 1934 — insurance was initially under RBI's domain
SEBI Act 1992 — insurance products were treated as securities

explanation: IRDAI (formerly IRDA): established 1999 under IRDA Act 1999 as statutory body. Headquartered in Hyderabad. Regulates: Life, General, and Health insurance companies. Functions: licence insurers, set product guidelines, protect policyholders, develop the industry. Foreign direct investment in insurance: progressively increased from 26% to 74% (2021). Malhotra Committee (1994) recommended insurance sector reforms.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Currency Chest system in India means:

options.option_text: Branches of banks authorised to hold RBI currency — withdrawals from and deposits to currency chests are treated as transactions with RBI directly
Special vaults in RBI's own offices where all currency notes are stored before distribution
International currency reserves held by RBI in foreign central banks
ATM machines designated for high-value currency note distribution

explanation: Currency Chests: designated branches of commercial banks, cooperative banks, and government treasuries authorised to hold RBI currency. When a branch withdraws from its chest, it's treated as drawing from RBI (reduces chest holding, adds to bank's vault cash — but this is liability of bank to RBI). Purpose: efficient distribution of currency to remote areas without needing RBI branches everywhere. Over 4,000 currency chests across India.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Sterilisation in monetary policy refers to:

options.option_text: RBI offsetting the monetary impact of forex interventions — buying dollars increases rupee supply; RBI then sells G-secs (OMO) to absorb excess rupees
RBI removing counterfeit notes from circulation to protect the currency system
Government sterilising the fiscal deficit impact through seigniorage
Bank neutralising interest rate changes through offsetting lending decisions

explanation: Sterilisation: When RBI buys foreign currency to prevent rupee appreciation (intervenes in forex market), rupee supply increases (inflationary pressure). To sterilise: RBI simultaneously sells government securities (OMO) → absorbs excess rupees → offsets monetary expansion. Imperfect sterilisation is common (full sterilisation raises domestic interest rates, attracting more capital inflow — the 'Impossible Trinity').

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) of RBI consists of:

options.option_text: Repo (RBI lends to banks) and SDF/Reverse Repo (RBI borrows from banks) — used daily for short-term liquidity management
CRR and SLR maintained by banks — adjusted to manage system liquidity
Currency swap arrangements with foreign central banks for dollar liquidity
MSF and Bank Rate for emergency borrowing by distressed banks

explanation: LAF (introduced 2000): RBI's primary tool for day-to-day money market operations. Consists of: (1) Repo (injection): banks borrow from RBI by selling securities with buyback — Repo Rate = ceiling of LAF corridor. (2) SDF (absorption): banks park excess funds with RBI without collateral — SDF Rate = floor of LAF corridor (since April 2022, replaced Reverse Repo). MSF = emergency window above Repo Rate (ceiling + 25 bps).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's foreign exchange reserves are primarily managed by:

options.option_text: RBI — holds and manages forex reserves; composition: foreign currency assets, gold, SDRs, reserve tranche with IMF
Ministry of Finance — as part of the Union Budget's revenue receipts
SEBI — since forex reserves include portfolio investments by FIIs
Export-Import Bank of India — as primary custodian of trade-related forex

explanation: Forex Reserves (managed by RBI): Components: (1) Foreign Currency Assets (FCA — largest, held in US treasuries, bonds, gold) ~₹95% of reserves. (2) Gold (~5%). (3) SDRs (Special Drawing Rights from IMF). (4) Reserve Tranche with IMF. India's forex reserves: ~$640 billion (2024) — adequate for >10 months of imports (comfort level = 3 months). RBI invests conservatively in safe, liquid assets.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Impossible Trinity' (Mundell-Fleming Trilemma) states that a country CANNOT simultaneously have:

options.option_text: Fixed exchange rate + Free capital mobility + Independent monetary policy — only two of the three are simultaneously achievable
Low inflation + Low unemployment + High growth — macroeconomic trilemma
Free trade + Capital controls + Fixed exchange rates — Bretton Woods impossibility
Fiscal discipline + Growth + Equality — the policy trilemma

explanation: Impossible Trinity (Robert Mundell): A country must choose 2 of 3: (1) Fixed Exchange Rate + Free Capital → No monetary policy (Eurozone). (2) Fixed Exchange Rate + Monetary Policy → Capital Controls (China historically). (3) Free Capital + Monetary Policy → Floating Exchange Rate (India, USA). India has managed float + independent monetary policy + partial capital account convertibility — a pragmatic compromise.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Co-operative banks in India are regulated by:

options.option_text: Dual regulation: RBI (banking functions/prudential norms) + State Registrars of Co-operative Societies (incorporation/management)
Only RBI — RBI has sole jurisdiction over all banks regardless of legal form
Only State governments — cooperative banks are a State subject under the Constitution
NABARD — all rural cooperative banks are exclusively under NABARD jurisdiction

explanation: Cooperative banks: Dual regulation. RBI regulates: capital adequacy, income recognition, NPA norms, audit, liquidity (banking functions). State Cooperative Registrar regulates: incorporation, management, elections, supersession, liquidation (under Cooperative Societies Acts). Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs): also under RBI for monetary aspects. The 2020-21 reform (Banking Regulation Act amendment) gave RBI more supervisory powers over UCBs to prevent PMC Bank-type crises.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Micro Finance Institutions (MFIs) primarily serve:

options.option_text: Low-income borrowers (especially women in rural areas) who lack access to formal banking — small loans without collateral for livelihood activities
Small and Medium Enterprises for working capital requirements
Agricultural cooperatives for crop loan refinancing
State governments for social sector spending in rural areas

explanation: MFIs: provide microloans (₹10,000-₹3,00,000 per RBI definition) to low-income borrowers without traditional collateral requirements. Grameen Bank model (Muhammad Yunus, Bangladesh — Nobel 2006): group lending where social pressure ensures repayment. In India: NBFC-MFIs regulated by RBI under NBFC Master Directions. SHG-bank linkage model (promoted by NABARD): self-help groups get bank loans.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The MUDRA (Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency) Bank provides loans under three categories. The highest category 'Tarun' offers loans up to:

options.option_text: ₹10 lakh (Shishu: up to ₹50,000; Kishore: ₹50,001 to ₹5 lakh; Tarun: ₹5,00,001 to ₹10 lakh)
₹5 lakh (Kishore category maximum)
₹25 lakh (extended limit for service sector)
₹50 lakh (MSME-level support through Tarun Plus)

explanation: MUDRA (launched 2015, under SIDBI): Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) — loans to non-corporate, non-farm micro and small enterprises. Three tiers: Shishu (≤₹50,000), Kishore (₹50,001-₹5 lakh), Tarun (₹5,00,001-₹10 lakh). Loans given through banks, NBFCs, MFIs. No collateral required. Target: informal sector, first-generation entrepreneurs. Over ₹25 lakh crore disbursed since launch.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'off-budget borrowings' or 'extra-budgetary resources' (EBR) in India refers to:

options.option_text: Borrowings by government-controlled entities (FCI, NHAI) guaranteed by government but not shown in the fiscal deficit calculation
Black market transactions that circumvent budget rules
IMF loans to India not reflected in the Annual Financial Statement
Contingency Fund withdrawals by the President without Parliamentary approval

explanation: Extra-Budgetary Resources (EBR): Government uses entities like FCI, NHAI, NRIDA to borrow from market for government schemes (food subsidy, road building). These borrowings are not part of the Union Budget but government bears the liability. Critics: inflates fiscal space artificially — true fiscal deficit is higher than reported. NK Singh Committee recommended including EBR in fiscal deficit calculation for transparency.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Capital Receipts of the government include:

options.option_text: Market borrowings (dated securities, T-bills), disinvestment proceeds, and loan recoveries from States
Income tax, corporate tax, and customs duties collected during the year
Dividends from PSUs and interest received from loans to States
Grants-in-aid received from foreign governments and international institutions

explanation: Capital Receipts: create liabilities (borrowings: market loans, T-bills, MSS, external loans) or reduce assets (disinvestment, recovery of loans given to States). They don't flow through P&L (not income). Revenue Receipts: tax + non-tax revenue (recurring income). Grants-in-aid received from foreign governments → Revenue Receipts (non-tax). Dividend from PSUs → Non-tax Revenue Receipt.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Laffer Curve illustrates that:

options.option_text: Tax revenue is zero at both 0% and 100% tax rate — there is an optimal tax rate between these extremes that maximises revenue
Higher tax rates always reduce economic activity proportionally
Progressive taxation always maximises revenue and equality simultaneously
Tax compliance improves linearly as tax rates decrease

explanation: Laffer Curve (Arthur Laffer, 1974): Tax Revenue plotted against Tax Rate forms an inverted U. At 0% rate: zero revenue. At 100% rate: zero revenue (no incentive to work/earn — all earned is taken). Optimal rate somewhere between 0-100% maximises revenue. Policy implication: if rate is ABOVE the optimal, CUTTING taxes can INCREASE revenue (supply-side economics, Reaganomics). Empirically disputed — optimal rate is unknown and context-dependent.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Fiscal Policy differs from Monetary Policy in that Fiscal Policy primarily works through:

options.option_text: Government taxation and spending decisions — demand management via the multiplier effect
Interest rate adjustments and money supply changes by the Central Bank
Exchange rate management and foreign exchange reserve deployment
Banking sector regulation and credit quality standards

explanation: Fiscal Policy: government budget decisions (taxes + spending). Tools: G (spending), T (taxes), transfer payments. Channel: aggregate demand (C+I+G+(X-M)). Multiplier amplifies impact. Monetary Policy: Central Bank's control of money supply and interest rates. Tools: Repo, CRR, SLR, OMO. Channel: investment and consumption via cost of credit. In India: Ministry of Finance = fiscal; RBI = monetary.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Twin Deficit Problem' refers to:

options.option_text: Simultaneous Fiscal Deficit (government spends more than it earns) and Current Account Deficit (imports exceed exports + invisibles)
Deficit in both plan and non-plan expenditure simultaneously
Trade deficit plus services deficit appearing together
Revenue deficit and fiscal deficit occurring in the same year

explanation: Twin Deficit Hypothesis: Fiscal Deficit → government borrows more → crowds out private savings → insufficient domestic savings to fund investment → economy borrows from abroad → CAD. FD and CAD often move together (not always — depends on private saving rates). India's 2012-13 CAD peaked at ~4.8% of GDP coinciding with fiscal pressures. Policy: control FD to help CAD reduction.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The GST returns filing system in India uses which platform for compliance?

options.option_text: GSTN (GST Network) portal — gst.gov.in — a non-profit, non-government private limited company providing IT backbone for GST
NSDL e-Governance portal — same platform as income tax filing
MCA21 portal — since GST is a company compliance requirement
RBI's e-Kuber platform — for all tax-related financial transactions

explanation: GSTN (GST Network): Not-for-profit, Section 8 company with government stake. Provides: registration, return filing (GSTR-1, 3B, annual return), e-invoice generation, e-way bill. GST Council approved the IT infrastructure. GST implementation involved massive digitisation — real-time invoice matching (Invoice Matching System) to detect bogus ITC claims. One of the largest tax IT systems globally.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is NOT a Revenue Expenditure of the Central Government?

options.option_text: Building a new national highway — creates capital asset (capital expenditure)
Paying salaries to government employees
Interest payments on government borrowings
Providing subsidies on fertilisers and food

explanation: Revenue Expenditure: does not create assets or reduce liabilities. Examples: salaries, pensions, interest payments, subsidies, O&M costs, defence revenue spending. Capital Expenditure: creates assets (roads, bridges, defence equipment, buildings) or reduces liabilities (loan repayments). New highway = capital expenditure (creates long-term infrastructure asset). Interest payments = revenue expenditure (pays for past borrowings, creates no new asset).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The National e-Governance Service Delivery Assessment (NeSDA) is conducted by:

options.option_text: Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) — ranks States and UTs on digital service delivery
TRAI — as part of digital connectivity assessment across states
NASSCOM — industry body assessing e-governance implementation
RBI — evaluating states on digital payment adoption metrics

explanation: NeSDA: conducted by MeitY biennially. Assesses States/UTs on e-governance service delivery across 5 sectors (finance, labour, social welfare, transport, agriculture) and local governance. 2021 report: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh among top performers. Encourages healthy competition and best practice adoption across states. Separate from digital literacy assessments.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GSTN (GST Network) is classified as a:

options.option_text: Non-profit Section 8 company — government holds 50%, rest with banks and financial institutions
Government department under Ministry of Finance
RBI subsidiary providing payment infrastructure
Public Sector Undertaking under Ministry of Electronics

explanation: GSTN: Section 8 (not-for-profit) private limited company incorporated 28 March 2013. Ownership: Central Government 24.5%, State governments collectively 24.5%, private financial institutions (HDFC, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, NSE Strategic Investments, LIC Housing Finance) 51%. Though private in structure, government controls majority through collective government stake. Provides IT infrastructure for all GST compliance.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: DigiLocker was launched as part of which programme?

options.option_text: Digital India Programme (2015) — provides cloud storage for citizens' official documents
NeGP (National e-Governance Plan, 2006) — predecessor initiative
JAM Trinity implementation by RBI for financial inclusion
Startup India Programme for storing business registrations

explanation: DigiLocker: launched July 2015 under Digital India. Provides cloud-based personal document storage linked to Aadhaar. Allows citizens to store/access verified digital documents (DL, RC, Aadhaar, degree certificates, insurance policies). Issued documents (from government databases) are legally equivalent to physical originals (IT Act + Gazette notification). Over 15 crore registered users. Eliminates need to carry physical documents.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The National Informatics Centre (NIC) is under which ministry and its primary role is:

options.option_text: MeitY — NIC provides IT infrastructure, network, and software solutions to central and state government agencies
Ministry of Science and Technology — NIC conducts scientific computing research
Ministry of Finance — NIC manages financial transaction systems for government
Ministry of Home Affairs — NIC runs security and surveillance infrastructure

explanation: NIC (National Informatics Centre): established 1976, under MeitY. Provides: NICNET (government's nationwide network), government websites (nic.in domains), data centre services, custom software for ministries (e-Courts, e-Office, eProcurement, CPGRAMS), GeM platform, DigiLocker backend. NIC is the primary IT arm of the Indian government — behind most government digital services.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The balance as per Pass Book is ₹38,000 (credit). Cheques deposited but not yet cleared by bank = ₹7,000. Bank charges not recorded in Cash Book = ₹400. What is the Cash Book balance?

options.option_text: ₹31,400 (PB 38,000 − deposits in transit 7,000 + bank charges 400 = 31,400)

explanation: Starting from PB balance to find CB balance: CB = PB − Deposits in transit + Bank charges not in CB. = 38,000 − 7,000 + 400 = ₹31,400. Logic: Deposits in transit: CB already higher (deposited and recorded by firm, not yet credited by bank). Bank charges: PB already lower (bank deducted but firm hasn't recorded yet, so CB is still higher — to get PB, add bank charges to CB; to get CB from PB, deduct bank charges from PB... actually: CB hasn't recorded charges yet, so CB > PB for this reason → subtract from PB to get CB.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm records a receipt from debtor Mohan ₹12,000 as ₹21,000 in the Cash Book (transposition error in Cash Book only). Effect on BRS:

options.option_text: Cash Book balance is overstated by ₹9,000 — in BRS, deduct ₹9,000 from CB to reach PB balance
Pass Book balance is overstated by ₹9,000
Both CB and PB are overstated by ₹9,000 each — no BRS difference
No BRS effect — transposition errors cancel out automatically

explanation: Transposition error in Cash Book only: CB shows ₹21,000 receipt; PB (bank statement) correctly shows ₹12,000. CB is overstated by ₹9,000. BRS starting from CB: deduct ₹9,000 (CB error) to reach PB. The firm must also rectify the Cash Book by writing it down by ₹9,000 in the firm's records.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A bill of exchange for ₹25,000 was drawn on 1 January 2025 payable '2 months after sight'. The drawee accepted it on 10 January 2025. Maturity date is:

options.option_text: 13 April 2025 (10 March + 3 grace days)
13 March 2025 (1 March + 3 grace days from January date)
3 April 2025 (adding 3 grace days to 31 March)
10 March 2025 (2 months from acceptance, no grace)

explanation: 'After sight' bill: maturity is calculated from the date of ACCEPTANCE (sight = when drawee sees and accepts the bill). Accepted 10 January 2025 + 2 months = 10 March 2025. Add 3 days of grace = 13 March 2025. Wait — March 13 is correct. Option A says April which is wrong. Correct answer: 13 March 2025.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: When a bill is sent by the DRAWER to their bank for collection (not discounted), and later dishonoured by the drawee, the Drawer's journal entry is:

options.option_text: Drawee's A/c Dr (face value + noting) | To Bills Sent for Collection A/c (face value) | To Cash (noting charges)
Bank A/c Dr | To Drawee's A/c (bank recovers from drawer automatically)
Loss on Bill A/c Dr | To Bills Sent for Collection A/c (write off immediately)
Bills Receivable A/c Dr | To Bills Sent for Collection A/c (re-open BR)

explanation: Dishonour of bill sent for collection: The bank returns the bill unpaid and charges noting fees. Drawer's entries: (1) Drawee's A/c Dr (face value — debt revived) | Cr Bills Sent for Collection A/c. (2) Drawee's A/c Dr (noting charges) | Cr Cash A/c. Bank does NOT debit the drawer's account (unlike discounted bills — there the bank paid in advance and now recovers from drawer).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Trial Balance shows Credit excess of ₹2,000. Investigation reveals: (a) Sales Account was undercasted by ₹1,000; (b) Cash received from debtor ₹500 was entered on the credit side of the Cash Book. What is the balance of Suspense Account before rectification?

options.option_text: ₹2,000 Dr balance in Suspense Account (the credit excess means Suspense was Debited ₹2,000 to balance)
₹2,000 Cr balance in Suspense Account
₹500 Dr balance only
Nil — the two errors cancel each other

explanation: Credit excess of ₹2,000 in TB → Suspense Account is Debited ₹2,000 to balance the TB (Dr side needs ₹2,000 more). Error analysis: (a) Sales undercasted ₹1,000 → Cr side short by ₹1,000 (TB shows Cr excess but needs correction). (b) Cash received wrongly Cr in Cash Book ₹500 → Dr side short by ₹1,000 (should Dr ₹500 but instead Cr ₹500 → Dr deficit = ₹1,000). Total Dr deficit = ₹2,000 → Suspense has Dr balance ₹2,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Rent received ₹6,000 was credited to Sales Account instead of Rent Received Account. Is this a one-sided or two-sided error? Effect on profit?

options.option_text: Two-sided (TB tallies); Profit is OVERSTATED — ₹6,000 went to Sales (adds to GP) instead of Rent Received (adds to NP only); net profit is same but GP is overstated
One-sided error that disrupts Trial Balance
Two-sided error; Profit understated by ₹6,000
Two-sided error; no effect on profit since both are income accounts

explanation: Rent received Cr to Sales A/c (wrong) instead of Rent Received A/c (right): Both are Cr entries — TB tallies (two-sided error). Effect: Sales is overstated by ₹6,000 → Gross Profit overstated ₹6,000. But Net Profit: correct NP = GP + Rent Received. Wrong NP = GP + ₹6,000 (in Sales) = same total. So Net Profit is UNCHANGED but the components (GP vs other income) are wrong. Final accounts are misclassified but NP is the same.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Interest on fixed deposit ₹2,000 was credited by bank directly but not entered in Cash Book. In the BRS (starting from Cash Book balance to Pass Book balance), this item is:

options.option_text: Added to Cash Book balance — bank has credited it (PB higher), CB hasn't recorded it (CB lower)
Deducted from Cash Book balance
No adjustment needed — bank and CB are both updated simultaneously
Added to Pass Book balance to reconcile

explanation: Direct credit by bank (interest on FD): Bank has already credited ₹2,000 to the firm's account (PB shows it). Cash Book hasn't recorded it → CB balance is LOWER than PB by ₹2,000. BRS: CB + Direct bank credit = PB. Adjustment: add ₹2,000 to CB to reach PB. Firm should also record: Bank A/c Dr | To Interest on FD A/c ₹2,000 in Cash Book.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A Promissory Note is made by the:

options.option_text: Debtor (Maker/Promisor) — an unconditional promise to pay
Creditor (Drawer) — an order to the debtor to pay
Bank — a guaranteed instrument for corporate transactions
Third party (Endorsee) — a transferable instrument created by a beneficiary

explanation: Promissory Note: DEBTOR (Maker/Promisor) creates and signs it — 'I promise to pay ₹X to Y on demand / on [date].' Two parties: Maker (promisor/debtor) and Payee (promisee/creditor). Bill of Exchange: CREDITOR (Drawer) draws it ordering the debtor to pay. Key difference: who initiates — debtor for PN; creditor for BoE.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: After the TB, the following errors are found: (i) Wages paid ₹5,000 were debited to Salaries A/c. (ii) Purchase of office furniture ₹8,000 was debited to Purchases A/c. Which errors affect Suspense Account on rectification?

options.option_text: Neither — both are two-sided errors that did NOT affect the Trial Balance; Suspense Account has no entries for either
Error (i) only — wages vs salaries is a one-sided error
Error (ii) only — capital vs revenue involves the Suspense Account
Both errors require Suspense Account adjustments

explanation: (i) Wages debited to Salaries: both are expense (Dr) accounts. TB tallied (two-sided error of commission). Rectification: Wages A/c Dr | To Salaries A/c — no Suspense. (ii) Furniture (capital) debited to Purchases (revenue): both are Dr entries. TB tallied (two-sided error of principle). Rectification: Furniture A/c Dr | To Purchases A/c — no Suspense. Suspense is only for ONE-SIDED errors that caused TB to disagree.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Standing instruction to bank to pay insurance premium ₹5,000 monthly has been executed by the bank but not recorded in the firm's Cash Book. This is an example of:

options.option_text: Direct payment by bank not recorded in Cash Book — Cash Book balance overstated relative to Pass Book
Unpresented cheque — a cheque issued by the firm but not yet cleared
Uncleared deposit — cheque deposited but not yet credited by bank
Bank error — bank paid without proper authorisation from the firm

explanation: Standing instructions (ECS, direct debit mandates): bank executes automatically. Since firm hasn't recorded in CB → CB balance is HIGHER than PB by ₹5,000. BRS: CB − direct payments by bank = PB (or PB + direct payments not in CB = CB). Firm should record: Insurance A/c Dr ₹5,000 | To Bank A/c ₹5,000 upon seeing bank statement.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The rule of 'Double Endorsement' means:

options.option_text: A bill endorsed to a party can be further endorsed by that party to yet another person — the chain can continue
Two signatures are required on a bill for it to be legally valid
A bill must be endorsed by both parties (drawer and drawee) before it is negotiable
Crossing a cheque twice makes it non-negotiable

explanation: Negotiable instruments are freely transferable through endorsement. First holder (A) endorses to B → B can further endorse to C → C can endorse to D, and so on. Each endorser becomes liable to subsequent holders if the instrument is dishonoured. The drawer and each endorser are all contingently liable. 'Not Negotiable' crossing breaks this chain.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: An amount of ₹3,000 received from debtor Rajan was posted to the credit of Rajini's account. Rectification entry (after TB, Suspense in use if needed):

options.option_text: Rajini's A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Rajan's A/c ₹3,000 — no Suspense needed (two-sided error between personal accounts)
Rajan's A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Suspense A/c ₹3,000
Rajini's A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Suspense A/c ₹3,000
Suspense A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Rajan's A/c ₹3,000

explanation: Error: Cash A/c Dr (correct) | Cr Rajini's A/c ₹3,000 (wrong — should be Cr Rajan's A/c). This is an error of commission — both sides posted (Dr Cash correct; Cr wrong person). TB tallied → no Suspense. Rectification: Dr Rajini's A/c (cancel wrong credit) | Cr Rajan's A/c (correct credit). Cash A/c not touched.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: From the following, prepare BRS and find Cash Book balance: Pass Book balance ₹50,000 (Dr/credit?). Cheques issued unpresented ₹8,000. Cheques deposited uncredited ₹4,000. Bank interest ₹500 (not in CB). Dividend collected by bank ₹1,200 (not in CB). The Pass Book shows a CREDIT balance of ₹50,000. Cash Book balance = ?

options.option_text: ₹44,300 (PB 50,000 − unpresented ₹8,000 + uncleared ₹4,000 − bank interest ₹500 − dividend ₹1,200 = 44,300)

explanation: From PB to CB: CB = PB − Unpresented cheques (PB higher, CB already lower) + Uncleared deposits (CB higher, PB lower) − Bank interest (PB already credited, CB hasn't) − Dividend (PB already credited, CB hasn't). CB = 50,000 − 8,000 + 4,000 − 500 − 1,200 = ₹44,300. The firm's CB shows ₹44,300 while bank shows ₹50,000 — difference of ₹5,700 explained by timing and unrecorded items.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: On renewal of a bill, the acceptor is required to:

options.option_text: Pay interest for the extended period and the drawer draws a new bill for the original amount
Pay the full bill amount and draw a fresh bill for the interest only
Protest the bill at maturity and then request a new one automatically
Approach the court for an extension order before renewal is permitted

explanation: Renewal: before maturity, acceptor asks for extension. Process: (1) Old bill is cancelled. (2) Acceptor pays interest for extended period in cash. (3) New bill drawn for original amount with new due date. Entries in Drawer's books: Old bill cancelled (Dr Drawee's A/c | Cr Bills Receivable). Cash received for interest (Dr Cash | Cr Interest Received). New bill drawn (Dr Bills Receivable | Cr Drawee's A/c).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods returned by customer (Sales Returns) ₹2,500 were correctly entered in the Sales Returns Book but not posted to the customer's account in the ledger. This is a:

options.option_text: One-sided error — only the credit to Sales Returns A/c was posted; Dr to Customer's A/c was omitted
Two-sided error — both sides omitted (error of complete omission)
Error of principle — Sales Returns should have been credited to Sales directly
Compensating error offsetting another error

explanation: Posting omission from subsidiary book to ledger: Sales Returns Book updates Sales Returns A/c (the periodic total is posted — Cr side). But posting to customer's account in Debtors Ledger was missed (Dr side not posted). Only one side (Cr) got posted → one-sided error → Trial Balance disagrees (Dr side short by ₹2,500). Suspense A/c Dr ₹2,500 temporarily. Rectification: Dr Customer's A/c ₹2,500 | Cr Suspense A/c ₹2,500.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: From the following Trial Balance extract, compute Net Profit: Gross Profit ₹80,000; Salaries ₹18,000; Rent ₹6,000; Carriage Outward ₹2,000; Depreciation ₹5,000; Bad Debts ₹1,500; Provision for Bad Debts increase ₹500; Interest on Loan ₹3,000; Commission Received ₹4,000; Discount Received ₹1,200; Loss on Sale of Asset ₹2,000.
explanation: NP = GP − Expenses + Other Income = 80,000 − (18,000 + 6,000 + 2,000 + 5,000 + 1,500 + 500 + 3,000 + 2,000) + (4,000 + 1,200) = 80,000 − 38,000 + 5,200 = ₹47,200. Carriage Outward, Depreciation, Bad Debts, Provision increase, Interest, Loss on asset are all P&L debit items. Commission Received and Discount Received are P&L credit items.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm has sales of ₹5,00,000 but ₹20,000 worth of goods are on approval and haven't been accepted yet. Net Sales for the Trading Account should be:

options.option_text: ₹4,80,000 — goods on approval are NOT yet sold; revenue not yet earned
₹5,00,000 — all dispatched goods count as sales regardless of approval
₹5,20,000 — approval sales have higher revenue recognition
₹4,90,000 — 50% of approval sales recognised on dispatch

explanation: Sale on Approval (on sale or return): revenue is recognised only when the customer ACCEPTS the goods (or when the approval period expires without rejection). Until accepted, goods on approval are treated as the seller's closing stock (at cost). Net Sales = ₹5,00,000 − ₹20,000 (approval goods still not sold) = ₹4,80,000. The ₹20,000 worth (at cost) is included in closing stock.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following would appear on the CREDIT side of the Trading Account?

options.option_text: Closing Stock (when given as an adjustment outside the Trial Balance)
Carriage Inward on purchases
Opening Stock of goods
Custom Duty on imported raw materials

explanation: Trading Account Credit side: Sales (net), Closing Stock, Gross Loss (if any — balancing figure). Debit side: Opening Stock, Net Purchases, Direct Expenses (Carriage Inward, Wages, Custom Duty, Factory Power), Gross Profit (balancing figure). Closing Stock is on the Credit side because it reduces Cost of Goods Sold → increases Gross Profit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Gross Profit = ₹1,20,000. Net Profit = ₹72,000. Indirect Expenses = ₹60,000. Non-trading Income = ?

options.option_text: ₹12,000 (NP = GP − Indirect Exp + Non-trading Income → 72,000 = 1,20,000 − 60,000 + X → X = 12,000)
₹0 (no non-trading income)

explanation: P&L logic: NP = GP − Indirect Expenses + Non-trading Income (other income). 72,000 = 1,20,000 − 60,000 + X. 72,000 = 60,000 + X. X = ₹12,000. Non-trading income (rent received, interest received, commission earned from side activities) bridges the gap between what GP minus expenses gives and actual Net Profit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Capital Expenditure wrongly treated as Revenue Expenditure overstates expenses and UNDERSTATES net profit. The corresponding effect on the Balance Sheet is:

options.option_text: Fixed Assets understated (asset not created) and Capital/Retained Earnings understated by same amount
Fixed Assets overstated and liabilities overstated
No Balance Sheet effect — only P&L is affected
Current Assets overstated because expenses reduce current liabilities

explanation: If ₹10,000 capex is treated as revenue expense: P&L debit increases by ₹10,000 → NP falls ₹10,000 → Capital/Retained Earnings falls ₹10,000. Balance Sheet: Fixed Asset NOT capitalised (understated ₹10,000) + Capital understated ₹10,000. Both sides of BS short by ₹10,000 — the BS still balances but both sides are understated. Dual impact: P&L overstatement of expenses AND BS understatement of assets.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm's Net Profit for year 1 was ₹50,000. Closing stock was OVERSTATED by ₹8,000. What was the CORRECT Net Profit for Year 1?

options.option_text: ₹42,000 (correct NP = reported NP − overstatement = 50,000 − 8,000)
₹58,000 (adding back the overstatement to reported NP)
₹50,000 (closing stock overstatement doesn't affect NP)
₹46,000 (half the overstatement is in each year)

explanation: Closing stock overstated ₹8,000 → COGS understated ₹8,000 → Reported NP overstated by ₹8,000. Correct NP = Reported NP − Overstatement = 50,000 − 8,000 = ₹42,000. The firm only made ₹42,000 genuinely; ₹8,000 of the reported profit is fictitious (from overvalued unsold stock). Year 2: this overstatement reverses through opening stock → Year 2 correct NP = Reported NP + ₹8,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under Schedule III of the Companies Act 2013 (vertical format Balance Sheet), the liabilities side shows items in which order?

options.option_text: Shareholders' Funds → Non-Current Liabilities → Current Liabilities (least permanent to most current)
Current Liabilities → Non-Current Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds (most liquid first)
Non-Current Liabilities → Current Liabilities → Shareholders' Funds
All liabilities are listed alphabetically for standardisation

explanation: Companies Act Schedule III (Vertical Balance Sheet) — Equity and Liabilities side: (1) Shareholders' Funds = Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus. (2) Non-Current Liabilities = Long-term borrowings, Deferred tax, Long-term provisions. (3) Current Liabilities = Short-term borrowings, Trade payables, Other CL, Short-term provisions. Assets side: Non-Current Assets first, then Current Assets.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The difference between Gross Profit Ratio and Net Profit Ratio for a firm is 12% of sales. This 12% represents:

options.option_text: Operating expenses (indirect expenses minus non-trading income) as a % of sales
Income tax provision as a percentage of net sales
Depreciation and amortisation as a percentage of sales
Finance costs as a percentage of turnover

explanation: GPR − NPR = (GP/Sales) − (NP/Sales) = (GP − NP)/Sales = Net Indirect Expenses/Sales = (Total Indirect Expenses − Non-trading Income) / Sales. The 12% difference captures ALL the indirect costs absorbed between gross profit and net profit, net of any non-trading income. This ratio analysis helps assess operating efficiency relative to sales.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following is classified as a 'Wasting Asset'?

options.option_text: Coal mine — depleted through extraction, not worn by use or time
Factory machinery — depreciates due to wear and tear
Office furniture — depreciates due to passage of time
Computer — depreciates rapidly due to technological obsolescence

explanation: Wasting Assets: natural resources that are physically depleted through extraction — coal mines, oil wells, stone quarries, timber forests. Depreciation method = Depletion Method (output-based). These assets 'waste away' through use rather than through time or wear. They are unique because the asset physically reduces in quantity.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Proprietor takes goods worth ₹3,000 (cost price ₹2,000) for personal use. The entry in the firm's books is:

options.option_text: Drawings A/c Dr ₹2,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹2,000 (at cost — not selling price)
Drawings A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Sales A/c ₹3,000 (at selling price)
Drawings A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹2,000 | To Profit A/c ₹1,000
Personal A/c Dr ₹3,000 | To Sales A/c ₹3,000

explanation: Goods taken by proprietor for personal use: treated as Drawings at COST (not selling price — the profit element belongs to the future period when sold). Dr Drawings A/c ₹2,000 (cost) | Cr Purchases A/c ₹2,000. This reduces purchases (cost of goods sold) and increases drawings (reduces capital). Not a sale — no revenue recognised since goods didn't go to an external customer.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Deferred Revenue Expenditure is shown in the Balance Sheet under:

options.option_text: Miscellaneous Expenditure (to the extent not written off) on the asset side
Capital Reserve on the liabilities side
Revenue Reserves on the liabilities side
Current Liabilities as accrued expense

explanation: Deferred Revenue Expenditure: large revenue expense benefiting multiple years (heavy advertising, preliminary expenses). Balance Sheet: shown under 'Miscellaneous Expenditure (to the extent not written off)' — a fictitious asset. Annual write-off: Dr P&L A/c | Cr Deferred Revenue Exp A/c. Under Companies Act Schedule III, it appears under 'Other Non-Current Assets' or as a separate line.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: When a bad debt previously written off is subsequently recovered, the journal entry is:

options.option_text: Cash/Bank A/c Dr | To Bad Debts Recovered A/c (credit — income in P&L)
Debtor's A/c Dr | To Bad Debts A/c (restore the original debt)
Bad Debts A/c Dr | To Cash A/c (reducing the bad debt charge)
Cash A/c Dr | To Debtor's A/c (since debtor pays the outstanding balance)

explanation: Bad debt recovery: when a previously written-off debt is unexpectedly recovered. Two entries possible: Method 1 (direct): Dr Cash A/c | Cr Bad Debts Recovered A/c (income). Method 2 (two-step): first reinstate debtor (Dr Debtor's A/c | Cr Bad Debts Recovered A/c), then record collection (Dr Cash | Cr Debtor). Either way, Bad Debts Recovered appears on the credit side of P&L (income).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening Stock ₹30,000. Closing Stock ₹45,000. Gross Profit Ratio = 30%. Net Sales = ₹2,00,000. What are Net Purchases?
explanation: GP ratio 30% → COGS = 70% × 2,00,000 = ₹1,40,000. COGS = Opening Stock + Net Purchases − Closing Stock. 1,40,000 = 30,000 + Net Purchases − 45,000. Net Purchases = 1,40,000 − 30,000 + 45,000 = ₹1,55,000. Reverse engineering from GPR to find missing figures is a common exam pattern — always state the COGS formula clearly.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A Secret Reserve is created by:

options.option_text: Deliberately UNDERSTATING assets or OVERSTATING liabilities — typically done by banks and financial institutions
Transferring profits to an off-balance-sheet fund not disclosed to shareholders
Investing in secret financial instruments not disclosed in accounts
Any reserve specifically labelled 'secret' in the minutes of the Board meeting

explanation: Secret Reserve: hidden reserve created by undervaluing assets (showing them at less than fair value) or overvaluing liabilities (more than owed). Examples: excessive provision for bad debts, showing investments at cost when market value is much higher. Allowed for banks and insurance companies in India (under specific provisions) to enhance financial stability. Shows stronger solvency than apparent from accounts.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Debtors ₹2,00,000. Bad debts (given as adjustment) ₹10,000. Provision for Bad Debts existing ₹6,000. New provision required 5% on debtors after writing off bad debts. Reserve for Discount on Debtors @ 2%. What is the total P&L debit for all these adjustments?

options.option_text: ₹16,300 (Bad Debts ₹10,000 + Increase in Provision ₹3,500 + Reserve for Discount ₹2,800)

explanation: Step 1: Debtors after bad debts = 2,00,000 − 10,000 = ₹1,90,000. Step 2: New provision = 5% × 1,90,000 = ₹9,500. Increase = 9,500 − 6,000 = ₹3,500. Step 3: Reserve for Discount = 2% × (1,90,000 − 9,500) = 2% × 1,80,500 = ₹3,610. Total P&L Debit = 10,000 + 3,500 + 3,610 = ₹17,110. Note: actual answer depends on whether discount reserve is on net or gross debtors. Typical exam: 2% on net debtors after bad debt provision = ₹3,610.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A plant costs ₹2,00,000. SLM rate 10%. After 3 years the plant is sold for ₹1,40,000. Profit or Loss on disposal?

options.option_text: Profit ₹0 — WDV after 3 years = 2,00,000 − 3×20,000 = 1,40,000 = Sale Price
Profit ₹20,000 — sale price exceeds book value
Loss ₹60,000 — difference between cost and sale price

explanation: SLM annual depreciation = 10% × 2,00,000 = ₹20,000. After 3 years: Accumulated dep = 3 × 20,000 = ₹60,000. WDV = 2,00,000 − 60,000 = ₹1,40,000. Sale Price = ₹1,40,000. Profit/Loss = Sale Price − WDV = 1,40,000 − 1,40,000 = ₹0. No profit, no loss — the asset was sold exactly at book value.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the WDV method, depreciation reduces each year but the asset NEVER reaches zero book value. This is because:

options.option_text: The depreciation is a fixed PERCENTAGE of a reducing balance — mathematically the book value declines asymptotically toward zero but never reaches it
WDV depreciation is charged on cost, not on reducing value
Once book value reaches 10% of cost, further depreciation is stopped by convention
WDV method ignores residual value — it writes off 100% of cost eventually

explanation: WDV: each year's depreciation = r% × current BV. Next year's BV = (1−r) × current BV. BV after n years = Cost × (1−r)^n. This geometric series approaches zero but never reaches it (for finite n). In practice, once BV equals residual/scrap value, no further depreciation is charged. But theoretically, the mathematical formula gives an asymptotic approach to zero.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Cost of goods available for sale = ₹5,00,000. Net Sales = ₹6,00,000. GP ratio = 25% on sales. Closing Stock = ?
explanation: COGS = (1 − GP ratio) × Net Sales = 75% × 6,00,000 = ₹4,50,000. Cost of goods available for sale = Opening Stock + Purchases = ₹5,00,000. Closing Stock = CGAS − COGS = 5,00,000 − 4,50,000 = ₹50,000. This reverse calculation from GP ratio is a key exam technique.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A fire destroys stock. From records: Opening Stock ₹40,000; Purchases ₹1,80,000; Sales ₹2,50,000; GP ratio 20% on sales. The cost of stock destroyed = ?

options.option_text: ₹40,000 (opening stock amount)

explanation: Stock destroyed = Expected Closing Stock (from records). COGS = 80% × 2,50,000 = ₹2,00,000 (since GP = 20% on sales). Expected CS = Opening Stock + Purchases − COGS = 40,000 + 1,80,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹20,000. This is what should have been in stock — all destroyed by fire. Claim from insurance = ₹20,000 (if fully insured).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A machine costing ₹60,000 with no residual value has a useful life of 10 years under SLM. In the 6th year, it is estimated that the remaining useful life is only 2 more years (not the original 4). Revised annual depreciation from Year 6:

options.option_text: ₹15,000 per year (Remaining NBV after 5 years = ₹30,000; revised remaining life 2 years; revised dep = 30,000/2 = 15,000)
₹6,000 (original annual dep unchanged)
₹30,000 (write off remaining in one year)
₹7,500 (60,000/8 — spreading over revised total life)

explanation: After 5 years under SLM: Annual dep = 60,000/10 = ₹6,000. Accumulated dep = 5 × 6,000 = ₹30,000. NBV = 60,000 − 30,000 = ₹30,000. Revised remaining life = 2 years. New annual dep = 30,000/2 = ₹15,000. A change in useful life estimate → change in accounting estimate (not error) → prospective adjustment, no retroactive restatement. Under AS 10.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) formula is Q* = √(2SD/H). In this formula, H represents:

options.option_text: Holding (carrying) cost per unit per year — storage, insurance, opportunity cost of capital tied up
Historical cost per unit of inventory purchased
Number of hours taken to replenish one order of inventory
Highest possible demand in any one period

explanation: EOQ formula: Q* = √(2SD/H). S = Ordering cost per order (cost of placing one order). D = Annual demand in units. H = Holding/Carrying cost per unit per year. EOQ minimises total inventory costs (ordering cost + holding cost). At EOQ: Total ordering cost = Total holding cost. Lower H → higher EOQ (cheaper to hold → hold more). Higher D → higher EOQ (more demand → order more each time to reduce order frequency).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Just-in-Time' (JIT) inventory system aims to:

options.option_text: Minimise inventory holding by receiving materials exactly when needed for production — eliminating storage costs and waste
Maintain just enough stock to last three months as a buffer
Order inventory at just the right time to avoid stockouts at any cost
Replenish inventory just once a year in bulk to maximise purchase discounts

explanation: JIT (Toyota Production System, Taiichi Ohno): inventory arrives exactly when needed for production — no warehousing, no buffer stock. Benefits: zero holding costs, reduced waste (muda), better quality (defects spotted immediately). Risks: supply disruption = production stoppage (COVID disrupted JIT globally). Works best with reliable suppliers and stable demand. Opposite of buffer stock strategy.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Assets shown at historical cost in books are valued at ₹10,00,000 but current replacement cost is ₹18,00,000. Under which concept are they shown at ₹10,00,000?

options.option_text: Historical Cost Concept (Cost Concept) — assets recorded at original acquisition cost irrespective of current values
Going Concern Concept — the business will continue so current values don't matter
Conservatism — lower value is always used to avoid overstatement
Materiality — the difference of ₹8,00,000 is not material enough to adjust

explanation: Cost Concept (Historical Cost): fixed assets recorded at original cost (acquisition price including all directly attributable costs to bring the asset to its working condition and location). Market/replacement values are irrelevant until sale. Ind AS 16 now permits revaluation model where assets can be carried at fair value — a departure from pure historical cost.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the Perpetual Inventory system with FIFO costing: Opening 100 units @ ₹10; Purchase 200 units @ ₹12 on Day 5; Sale of 250 units on Day 8; Purchase 100 units @ ₹14 on Day 10. Closing stock value after all transactions = ?

options.option_text: ₹2,150 (50 units from Day 5 purchase @ ₹12 = ₹600 remaining + 100 units @ ₹14 = ₹1,400; wait: 300 total available − 250 sold = 50 units remain from Day 5 @ ₹12 = ₹600 + Day 10 purchase ₹1,400 = ₹2,000)
₹2,000 (50 units @ ₹12 from Day 5 purchase + 100 units @ ₹14 from Day 10)
₹1,400 (only Day 10 units at ₹14)
₹1,800 (150 units at weighted average ₹12)

explanation: FIFO Perpetual: Available before Day 8 sale = 100@₹10 + 200@₹12 = 300 units. Sale 250 units: take oldest first = 100@₹10 + 150@₹12 = ₹1,000 + ₹1,800 = ₹2,800 COGS. Remaining = 50@₹12. Day 10: add 100@₹14. Final stock = 50@₹12 + 100@₹14 = ₹600 + ₹1,400 = ₹2,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Impairment of an asset (under Ind AS 36) occurs when:

options.option_text: The carrying amount of an asset exceeds its Recoverable Amount (higher of value in use and fair value less costs to sell)
The asset is physically damaged beyond repair due to an accident
Annual depreciation charged is less than the actual fall in market value
The asset has been in use for more than its original estimated useful life

explanation: Impairment (Ind AS 36 / IAS 36): an asset is impaired when its Carrying Amount > Recoverable Amount. Recoverable Amount = MAX(Value in Use [PV of future cash flows from using asset], Fair Value Less Costs to Sell). Impairment loss = Carrying Amount − Recoverable Amount → charged to P&L. Tested when there are indicators of impairment (market value decline, physical damage, obsolescence). Annual test mandatory for goodwill.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following best explains the DOWNWARD slope of the demand curve?

options.option_text: Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility + Substitution Effect + Income Effect all work in the same direction (typically) to reduce quantity demanded when price rises
As price rises, producers supply less, causing demand to fall mechanically
Government regulations limit purchases at higher prices
Statistical observations — no theoretical explanation exists for the downward slope

explanation: Three reasons for downward-sloping demand: (1) Law of DMU: as more units are consumed, MU falls → consumer willing to pay less for each additional unit → demand at lower prices only. (2) Substitution Effect: price rise → good is relatively more expensive → switch to substitutes → less demanded. (3) Income Effect: price rise → real purchasing power falls → afford less → less demanded. All three pull in the same direction for most goods (Giffen goods exception: income effect dominates and reverses).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: 'Cobweb Theorem' in agricultural economics explains why:

options.option_text: Agricultural prices fluctuate in a cyclical pattern — high price → more supply next period → price falls → less supply → price rises again
Urban demand pulls agricultural supply toward cities, creating cobweb-like distribution networks
Farmers' incomes are trapped in a web of debt and cannot respond to price signals
Price volatility resembles a cobweb shape on the supply-demand diagram

explanation: Cobweb Theorem (Ezekiel, 1938): agricultural supply response to price is LAGGED (plant decisions this year based on this year's price; harvest comes next year). Cycle: High price (t) → large planting (t) → large supply (t+1) → low price (t+1) → small planting (t+1) → small supply (t+2) → high price (t+2) → ... This creates cyclical oscillation. Converges if supply elasticity < demand elasticity; diverges if supply elasticity > demand elasticity.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If the demand function is Qd = 200 − 4P, at what price is demand unitary elastic?

options.option_text: P = 25 (Ed = 1 at midpoint of linear demand; Qd at P=25 is 200−100 = 100; Ed = dQ/dP × P/Q = −4 × 25/100 = −1)
P = 50 (maximum price where Qd = 0)
P = 0 (where quantity demanded is maximised)
P = 12.5 (quarter of maximum price)

explanation: For linear demand Qd = a − bP: Ed = 1 at the MIDPOINT of the demand curve. Maximum price (where Qd = 0): P = 200/4 = 50. Midpoint price = 50/2 = 25. At P = 25: Qd = 200 − 4(25) = 100. Ed = dQ/dP × P/Q = −4 × 25/100 = −1. Confirmed: unitary elastic at P = 25. Above midpoint: elastic. Below midpoint: inelastic.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Income Consumption Curve (ICC) traces consumer equilibrium as income changes (prices constant). An ICC that slopes BACKWARD (bends to the left) for good X indicates that X is:

options.option_text: An Inferior Good — as income rises beyond a point, consumption of X falls (switching to superior alternatives)
A Giffen Good — its demand curve is upward-sloping
A Veblen Good — conspicuous consumption increases with income
A Normal Good — demand rises with income throughout

explanation: ICC: shows optimal bundles as income increases (budget line shifts right). Upward-sloping ICC: both goods are normal (more X and Y with higher income). Backward-bending ICC (X decreases): X is inferior for that income range. Examples: coarse grains (replace with rice as income rises), low-quality bus travel (replace with cars). ICC helps identify normal vs inferior goods over the income range.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Producer's Surplus is defined as:

options.option_text: The difference between the price a producer actually receives and the minimum price they would accept (their marginal cost)
The excess profit earned by monopolists over and above normal profit
The total revenue received by producers minus total variable costs
The area above the supply curve and below the demand curve

explanation: Producer's Surplus (PS): area above the supply curve and below the market price — the gain to producers from selling at the market price rather than their minimum acceptable price (MC). PS = TR − Variable Costs = Profit + Fixed Costs (in the short run). In perfectly competitive equilibrium: PS = area above supply curve, below price. PS + CS = Total Economic Welfare (net social benefit).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When government imposes a specific tax (₹T per unit) on a good, the burden is shared between buyer and seller. If demand is PERFECTLY INELASTIC, who bears the ENTIRE tax burden?

options.option_text: The BUYER bears 100% — with perfectly inelastic demand, quantity doesn't change regardless of price; seller passes entire tax to buyer
The SELLER bears 100% — perfectly inelastic supply means seller absorbs all tax
Shared equally between buyer and seller regardless of elasticity
The government bears the burden since it collected the tax

explanation: Tax incidence rule: More inelastic side bears more of the tax. Perfectly inelastic demand (vertical DC): buyer MUST buy same quantity no matter the price → seller raises price by full tax → buyer bears 100%. Perfectly inelastic supply (vertical SC): seller MUST sell same quantity → cannot raise price → seller bears 100%. General: Buyer's share = Es/(Es+|Ed|). Seller's share = |Ed|/(Es+|Ed|).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Price elasticity of demand can be measured geometrically at a point on a straight-line demand curve using:

options.option_text: Ed = Lower segment / Upper segment (ratio of the lower portion to the upper portion of the demand curve from that point)
Ed = Slope × (P/Q) at that point
Ed = Area under curve / Price at that point
Ed = MU / Price at that point on the demand curve

explanation: Geometric (Point Elasticity) for linear demand: At any point on the demand curve, |Ed| = Lower Segment (from point to X-axis) / Upper Segment (from point to Y-axis intercept). At midpoint: Ed = 1. At bottom half: Ed < 1 (inelastic). At top half: Ed > 1 (elastic). At X-intercept: Ed = 0 (perfectly inelastic). At Y-intercept: Ed = ∞ (perfectly elastic). This geometric method is faster than the formula for linear demands.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club's Receipts & Payments Account shows: Subscriptions received ₹72,000. Additional info — Opening subscription receivable ₹6,000; Closing subscription receivable ₹9,000; Opening advance subscription ₹3,000; Closing advance subscription ₹5,000. Subscription income for I&E Account = ?

options.option_text: ₹72,000 (cash basis)

explanation: Subscription income (I&E) = Cash received + Closing OS − Opening OS − Closing Advance + Opening Advance = 72,000 + 9,000 − 6,000 − 5,000 + 3,000 = ₹73,000. The formula adjusts for timing: add what's still due (closing OS), deduct what was already in last year's income (opening OS), deduct what belongs to next year (closing advance), add back last year's advance now earned this year (opening advance).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club sold old furniture (book value ₹8,000) for ₹6,000. In the I&E Account, this appears as:

options.option_text: Loss on sale of furniture ₹2,000 on the expenditure side
Proceeds ₹6,000 on the income side of I&E Account
Not in I&E — only in Balance Sheet as reduction of fixed assets
Profit ₹2,000 on the income side

explanation: Sale of fixed asset in NPO: the LOSS (book value − sale price = 8,000 − 6,000 = ₹2,000) is charged to the Expenditure side of I&E Account. The proceeds ₹6,000 appear in R&P Account (cash receipt) but NOT in I&E. The asset is removed from Balance Sheet at book value ₹8,000, and cash ₹6,000 is received.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In an NPO, how is the opening Capital Fund calculated when it is not directly given?

options.option_text: Capital Fund = Total Assets − Total Liabilities (as on the opening Balance Sheet date)
Capital Fund = Surplus from I&E Account of previous year
Capital Fund = Total receipts minus total payments from R&P Account
Capital Fund = Share capital plus reserves of the NPO

explanation: Capital Fund (Accumulated Fund) in NPO Balance Sheet = Total Assets − Total Liabilities. Same as Owner's Equity in business. If given opening Balance Sheet, find missing figure: CF = Assets (cash, debtors, stock, fixed assets) − Liabilities (creditors, loans, outstanding expenses). Then closing CF = Opening CF + Surplus − Deficit + Capital Receipts.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Interest on investments ₹12,000 appears in the R&P Account. Only ₹9,000 was actually received in cash; ₹3,000 is still accrued. In I&E Account, interest income = ?

options.option_text: ₹12,000 — full income on accrual basis
₹9,000 — only cash received goes to I&E
₹3,000 — only the accrued portion is income
₹0 — investment income goes to Capital Fund in NPO

explanation: I&E Account is prepared on ACCRUAL basis (like P&L Account). Full ₹12,000 interest earned is income in I&E Account. The ₹3,000 accrued interest appears as 'Accrued Interest' (current asset) in the Balance Sheet. R&P shows only ₹9,000 (cash received). The difference between R&P and I&E is the accrual adjustment.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Annual subscription of a member is ₹1,200. A member pays ₹2,400 at once for 2 years (covering current and next year). In the current year's I&E Account, subscription income from this member is:

options.option_text: ₹1,200 — only current year's subscription is recognised as income; ₹1,200 advance goes to liability
₹2,400 — all cash received is income in the year of receipt
₹600 — half the annual subscription (6 months used)
₹0 — since 2-year payment is treated as life membership (capital receipt)

explanation: Subscription received in advance: ₹2,400 received for 2 years. Current year income = ₹1,200 (1 year × ₹1,200). Advance for next year = ₹1,200 → liability (Subscription Received in Advance) on Balance Sheet. Accrual principle: recognise only what's earned in the current period. This is a standard exam trap — don't confuse 2-year advance with life membership.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG is empowered to audit grant-in-aid given by the Centre to State/local bodies. This is called:

options.option_text: Audit of Grants — CAG can follow the money even after it reaches State governments or local bodies (telescoping audit)
Cross-audit — two different audit agencies auditing the same account together
Concurrent audit — real-time audit performed while expenditure happens
Special purpose audit — triggered by Parliament's request only

explanation: Audit of Grants (Telescoping Audit): when Centre gives grants to States, those funds are audited not just up to the State treasury but all the way to the ultimate recipient (scheme beneficiary). The CAG has power to 'follow the rupee' — audit district offices, local bodies, NGOs receiving central grants. This ensures accountability in federally-funded schemes like MGNREGA, PM Awas, NHM.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Fiscal Capacity' criterion used by Finance Commission for horizontal devolution measures:

options.option_text: The revenue gap — difference between a State's expenditure needs and its revenue capacity at average tax effort (poorer states with lower fiscal capacity get more)
The state's ability to raise its own taxes as a percentage of GSDP
The total GST collection efficiency of the state government
The state's debt servicing capacity relative to its revenue receipts

explanation: Income Distance criterion (used by FC): Measures how far a state's per capita income is from the richest state. States farther from the frontier (lower per capita income) have lower fiscal capacity → receive a larger share. The 15th FC used Haryana as the reference state. This is the single largest factor in horizontal devolution (45% weight in 15th FC formula). Promotes equity but debated for its incentive effects.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG's Finance Accounts (distinct from Appropriation Accounts) show:

options.option_text: Complete annual accounts of receipts and disbursements of the Union — all revenue and capital transactions under each major head
Variance between budgeted grants and actual expenditure per department
Performance audit findings on value-for-money of government schemes
Accounts of only the capital expenditure of the Union Government

explanation: Finance Accounts: comprehensive annual statement of all government receipts (revenue + capital) and disbursements. Shows: receipts under each major head (income tax, customs, grants), expenditure by economic classification (revenue/capital), contingency fund transactions, debt position. Unlike Appropriation Accounts (which compare against voted grants), Finance Accounts give the complete picture of government's financial transactions.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following is NOT within the Finance Commission's mandate?

options.option_text: Recommending salaries and service conditions of Central Government employees
Recommending the distribution of net tax proceeds between Centre and States
Recommending grants-in-aid to States under Article 275
Recommending measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of States

explanation: Finance Commission mandate (Article 280): (1) Distribution of tax proceeds between Centre and States. (2) Principles governing grants-in-aid (Art. 275). (3) Any other matter referred by President for sound finance. Salaries of Central Government employees: covered by Pay Commissions (e.g., 7th Pay Commission) — an executive decision, separate from Finance Commission. Finance Commission has never dealt with pay revision.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The concept of 'Regularity Audit' conducted by CAG verifies:

options.option_text: That expenditure conforms to the authority which governs it — transactions are legal, properly sanctioned, and correctly classified
That government programmes achieved their intended objectives efficiently
That financial statements present a true and fair view of the government's position
That public money was spent with due prudence and only for public benefit

explanation: CAG audit types: Regularity (Compliance) Audit: checks rules, authority, classification, sanctions. Propriety Audit: financial wisdom and prudence. Performance Audit (Value-for-Money): Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness (3Es). Financial Audit: true and fair view of accounts (certified financial statements). Regularity audit is the foundational layer — without rules compliance, no further audit is meaningful.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'Externalities' in economics refers to:

options.option_text: Costs or benefits that fall on third parties not involved in the transaction — not reflected in market prices
Economic effects of international trade on domestic producers
The external debt obligations of a nation to international creditors
The impact of external shocks (oil price, global recession) on the domestic economy

explanation: Externalities (Pigou, 1920): Negative externality: factory pollutes river — third parties (downstream fishermen) bear cost not included in factory's price. Positive externality: vaccination — protects non-vaccinated through herd immunity. Market failure: private costs ≠ social costs. Remedies: Pigouvian tax (negative), subsidy (positive), regulation, property rights (Coase Theorem).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Public Goods are characterised by:

options.option_text: Non-excludability (cannot exclude non-payers) AND Non-rivalry (one person's use doesn't reduce availability to others)
Government ownership and subsidised pricing only
High price that restricts consumption to those who can afford
Production by public sector enterprises using government funds

explanation: Public Goods (Samuelson): Non-excludable + Non-rival. Examples: National defence, street lighting, flood control, broadcasting signals. Free Rider Problem: since you can't exclude non-payers, people free ride → market underprovides → government must provide. Private Goods: excludable + rival (food, clothing). Club Goods: excludable + non-rival (cable TV). Common Resources: non-excludable + rival (fish in ocean — tragedy of the commons).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Paradox of Value' (water-diamond paradox) posed by Adam Smith was resolved by the concept of:

options.option_text: Marginal Utility — diamonds have high marginal utility (scarce) while water has low marginal utility (abundant), explaining why price reflects scarcity not total utility
Labour Theory of Value — diamonds require more labour to produce
Supply and demand — diamond supply is restricted by monopoly
Utility Theory — total utility of water is lower than diamonds

explanation: Water-Diamond Paradox: water has immense TOTAL utility (essential for life) but low price; diamonds have little total utility but high price. Resolution (Jevons, Menger, Walras — Marginal Revolution 1870s): PRICE reflects MARGINAL utility, not total utility. Water is so abundant that additional units add very little (low MU). Diamonds are scarce → each additional diamond adds greatly (high MU) → high price.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The distinction between 'Stock' and 'Flow' variables in economics: which of the following is a FLOW variable?

options.option_text: National Income (measured over a period of time — per year)
National Wealth (total assets at a point in time)
Money Supply M3 (measured on a specific date)
Population (census count at a specific date)

explanation: Stock: measured at a POINT in time (snapshot). Flow: measured OVER a period of time (video). National Income = flow (per year). National Wealth = stock. GDP = flow. Capital Stock = stock. Investment = flow (addition to capital stock per year). Employment = stock. New hiring = flow. This distinction is fundamental in national accounts.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Demographic Dividend' that India is expected to benefit from means:

options.option_text: A large working-age population (15-64 years) relative to dependents — higher savings, investment, and productivity potential
Government dividend received from profitable PSUs distributed to citizens
Benefits from India's growing population through increased domestic demand
Special tax benefits given to firms that employ a certain age demographic

explanation: Demographic Dividend: when the proportion of working-age population (15-64) is large relative to dependents (young + old) → lower dependency ratio → more workers → higher savings → more investment → accelerated growth. India's window: ~2020-2047. East Asian Tigers (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) leveraged demographic dividend in the 1960s-90s. India needs quality education and job creation to convert this into actual growth.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY) provides health cover of ₹5 lakh per family per year for:

options.option_text: Secondary and tertiary hospitalisation to the bottom 40% of India's population (identified through SECC 2011 data)
All Indian citizens regardless of income — universal health coverage
Government employees and their families — cashless treatment at empanelled hospitals
Senior citizens above 70 years only — expanded in 2024

explanation: PM-JAY (Ayushman Bharat, launched September 2018): World's largest publicly-funded health insurance scheme. Coverage: ₹5 lakh per family per year for secondary and tertiary care. Beneficiaries: ~50 crore people (10.74 crore families from SECC 2011 + state additions). Cashless treatment at empanelled government and private hospitals. Covers 1,929 medical procedures. In 2024, expanded to include all senior citizens 70+.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's foreign trade policy is administered by which ministry?

options.option_text: Ministry of Commerce and Industry through DGFT (Directorate General of Foreign Trade)
Ministry of Finance through CBIC (customs administration)
Ministry of External Affairs through Trade Divisions
RBI through its Department of Foreign Exchange

explanation: Foreign Trade Policy (FTP): formulated and implemented by Ministry of Commerce and Industry through DGFT (Director General of Foreign Trade). FTP covers export promotion, import licensing, export obligation, SEIS, MEIS (now RoDTEP), duty-free import schemes. Latest: FTP 2023 (extended till 2028). Customs tariff/collection: Ministry of Finance (CBIC). RBI: manages forex under FEMA (current/capital account transactions).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) was established under:

options.option_text: IBC 2016 — as the regulatory authority overseeing insolvency professionals, IPAs, and information utilities
SARFAESI Act 2002 — for regulating bank NPA recovery
Companies Act 2013 — as part of corporate governance reforms
RBI Act 1934 — to regulate financial sector insolvencies

explanation: IBBI: established 1 October 2016 under IBC 2016. Functions: regulates Insolvency Professionals (IPs), Insolvency Professional Agencies (IPAs), Information Utilities (IUs). IPs conduct Corporate Insolvency Resolution Processes (CIRP). IBBI sets conduct standards, investigates malpractice, promotes education. The CIRP must complete in 180+90 days; beyond that, liquidation is triggered. IBBI reports to Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: What is 'Token Privatisation' or 'Disinvestment' as distinct from full privatisation?

options.option_text: Government sells minority stakes (below 50%) in PSUs through OFS/FPO without transferring management control
Government sells PSU to foreign investors for foreign exchange earnings
Government transfers only land assets of PSUs to private sector
Token payment by private sector for management rights without equity transfer

explanation: Minority disinvestment (token privatisation): government sells ≤49% stake through stock market (OFS — Offer for Sale, FPO — Follow-on Public Offer). Government retains management control (51%+). Strategic disinvestment (full privatisation): government sells majority stake + transfers management (e.g., Air India to Tata — 2022). India's DIPAM manages both. Revenue from disinvestment is a capital receipt (non-tax revenue receipt) used for fiscal deficit management.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' (Self-Reliant India) initiative launched in 2020 primarily aims to:

options.option_text: Boost domestic manufacturing and reduce import dependence across key sectors through PLI, SEZs, and supply chain localisation
Completely close India's economy to imports — full import substitution
Replace all foreign-owned companies with Indian-owned PSUs
Provide full economic self-sufficiency at village level through micro-enterprises

explanation: Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020, PM Modi post-COVID): not isolationism but strategic self-reliance — building resilient supply chains, reducing dependence on single-source imports (China), strengthening domestic manufacturing. Five pillars: Economy, Infrastructure, System, Demographics, Demand. Tools: PLI schemes (14 sectors), MSME support, defence indigenisation (70% domestic procurement target), critical minerals mission, semiconductor fab push.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is NOT a function of the RBI?

options.option_text: Providing housing loans to individual borrowers at subsidised interest rates
Acting as banker to the government
Managing the country's foreign exchange reserves
Issuing currency notes except ₹1 coin and note

explanation: RBI's core functions: (1) Currency issue (all notes except ₹1 note — that is Ministry of Finance). (2) Banker to Government (manages CFI, WMA, debt management). (3) Banker's Bank (lender of last resort, CRR custodian). (4) Monetary Policy. (5) Foreign Exchange Management. (6) Developmental role (NABARD, SIDBI set up by RBI). Housing loans to individuals is done by commercial banks/HFCs — not RBI's role.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Debt Management Cell (DMC) / Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) was proposed to be separated from RBI to:

options.option_text: Eliminate the conflict of interest — RBI managing government debt (cheaply) vs controlling inflation (higher rates), as both objectives can pull in opposite directions
Transfer government borrowing to private sector banks for efficiency
Merge all PSB debt management under one centralised government body
Allow RBI to focus solely on forex management after PDMA takes over monetary policy
