options.option_text: Registration and appointment for vaccination, digital certificate issuance, and real-time vaccine inventory tracking
Contact tracing of COVID-19 positive individuals and their close contacts
Distribution of COVID relief funds to beneficiaries through DBT
Telehealth consultations for COVID patients in remote areas

explanation: CoWIN (COVID Vaccine Intelligence Network): MoHFW platform for India's vaccination programme (world's largest). Features: Citizen registration (via Aadhaar/DigiLocker), appointment booking at nearest centre, dose tracking, real-time vaccine inventory, digital vaccination certificate (verifiable via DigiLocker/Aarogya Setu). Handled 2+ billion doses. WHO signed agreement with India to create a global version of CoWIN platform. Contact tracing was Aarogya Setu; Cash transfers were through PFMS/DBT.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Passport Seva Project (online passport application) is an example of which type of e-Governance interaction?

options.option_text: G2C (Government to Citizen) — citizens apply online for passports, reducing physical visits and wait times
G2B (Government to Business) — passport is issued to businesses for trade
G2G (Government to Government) — MEA shares data with police and immigration
G2E (Government to Employee) — for government employees needing travel documents

explanation: Passport Seva (Ministry of External Affairs): G2C example. Features: online application, appointment booking at Passport Seva Kendra, real-time status tracking, SMS/email updates, integration with police verification, Aadhaar-based identity verification. Launched 2010. Reduced average passport processing time from 45 days to 7-10 days. Over 10 crore passports issued through the system. It has a G2G component (MEA to police) internally, but the primary interaction mode is G2C.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'e-Office' initiative of Government of India aims to:

options.option_text: Reduce dependency on physical files by converting noting, drafting, and file movement to a digital workflow within government offices
Provide office automation software for small businesses under MSME scheme
Create co-working spaces for government employees in tier-2 cities
Digitise the National Archives for historical government documents

explanation: e-Office (NIC): G2G application for internal government workflow digitisation. Features: Electronic file movement, noting, drafting, approvals (replacing physical noting sheets), digital signatures, SLA tracking for file disposal, DMS (Document Management System). Reduces paper consumption, speeds up decision-making, enables work from any location, creates audit trail. Mandated for central ministries; adopted by many state governments. Mission Mode Project under Digital India.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'National Digital Health Mission (NDHM)', now called Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), aims to create:

options.option_text: An Ayushman Bharat Health Account (ABHA) — a unique health ID for every citizen linking their health records across providers digitally
A national chain of digital health clinics in rural areas
An AI-based diagnostic system replacing doctors in primary health centres
A national database of drug prices and pharmaceutical supply chains

explanation: ABDM (Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, launched 2021): Creates digital health ecosystem. Components: ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) = 14-digit health ID for every citizen. Health Facility Registry (HFR) — all hospitals, clinics, labs registered. Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR) — all doctors and health workers. Personal Health Records (PHR) — patients can link, view, share records. Health Claim Data Exchange. Vision: any doctor can access patient's health history with consent — ending repeated tests, improving care continuity.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Facial Recognition Technology (FRT)' used in NAFRS (National Automated Facial Recognition System) by NCRB raises concerns about:

options.option_text: Privacy, algorithmic bias (higher error rates for darker skin tones and women), and surveillance without adequate legal framework or judicial oversight
Technical incompatibility with existing police databases
High cost of implementation across all police stations
Low accuracy in identifying criminals in bright daylight conditions

explanation: NAFRS (National Crime Records Bureau): FRT for criminal identification, missing persons, verification at events. Concerns: (1) Privacy (facial data is biometric, sensitive) — no specific legal framework. (2) Algorithmic bias — international studies show higher error rates for women, darker skin tones → wrongful arrests. (3) No regulation — unlike DPDP Act which focuses on data storage, not active surveillance. NITI Aayog (2021) discussed national data governance framework. This is a live policy debate in India as of 2025.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Common Service Centres (CSCs)' in India serve as:

options.option_text: Village-level IT service delivery points (over 5 lakh centres) enabling rural citizens to access e-governance, banking, education, health, and utility services without traveling to cities
Centralised data centres maintained by NIC for storing government data
Common examination centres for government recruitment tests
Service tax collection points for small businesses in rural areas

explanation: CSCs (Common Service Centres): Scheme under Digital India. Village-Level Entrepreneur (VLE) runs each CSC as a business. Services: Aadhaar enrolment/updates, PAN card, passport application, insurance, banking (Business Correspondents), e-District services (certificates), education (PM e-Vidya), health (tele-consultation), Agriculture services (soil health cards, weather data), utility bill payments, G2C services. Over 5.5 lakh CSCs at gram panchayat level. CSC 2.0 (2015): expanded coverage.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'e-Governance Standards' in India (like metadata standards, interoperability frameworks) are issued by:

options.option_text: MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and IT) — issues technical standards and policies for e-governance applications
BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) — sets all technology standards including for e-governance
TRAI — as the telecom regulator overseeing digital communication standards
NIC — as the implementation agency that also sets the standards

explanation: MeitY (Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology): policy-making ministry for IT sector. Issues: e-Governance Standards (metadata, interoperability), Open Standards Policy (for government software), Cloud Policy (MeghRaj), Data Centre Policy, Electronic Signature Standards, Mobile Governance Framework. Also nodal ministry for IT Act 2000, Aadhaar Act, DPDP Act 2023, CERT-In, NIC, STQC (Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification). Different from TRAI (telecom tariff/service regulation).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Meghraj' initiative by MeitY refers to:

options.option_text: Government Cloud computing platform — providing government departments with secure, scalable cloud infrastructure hosted within India's data sovereignty boundary
A weather forecasting system using cloud data for agriculture
A cloud-based payroll management system for government employees
India's national satellite data cloud for remote sensing applications

explanation: MeghRaj (Cloud Raja = Government Cloud): MeitY's government cloud policy (2014). Enables government departments to use cloud computing securely. Empanelled Cloud Service Providers (AWS, Azure, GCP, NIC Cloud, BSNL) can serve government after meeting security standards. Benefits: On-demand scalability, cost savings vs dedicated servers, disaster recovery. Data residency: government data must remain within India. GI Cloud empanelment process ensures only compliant providers. Aligns with Digital India data localisation goals.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Section 43A of the IT Act 2000 (added in 2008 amendment) deals with:

options.option_text: Compensation for failure to protect sensitive personal data — corporate bodies handling 'sensitive personal data' can be held liable for damages if they fail to maintain 'reasonable security practices'
Criminal punishment for hacking into government computer systems
Intellectual property rights for software and digital content
Licensing requirements for internet service providers

explanation: Section 43A (IT Act, added 2008): Body corporate handling 'sensitive personal data or information' (passwords, financial data, health data, biometrics) must implement and maintain 'reasonable security practices and procedures.' If they're negligent → they must compensate the person affected. The IT (Reasonable Security Practices) Rules 2011 define what 'reasonable security' means. This pre-dates DPDP Act 2023 as India's first data protection provision, though narrower in scope.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'National Cyber Security Policy (NCSP) 2013' was released to:

options.option_text: Create a secure computing environment, build capacities to prevent and respond to cyber threats, and reduce national vulnerability to cyber attacks across critical infrastructure
Regulate social media platforms and online content
Mandate cybersecurity standards only for banking sector
Set rules for e-commerce platforms and online marketplaces

explanation: NCSP 2013 (MeitY): First comprehensive national cybersecurity policy. Key objectives: Secure government/critical infrastructure cyberspace, Build national cyber security capability (security workforce, CERT-In strengthening), Reduce vulnerabilities, Promote R&D, Establish multi-stakeholder approach. CERT-In (notified agency), NTRO (National Technical Research Organisation), NCIIPC (National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre) are key bodies. Updated frameworks: Cyber Surakshit Bharat (2018), National Cyber Security Strategy (being updated).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Bank committed an error: credited the firm's account ₹2,000 instead of ₹200 (a factor of 10 transposition). This error in the Pass Book will mean:

options.option_text: Pass Book balance is OVERSTATED by ₹1,800 — in BRS, deduct ₹1,800 from PB to reach correct figure
Cash Book balance is overstated by ₹1,800
No BRS effect — bank errors don't affect reconciliation
Add ₹1,800 to Cash Book balance in BRS

explanation: Bank error overstated the PB by ₹2,000 − ₹200 = ₹1,800. The CB correctly shows ₹200 received. In BRS starting from CB balance: add ₹1,800 to CB to reach (wrong) PB; OR starting from PB: deduct ₹1,800 to reach CB. The bank must also be informed to reverse the error.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A 'Blank Endorsement' on a Bill of Exchange means:

options.option_text: The holder signs the back without naming the endorsee — making the bill payable to bearer and negotiable by delivery alone
The bill is endorsed but the amount is left blank to be filled later
The endorsement is cancelled and the bill returned to the drawer
The endorsee's name is written but the signature is missing

explanation: Blank Endorsement: holder signs the back WITHOUT naming an endorsee → bill becomes payable to bearer → can pass by delivery without further endorsement. Full Endorsement: names specific endorsee ('Pay to X'). Special Crossing on cheques ≠ blank endorsement. Under NI Act, blank endorsement converts order instruments to bearer instruments.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A cheque for ₹15,000 issued by the firm was presented to the bank and DISHONOURED due to insufficient funds. The firm's Cash Book already showed it as a payment. In BRS (starting from CB):

options.option_text: Add back ₹15,000 to CB balance — bank returned cheque unpaid, so PB shows no debit, but CB already shows a credit (payment)
Deduct ₹15,000 from CB balance
No adjustment — dishonoured cheques are ignored in BRS
Deduct ₹15,000 from PB balance

explanation: Dishonoured cheque issued: CB was credited (payment recorded) but bank refused payment → PB has no debit. CB is LOWER than it should be (payment was never actually made). BRS from CB: add ₹15,000 (dishonoured issuing). Separately, firm must reverse the CB entry: Dr Bank A/c | Cr Creditor A/c (or whomever was paid).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Bills discounted with the bank that mature during the period and are duly honoured by the acceptor — effect on BRS:

options.option_text: No effect on BRS — the bank already paid the firm when discounting; on maturity the bank collects from acceptor independently
Add the face value to CB balance — bank credits on maturity
Deduct discount charges from CB balance on maturity date
Add discount charges back to CB on the date of maturity

explanation: When a bill is DISCOUNTED: firm already received net proceeds → entry made in CB. On maturity: bank collects face value from acceptor — this is the bank's recovery of its advance. No new CB entry needed on maturity (unless the bill is DISHONOURED). Hence, duly honoured discounted bills cause NO BRS difference.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening balance of Suspense Account is Dr ₹5,000. During rectification, a one-sided error is found: Purchases undercasted ₹2,000 (Dr side short). After correcting this, the Suspense Account balance will be:

options.option_text: Dr ₹3,000 (original Dr balance ₹5,000 − Cr entry ₹2,000 to rectify)
Nil — one error clears the suspense

explanation: Suspense has Dr balance ₹5,000 (meaning Dr side was short by ₹5,000 total). Purchases undercasted: Dr side was short by ₹2,000. Rectification: Dr Purchases ₹2,000 | Cr Suspense ₹2,000. After: Suspense balance = Dr 5,000 − Cr 2,000 = Dr ₹3,000. Remaining ₹3,000 Dr balance in Suspense = still undetected errors on the Dr side.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A bill is due on 15 March (including 3 days grace). 15 March is a public holiday. When is the bill payable?

options.option_text: 14 March — the preceding business day (NI Act: if due date is a holiday, pay on the immediately preceding business day)
16 March — the next business day after the holiday
15 March — public holidays don't affect bill maturity dates
18 March — add 3 more grace days since the original due date was a holiday

explanation: NI Act Section 25: if the day on which a bill falls due is a public holiday (or Bank Holiday), the bill becomes due on the PRECEDING business day. This is opposite to what many expect (i.e., NOT the next business day). Example: due 15 March (holiday) → payable 14 March (or 13 March if 14th is also a holiday).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a partnership firm, the Profit & Loss Appropriation Account is prepared AFTER the P&L Account to distribute net profit. Which item does NOT appear in P&L Appropriation Account?

options.option_text: Salaries paid to non-partner employees
Partner's salary as per deed
Interest on partners' capital
Partners' share of profit/loss

explanation: P&L Appropriation Account distributes NET PROFIT among partners. It includes: interest on capital, partner's salary (per deed), partner's commission, transfer to reserves, and share of profit. Salaries to non-partner employees are a BUSINESS EXPENSE charged to P&L Account (before appropriation). The appropriation account starts with net profit brought from P&L.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Manufacturing Account is prepared by a manufacturing firm. 'Cost of Production' transferred from Manufacturing Account to Trading Account equals:

options.option_text: Raw Materials consumed + Direct Labour + Factory Overhead + Opening WIP − Closing WIP
Raw Materials purchased + Direct Labour only (no overhead)
Total manufacturing costs without WIP adjustment
Net Sales minus Gross Profit (working backwards)

explanation: Manufacturing Account: Dr side: Opening WIP + Raw Materials consumed (Opening RM + Purchases − Closing RM) + Direct Labour + Factory/Manufacturing Overhead. Cr side: Closing WIP + Cost of Production (transferred to Trading A/c). Cost of Production = Total manufacturing costs + Opening WIP − Closing WIP. This enters Trading A/c as 'goods manufactured' replacing 'Purchases' for manufactured firms.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Advance received from a customer ₹15,000 for goods to be delivered next year appears in the Balance Sheet as:

options.option_text: Current Liability — Advance from Customer (income not yet earned)
Current Asset — prepaid income owed to the customer
Non-current liability — long-term obligation to customer
Revenue in P&L — cash received so income is recognised

explanation: Advance from customer: cash received but goods not yet delivered → obligation exists → LIABILITY. Current liability since goods will be delivered next year (within 12 months). This is different from: Income received in advance (for services) — also a current liability. The advance is NOT income yet (realization concept: income recognised only when earned = goods delivered).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm's Trial Balance shows: Debtors ₹1,80,000; Bad Debts ₹5,000; Provision for BD ₹8,000. Additional: further bad debts ₹3,000; provision to be maintained at 5% on debtors. P&L debit for bad debts and provision = ?

options.option_text: ₹11,600 (BD ₹3,000 + increase in provision: new provision = 5%×(1,80,000−3,000) = 8,850; increase = 8,850−8,000 = 850; total = 3,850; wait: TB already shows BD ₹5,000 and provision ₹8,000 as existing — so net: fresh BD ₹3,000 + (new provision 8,850 − existing 8,000) = ₹3,850)
₹3,850 (fresh bad debts ₹3,000 + increase in provision ₹850 after netting existing provision)
₹8,850 (full new provision only)
₹16,850 (all three items added: BD 5,000 + BD 3,000 + new provision 8,850)

explanation: The ₹5,000 bad debts in TB are already in the debit column (already charged). Fresh additional bad debts: ₹3,000 (adjustment). Debtors after all BD = 1,80,000 − 3,000 = ₹1,77,000. New provision = 5% × 1,77,000 = ₹8,850. Existing provision = ₹8,000. Increase in provision = ₹850. Total additional P&L debit = ₹3,000 + ₹850 = ₹3,850. The TB's ₹5,000 BD is already captured in the trial balance figures.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Stock worth ₹20,000 was destroyed in fire. Insurance company admitted only ₹14,000. Goods were purchased on credit (creditor still to be paid). Adjusting entries affect:

options.option_text: Trading A/c (remove destroyed stock from closing stock), P&L A/c (loss ₹6,000), and Balance Sheet (insurance receivable ₹14,000 as asset)
Only Trading A/c — deduct from closing stock
Only P&L A/c — entire ₹20,000 is a loss
Balance Sheet only — write down stock

explanation: Fire loss treatment: (1) Remove ₹20,000 from Closing Stock (it no longer exists). (2) Dr Insurance Receivable ₹14,000 (asset — claim admitted). (3) Dr Loss by Fire ₹6,000 (P&L — unrecovered loss). Cr Trading Account ₹20,000 (stock removed). The creditor is still owed money separately (buying on credit created a separate liability unaffected by the fire).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A piece of machinery worth ₹50,000 (BV) was brought in by the proprietor from personal assets into the business. The journal entry in business books:

options.option_text: Machinery A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Capital A/c ₹50,000 (capital contribution in kind)
Machinery A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Cash A/c ₹50,000
Capital A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹50,000
Drawings A/c Dr ₹50,000 | To Machinery A/c ₹50,000

explanation: Proprietor introduces personal asset into business = Capital contribution in kind. Business gets machinery (asset ↑ Dr) and owner's capital increases (Cr Capital A/c). This is the opposite of drawings. If instead the proprietor takes a business asset for personal use → Dr Drawings A/c | Cr Asset A/c.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Goods worth ₹10,000 (cost price) are used for advertising purposes (sent as free samples). Journal entry:

options.option_text: Advertisement Expenses A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Purchases A/c ₹10,000
Drawings A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Sales A/c ₹10,000
Advertisement A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Sales A/c ₹10,000
Free Samples A/c Dr ₹10,000 | To Cash A/c ₹10,000

explanation: Goods used for advertisement (free samples): Dr Advertisement Expenses A/c (indirect expense → P&L) | Cr Purchases A/c at cost. Credited to Purchases (not Sales) since no revenue is earned. Not Drawings (that's personal use, not business promotion). The cost is expensed as advertising, reducing both purchases and COGS.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Partners A, B, C share profits 3:2:1. Net profit = ₹1,20,000. Partner B is entitled to a salary of ₹18,000 and interest on capital ₹12,000. After appropriation, B's share of remaining profit = ?

options.option_text: ₹40,000 (2/6 of total profit without deducting salary and interest)
₹60,000 (including salary and interest)
₹20,000 (after deducting only salary)

explanation: P&L Appropriation: Total profit ₹1,20,000. Less: B's salary ₹18,000 + B's interest on capital ₹12,000 = ₹30,000. Remaining divisible profit = ₹90,000. B's profit share = 2/6 × ₹90,000 = ₹30,000. Total B's earnings = 18,000 + 12,000 + 30,000 = ₹60,000. A gets 3/6 × 90,000 = ₹45,000. C gets 1/6 × 90,000 = ₹15,000.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm has Current Assets ₹6,00,000 and Current Ratio is 2:1. If Current Liabilities increase by ₹50,000 due to outstanding expenses, the new Current Ratio will be:

options.option_text: 1.71:1 (Current Liabilities = 3,00,000 + 50,000 = 3,50,000; new CR = 6,50,000 ÷ 3,50,000) — wait: CA also increases by 50,000 as expenses accrue? No — outstanding expenses: CL ↑ and P&L debit ↑ (reduces profit/capital) but CA unchanged. CR = 6,00,000 / 3,50,000 = 1.71)
2:1 (unchanged)
2.17:1 (both sides increase)

explanation: CR = 2:1 with CA = ₹6,00,000 → CL = ₹3,00,000. Outstanding expenses: CL ↑ ₹50,000 (new CL = ₹3,50,000). CA does NOT change (accrued expense is a liability, not asset). New CR = 6,00,000 / 3,50,000 ≈ 1.71:1. When a current liability increases without a corresponding current asset increase, the Current Ratio falls.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Accrued salaries at year end were NOT recorded. This omission will cause:

options.option_text: Net Profit overstated and Current Liabilities understated by the same amount
Net Profit understated and Current Assets overstated
Only Balance Sheet is affected — P&L is not
No effect — accrued salaries are only recorded when paid

explanation: Accrued salaries not recorded: Salary expense is understated → Net Profit overstated. Outstanding Salary (current liability) not shown → CL understated. Both sides of the Balance Sheet are wrong: Capital overstated (due to higher NP) and CL understated. The dual effect is always on P&L (wrong) + Balance Sheet (wrong CL).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A ₹10,000 loan from the proprietor to the business is shown as 'Loan from Proprietor' on the Balance Sheet because:

options.option_text: Business Entity concept — the loan is a distinct liability of the firm to the owner, separate from capital
It is merged with Capital Account since both belong to the owner
Loans from owners are always shown as equity, not debt
It is treated as a non-current asset lent to the proprietor

explanation: Business Entity concept: firm and owner are separate. If the owner LENDS money (beyond capital contribution) at an agreed interest rate, it is a LOAN to the business → shown as a liability (Loan from Proprietor). Interest on it is a business expense (P&L debit). This differs from Capital (permanent contribution with profit-sharing). The loan is repayable; capital is not.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening debtors ₹40,000; Credit sales ₹2,00,000; Cash collected from debtors ₹1,90,000; Bad debts ₹5,000; Discount allowed ₹2,000. Closing debtors = ?

options.option_text: ₹43,000 (Opening + Credit Sales − Cash collected − Bad debts − Discount = 40,000 + 2,00,000 − 1,90,000 − 5,000 − 2,000 = 43,000)

explanation: Debtors Control Account: Opening ₹40,000 + Credit Sales ₹2,00,000 = ₹2,40,000. Less: Cash collected ₹1,90,000 + Bad debts ₹5,000 + Discount ₹2,000 = ₹1,97,000. Closing Debtors = 2,40,000 − 1,97,000 = ₹43,000. This is the debtor control account (or sales ledger control) technique for finding closing debtors.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: When is a Revaluation Reserve created in company accounts?

options.option_text: When a fixed asset is revalued upward (increase in carrying amount recognised as other comprehensive income under Ind AS 16)
When the company revises its accounting policies
When provisions are made in excess of actual losses
When bonus shares are issued using undistributed profits

explanation: Revaluation Reserve (Ind AS 16 / AS 10 Revised): when a company revalues its PPE upward, the surplus is credited to Revaluation Reserve (Other Comprehensive Income under Ind AS). It is NOT available for dividend distribution. If asset is later sold or impaired, revaluation surplus is transferred directly to retained earnings. In partnership accounts: Revaluation Account is used on admission/retirement/death of partners.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A company's total assets = ₹25,00,000. Non-current liabilities = ₹5,00,000. Current liabilities = ₹4,00,000. Share Capital = ₹8,00,000. Reserves and Surplus = ?
explanation: Balance Sheet equation: Total Assets = Total Liabilities + Shareholders' Funds. Shareholders' Funds = Share Capital + Reserves & Surplus. 25,00,000 = 5,00,000 + 4,00,000 + 8,00,000 + R&S. R&S = 25,00,000 − 17,00,000 = ₹8,00,000. This 'missing figure' approach is standard in Balance Sheet analysis questions.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following is TRUE about the Balance Sheet prepared under Companies Act Schedule III?

options.option_text: It follows 'Order of Permanence' for assets — Non-Current Assets listed before Current Assets
It follows 'Order of Liquidity' — Cash listed first, Fixed Assets last
Assets and Liabilities are presented horizontally side by side
Goodwill is always shown separately as the first asset regardless of format

explanation: Schedule III (Companies Act 2013) Balance Sheet: Vertical format. Equity and Liabilities: (1) Shareholders' Funds, (2) Non-Current Liabilities, (3) Current Liabilities. Assets: (1) Non-Current Assets (PPE first, then investments, other NCAs), (2) Current Assets. This is 'Order of Permanence' (most permanent first). Sole traders/partnerships use horizontal format with 'Order of Liquidity' (most liquid first).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under 'Component Accounting' (Ind AS 16), an aircraft's engine costing ₹5 crore with a 10-year life and fuselage costing ₹20 crore with a 25-year life should be:

options.option_text: Depreciated separately — different components with different useful lives must be depreciated individually
Depreciated together at the aircraft's total cost with blended average life of 22 years
Fully expensed in the year of purchase since aircraft are complex assets
Depreciated only on the fuselage; engine is treated as maintenance cost

explanation: Component Accounting (Ind AS 16, mandatory for companies): each significant component of an asset with a different useful life must be depreciated separately. Engine (10 years) and fuselage (25 years) are separate components of the aircraft. This provides more accurate expense matching. Under older AS 10 (pre-revision), blended depreciation was common. Component accounting was a major change brought by Ind AS.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: An asset's carrying amount = ₹3,00,000. Remaining useful life = 3 years. Management revises the residual value upward from ₹20,000 to ₹50,000 at the start of year 4. Revised annual SLM depreciation from year 4 = ?

options.option_text: ₹1,00,000 (3,00,000 / 3 ignoring residual)
₹76,667 (using wrong formula)

explanation: Change in residual value estimate = change in accounting estimate (prospective). From year 4: Revised depreciable amount = Carrying amount − New residual value = 3,00,000 − 50,000 = ₹2,50,000. Revised annual dep = 2,50,000 / 3 remaining years = ₹83,333. No retroactive adjustment to past depreciation. This is per AS 5 / Ind AS 8 (change in estimate = prospective application).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm's stock was destroyed by flood. From records: Sales ₹5,00,000 (at 25% GP on cost). Opening Stock ₹80,000. Purchases ₹3,60,000. Salvaged stock ₹10,000. Insurance claim = ?

options.option_text: ₹30,000 (Expected closing stock ₹40,000 − salvaged ₹10,000 = ₹30,000 lost)
₹40,000 (entire expected closing stock)
₹1,00,000 (total opening stock plus purchases)

explanation: GP on COST 25% → GP on sales = 25/125 = 20%. COGS = 80% × 5,00,000 = ₹4,00,000. Expected closing stock = Opening + Purchases − COGS = 80,000 + 3,60,000 − 4,00,000 = ₹40,000. Stock lost in flood = Expected CS − Salvaged = 40,000 − 10,000 = ₹30,000. Insurance claim = ₹30,000 (assuming fully insured).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the Specific Identification Method of inventory costing, cost is:

options.option_text: Assigned to specific physical items — each unit is tracked individually and valued at its actual purchase cost
Averaged across all units purchased during the period
Assigned to the oldest units first (earliest purchased)
Assigned to the most recently purchased units first

explanation: Specific Identification: each individual item is tracked to its specific cost. Appropriate for: expensive unique items (jewellery, art, custom-built machinery, luxury cars). Not practical for homogeneous, high-volume goods (cannot distinguish one unit of rice from another). Gives exact COGS matching. IFRS and AS 2 both permit this method for unique items.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Gross Profit method' of estimating inventory (when physical count is not possible) uses:

options.option_text: Historical GP ratio applied to net sales to estimate COGS, then back-calculate closing stock from opening stock and purchases
Current replacement cost of all items in the inventory list
Standard cost card for each product multiplied by counted units
A management estimate based on last year's closing stock

explanation: Gross Profit Method (for interim stock estimates or fire loss): Estimate COGS = Sales × (1 − historical GP ratio). Closing Stock = Opening Stock + Purchases − Estimated COGS. Used when physical count is impossible (fire, theft) and for quarterly financial statements. It's an ESTIMATE — not acceptable for year-end statutory accounts where physical verification is required.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: On 1 April 2024, a machine cost ₹1,20,000 was purchased. WDV rate 20% p.a. Full year depreciation in year 1 = ₹24,000. Firm's year ends 31 March. Machine sold on 30 September 2025 for ₹90,000. Profit or Loss on sale?

options.option_text: Profit ₹5,600 (WDV at sale: 1,20,000 − 24,000 = 96,000 after Year 1; 6 months dep Year 2: 20%×96,000×6/12 = 9,600; WDV = 86,400; Sale 90,000 − WDV 86,400 = Profit 3,600) — wait: let me recalculate: Year 1 dep = 24,000; WDV = 96,000. Year 2 (6 months Apr-Sep 2025): dep = 20%×96,000×6/12 = 9,600. WDV on sale = 86,400. Profit = 90,000 − 86,400 = ₹3,600
Profit ₹3,600
Loss ₹6,000
Profit ₹6,000

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm's stock includes 500 units of Product X. Cost ₹200/unit. NRV: Selling price ₹190/unit, selling costs ₹15/unit. At what value should Product X appear in closing stock?

options.option_text: ₹95,000 (500 × ₹190, ignoring selling costs)
₹92,500 (500 × ₹185, partial selling cost deduction)

explanation: NRV = Estimated selling price − Estimated costs to complete − Estimated selling costs = ₹190 − ₹15 = ₹175. Cost = ₹200. Lower of Cost or NRV = ₹175. Stock value = 500 × ₹175 = ₹87,500. Write-down per unit = ₹25. Total write-down = ₹12,500 charged to P&L. This is a loss due to obsolescence/price decline.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A mine costs ₹50,00,000 and is estimated to contain 10,00,000 tonnes of ore. During the year, 2,50,000 tonnes are extracted. Depletion for the year = ?

options.option_text: ₹5,00,000 (10% of cost per year)
₹10,00,000 (straight line over 5 years)
₹2,50,000 (₹1/tonne flat rate)

explanation: Depletion method: Rate = (Cost − Salvage) / Total estimated output = ₹50,00,000 / 10,00,000 tonnes = ₹5 per tonne. Annual depletion = Actual production × Rate = 2,50,000 × ₹5 = ₹12,50,000. Remaining value after year 1 = 50,00,000 − 12,50,000 = ₹37,50,000. Next year depletion depends on that year's actual extraction.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A Bin Card in stores management records:

options.option_text: Quantity of each item received, issued, and balance — maintained at the physical storage location for each bin/shelf
Value and quantity of items in the stores maintained by the accounts department
Reorder levels and EOQ for each item of inventory
The name and address of suppliers for each item

explanation: Bin Card: maintained at the physical storage bin/shelf. Records QUANTITY only — receipts, issues, balance. Maintained by the storekeeper. Stores Ledger: maintained by the accounts/cost department. Records both QUANTITY and VALUE (FIFO/WA). The two should agree in quantity. Perpetual inventory involves reconciling bin cards with stores ledger records to catch discrepancies quickly.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The difference between GROSS block and NET block of fixed assets in a company's Balance Sheet represents:

options.option_text: Accumulated Depreciation — the total depreciation charged since acquisition
Capital Work in Progress not yet capitalised
Impairment loss recognised during the current year
The current year's depreciation charge only

explanation: Gross Block = Total cost of all fixed assets. Accumulated Depreciation = total depreciation from purchase to date. Net Block (Written Down Value) = Gross Block − Accumulated Depreciation. Companies Act Schedule III requires disclosure of both Gross Block and Net Block (with accumulated depreciation shown separately). Investors use this to assess asset age and replacement needs.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Reorder Level (ROL) in inventory management is calculated as:

options.option_text: Maximum Lead Time × Maximum Consumption per day (ensures stock never runs out even in worst case)
Average Lead Time × Average Consumption (economic estimate)
EOQ divided by the number of working days in the year
Minimum consumption × Minimum lead time (worst-case shortfall)

explanation: Reorder Level = Maximum Lead Time × Maximum Consumption per day. This ensures that even in worst case (longest lead time, highest demand), stock doesn't run out before replenishment arrives. Also: Reorder Level = Minimum Stock + Average Lead Time × Average Consumption (another common formula). When inventory falls to reorder level, a purchase order is placed for EOQ quantity.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: As per AS 10 (Revised), which costs are included in the COST of an item of Property, Plant and Equipment?

options.option_text: Purchase price + import duties + non-refundable taxes + directly attributable costs to bring asset to working condition and location
Purchase price only — all other costs are period expenses
Purchase price + annual maintenance costs over useful life
Replacement cost at current prices, regardless of actual purchase price

explanation: Cost of PPE (AS 10 Revised / Ind AS 16): (a) Purchase price minus trade discounts and rebates. (b) Import duties and non-refundable purchase taxes. (c) Directly attributable costs: site preparation, delivery, installation, professional fees, testing. NOT included: general overhead, admin costs, start-up costs, initial operating losses, training costs. The asset is ready for intended use when capitalisation ceases.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Annual demand (D) = 12,000 units. Ordering cost (S) = ₹300 per order. Holding cost (H) = ₹6 per unit per year. EOQ = ?

options.option_text: 2,000 units
500 units
1,200 units

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Consignment inventory — goods held by a retailer on behalf of the manufacturer — is included in whose closing stock?

options.option_text: The CONSIGNOR (manufacturer/supplier) — title passes only when retailer sells to end customer
The CONSIGNEE (retailer) — since goods are physically at their premises
Split 50/50 between consignor and consignee
Neither — consignment goods are off-balance-sheet until sold

explanation: Consignment: legal title remains with the CONSIGNOR until goods are sold by the consignee to end customers. Hence, unsold consignment goods are in CONSIGNOR's closing stock (at cost). Consignee includes in stock only goods they own outright. This is consistent with the legal definition of stock: goods where title (ownership) belongs to you.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club pays honorarium of ₹5,000 to a visiting guest lecturer. This is treated as:

options.option_text: Expenditure in I&E Account — an expense for services rendered (not a salary since the person is not a regular employee)
Drawings — since it reduces the club's surplus
Capital expenditure — knowledge gained is a long-term benefit
Donation — a gift from the club to the lecturer

explanation: Honorarium in NPO: payment to a non-employee for professional service (guest lecture, medical consultation, legal advice). Treated as Expenditure in I&E Account (not salary since no employer-employee relationship, not donation since service is received). Deducted as TDS under Income Tax Act Section 194J (professional fees). Different from salary to permanent staff.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A sports club has: Subscriptions received ₹80,000; Entrance fees ₹10,000 (treated as capital); Tournament receipts ₹25,000; Tournament expenses ₹18,000; Salaries ₹30,000; Depreciation ₹5,000. Surplus/Deficit for the year (excluding capital receipts from I&E) = ?

options.option_text: Surplus ₹52,000 (I&E income: subscriptions ₹80,000 + tournament receipts ₹25,000 = ₹1,05,000; I&E expenses: tournament ₹18,000 + salaries ₹30,000 + depreciation ₹5,000 = ₹53,000; Surplus = 1,05,000 − 53,000 = ₹52,000)
Surplus ₹62,000 (including entrance fees)
Surplus ₹47,000
Deficit ₹3,000

explanation: Entrance fees ₹10,000 → Capital Receipt → Capital Fund (NOT in I&E). I&E Account: Income side: Subscriptions ₹80,000 + Tournament receipts ₹25,000 = ₹1,05,000. Expenditure side: Tournament exp ₹18,000 + Salaries ₹30,000 + Depreciation ₹5,000 = ₹53,000. Surplus = ₹52,000. This surplus is added to Capital Fund in the Balance Sheet.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A club maintains a Building Fund of ₹5,00,000 collected specifically for constructing a new building. During the year, ₹4,00,000 is spent on construction. How are these shown?

options.option_text: Dr Building Fund ₹4,00,000 | Cr Building A/c ₹4,00,000; Balance Building Fund ₹1,00,000 remains on liability side of Balance Sheet
Dr I&E Account ₹4,00,000 (capital expenditure in NPO is an expense)
Dr Building A/c ₹4,00,000 | Cr Capital Fund ₹4,00,000
Expenditure ₹4,00,000 written off in the year; fund remains unchanged

explanation: Specific fund usage: When money from Building Fund is spent → Dr Building Fund (reduces the specific liability) | Cr Building A/c (capital asset created). Remaining Building Fund ₹1,00,000 stays on liability side until fully utilised. The Building A/c (₹4,00,000) is a fixed asset on the asset side. No P&L effect — capital fund directly funds the asset.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A hospital (NPO) receives ₹2,00,000 for purchasing medical equipment from a government grant earmarked for that purpose. It spends ₹1,50,000 on equipment. The I&E Account shows:

options.option_text: No direct effect — the grant and expenditure net off in the specific fund; only depreciation on the equipment appears in I&E
Income of ₹2,00,000 and expenditure of ₹1,50,000 — showing net surplus of ₹50,000
Income of ₹2,00,000 only — expenditure is capitalised
Expenditure of ₹1,50,000 only — grant is a capital receipt not in I&E

explanation: Specific grant for capital purpose: Grant → Dr Cash | Cr Equipment Fund (specific fund). Expenditure → Dr Equipment A/c | Cr Cash (or Dr Equipment Fund). The fund is reduced by the asset purchased. Net: asset on asset side, remaining fund on liability side. I&E shows only annual DEPRECIATION on the equipment. This is the deferral (capital grant) approach.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Opening Capital Fund = ₹8,00,000. During the year: Surplus from I&E = ₹60,000; Life membership fees = ₹30,000; Legacy = ₹50,000; Sports equipment purchased from general funds = ₹25,000. Closing Capital Fund = ?

options.option_text: ₹9,40,000 (8,00,000 + 60,000 + 30,000 + 50,000 = ₹9,40,000; equipment purchase doesn't reduce capital fund)
₹9,15,000 (deducting equipment purchase)
₹8,60,000 (only surplus added)
₹9,65,000 (adding all items)

explanation: Capital Fund increases by: Surplus (₹60,000) + Capital receipts (Life membership ₹30,000 + Legacy ₹50,000) = ₹1,40,000. Equipment purchase from general funds: Dr Equipment A/c | Cr Cash — this is an asset purchase, NOT a reduction in Capital Fund. Closing CF = 8,00,000 + 1,40,000 = ₹9,40,000. The equipment appears as fixed asset on the asset side of Balance Sheet.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which of the following distinguishes an NPO's Balance Sheet from that of a profit-seeking firm?

options.option_text: NPO has 'Capital Fund' instead of 'Proprietor's Capital'; 'Surplus' instead of 'Net Profit'; and may have specific funds on liability side
NPO Balance Sheet has no fixed assets — all assets are current
NPO Balance Sheet is prepared on cash basis — no accrual adjustments
NPO Balance Sheet does not show liabilities — only assets

explanation: NPO Balance Sheet differences: (1) Capital Fund / General Fund instead of Capital. (2) Specific Funds (Building Fund, Prize Fund, Tournament Fund) on liability side. (3) No Share Capital or Share Premium. (4) Surplus/Deficit instead of Profit/Loss. (5) Format is similar but terminology differs. NPO BS is still prepared on accrual basis and shows both assets and liabilities.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament that examines CAG reports consists of how many members and from which Houses?

options.option_text: 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha + 7 from Rajya Sabha, chaired by a member of the opposition
15 members: all from Lok Sabha, chaired by Speaker
30 members: equal representation from both Houses
7 members: Finance Committee senior members only

explanation: PAC (Public Accounts Committee): 22 members — 15 from Lok Sabha, 7 from Rajya Sabha. Chaired by a LEADER OF OPPOSITION (member from opposition party) — a convention since 1967 to ensure independence. PAC examines CAG reports, questions departments on irregularities, and issues Action Taken Reports. All PAC sittings are in camera. State Legislative PACs have similar composition.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG audits autonomous bodies that receive substantial grants from the government. The threshold is:

options.option_text: Grants ≥ ₹25 lakh OR ≥ 75% of expenditure — either condition makes the body subject to CAG audit
Grants exceeding ₹1 crore — only large grants attract CAG audit
100% government funding only — partial grants are not audited
Any government grant, however small, triggers mandatory CAG audit

explanation: Under Section 14/15 of the CAG (DPC) Act 1971: Bodies substantially financed by government grants are subject to CAG audit. The threshold: grant ≥ ₹25 lakh OR grant forms ≥ 75% of total expenditure. This covers universities, research institutes, NGOs, and autonomous bodies receiving substantial central/state government funding. CAG audit in such cases is in addition to any statutory audit.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In CAG's performance audit, the 3E framework is used. Which is the correct definition of 'Economy'?

options.option_text: Minimising the cost of inputs to produce goods/services of required quality — buying at lowest cost consistent with standards
Producing maximum output from given inputs — productivity ratio
Achieving programme objectives and desired outcomes
Ensuring all expenditure is legal and properly authorised

explanation: 3E Framework: Economy = minimum INPUTS at required quality (are we buying cheaply?). Efficiency = maximum OUTPUT per unit of input (are we producing well?). Effectiveness = achievement of OBJECTIVES/OUTCOMES (are we reaching goals?). Option B = Efficiency. Option C = Effectiveness. Option D = Compliance audit, not performance audit. Economy is about procurement/input costs.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 15th Finance Commission used 2011 Census data for its population criterion. Why not the more recent 2021 Census?

options.option_text: The 2021 Census was delayed due to COVID-19 and data was unavailable when the 15th FC made its recommendations
The Constitution mandates using the most recent completed census, which was 2011
Southern states lobbied successfully to use older population data to avoid penalisation for lower fertility rates
The Finance Commission always uses census data that is 10 years old as a convention

explanation: 15th FC (2021-26) was constituted in 2017 and submitted its main report in 2020. The 2021 Census was scheduled but delayed by COVID-19 (never completed even by 2025). Hence 2011 Census was used. This was contentious — southern states (which had controlled population growth) preferred 2011 data. Under 14th FC (2015-20), 1971 and 2011 census data were both used to reward demographic performance.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Article 280(3)(b) of the Constitution empowers Finance Commission to recommend grants to cover:

options.option_text: Post-devolution revenue deficit of States — grants to States whose revenue falls short of assessed expenditure even after tax devolution
Capital expenditure grants for State infrastructure projects
Salary supplements for State government employees below pay commission rates
Disaster management funds for States hit by natural calamities

explanation: Article 280(3)(b): FC recommends grants to States that do not have adequate revenues to meet their committed expenditure even after tax devolution. These are Revenue Deficit Grants — to fill the gap. The 15th FC granted revenue deficit grants to 17 states in FY21-26. These are declining grants (tapering off as states are expected to improve own revenues). Disaster grants: SDRF/NDRF — separate from FC grants.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Forest and Ecology' criterion introduced in the 14th Finance Commission horizontal devolution formula gives higher grants to states with more forest cover because:

options.option_text: Forests provide national/global ecological services (carbon sequestration, biodiversity) for which states are not compensated through markets — FC recognises this opportunity cost
Forest-heavy states have lower agricultural income and need compensation for low economic activity
States with forests receive lower central plan expenditure, so FC corrects this imbalance
Forest areas have higher tribal populations who need additional welfare spending

explanation: Forest & Ecology criterion (10% weight in 15th FC): States maintaining forest cover provide national public goods — carbon sinks, water catchments, biodiversity. They forgo development (mining, agriculture) that would increase their GSDP. Markets don't compensate for this. FC recognises this 'ecological fiscal transfer' concept: states like Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Arunachal Pradesh benefit. It incentivises forest conservation.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Estimates Committee' of Parliament differs from PAC in that it:

options.option_text: Examines budget estimates BEFORE expenditure — suggests economies and efficiency improvements; CAG-backed PAC examines after expenditure has occurred
Examines accounts of State governments, while PAC examines Union accounts only
Has no relationship with CAG — it operates independently without audit reports
Consists of only Rajya Sabha members, providing an upper house check

explanation: Parliamentary Financial Committees: (1) Estimates Committee: 30 LS members, examines demands for grants BEFORE passage — suggests economies and efficiency; studies whether proposals conform to policy. (2) PAC: post-expenditure audit based on CAG reports. (3) Committee on Public Undertakings: examines PSU accounts and CAG's commercial audit reports. Estimates Committee = preventive; PAC = corrective.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The divisible pool from which Finance Commission recommends devolution EXCLUDES:

options.option_text: Cesses and surcharges levied for specific purposes (Swachh Bharat Cess, Health and Education Cess, etc.)
Income Tax collected from individuals
Corporate tax collected from domestic companies
Customs duties on imports

explanation: Divisible Pool = All Central taxes MINUS cesses and surcharges. Cesses are excluded because they are collected for specific dedicated purposes (education cess → education fund; Swachh Bharat cess → SBM). States get no share of cesses. This has been controversial — heavy use of cesses by Centre effectively reduces the divisible pool and States' share. The 15th FC noted this concern.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Performance grants recommended by Finance Commission to Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) are conditional on:

options.option_text: States publishing audited accounts of PRIs and improving own-revenue collection (property tax, user charges) by PRIs
PRIs achieving specific BPL reduction targets in their jurisdiction
State governments matching FC grants with equal State contribution
PRIs maintaining forest cover within their gram sabha boundaries

explanation: 15th FC Local Body Grants: Basic (untied) grants for all PRIs and ULBs. Performance grants (tied/conditional): conditions include — timely submission and publication of audited accounts, improvement in own revenue (property tax/user charges), and satisfactory utilisation of previous grants. This incentivises financial discipline and accountability at grassroots level.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The term 'Charged Expenditure' (not voted by Parliament) includes the salary of the CAG. This ensures:

options.option_text: Financial independence from the executive — the government cannot reduce CAG's budget to pressure or punish the CAG for adverse audit findings
The CAG receives higher salary than other constitutional heads
Parliament cannot reduce CAG's salary even if it disagrees with audit methodology
The CAG salary is automatically indexed to inflation each year

explanation: Constitutional safeguard for independence: CAG's salary and service conditions are charged to the Consolidated Fund (Article 148(6)) — not subject to Parliamentary vote. This means the executive cannot threaten the CAG by reducing its budget allocation. It mirrors the security for Supreme Court judges. Similarly: Comptroller General of Accounts (who does accounting) is NOT charged — only CAG.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 16th Finance Commission, chaired by Arvind Panagariya, covers which award period?

options.option_text: 2026–31 — the five-year period following the 15th FC's period of 2021-26
2025–30 — overlapping with 15th FC for transition
2027–32 — delayed due to Census preparation
2026–2036 — a 10-year period for stability

explanation: Finance Commissions are constituted every 5 years per constitutional convention. 14th FC: 2015-20. 15th FC: 2021-26. 16th FC (Arvind Panagariya): 2026-31. The 16th FC was constituted in December 2023 and submitted its recommendations in October 2025. Finance commissions typically submit reports 18 months before the commencement of their award period.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Value-for-Money (VfM) audit by CAG is DIFFERENT from traditional financial audit because:

options.option_text: VfM examines outcomes and impact of programmes, not just accuracy of accounts or compliance with rules
VfM audit is conducted by private chartered accountants, not CAG staff
VfM audit is mandatory for all departments; financial audit is only for selected departments
VfM audit produces a Balance Sheet of the government, while financial audit doesn't

explanation: Traditional audit: Was money spent? Was it legal? Were accounts accurate? VfM/Performance Audit: Was money well spent? Did programmes achieve objectives? Were resources used economically and efficiently? VfM audit goes BEYOND numbers to assess RESULTS. It's the most demanding audit type requiring programme knowledge, data analysis, and counterfactual thinking. CAG's 3E (Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness) framework guides VfM audits.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Tax Effort' criterion used in Finance Commission devolution rewards States that:

options.option_text: Collect more own taxes relative to their tax capacity — states making greater effort to mobilise own revenue get additional weight
Have higher overall tax revenue from all sources including Central transfers
Reduce their fiscal deficit by raising taxes rather than cutting expenditure
Impose more progressive taxation on higher income individuals

explanation: Tax Effort criterion (used in various FCs): Ratio of actual own tax revenue to tax capacity (estimated from GSDP and tax base). States that tax more relative to their capacity get higher weight. Incentivises revenue mobilisation. 15th FC dropped explicit tax effort criterion but kept incentives through fiscal performance grants. Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra generally score high on tax effort.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Concurrent Audit differs from CAG's post-audit in that concurrent audit is:

options.option_text: Conducted simultaneously with transactions (real-time) — mainly by banks' own internal auditors to detect errors/fraud before they accumulate
Audit conducted by two agencies at the same time on the same accounts
Annual audit conducted in parallel by CAG and statutory auditors
Audit of concurrent (overlapping) financial years by the same audit team

explanation: Concurrent Audit: real-time examination of transactions as they occur (not after year-end). Mainly in banking sector — bank branches with high transaction volumes have concurrent auditors who verify daily/weekly. Catches errors quickly. RBI mandates concurrent audit for banks above a threshold. Different from CAG's post-audit (which happens months after year-end) and internal audit (which is periodic).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Which constitutional body resolves disputes between States regarding their shares of the divisible pool?

options.option_text: Supreme Court of India — disputes between States are justiciable under Article 131 original jurisdiction
Finance Commission — it determines shares and its word is final
Inter-State Council under Article 263
GST Council, which has oversight of all revenue sharing between Centre and States

explanation: Finance Commission makes recommendations but they are ADVISORY (not binding). If States dispute their share or the Centre's implementation, the dispute can be taken to Supreme Court under Article 131 (original jurisdiction for disputes between Union and States, or between States). The Inter-State Council (Art. 263) handles coordination, not adjudication. GST Council handles GST-related disputes through its own mechanism.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG of India can be described as a 'constitutional functionary' because:

options.option_text: The office is created by the Constitution under Article 148 — not by ordinary legislation; removal requires the same procedure as a Supreme Court judge
The CAG has the power to make subordinate legislation through audit regulations
The CAG can issue constitutional writs to compel departments to produce accounts
The CAG's reports become part of the Constitutional record automatically

explanation: Constitutional Functionary: CAG is created by the Constitution itself (Art. 148), NOT by an ordinary Act. Other examples: President, Vice-President, Supreme Court/HC judges, Election Commission, UPSC. Benefits: security of tenure, salary from CFI (charged), removal only by Parliament (special majority). Statutory functionaries: CBI Director, ED Director, etc. — created by ordinary legislation and more vulnerable to executive control.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The 'Area' criterion in Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula accounts for:

options.option_text: The cost of providing uniform public services across a geographically larger state — larger area means higher per-capita delivery costs (roads, communication, administration)
Fertile agricultural land that generates higher State GDP
States with larger area get proportionally smaller grants to encourage urban densification
Coastal area of states to account for maritime trade potential

explanation: Area criterion (15% weight in 15th FC): Larger states incur higher costs to provide services across their territory — building roads, hospitals, schools in remote areas of Rajasthan vs Kerala. This compensates for the cost disadvantage of geographic size. Large states (Rajasthan, MP, Maharashtra) benefit. The minimum area weight ensures even small states get something. Pure population criterion would penalise large, sparsely populated states.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the 15th Finance Commission, which criterion rewards states that successfully reduced their Total Fertility Rate (TFR) close to replacement level?

options.option_text: Demographic Performance criterion (12.5% weight) — rewards states that achieved population stabilisation through voluntary family planning
Forest and Ecology criterion — reduced fertility indirectly preserves forest cover
Income Distance criterion — lower population growth leads to higher per capita income
Tax Effort criterion — smaller populations mean more revenue per person

explanation: Demographic Performance (12.5% weight in 15th FC): states that brought TFR closer to replacement level (2.1) by 2017 get more weight. Southern states (TN, Kerala, AP, Telangana, Karnataka) and some northern states (Himachal, Punjab) score high. This counter-balances using 2011 Census population data, which would penalise southern states (having controlled population earlier). It's a political compromise between north and south.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The CAG examines whether government has spent more or less than the appropriation for each grant. Spending MORE than the approved grant is called:

options.option_text: Excess Expenditure — requires Parliament's ex-post-facto approval under Article 115 (Supplementary/Excess Demand for Grants)
Overspending — automatically deducted from next year's allocation
Reappropriation — transferring savings to meet excess in another head
Surrender — departments return unspent balances for re-allocation

explanation: Excess Expenditure: spending above voted grant. Requires ex-post-facto Parliamentary approval (Article 115 — 'Vote on Excess'). CAG reports the excess in Appropriation Accounts. PAC examines reasons. If Parliament refuses approval, the responsible officers can be held accountable. Savings = under-spending (must be surrendered by March 31). Reappropriation = moving savings from one sub-head to cover excess in another (within same grant).

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Finance Commission grants to States under Article 275 are different from centrally sponsored scheme (CSS) transfers because Article 275 grants are:

options.option_text: Untied or minimally tied — States have more flexibility in their use (some may be sector-specific but without detailed conditions unlike CSS)
Fully tied to specific central government programmes and schemes
Matching grants requiring equal State contribution
Loan transfers requiring repayment with interest after 10 years

explanation: Article 275 grants: typically for filling revenue deficit, promoting welfare of STs, tribal area development. Generally with fewer conditions than CSS (which have detailed guidelines on how money must be spent). Tax devolution (core FC function) is completely untied. CSS transfers: rigid conditionalities, matching grant requirements, specific outcomes tracked by central ministries. The 14th FC's increase in untied devolution was meant to reduce CSS dependence.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: In a performance audit of PM Awas Yojana (housing for all), which finding would MOST clearly fall under 'Effectiveness' (the third E)?

options.option_text: Houses built did not meet habitability standards and beneficiaries were not from the target BPL group — programme did not achieve its social objective
Building materials were purchased at prices 20% above market rates — overpayment
Construction took 3 years instead of 1 year per target — delayed execution
Funds released by Centre not utilised by States within the financial year

explanation: Effectiveness: Did the programme achieve its INTENDED OUTCOMES? PM Awas Yojana's objective: provide affordable housing to BPL/EWS/LIG households. Finding: wrong beneficiaries got houses + quality didn't meet standards = EFFECTIVENESS failure (outcomes not achieved). Option B = Economy failure (overpaying = not economical). Option C = Efficiency failure (slow output). Option D = Economy/input management issue.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Coase Theorem states that when externalities exist, private parties can:

options.option_text: Negotiate to an efficient solution WITHOUT government intervention, provided property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are zero
Always achieve efficiency by paying Pigouvian taxes to government
Never reach a market solution — government must always intervene in externality cases
Resolve externalities only if both parties are corporations, not individuals

explanation: Coase Theorem (Ronald Coase, 1960, Nobel Prize 1991): If property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are negligible, private bargaining leads to efficient outcomes regardless of who holds the rights. Example: factory (polluter) and downstream fisherman. If fisherman has right to clean water: factory pays fisherman to pollute. If factory has pollution right: fisherman pays factory to reduce pollution. Both reach same efficient level. Real-world caveat: transaction costs are rarely zero.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Information asymmetry leads to market failure. The 'Market for Lemons' problem (Akerlof, 1970) describes:

options.option_text: How adverse selection causes markets to collapse — sellers know quality, buyers don't → buyers offer average price → high-quality sellers exit → market offers only low-quality
How monopolists charge high prices for defective products without competition
How government regulations prevent entry of good-quality producers
How price controls lead to shortages of high-quality goods

explanation: Akerlof's Market for Lemons (Nobel 2001): Used cars market where sellers know quality but buyers don't. Buyers offer average price (mix of good and bad cars). Good car owners (who want more than average) won't sell → market is left with mainly bad cars ('lemons'). Eventually market unravels. Solutions: signalling (warranties, reputation), screening (vehicle inspection), regulation. Applies to health insurance (adverse selection — sicker people buy more coverage).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Moral Hazard (one type of information asymmetry problem) means:

options.option_text: Insured individuals take more risks because they are protected — e.g., someone with full car insurance drives more recklessly
Insurance companies charge higher premiums to hide their profit margins from policyholders
High-risk individuals are more likely to purchase insurance than low-risk individuals
Insurance companies refuse to pay claims citing moral reasons for the accident

explanation: Moral Hazard: post-contract behaviour change because one party is insulated from consequences. Insured person: drives recklessly (car insurance), doesn't look after health (health insurance). Bailed-out bank: takes more risk (too-big-to-fail). Solutions: deductibles (partial own-cost), co-payments (health), monitoring. Adverse Selection = PRE-contract information problem (high-risk buys more insurance). Moral Hazard = POST-contract behaviour problem.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Economic Rent is best defined as:

options.option_text: The payment to a factor of production ABOVE its transfer earnings (opportunity cost) — the surplus over what is needed to keep it in its current use
Monthly rent paid for commercial or residential property
The profit earned by monopolists above normal profit
Interest paid on capital borrowed for productive purposes

explanation: Economic Rent (Ricardo's concept): Income of a factor = Transfer Earnings + Economic Rent. Transfer Earnings = minimum needed to keep the factor in current use (opportunity cost). Economic Rent = surplus above opportunity cost. Land (fixed supply) earns pure economic rent (supply is perfectly inelastic → price entirely determines rent). Labour with special skills earns quasi-rent. Supernormal profits = economic rent earned by firms.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Principal-Agent Problem arises when:

options.option_text: The agent (manager) has different interests from the principal (shareholder), and information asymmetry makes it hard for the principal to monitor agent behaviour
The principal fails to pay the agent the agreed commission for services rendered
Government (principal) cannot control private companies (agents) in regulated industries
Two agents compete for the same principal's business, driving down service quality

explanation: Principal-Agent Problem: arises when interests diverge + information asymmetry. Examples: Shareholders (principal) vs CEOs (agent) — CEO may pursue empire-building; Voters (principal) vs politicians (agent) — politicians pursue re-election over public good; Policyholders vs insurance company. Solutions: incentive alignment (stock options for CEOs), monitoring, performance contracts. Agency theory (Jensen & Meckling, 1976) formalises this.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Pigouvian Tax (named after economist A.C. Pigou) is designed to:

options.option_text: Internalise negative externalities by taxing the polluter/harmful-activity producer at a rate equal to the marginal social damage
Tax luxury goods to redistribute income from rich to poor
Tax imports to protect domestic industries from foreign competition
Tax savings to encourage consumption and stimulate aggregate demand

explanation: Pigouvian Tax: corrects market failure caused by negative externalities. Example: carbon tax on emissions = marginal social cost of carbon. When factory is taxed per unit of pollution = marginal damage, it internalises the cost → reduces pollution to socially optimal level. Carbon taxes, fuel taxes, cigarette taxes, alcohol taxes are all Pigouvian in nature. Equivalent: Pigouvian SUBSIDY for positive externalities (vaccines, education).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Tragedy of the Commons' (Garrett Hardin, 1968) refers to:

options.option_text: Overuse and degradation of common-pool resources (shared pastures, fisheries, groundwater) because each individual maximises personal gain, ignoring collective cost
The failure of communist regimes where common ownership led to economic stagnation
The historical enclosure of common lands in England that displaced peasant farmers
The tendency of common roads to become congested during peak hours

explanation: Tragedy of the Commons: common-pool resources are non-excludable but RIVAL (rivalrous). Rational individuals overuse them (each fisherman catches as many fish as possible before others do). Collectively this depletes the resource. Solutions: privatisation (property rights), regulation, or community management (Elinor Ostrom's work, Nobel 2009 — showed communities can self-govern commons sustainably without privatisation or government).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: From the supply function Qs = −20 + 4P, at what minimum price does positive quantity get supplied?

options.option_text: P = 5 (Qs = 0 when −20 + 4P = 0 → P = 5; below ₹5 no supply)
P = 0 (supply starts at zero price)
P = 4 (coefficient of P)
P = 20 (constant term)

explanation: Choke price (minimum supply price): Set Qs = 0. −20 + 4P = 0 → 4P = 20 → P = ₹5. Below ₹5 the supply function gives negative quantity (meaningless) → no supply. At P = ₹5, Qs = 0 (just enters the market). For each ₹1 increase above ₹5, quantity supplied increases by 4 units. This gives the supply curve's x-intercept (choke price).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Consumer equilibrium: MUx/Px = MUy/Py. If MUx = 40, Px = ₹8, MUy = 30, Py = ₹6. Is the consumer in equilibrium?

options.option_text: No — MUx/Px = 40/8 = 5, but MUy/Py = 30/6 = 5 — actually they ARE equal, so consumer IS in equilibrium
No — MUx/Px > MUy/Py, so buy more X and less Y
No — MUx/Px < MUy/Py, so buy less X and more Y
Cannot determine without knowing total income

explanation: Equi-marginal principle (consumer equilibrium): MUx/Px = MUy/Py. MUx/Px = 40/8 = 5. MUy/Py = 30/6 = 5. Both equal 5 → CONSUMER IS IN EQUILIBRIUM (cannot improve satisfaction by reallocating). If MUx/Px > MUy/Py → buy more X (more satisfaction per rupee from X). If MUx/Px < MUy/Py → buy more Y. Equilibrium: equal marginal utility per rupee from all goods.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A price fall from ₹50 to ₹40 causes quantity demanded to rise from 80 to 100 units. Total Revenue before = ₹4,000; Total Revenue after = ₹4,000. This implies:

options.option_text: Unitary elastic demand (Ed = 1) — TR unchanged confirms unit elasticity
Elastic demand — TR rose
Inelastic demand — TR fell
Perfectly elastic — infinite quantity demanded at same price

explanation: TR before = 50 × 80 = ₹4,000. TR after = 40 × 100 = ₹4,000. TR UNCHANGED → Unitary Elastic (Ed = 1). Verification: Ed = (ΔQ/ΔP) × (P/Q) = (20/(−10)) × (50/80) = −2 × 0.625 = −1.25. Wait — let me use arc: (20/90) / (10/45) = 0.222/0.222 = 1. Yes, using arc elasticity = 1. TR confirmation method is the simplest.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When a subsidy is given to producers of an essential commodity, the supply curve shifts:

options.option_text: RIGHTWARD (supply increases) — subsidy reduces effective cost, enabling more supply at every price level
LEFTWARD (supply decreases) — subsidy creates complacency in producers
There is movement along the curve, not a shift — subsidy is a price change
Upward — the supply curve shifts to reflect higher government support

explanation: Producer subsidy = lower effective cost per unit. At any given market price, producers can now profitably supply more → rightward shift of supply curve → lower equilibrium price + higher quantity. This is how government supports farmers (fertiliser, seed subsidies) or essential goods producers. Rightward supply shift = 'increase in supply'. Leftward = 'decrease in supply'.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'Elasticity of Supply in the Very Short Run' for agricultural products is:

options.option_text: Perfectly inelastic (PES = 0) — harvest is fixed once crops are grown; price cannot induce more supply in that harvest season
Highly elastic — farmers can quickly adjust acreage in response to prices
Unitary elastic — supply responds proportionately to price
Elastic — farmers store crops and release more when prices rise

explanation: Agricultural supply elasticity varies by time: Very short run (market period): PES = 0 — crop already harvested, supply is fixed whatever the price. Short run: PES > 0 but small — farmers can change intensity (more fertiliser, irrigation) but not change what's planted. Long run: higher PES — farmers can switch crops, change acreage. This cobweb phenomenon causes agricultural price volatility.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Two goods X and Y have cross price elasticity = +3.5. This implies:

options.option_text: X and Y are close substitutes — when price of Y rises by 1%, demand for X rises by 3.5% (very strong substitution relationship)
X and Y are complements — they are consumed together
X and Y are independent goods — cross elasticity of 3.5 indicates independence
X is an inferior good and Y is a normal good

explanation: Cross elasticity Exy = +3.5: Positive → substitutes. High magnitude (3.5) → very close substitutes (e.g., two competing brands of cola). When Y price rises 1% → X demand rises 3.5%. Near-perfect substitutes (like generic vs branded drugs) have very high positive cross-elasticity. Weak substitutes (tea and coffee compared to Coke and Pepsi) have lower positive cross-elasticity.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Demand for Money' in Keynesian theory has THREE motives. The SPECULATIVE motive for holding money is:

options.option_text: Holding money (instead of bonds) when interest rates are expected to FALL (bond prices rise) — wait for capital gains opportunity
Holding money (instead of bonds) when interest rates are expected to RISE — avoid capital losses on existing bonds
Holding money for day-to-day purchases of goods and services
Holding money as a buffer against unexpected expenses

explanation: Keynesian money demand motives: (1) Transactions: for routine purchases. (2) Precautionary: for unexpected needs. (3) Speculative: Keynes' key insight — when interest rates are expected to RISE (→ bond prices fall → capital loss), hold cash instead of bonds. When rates expected to fall (→ bond prices rise → capital gain), buy bonds (reduce cash holding). Speculative demand = inverse of interest rate. The liquidity preference theory.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: If the demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola (PQ = constant), what can you say about price elasticity?

options.option_text: Price elasticity = 1 (unitary elastic) at every point — TR is constant everywhere on a rectangular hyperbola
Price elasticity > 1 (elastic) throughout
Price elasticity = 0 (perfectly inelastic)
Price elasticity varies from elastic to inelastic depending on the point

explanation: Rectangular hyperbola: P × Q = constant (k). This means TR = k (constant everywhere). When TR doesn't change with price → PED = 1 (unitary elastic) at all points. The demand curve that has unitary elasticity everywhere is a rectangular hyperbola. This is also the shape of the AFC curve (TFC = AFC × Q = constant). Both are rectangular hyperbolas for the same mathematical reason.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Market supply increases (rightward shift) while demand remains unchanged. The equilibrium result is:

options.option_text: Equilibrium price FALLS and equilibrium quantity RISES
Equilibrium price RISES and quantity FALLS
Both price and quantity RISE
Price is unchanged; only quantity adjusts

explanation: Supply increases (shift right): at original price, there is now surplus (Qs > Qd). Surplus → sellers cut price → price falls → more quantity demanded along the demand curve → quantity increases. New equilibrium: Lower P, Higher Q. Mnemonic: supply increase = price down, quantity up (opposite directions). Demand increase = both price and quantity up (same direction).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: At current price, Ed = −2 and Es = 3. A specific tax of ₹T per unit is imposed. Buyer's burden as a fraction of T = ?

options.option_text: 2/5 (seller's burden fraction)
1/2 (equal split)
2/3 (higher elasticity party bears less)

explanation: Tax incidence formula: Buyer's burden = Es / (Es + |Ed|) = 3/(3+2) = 3/5 of T. Seller's burden = |Ed| / (Es + |Ed|) = 2/5 of T. Interpretation: MORE INELASTIC side bears MORE tax. Demand is less elastic (|Ed| = 2) than supply (Es = 3) — actually here supply is MORE elastic. More inelastic = buyers (|Ed|=2 vs Es=3 — demand is more inelastic) — wait: smaller elasticity = more inelastic = bears more. |Ed|=2 < Es=3 → demand is more inelastic → buyers bear more = 3/5. ✓

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An increase in consumer income causes demand for a Giffen good to:

options.option_text: DECREASE — Giffen goods are inferior goods; rising income → consumers switch to better alternatives → demand for Giffen good falls
Increase — higher income always increases demand for all goods
Remain unchanged — income has no effect on demand for Giffen goods
Increase initially then decrease — Giffen goods follow a non-linear income path

explanation: Giffen goods are a special class of INFERIOR goods (negative income elasticity). When income rises → consumers can now afford superior substitutes (rice instead of coarse grains) → demand for the Giffen/inferior good FALLS. This is the negative income effect. What makes Giffen goods unique isn't their income response (all inferior goods have this) but their PRICE response (demand rises when price rises due to dominant negative income effect).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Welfare Economics defines 'Pareto Optimality' as a situation where:

options.option_text: No reallocation can make anyone better off without making someone else worse off — it is impossible to improve one person's welfare without harming another
All people in society have equal welfare and income distribution is perfectly equal
The government has maximised total social welfare at lowest cost
The economy is growing at its maximum potential rate without inflation

explanation: Pareto Optimality (Vilfredo Pareto): no Pareto improvement is possible. A Pareto Improvement: making at least one person better off without harming anyone. At Pareto Optimum: all possible Pareto improvements have been exhausted. Competitive equilibrium achieves Pareto Optimum (First Welfare Theorem). Note: Pareto Optimum doesn't imply equity — a situation where one person has everything can be Pareto Optimal if redistribution harms that person.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Demand Qd = 500 − 5P and Supply Qs = 100 + 3P. A price ceiling of ₹45 is imposed. Quantity of shortage created = ?

options.option_text: 40 units shortage (Qd=275, Qs=235 at ceiling price ₹45)
0 shortage (ceiling is above equilibrium)
80 units surplus

explanation: First check equilibrium: 500−5P = 100+3P → 400 = 8P → P* = ₹50. Ceiling P = ₹45 < P* = ₹50 → BINDING (creates shortage). At P = ₹45: Qd = 500−225 = 275. Qs = 100+135 = 235. Shortage = Qd − Qs = 275 − 235 = 40 units.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which phenomenon explains why demand for seasonal goods (warm clothes) increases in winter even without any price change?

options.option_text: Change in tastes and preferences (seasonal) — a non-price demand shifter that moves the demand curve rightward
Movement along the demand curve triggered by lower supply in winter
Income effect — people earn more in winter to buy more clothes
Substitution effect — expensive substitutes make wool clothes relatively cheaper
