explanation: Seasonal demand: temperature change → consumers' preference for warm clothing increases → demand curve shifts RIGHT without any price change. This is a 'change in demand' (not change in quantity demanded). Demand shifters include: income, prices of related goods, tastes/preferences (including seasonal), expectations, population. Price change → movement along curve (change in QD). All other factors → shift of curve (change in demand).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A market with a single buyer (monopsony) will result in:

options.option_text: Employment below the competitive level and wage below the competitive wage — the monopsonist sets MFC > wage, restricts hiring to maximise profit
Higher wages because the single buyer has to attract all available workers
Higher employment than competition because monopsonist can plan better
Same outcomes as competitive market if the monopsonist is regulated

explanation: Labour monopsony: single employer in a town. Supply of labour is upward sloping (must pay more to attract more workers). MFC (marginal factor cost) > wage (since to hire one more worker, must raise wage for ALL workers). Monopsonist: hire where MRP = MFC → quantity < competitive equilibrium; pay the supply curve wage (less than competitive). Result: exploitatively low wages, under-employment. Minimum wage can INCREASE employment in monopsony (unlike competitive market).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Hicks Decomposition' separates the price effect on demand into:

options.option_text: Substitution Effect (holding REAL UTILITY constant — compensated demand) and Income Effect
Price Effect and Quantity Effect (two separate demand responses)
Short-run Effect and Long-run Effect on consumer behaviour
Supply Effect and Demand Effect on equilibrium quantity

explanation: Hicks Decomposition (JR Hicks): Price effect = Substitution effect (hold utility constant = move along same IC to new price ratio) + Income effect (shift to new IC with changed purchasing power). SE is always negative (own price rises → consume less of that good). IE: normal good (negative = buy less when price rises, income falls). Giffen: IE so positive it overwhelms SE. Slutsky Decomposition: alternative — holds REAL INCOME (purchasing power) constant.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A firm under perfectly elastic supply (PES = ∞) faces a tax. Who bears the entire tax burden?

options.option_text: The BUYER bears 100% — perfectly elastic supply means sellers supply at exactly their cost; any tax shifts full burden to consumers
The SELLER bears 100%
Tax is shared equally
Cannot determine without demand elasticity

explanation: Tax incidence: Buyer's share = Es / (Es + |Ed|). If Es = ∞: buyer's share = ∞/(∞ + |Ed|) = 1 (100%). Seller's share = |Ed|/(∞ + |Ed|) = 0. Perfectly elastic supply: seller will not accept a lower price (supply curve is horizontal at minimum cost). Any tax → seller raises price by full tax amount → buyer pays all. Example: competitive labour market with perfectly elastic labour supply.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When both DEMAND and SUPPLY DECREASE simultaneously, equilibrium quantity will:

options.option_text: Definitely DECREASE — both shifts reduce quantity; price effect is ambiguous (depends on relative magnitudes)
Definitely INCREASE — reduced supply raises price which attracts more demand
Remain unchanged — the two effects cancel out exactly
Definitely DECREASE and price will definitely DECREASE too

explanation: Simultaneous shifts analysis: Demand ↓ (leftward): Q↓, P↓. Supply ↓ (leftward): Q↓, P↑. Combined: Quantity effect: BOTH push quantity DOWN → Q definitely ↓. Price effect: demand ↓ pushes P down; supply ↓ pushes P up → AMBIGUOUS (depends on relative shifts). If demand decreases more: P falls. If supply decreases more: P rises. If equal: P unchanged.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: An 'Indifference Map' consists of:

options.option_text: A family of indifference curves, where higher curves represent higher utility levels — a complete representation of consumer preferences
A single indifference curve showing all utility-maximising combinations
A mapping of price-quantity combinations for different income levels
A diagram showing all feasible consumption bundles within a budget constraint

explanation: Indifference Map: set of all possible ICs for a consumer. Each IC represents a different (higher or lower) utility level. Higher IC = more preferred (dominant bundle — more of everything). Lower IC = lower utility. ICs cannot intersect (transitivity). Budget line tangent to HIGHEST ATTAINABLE IC = consumer equilibrium. The map allows derivation of demand curves by changing prices and tracking equilibrium shifts.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Deadweight Loss from a tax on a good occurs because:

options.option_text: Mutually beneficial trades that would have occurred in the absence of the tax no longer take place — the gap between buyer's willingness to pay and seller's supply cost exceeds the tax
The tax revenue collected by the government is wasted on inefficient spending
Sellers reduce quality to maintain profits after paying the tax
Consumers reduce consumption below what is socially optimal

explanation: Tax Deadweight Loss (Harberger Triangle): the tax drives a wedge between buyer's price (Pb) and seller's price (Ps). Transactions where buyer's WTP > Ps but < Pb no longer occur. These are 'missing trades' — welfare that neither buyer, seller, nor government captures. DWL = ½ × tax rate × change in quantity. Higher tax and/or higher elasticity → larger DWL. DWL is the efficiency cost of taxation.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Qd = 400 − 2P; Qs = 50 + P. A tax of ₹30/unit is imposed on sellers. New equilibrium price paid by buyers and received by sellers = ?

options.option_text: Buyers pay ₹140; sellers receive ₹110 (old equilibrium: P*=116.67 approx; with tax: new supply Qs=50+(P−30)=−20+P rearranged: Qs=50+P−30=20+P... 400−2P=20+P → 380=3P → P paid = ₹126.67, Ps = ₹96.67)
Buyers pay ₹126.67; Sellers receive ₹96.67
Buyers pay ₹116.67; Sellers receive ₹86.67
Buyers pay ₹146.67; Sellers receive ₹116.67

explanation: Without tax: Qd = Qs → 400−2P = 50+P → P* = 350/3 ≈ ₹116.67. With tax ₹30 on sellers: supply shifts → Qs = 50 + (Pb−30) where Pb = buyer's price. Set equal: 400−2Pb = 50 + (Pb−30) = 20+Pb. 380 = 3Pb. Pb = ₹126.67. Ps = Pb − Tax = 126.67 − 30 = ₹96.67. Buyer's burden = 126.67 − 116.67 = ₹10/unit. Seller's burden = 116.67 − 96.67 = ₹20/unit. Tax split 10:20 (buyer:seller).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Law of Demand' assumes 'other things equal (ceteris paribus)'. Which of these is NOT held constant in this assumption?

options.option_text: The price of the good itself — this is the variable being changed to trace the demand curve
Consumer income levels
Prices of related goods (substitutes and complements)
Consumer tastes and preferences

explanation: Ceteris paribus (other things equal) in demand analysis: HELD CONSTANT: consumer income, prices of related goods, tastes/preferences, expectations, number of buyers. NOT HELD CONSTANT (the variable): the PRICE OF THE GOOD ITSELF — this changes to trace out the demand curve. When price changes → movement along the demand curve. When anything 'held constant' changes → the demand curve SHIFTS.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A machine's component (engine) costs ₹50,000 with 5-year life. The remaining frame costs ₹1,50,000 with 15-year life. Under component accounting (Ind AS 16), which depreciation treatment is correct?

options.option_text: Engine: ₹10,000/year (50,000/5); Frame: ₹10,000/year (1,50,000/15) — separately depreciated
Entire machine ₹2,00,000 depreciated over 15-year blended life at ₹13,333/year
Only the engine is depreciated; frame is not depreciated separately
Both components depreciated over 5 years (shortest life) for conservatism

explanation: Component Accounting (Ind AS 16): each significant component with different useful life must be depreciated separately. Engine (₹50,000, 5 years) → ₹10,000/year. Frame (₹1,50,000, 15 years) → ₹10,000/year. Total annual depreciation = ₹20,000 (vs ₹13,333 under blended approach). This gives more accurate expense matching over the asset's life.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Closing stock includes 200 units of Product Y. Cost = ₹80/unit. Estimated selling price = ₹85/unit. Estimated cost to complete = ₹12/unit. Selling commission = ₹5/unit. NRV = ? How should it be valued?

options.option_text: ₹68/unit (NRV = 85 − 12 − 5 = ₹68 < Cost ₹80 → value at NRV ₹68/unit; total = ₹13,600)
₹80/unit (at cost — NRV not calculated)
₹85/unit (at selling price)
₹75/unit (deducting only selling commission)

explanation: NRV = Est. selling price − Est. costs to complete − Est. selling costs = 85 − 12 − 5 = ₹68. NRV (₹68) < Cost (₹80) → value at NRV. Write-down = ₹12/unit × 200 = ₹2,400 charged to P&L. Total closing stock = 200 × ₹68 = ₹13,600.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Under the Straight Line Method, a firm charges identical depreciation each year. This means the NET BOOK VALUE (NBV) falls:

options.option_text: In a straight line (linearly) — equal reduction each year until reaching residual value
Exponentially — faster in early years, slower later
In an S-curve — slow initially, fast in middle years, slow at end
NBV remains constant — only the depreciation account increases

explanation: SLM: same amount charged each year → NBV falls by equal steps → straight line graph of NBV over time. WDV: higher depreciation early → NBV falls steeply at first → exponential decline. SLM NBV graph: a straight line from Cost at Year 0 to Residual Value at Year n.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm discovers ₹5,000 worth of damaged stock included in closing stock. The stock is damaged and unsaleable. The correct adjustment:

options.option_text: Reduce closing stock by ₹5,000 (charge loss to Trading Account) — unsaleable stock has zero NRV
Keep in closing stock at ₹5,000 until it is actually discarded
Increase closing stock provision by ₹5,000 to offset the damage
Write off ₹5,000 from Capital Account — abnormal loss bypasses P&L

explanation: Unsaleable stock → NRV = ₹0 (cannot be sold). Lower of Cost or NRV = ₹0. Write down from ₹5,000 to ₹0 → charge ₹5,000 to P&L as write-down expense. Effectively, closing stock falls by ₹5,000 → COGS increases ₹5,000 → Gross Profit falls ₹5,000. The AS 2 / Ind AS 2 principle: never carry inventory above its NRV.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: An asset with cost ₹1,00,000 and estimated useful life 10 years (no residual value) is depreciated under SLM. At the END of Year 7, it is decided the remaining useful life is only 1 more year. Carrying amount at end of Year 7 before revision = ₹30,000. Revised depreciation for Year 8 = ?

options.option_text: ₹30,000 — full remaining book value written off in 1 year
₹10,000 — original annual SLM rate unchanged
₹15,000 — half the remaining balance per year
₹0 — asset already fully depreciated per original schedule

explanation: After Year 7: NBV = ₹30,000 (10,000/year × 7 years = ₹70,000 dep; NBV = ₹30,000). Revised remaining life = 1 year. Revised annual dep = ₹30,000/1 = ₹30,000. At end of Year 8: NBV = ₹0. Change in estimate is prospective (no catch-up). Full ₹30,000 charged in Year 8.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: A firm applies the 'Lower of Cost or NRV' rule on an aggregate portfolio basis. Item A: Cost ₹100, NRV ₹90. Item B: Cost ₹80, NRV ₹95. Portfolio total: Cost ₹180, NRV ₹185. Inventory value = ?

options.option_text: ₹180 (portfolio: NRV ₹185 > Cost ₹180 → value at Cost)
₹185 (at NRV)
₹175 (item-by-item: A at ₹90 + B at ₹80)
₹170 (conservative — apply NRV to all items)

explanation: If portfolio (aggregate) basis is used: Total NRV ₹185 > Total Cost ₹180 → value at cost ₹180. Item-by-item basis (required by AS 2): A = min(100,90)=90; B = min(80,95)=80; Total = ₹170. AS 2 / IAS 2 requires ITEM-BY-ITEM basis. Portfolio basis gives different (higher) result. This question illustrates why AS 2 specifies item-by-item — it's more conservative and more accurate.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Capital Work in Progress (CWIP) represents:

options.option_text: Assets under construction/installation that are not yet ready for use — shown separately in Balance Sheet; no depreciation charged until the asset is complete and put to use
Finished goods in process of being moved from factory to warehouse
Work-in-process inventory partially completed in the factory
Depreciation provision set aside for capital asset replacement

explanation: CWIP: Fixed assets still being constructed/installed — building under construction, plant being commissioned. Costs accumulate in CWIP account. No depreciation until asset is 'available for use'. Once complete: transfer CWIP → Fixed Asset account; then start depreciating. Under Ind AS 16: qualifying borrowing costs (interest on construction loan) can be capitalised into CWIP during construction period.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: Safety Stock in inventory management is the buffer maintained to:

options.option_text: Guard against demand uncertainty and supply lead-time variability — prevents stockouts if demand is higher than expected or delivery is delayed
Ensure the fire safety requirements for the storage warehouse are met
Provide minimum capital investment in inventory as required by auditors
Keep EOQ levels balanced with minimum stock requirements

explanation: Safety Stock = extra inventory held above expected demand during lead time. Formula (simple): Safety Stock = (Max lead time − Avg lead time) × Avg daily demand. Higher uncertainty → larger safety stock. Too much: holding costs. Too little: stockouts (lost sales, customer dissatisfaction). Trade-off between service level and inventory cost. ABC analysis: A items may have higher safety stock despite higher holding cost due to criticality.

subject: Finance & Accounts
stem: The formula for Maximum Stock Level is:

options.option_text: Reorder Level + Reorder Quantity − (Minimum Lead Time × Minimum Consumption)
EOQ + Safety Stock
Average daily consumption × Maximum storage capacity
Reorder Level + Minimum Stock Level

explanation: Stock Level formulas: Maximum Stock Level = ROL + ROQ − (Min LT × Min Consumption). Minimum Stock Level = ROL − (Avg LT × Avg Consumption). Reorder Level = Max LT × Max Consumption. These are classic cost accounting inventory control formulas. Maximum stock: stock should never exceed this level (avoids excess holding costs and obsolescence risk).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Multiplier-Accelerator Interaction' in business cycle theory explains:

options.option_text: How an initial investment triggers income growth (multiplier) which induces further investment (accelerator), creating cyclical amplification — explains booms and busts
The mathematical product of fiscal multiplier and monetary accelerator rates
How tax multipliers and subsidy accelerators interact in fiscal policy
The compound interest effect on government debt growth

explanation: Multiplier-Accelerator (Samuelson 1939): Multiplier: initial investment → income rises (multiple). Accelerator: rising income → firms need more capital → induced investment. This new investment triggers more multiplier effect → more income → more investment → boom. When growth slows: fewer induced investment → reverse multiplier → recession. The two interact to generate endogenous business cycles without external shocks. Hicks (1950) showed this generates cyclical fluctuations.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When price of Good X rises by 10%, demand for Good Y rises by 4%. Cross Price Elasticity = +0.4. Demand for Good X itself falls by 8% (own price elasticity = −0.8). Good X's TR after the price rise:

options.option_text: TR RISES (own PED |−0.8| < 1 → inelastic; price rise increases TR)
TR FALLS (elastic demand)
TR unchanged (unit elastic)
Cannot be determined without revenue data

explanation: |Ed| = 0.8 < 1 → inelastic demand for X. Rule: when demand is inelastic, price rise → TR RISES. Price ↑ 10%; Quantity ↓ 8% → net TR change ≈ +10% − 8% = +2% (approximate). TR = P×Q → P rises more than Q falls → TR rises. Cross elasticity of Y is supplementary info (testing if you distinguish Ed from Exy).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Revealed Preference approach allows us to test the 'Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)'. WARP is violated when:

options.option_text: A consumer chooses bundle A when B is affordable, BUT later chooses B when A is also affordable — inconsistent preferences
A consumer changes preference between two goods over time naturally
The consumer's demand curve is downward sloping as price rises
Marginal utility declines as consumption increases

explanation: WARP: if A is 'revealed preferred' to B (A chosen when both affordable) → B can never be revealed preferred to A (B cannot be chosen when A is also affordable). WARP violation = inconsistent choices = irrational consumer. WARP is the minimum rationality requirement in revealed preference theory. Strong Axiom of Revealed Preference (SARP): extends to chains of revealed preference (transitivity over multiple choices).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Long-run supply in a perfectly competitive increasing-cost industry is:

options.option_text: Upward sloping — as industry expands, input prices rise (e.g., specialised labour becomes scarce), raising LR equilibrium price
Perfectly elastic (horizontal) — constant cost industry
Downward sloping — industry expansion creates external economies reducing costs
Same as the short-run supply curve

explanation: LRS curve types: Constant cost (input prices stable as industry expands): LRS horizontal. Increasing cost (input prices rise as industry expands — competition for inputs): LRS upward sloping. Decreasing cost (external economies as industry grows): LRS downward sloping. Most industries in reality are increasing cost (oil, minerals, specialised skills) → LRS upward sloping, though less steep than SR supply.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A monopolist with demand P = 120 − Q and TC = 100 + 20Q. Maximum profit and the output at which it occurs:

options.option_text: Q=100, Profit=₹0

explanation: MR = dTR/dQ = d((120−Q)Q)/dQ = 120−2Q. MC = dTC/dQ = 20. MR=MC: 120−2Q=20 → Q=50. P = 120−50 = ₹70. Profit = TR−TC = (70×50) − (100+20×50) = 3,500 − 1,100 = ₹2,400. Under competition: P=MC → Q=100, P=20, TR=TC=2,100, Profit=0. Monopoly restriction: Q=50 vs 100; P=70 vs 20; Deadweight loss = ½×50×50=₹1,250.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In Chamberlin's monopolistic competition, the long-run tangency equilibrium means the firm produces:

options.option_text: To the LEFT of minimum AC — output is less than the cost-minimising level, creating 'excess capacity'
At minimum AC — most efficient production
To the right of minimum AC — over-producing relative to minimum cost
At the intersection of MC and AC — where profit is maximised

explanation: Monopolistic competition LR: downward-sloping demand tangent to AC. This tangency MUST occur to the left of AC minimum (since both demand and AC are falling at that point — a downward-sloping line can only be tangent to a U-shaped curve on its falling portion). Firm produces at OUTPUT < optimal scale. Gap between actual output and min-AC output = EXCESS CAPACITY = 'cost of monopolistic competition.'

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) used to measure market concentration is calculated as:

options.option_text: Sum of squares of each firm's market share — HHI close to 10,000 means pure monopoly; close to 0 means perfect competition
Number of firms multiplied by average market share
Market share of top 4 firms (CR4 ratio)
Standard deviation of market shares across all firms

explanation: HHI = Σ(si²) where si = market share of firm i in percentage. Pure monopoly: 100² = 10,000. Equal 10 firms: 10×(10²) = 1,000. DOJ (US) thresholds: HHI < 1,500 = competitive; 1,500-2,500 = moderately concentrated; > 2,500 = highly concentrated. CCI uses HHI for merger review in India. CR4 (4-firm concentration ratio) is simpler but less information-rich than HHI.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A perfectly competitive firm in the SHORT RUN can earn supernormal profit if:

options.option_text: Market price (P) > Average Total Cost (ATC) at the profit-maximising output — in LR, entry erodes this profit
Price equals MC — the firm is at the profit-maximising point
Price is below AVC — firm should shut down temporarily
The firm is largest in the industry and has cost advantages

explanation: PC short run: price set by market (exogenous). Firm maximises: P=MC. If at that output, P > ATC → supernormal profit = (P−ATC) × Q. In long run: profits attract entry → supply rises → price falls → P = ATC (zero economic profit). Supernormal profit in PC is temporary — only in short run before entry equilibrates. Unlike monopoly (entry barriers → supernormal profit in LR too).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Network Effects (or network externalities) are best described as:

options.option_text: The value of a product/service INCREASES as more people use it — e.g., a messaging app becomes more valuable as more friends join
External benefits from a product that accrue to non-users (like vaccines)
Cost savings from expanding a computer network's bandwidth
Benefits from being part of a business networking association

explanation: Network effects / network externalities: each additional user adds value for ALL existing users. Positive feedback → 'winner takes all' tendency. Examples: WhatsApp, Facebook (direct network effect — value from other users). Credit cards (indirect: more merchants → more users → more merchants). Railway networks, power grids. Explains why tech markets tend toward monopoly/duopoly (GAFA). Metcalfe's Law: network value ∝ n² (n = number of users).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Two-part tariff pricing (entry fee + per-unit price) is used by monopolists to:

options.option_text: Extract consumer surplus — charge an entry fee equal to total CS and price at MC; this achieves monopoly profit without distorting output
Cross-subsidise poor consumers using profits from rich consumers
Bundle multiple products together at a combined discount price
Practice third-degree price discrimination by segment

explanation: Two-Part Tariff: Entry fee (T) + per-unit price (p). Optimal: set p = MC (efficient output) → charge entry fee T = Consumer Surplus at that p. CS extracted = monopoly profit. Examples: amusement parks (entry ticket + per-ride fee), razors + blades, printers + cartridges, SaaS subscription + per-use fee. Efficient because P=MC (no deadweight loss) but CS fully extracted by the monopolist as the entry fee.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The CCI can examine 'Anti-Competitive Agreements' under Section 3 of the Competition Act. Which agreement is 'per se' illegal (presumed anti-competitive without needing to prove market effect)?

options.option_text: Horizontal price fixing, market sharing, bid rigging, and output limitation agreements between competitors
Vertical agreements between manufacturer and distributor on resale price
Exclusive dealing agreements between firms in different industries
Technology licensing agreements between companies in different countries

explanation: Competition Act Section 3(3): Horizontal agreements (between competitors at the same level) on price, market sharing, bid rigging, output limitation are 'presumed to have an appreciable adverse effect on competition' — per se illegal (burden shifts to parties to prove otherwise). Section 3(4): Vertical agreements (between firms at different supply chain levels) are not per se illegal — assessed under 'rule of reason' (actual market effect must be shown). CCI has penalised cement companies, tyre companies for cartelisation under S.3(3).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under 'Ramsey Pricing' (for regulated natural monopolies), the optimal prices for multiple services should be set such that:

options.option_text: Services with MORE INELASTIC demand bear higher markups above MC — deviations from MC are inversely proportional to elasticity (to minimise deadweight loss while covering fixed costs)
All services are priced at marginal cost regardless of demand elasticity
All services are priced at average cost equally regardless of usage
Services with higher demand get lower prices (economies of scale)

explanation: Ramsey Pricing (Frank Ramsey, 1927): For a natural monopoly that must cover fixed costs but minimise deadweight loss: markup above MC = k/|Ed| where k is a constant. Inelastic demand goods (necessities) bear higher markup. Elastic demand goods have markup closer to MC. Counterintuitive from equity standpoint (necessities more expensive relative to cost). Used for: telecoms, electricity, railways — multiple services with different elasticities needing common infrastructure cost recovery.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Oligopoly market structure is characterised by a KINKED demand curve. What does the 'kink' in the demand curve imply about price changes?

options.option_text: Rivals match price cuts (making demand inelastic below kink) but ignore price rises (making demand elastic above kink) — so firm has no incentive to change price either way
Price can never change once set — the kink freezes the price permanently
Demand becomes perfectly elastic above and below the kink
The kink represents the cartel price, which all members agree to maintain

explanation: Sweezy's Kinked Demand (1939): Above kink price: rivals don't match price rise → this firm loses customers → elastic demand. Below kink: rivals match price cut → all lose revenue together → inelastic demand. Firm loses either way: raising price → lose customers; cutting price → price war, lower TR. Result: 'price rigidity' — firms rarely change prices even when costs change (MC can shift without changing Q* as long as new MC passes through the discontinuous MR gap at the kink).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under 'Predatory Pricing', a dominant firm:

options.option_text: Sets prices BELOW cost temporarily to drive out rivals, then raises prices once competition is eliminated
Sets prices very high (predatory to consumers) to maximise short-term profits
Prices at exactly marginal cost to prevent entry (Limit Pricing)
Matches a competitor's price to maintain market share (Price Matching)

explanation: Predatory Pricing: dominant firm prices below AVC (or below cost) to make it impossible for rivals/entrants to survive. Once rivals exit → raise prices to monopoly level. CCI Section 4 includes predatory pricing as abuse of dominant position. Challenge: proving intent (was below-cost pricing predatory or just competitive?). Classic cases: Standard Oil (1909), AKZO (EC), Brooke Group (US). Indian case: MCX-SX accused NSE of predatory pricing in currency derivatives.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'S-C-P (Structure-Conduct-Performance) Paradigm' in industrial organisation economics states:

options.option_text: Market STRUCTURE (concentration, barriers to entry) determines firm CONDUCT (pricing, advertising) which determines market PERFORMANCE (efficiency, innovation, profitability)
Firm performance determines market structure through survival of the fittest
Government supply-side policy determines competitive conduct and market outcomes
Structural reforms, capital reforms, and productivity reforms sequentially improve performance

explanation: S-C-P Paradigm (Mason, Bain, 1950s): Structure: number of firms, entry barriers, product differentiation, cost structures. Conduct: pricing strategy, advertising, collusion, R&D, innovation. Performance: allocative efficiency, technical efficiency, rate of progress, profitability. Policy implication: regulate structure (antitrust) → good conduct → good performance. Critics: reverse causation possible (good performance firms create their own market structure).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Bundling as a pricing strategy (selling two products together at one price) can benefit a monopolist because:

options.option_text: It reduces willingness-to-pay heterogeneity across consumers — bundles extract more surplus than selling individually when valuations for products are negatively correlated
It always forces consumers to buy products they don't need
It reduces the monopolist's production costs through economies of scope
It is illegal under competition law in all jurisdictions

explanation: Bundling: selling A+B together at a joint price. Pure Bundling: only bundle sold. Mixed Bundling: bundle + individual options. Effective when consumer valuations are negatively correlated (person who values A more values B less) — averaging the valuations via the bundle extracts more CS than individual pricing. Microsoft bundled Windows + IE (antitrust case). Tying: requires purchase of a second product to get the first (can be anti-competitive abuse of dominance).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's ranking in the World Bank's 'Ease of Doing Business (EoDB)' index improved dramatically between 2014 and 2020. This improvement primarily resulted from:

options.option_text: Reforms in 10 indicator areas including starting a business (SPICe+), construction permits (online approvals), getting electricity, tax payment (GST), contract enforcement (commercial courts)
Reduction in income tax rates making India more attractive for investment
Increase in FDI limits across all sectors automatically improving the ranking
Improvement in India's GDP growth rate signalling economic strength

explanation: India's EoDB rank: 142nd (2014) → 63rd (2019). 10 indicators: Starting Business, Construction Permits, Getting Electricity, Registering Property, Getting Credit, Protecting Minority Investors, Paying Taxes (GST), Trading Across Borders, Enforcing Contracts (commercial courts), Resolving Insolvency (IBC). Delhi and Mumbai are the sample cities. World Bank discontinued EoDB in 2021 after methodology concerns. Replaced by 'Business Ready (B-READY)' assessment from 2024.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana — Urban (PMAY-U)' aims to:

options.option_text: Provide housing for all urban poor by 2022 (extended) through four verticals: In-situ slum redevelopment, Credit Linked Subsidy, Affordable Housing in Partnership, Beneficiary-Led Construction
Build government rental housing colonies in metro cities only
Provide housing loans at zero interest for all urban residents
Demolish slums and relocate inhabitants to rural areas

explanation: PMAY-Urban (launched June 2015): 'Housing for All' by 2022. Four verticals: (1) In-situ Slum Redevelopment (ISSR) — use land as resource. (2) Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme (CLSS) — interest subsidy 3-6.5% for EWS/LIG/MIG categories. (3) Affordable Housing in Partnership (AHP) — joint public-private development. (4) Beneficiary Led Construction/Enhancement (BLC). Targeted 1.12 crore houses. Technology Innovation Grant (TIG) for new construction technologies. PMAY-Gramin: separate rural scheme.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which scheme provides ₹2 lakh insurance for accidental death/permanent disability to bank account holders aged 18-70 years at ₹20/year premium?

options.option_text: Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) — accidental death insurance
Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) — life insurance
Atal Pension Yojana (APY) — pension scheme for unorganised sector
PM Vaya Vandana Yojana — senior citizen pension scheme

explanation: Jan Suraksha Schemes (launched May 2015, FM Arun Jaitley): PMSBY: Accidental death/disability insurance, ₹2 lakh cover, ₹20/year premium, renewable, for 18-70 age group via bank auto-debit. PMJJBY: Life insurance (all causes), ₹2 lakh, ₹436/year premium, 18-50 age group. APY: Pension for unorganised sector, 18-40 age group. PMSBY is for ACCIDENT only; PMJJBY is for all causes of death. Both auto-renewed from bank account.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Naagrik)' scheme aims to:

options.option_text: Make regional air connectivity affordable — subsidise airfares on underserved routes (at ₹2,500 for 1-hour flights) to connect tier-2/tier-3 cities
Provide subsidised drone deliveries to rural areas for agricultural inputs
Connect all Indian cities with high-speed rail by 2030
Upgrade all existing airports to international standards

explanation: UDAN: Regional Connectivity Scheme (RCS) under Ministry of Civil Aviation. Launched 2016. Viability Gap Funding (VGF) shared between Centre-State-airlines to subsidise fares. Caps fares at ₹2,500 for 1-hour flights. Activated unserved/underserved airports. Over 400 UDAN routes. Part of National Civil Aviation Policy 2016. 'UDAN 4.0' expanded to North-East, Hilly areas, Helicopter routes. By 2025: 70+ airports connected under UDAN.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Human Development Report (HDR) 2023-24 ranked India at approximately:

options.option_text: 134th out of 193 countries — in the 'Medium Human Development' category (below Sri Lanka at 78 but above several South Asian and African nations)
Top 50 — India ranks among high development nations due to IT sector
Bottom 20 — persistent poverty pulls India below most developing nations
No rank — India doesn't participate in HDI ranking

explanation: UNDP HDR: India's HDI rank has improved from ~134-136 range. HDI score ~0.644 (2022 data). Category: Medium Human Development. Life expectancy: ~67-68 years. Mean years of schooling: ~6.5 years. GNI per capita (PPP): ~$6,500-7,000. India ranks higher than Bangladesh and Pakistan but significantly below Sri Lanka, China, Brazil. Kerala and Delhi if treated as countries would rank in High Development; Bihar and UP would rank much lower.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following is the correct description of 'Stagflation'?

options.option_text: Simultaneous high inflation AND high unemployment — challenging for policymakers since standard tools treat them as trade-offs (Phillips Curve breakdown)
Very slow economic growth (stagnation) without inflation
Inflation caused by stagnant supply in one sector only
High growth with stable prices — an ideal economic condition

explanation: Stagflation: Stagnation + Inflation simultaneously. Caused by supply shocks (oil price shock 1973 — OPEC embargo). Standard demand-side tools fail: raise rates to fight inflation → worsen recession; stimulate demand to reduce unemployment → worsen inflation. 1970s stagflation in USA/UK broke Keynesian consensus, led to Monetarism (Friedman) and supply-side economics (Reagan/Thatcher). India faced mild stagflation episodes post-2009 global crisis.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GDP growth was 7%. Population growth was 2%. Approximate growth in Real GDP per capita was:

options.option_text: ~5% (GDP growth − population growth = 7% − 2% = 5% per capita income growth)
9% (GDP + population)
7% (GDP growth is the same as per capita)
3.5% (GDP growth / 2)

explanation: Real per capita GDP growth ≈ Real GDP growth − Population growth (approximate). Exact: per capita = (1+g_GDP)/(1+g_pop) − 1. Approximate: g_GDP − g_pop = 7% − 2% = 5%. At 5% per capita growth, incomes double every ~14 years (rule of 70: 70/growth rate = doubling time). This is why countries with lower population growth rates tend to have faster per capita income growth, even with same GDP growth.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN)' enables tax authorities to:

options.option_text: Cross-verify Input Tax Credit (ITC) claims by matching invoices between buyer and seller — preventing fraudulent ITC claims
Automatically compute and transfer GST to states based on consumption patterns
Provide real-time credit to businesses based on their GST filing history
Replace all physical tax offices with digital-only administration

explanation: GSTN's key function: Invoice matching. Every supplier uploads invoices (GSTR-1); every buyer claims ITC (GSTR-2B generated automatically from GSTR-1 data). Tax authorities can compare claimed ITC with actual supplier uploads → catch fraudulent ITC claims. Fake invoice frauds: supplier raises invoices without actual goods to enable buyers to claim ITC without paying tax. E-invoicing (mandatory from 2020, phased rollout) further strengthened real-time verification.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's National Statistical Office (NSO) releases GDP estimates in a phased manner. The 'First Advance Estimate' of GDP is released in:

options.option_text: January (of the fiscal year in progress) — based on available data from April-September plus projections; used for Budget preparation
March (end of the fiscal year) — after all data is compiled
June (3 months after FY end) — preliminary estimate
December of the previous year — annual projection before the year starts

explanation: GDP release timeline: First Advance Estimate (FAE): January 7-10 (during the ongoing FY, based on 7 months data). Used by Finance Ministry for Budget. Second Advance Estimate (SAE): February end. First Provisional Estimate (May). Final Estimates: successive revisions over 2-3 years. GDP data has multiple rounds of revision as more complete data becomes available. The 'backcast' revision for base year change (2011-12) significantly changed historical estimates.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Pradhan Mantri Kisan Maan Dhan Yojana (PM-KMY)' provides:

options.option_text: Voluntary pension scheme for small and marginal farmers — minimum pension of ₹3,000 per month after age 60 with 50:50 premium co-contribution by farmer and government
Free health insurance of ₹5 lakh to all farmers
Crop loan waiver for indebted farmers with less than 2 hectares
Life insurance of ₹2 lakh for farmers who die in accidents

explanation: PM-KMY (launched August 2019): Pension scheme for small and marginal farmers (landholding ≤ 2 hectares), aged 18-40 at entry. Target: ₹3,000/month pension at age 60. Premium: farmer pays ₹55-₹200/month depending on age; government co-contributes equal amount. Managed by LIC. Entry ages 18-40 with corresponding premiums. Optional exit allowed. Different from PM-KISAN (direct income support) and PMSBY/PMJJBY (insurance).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Semiconductor Mission' (2021) aims to:

options.option_text: Develop India's domestic semiconductor (chip) fabrication ecosystem — reduce import dependence on Taiwan/China for chips critical for electronics, defence, EVs, telecom
Train 10 lakh software engineers in semiconductor programming
Export surplus electricity to neighbouring countries through semiconductor grid
Regulate domestic prices of mobile phones containing imported semiconductor chips

explanation: India Semiconductor Mission (ISM, 2021, ₹76,000 crore scheme): Set up domestic fab (fabrication facility), ATMP (Assembly, Testing, Marking and Packaging), and design ecosystem. Incentives: 50% capital subsidy for new fabs. Key deals: Tata Electronics + PSMC (Taiwan) — 28nm chip fab; CG Power + Renesas + Stars Microelectronics ATMP; Kaynes + Sensata ATMP. India currently designs chips (fabless: Qualcomm, Intel design in India) but doesn't fabricate them. Mission: change that by 2026-28.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'National Monetisation Pipeline (NMP)' announced in 2021 involves:

options.option_text: Monetising brownfield (existing) public infrastructure assets by leasing them to private sector for operation while government retains ownership — targeting ₹6 lakh crore over FY22-25
Selling government land banks to private developers
Privatising all public sector undertakings over a 4-year period
Issuing infrastructure bonds backed by public sector assets

explanation: NMP (Launched August 2021, NITI Aayog): Monetise BROWNFIELD assets (already built infrastructure) — toll roads, railway stations, airports, power transmission lines, gas pipelines, telecom towers, sports stadiums. Methods: InvIT/ReIT, PPP, OMT (Operate Maintain Transfer). Government RETAINS ownership; private sector pays upfront/annual lease for operating rights. Revenue recycled into new GREENFIELD infrastructure. Target: ₹6 lakh crore (FY22-25). Roads (27%), Power (28%), Railways (25%) are major sectors.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India achieved which milestone in 2021-22 to become the 5th largest economy in the world?

options.option_text: Surpassed United Kingdom's nominal GDP (in USD terms) to become the world's 5th largest — helped by GBP depreciation and India's post-COVID recovery
Surpassed Japan to become the 3rd largest economy
Surpassed Germany to become the 4th largest economy
Surpassed China to become the 2nd largest in Asia

explanation: India overtook UK to become 5th largest (nominal GDP) in Q4 FY22 (early 2022). Factors: India's post-COVID growth recovery + GBP weakness vs USD. GDP rankings (nominal, 2024-25): 1. USA (~$28 trillion). 2. China (~$18T). 3. Germany (~$4.5T). 4. Japan (~$4.2T). 5. India (~$3.9T). At PPP, India is 3rd (after USA and China). By 2030, India is projected to be 3rd largest nominal GDP economy.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'One District One Product (ODOP)' initiative under MSME Ministry aims to:

options.option_text: Identify and develop one unique traditional or handcrafted product per district to promote local industries, exports, and GI-tagged specialties
Establish one large manufacturing factory in every district headquarters
Supply one essential product (rice/wheat) to every district from government depots
Allow each district to have only one dominant private sector company

explanation: ODOP: Launched in Uttar Pradesh (2018) → scaled nationally. Each district identifies its speciality — Aligarh locks, Moradabad brassware, Varanasi silk, Agra footwear, etc. Support: financial assistance, technology upgrades, market access, export promotion, GI tagging, common facility centres. PM Vishwakarma scheme (2023) extended artisan support. Also integrated into district export promotion under the Foreign Trade Policy. Helps reduce regional inequality by developing local value chains.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Viksit Bharat 2047' (Developed India by 2047) vision targets achieving approximately what per capita income?

options.option_text: ~USD 18,000-20,000 per capita (close to current developed country threshold) — from current ~USD 2,500; requires sustained 7-8% GDP growth for 25 years
USD 5,000 (modest target focusing on basic human development)
USD 50,000 (US-level income by 2047)
No specific target — it's a qualitative vision statement only

explanation: Viksit Bharat 2047 (PM Modi, India@100 vision): Aims to make India a developed nation by 2047 (100th independence anniversary). Target: India to become a developed economy — implies per capita income of roughly $18,000-20,000 (World Bank 'high income' threshold is ~$14,005+). Requires GDP to grow to $30-35 trillion (from ~$4 trillion today). Key pillars: Poverty elimination, strong infrastructure, skilled workforce, manufacturing leadership, technological innovation, good governance.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Electricity (Amendment) Act 2022 aims to:

options.option_text: Introduce distribution sector competition — allow multiple distribution companies in one area so consumers can choose their electricity supplier
Privatise all state electricity boards immediately
Set a maximum price for electricity across all states uniformly
Transfer electricity regulation from states to Centre entirely

explanation: Electricity Amendment Bill 2022 (passed Lok Sabha 2023, pending Rajya Sabha): Key reform — allow multiple distribution licensees in a given area (currently each state DISCOM has monopoly). Consumer can choose supplier. Network (wires) remains with existing DISCOM; only supply is open to competition. Other provisions: National Renewable Energy Policy, stricter RPO enforcement, cross-subsidy reduction. States resist (power is Concurrent List subject). Also: Direct Benefit Transfer for electricity subsidies.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Model Tenancy Act 2021' (MTA) addresses India's housing problem by:

options.option_text: Providing a balanced legal framework for rental housing — faster dispute resolution, security deposit limits (2 months for residential), and enabling vacant properties to be offered for rent without fear of illegal occupation
Allowing government to acquire private properties from landlords for public housing
Setting maximum rental rates in all cities to make housing affordable
Exempting rental income from all income taxes to encourage landlords

explanation: MTA 2021 (template for states to adopt): Balance tenant-landlord rights. Key provisions: Written mandatory agreement, notice periods (1 month rent arrear → notice, 2 months → eviction proceedings). Security deposit: ≤2 months for residential, ≤6 months commercial. Fast-track Rent Court and Rent Authority for disputes. Aims to: Unlock 1 crore+ vacant urban properties (owners fearful of non-eviction under old laws). Encourage institutional rental housing. Adopted by some states; others still have old Rent Control Acts (protecting tenants but discouraging supply).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Agricultural Market Reform' (APMC reforms) introduced by the central government in 2020 (later repealed) sought to:

options.option_text: Allow farmers to sell produce outside APMC mandis directly to traders, processors, and exporters — ending the state-regulated mandi monopoly on agricultural sales
Abolish MSP (Minimum Support Price) for agricultural commodities
Mandate that all agricultural land be consolidated into cooperative farms
Allow foreign companies to directly purchase farmland from farmers

explanation: Three Farm Laws (2020, repealed November 2021 after farmer protests): (1) Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act: allow sale outside APMC mandis, no mandi tax outside. (2) Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act: contract farming framework. (3) Essential Commodities (Amendment) Act: remove stock limits on agricultural commodities. Main concerns: state revenue loss (mandi taxes), fear of corporate exploitation, MSP not guaranteed. Eventually withdrawn after 13 months of protests.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'National Logistics Policy 2022' aims to reduce India's logistics cost as a percentage of GDP from current ~13-14% to:

options.option_text: ~8% (comparable to global benchmarks like China and USA) by 2030 — through infrastructure, process, and digital integration improvements
2% — complete elimination of logistics inefficiency
20% — temporarily increasing to build better infrastructure
The policy doesn't set a specific target percentage

explanation: National Logistics Policy 2022 (PM Modi, September 2022): India's logistics costs ~13-14% of GDP vs 8% in developed countries — this extra cost makes Indian exports less competitive. Target: reduce to global benchmark level by 2030. Key: PM GatiShakti (multimodal connectivity), Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP — data integration across transport modes), Ease of Logistics (ELOG) services, warehousing rationalisation, skill development for logistics workforce. 'Logistics' added as a priority sector for bank credit.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'National Quantum Mission (NQM)' launched in 2023 primarily aims to:

options.option_text: Develop quantum computers, quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum materials — achieving technological leadership in quantum technologies by 2031
Provide free quantum chemistry education at all IITs
Build quantum cryptography for India's diplomatic communication
Research quantum physics for fundamental science Nobel prize pursuit

explanation: NQM (approved Cabinet May 2023, ₹6,003 crore, 8-year): India's strategic investment in quantum technology. Four thrusts: (1) Quantum Computing (50-1000 qubit computers by 2031). (2) Quantum Communication (quantum-safe encrypted network). (3) Quantum Sensing and Metrology (ultra-precise sensors). (4) Quantum Materials and Devices. Run by Department of Science and Technology (DST). India joins USA, China, EU in national quantum missions. Use cases: drug discovery, cryptography, materials science, optimisation problems.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023' introduced a new concept of 'Towns of Export Excellence (TEE)'. Towns can be designated as TEE if they produce exports of at least:

options.option_text: ₹750 crore per year — qualifying for special policy support, common service provider benefits, and export promotion infrastructure
₹100 crore per year
₹10,000 crore per year — only major export hubs qualify
Any amount — all towns with any export can be designated

explanation: FTP 2023 (released April 2023, valid till 2028): Introduced 'Towns of Export Excellence (TEE)' for clusters producing ≥₹750 crore exports p.a. (reduced from earlier ₹1,000 crore threshold). Benefits: priority access to Export Promotion Fund, common service providers for testing/certification, preferential credit. Also: RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported Products) continued, Amnesty scheme for pending cases, 4D targets (Develop, Diversify, Deepen, De-risk).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act' requires the Centre to lay before Parliament a 'Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement (FPSS)'. FPSS must explain:

options.option_text: Deviations from FRBM targets in current year and strategy for achieving targets — including rationale for any escape clauses invoked
The government's 5-year development plan and investment programme
Ministry-wise performance against budgetary allocations of previous year
Comparison of India's fiscal position with other G20 economies

explanation: FRBM Act requires 3 statements with Budget: (1) MTFP: 3-year rolling targets. (2) FPSS: Rationale for departure from targets if any, corrective measures. (3) Macroeconomic Framework Statement: GDP, inflation, BoP projections. If escape clause invoked (natural calamity, national security, structural reform year, negative growth or 50%+ fall in revenue growth): FPSS must explain why and when normal trajectory resumes. Parliament uses these to hold government accountable.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's RBI Act Section 24 empowers RBI to issue currency notes of which denominations?

options.option_text: ₹2 and above — all denomination notes except ₹1 note which is issued by Ministry of Finance (signed by Finance Secretary, not RBI Governor)
Only ₹500 and ₹2,000 denomination notes
All denominations including ₹1 — RBI is the sole issuer of all currency
Only notes above ₹100 — smaller notes are issued by commercial banks

explanation: Currency Issuing Authority: RBI issues all bank notes ₹2 and above (₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500, ₹2000). Signed by RBI Governor. ₹1 note (and coins): issued by Government of India (Ministry of Finance, signed by Finance Secretary) — though RBI distributes coins. ₹2,000 notes were discontinued (not in circulation from FY24). This distinction is a frequent exam question.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: When government expenditure > government revenue and the difference is financed by borrowing, the impact on financial markets is:

options.option_text: Government bonds supply increases → bond prices fall → bond yields rise → interest rates rise ('crowding out' private investment via higher rates)
More money in economy from government spending → interest rates fall
No impact on financial markets — government borrowing is self-financing
Stock market rises as government expenditure boosts corporate revenues

explanation: Crowding Out mechanism: Government deficit → issues more bonds → bond supply ↑ → bond prices fall (price and yield inversely related) → bond yields/interest rates RISE → private borrowing becomes expensive → private investment falls ('crowded out'). If economy at full employment: complete crowding out. If slack: partial crowding out (Keynesian view). RBI can monetise deficit (print money) to avoid crowding out but causes inflation. FRBM limits monetisation.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'National Pension System (NPS)' replaced the 'Old Pension Scheme (OPS)' for Central Government employees from:

options.option_text: 1 January 2004 — NPS introduced for all central government employees joining service from this date
1 April 1991 — along with LPG economic reforms
1 April 2014 — when PM Modi government came to power
1 January 2010 — NPS was opened to all citizens

explanation: NPS: introduced 1 January 2004 for new central government employees (excluding Armed Forces). OPS was defined benefit (50% of last drawn salary as pension — unfunded liability). NPS is defined contribution (employee + government each contribute 10% of salary+DA; employee manages funds across NPS fund managers; retirement corpus depends on contributions and returns). States can choose: most states adopted NPS; some (Rajasthan, Jharkhand, etc.) reverted to OPS. NPS opened to all citizens 2009. PFRDA (2003) regulates NPS.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Package (PMGKP) announced in March 2020 was significant because:

options.option_text: It was India's largest-ever direct cash transfer and food security package (₹1.7 lakh crore) to protect the vulnerable during COVID-19 lockdown
It permanently reformed the Mahatma Gandhi NREGA scheme
It introduced universal basic income for all rural households
It was the first ever government stimulus package in India's history

explanation: PMGKP (26 March 2020, ₹1.70 lakh crore): India's COVID economic relief. Components: 80 crore ration card holders get free 5 kg wheat/rice for 3 months (later extended). Women Jan Dhan account holders: ₹500/month for 3 months. Farmers: ₹2,000 advance under PM-KISAN. Construction workers: ₹31,000 crore from Building Workers Welfare Fund. Senior citizens/widows/disabled: ₹1,000. Healthcare workers insurance ₹50 lakh. Free cylinders to PM Ujjwala beneficiaries. Total 8+ packages followed.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which article empowers Parliament to impose duties and taxes NOT mentioned in the Union List?

options.option_text: Article 248 (Residuary Powers) — Parliament has power to make laws on subjects not in any of the three lists, including taxation
Article 110 (Money Bill definition)
Article 265 (No tax shall be levied without authority of law)
Article 280 (Finance Commission)

explanation: Article 248: Residuary powers of Parliament — Parliament has exclusive power to make laws on matters not enumerated in Union List, State List, or Concurrent List. Entry 97 of Union List (Residuary) specifically: 'Any other matter not enumerated in List II or List III including any tax not mentioned in either of those Lists.' This was used to justify service tax (before it was explicitly included), and helps in taxation of emerging digital activities. Article 265: No tax without law. Article 112: Budget.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Fifteen Finance Commission' (15th FC) devolved the highest-ever percentage to States and recommended 'Performance-Based Grants'. The total devolution (including all grants) as percentage of Centre's gross revenue was approximately:

options.option_text: ~42% (41% tax devolution + grants under Art.275 + disaster grants + local body grants — total broadly in 40-45% range)
25% (only the core 15th FC devolution)
60% — States retain majority of Central revenues
Exactly 41% — same as the 15th FC devolution percentage

explanation: 15th FC total transfers: 41% tax devolution from divisible pool. Plus: Revenue Deficit Grants (Art 275), Disaster Management grants, Local Body grants, sector-specific grants for health, education. Total resource transfer to States from Centre (including CSS, NCA, etc.) is typically 55-60% of Central revenues when everything is included. The 41% is specifically the share from the divisible pool of central taxes. Total resource sharing including plan transfers runs higher.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act 2017' guaranteed States:

options.option_text: 14% annual growth in their GST revenue for 5 years (FY18-22) using FY15-16 as base year — if actual GST revenue fell short, Centre compensated from cess collections
Equal distribution of GST among all states regardless of consumption
Immunity from fiscal deficit targets for 5 years post-GST implementation
Priority in Finance Commission devolution for 5 years to offset revenue loss

explanation: GST Compensation: States feared revenue loss from subsuming state taxes into GST. The Compensation Act guaranteed 14% p.a. protected revenue growth (compounded on FY16 base = FY17 base revenue). GST compensation cess collected on demerit goods deposited in Compensation Fund → paid monthly to states with shortfall. COVID (FY21-22): cess collections collapsed, Centre borrowed ₹1.1 lakh crore on behalf of States. The 5-year guarantee ended June 2022. States' demand: extend compensation or reduce rates on some items.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Green Budget Tagging' initiative in India's Union Budget classifies government expenditure based on:

options.option_text: Environmental impact — identifies allocations for climate-related activities like clean energy, sustainable transport, pollution control, green infrastructure (climate finance tracking)
Environmental pollution fines collected and budgeted for cleanup
Green card entry fees for foreign tourists to national parks
Agricultural green revolution spending as a separate budget category

explanation: Green Budget Tagging: India introduced this in Union Budget 2023-24, classifying expenditure across 4 categories: mitigation, adaptation, co-benefits, biodiversity. Example: PM Surya Ghar (rooftop solar), PM Kisan (agriculture), FAME-2 (EVs), national highways (green mobility) tagged. Aligns with India's NDC (Nationally Determined Contributions) for Paris Agreement. Helps track climate finance and informs investor decisions on sovereign green bonds. India issued Sovereign Green Bonds in January 2023 (₹16,000 crore).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: What is 'Seigniorage' in public finance?

options.option_text: Revenue earned by the government from issuing currency — the difference between the face value of money and the cost of producing it
Tax collected from lords and landlords (seigneurs) on land revenue in medieval system
Profit made by banks from interest rate spread between deposits and loans
Fine collected from firms for violation of competition norms

explanation: Seigniorage: ₹500 note costs ₹3-5 to print. Face value = ₹500. Seigniorage = ₹495-497 (per note). The government earns this as non-tax revenue. Excessive money printing to finance deficit = 'inflation tax' (a form of seigniorage). RBI transfers its surplus (from seigniorage, OMO operations, etc.) to government as dividend. Digital payments reduce seigniorage as less physical currency is needed. Historically, monarchs clipped coins (reduced metal content) = debasement = a form of seigniorage.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under India's MSS (Market Stabilisation Scheme), the bonds issued are different from regular government borrowings because:

options.option_text: MSS bonds are specifically to absorb excess liquidity caused by large capital inflows — proceeds kept in a separate MSS account with RBI, not usable for government expenditure
MSS bonds have higher interest rates to attract more investors
MSS bonds are guaranteed by IMF for foreign investors
MSS bonds are issued by state governments, not the Centre

explanation: MSS (Market Stabilisation Scheme, 2004): Tool for sterilising capital inflows. When massive FII/FDI inflows → excess rupee liquidity in banking system → inflationary pressure. RBI absorbs via MSS bonds (issued under government's name but proceeds locked in RBI account — government CANNOT use this money). Net: bonds absorb liquidity without boosting government spending. Different from regular borrowing (which funds expenditure). MSS issuance counted in India's fiscal deficit (adding to government debt) but no expenditure counterpart.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's Indirect Tax structure before GST had a problem called 'cascading effect' or 'tax on tax'. GST eliminated this by:

options.option_text: Allowing Input Tax Credit (ITC) at every stage — businesses deduct tax paid on inputs from tax collected on outputs, so tax is levied only on value added at each stage
Replacing all indirect taxes with a single income tax
Reducing all tax rates to single digits across all commodities
Collecting tax only at the final retail stage, not at manufacturing or wholesale

explanation: Pre-GST cascading: Manufacturer pays excise on output. Wholesaler pays VAT on price including excise (tax on tax). Retailer pays VAT on price including VAT (further cascading). Total tax burden > statutory rate. GST with ITC: Each stage charges GST on full sale price but claims credit for GST paid on inputs. Net tax at each stage = GST on value added only. Zero cascading. Revenue-neutral rate (RNR) study estimated cascading added 25-30% to pre-GST effective tax rates on some goods.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Mundell-Fleming Model' extends IS-LM to an open economy. Under FIXED exchange rate and PERFECT capital mobility, fiscal policy is:

options.option_text: Completely EFFECTIVE — fiscal expansion raises income, attracting capital inflow which prevents crowding out (central bank buys forex, expands money supply automatically)
Completely INEFFECTIVE — monetary expansion always offsets fiscal impulse
Partially effective — depends on elasticity of capital flows
Ineffective because exchange rate prevents income changes

explanation: Mundell-Fleming Model: Fixed rate + Perfect capital mobility: Fiscal policy IS effective. G↑ → IS shifts right → income rises → interest rate rises → capital inflows → currency appreciation pressure → central bank buys foreign currency (sells domestic) → LM shifts right → income rises further (full multiplier effect without crowding out). Monetary policy INEFFECTIVE (fixed rate: any money expansion → capital outflow → bank must buy domestic currency back → LM returns to original position). Opposite under floating exchange rates.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Sovereign Gold Bonds (SGBs)' serve which dual purpose for the government?

options.option_text: Reduce physical gold import demand (substitute gold investment with financial instrument) AND reduce fiscal deficit by mobilising funds at lower cost than market borrowing
Promote gold exports by creating a domestic gold futures market
Allow RBI to directly invest in gold as reserve asset
Provide tribal communities a way to monetise their traditional gold holdings

explanation: SGBs (RBI issues on behalf of government since November 2015): 8-year tenure, 2.5% interest p.a. on issue price + capital appreciation. Redeemable early (5th year onward). Capital gains tax exempt on maturity. Purpose: (1) Shift gold demand from physical to financial → reduce gold imports → improve Current Account (India imports ~800 tonnes gold p.a. = ~$35-40bn drain). (2) Funds borrowed at 2.5% vs market rate of 7% → fiscal savings. RBI stopped new SGB issuances in 2024 amid gold price rise making them costly.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT)' was constituted to:

options.option_text: Provide a dedicated appellate body for GST disputes between taxpayers and GST authorities — before High Court, resolving at lower cost and faster than courts
Set GST rates on new products not included in initial GST schedule
Arbitrate disputes between Centre and States on GST revenue sharing
Prosecute GST fraud cases under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act

explanation: GSTAT: A quasi-judicial authority for second appeal in GST matters. Hierarchy: Adjudicating authority (officer) → First appellate authority (Commissioner/Joint Commissioner) → GSTAT → High Court → Supreme Court. GSTAT reduces burden on courts and provides uniformity in GST interpretation. Long delayed — finally constituted in 2023 after years of delay due to disagreements on composition. National Bench in Delhi; State Benches in major cities.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Revenue Expenditure to Capital Expenditure Ratio' — when this ratio is HIGH, it indicates:

options.option_text: Government is spending more on consumption (salaries, subsidies, interest) relative to asset creation — limiting long-term growth potential and fiscal quality
Government is productively investing in infrastructure — high capex is good
Revenue collection is higher than capital receipts
The government has successfully reduced subsidies and cut waste

explanation: Quality of expenditure metric: High Rev/Cap ratio → 'unproductive' spending dominates. Revenue exp (salaries, pensions, subsidies, interest) → consumption, no assets. Capital exp (roads, dams, railways, hospitals) → asset creation, future productivity, multiplier effect. India's capex push in Union Budget 2021-24 (from 1.7% of GDP in FY20 to 3.3% in FY24) was to improve this ratio. IMF recommends countries track 'public investment' as key fiscal quality indicator.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A monopoly firm has MR = 0 at its profit-maximising output. What is the price elasticity of demand at this output?

options.option_text: Ed = −1 (unitary elastic) — MR = P(1 + 1/Ed); MR=0 → 1+1/Ed=0 → Ed=−1
Ed = 0 (perfectly inelastic)
Ed = −∞ (perfectly elastic)
Cannot be determined without knowing price

explanation: MR = P(1 + 1/Ed). Setting MR = 0: P(1 + 1/Ed) = 0. Since P ≠ 0: 1 + 1/Ed = 0 → Ed = −1. Monopolist MAXIMISES TOTAL REVENUE at the point where MR = 0 (unitary elastic demand). But profit maximisation (MR = MC) occurs where MC > 0, hence profit-maximising output is where MR = MC > 0, which is in the elastic range (|Ed| > 1). The MR = 0 point = TR maximum, not profit maximum.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In the Stackelberg leadership model, the leader firm chooses output FIRST knowing the follower's reaction function. Compared to Cournot Nash equilibrium:

options.option_text: Leader produces MORE than Cournot output; follower produces LESS; total output is HIGHER than Cournot; price is LOWER
Both leader and follower produce same as Cournot
Leader produces less; follower produces more than Cournot
Total output is the same as Cournot but distribution shifts

explanation: Stackelberg model (Stackelberg, 1934): Leader commits to large output, knowing follower will produce less (follower's reaction function shows: higher Q_leader → lower Q_follower). Leader's first-mover advantage allows it to capture more market share. Total output (Q_L + Q_F) > Cournot total → lower price. Leader earns MORE than Cournot profit; follower earns LESS. Example: Market leader vs market follower strategies in oligopolistic industries.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A market with free entry has firms earning zero economic profit in the long run. This is a feature of:

options.option_text: Both Perfect Competition AND Monopolistic Competition — free entry erodes supernormal profits in both structures
Perfect Competition only — MC firms retain some profit due to differentiation
Monopolistic Competition only — PC firms always make losses
Neither — zero profit is impossible with free entry as firms won't enter

explanation: Zero economic profit in LR: both PC and Monopolistic Competition achieve this via free entry. Supernormal profit → firms enter → demand for existing firms falls → price falls → zero profit. Difference: PC at zero profit also achieves productive (P = min ATC) and allocative (P = MC) efficiency. MC at zero profit: P = ATC but P > MC and P > min ATC (excess capacity). The mechanism (entry) is the same; the efficiency outcome differs.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'GeM (Government e-Marketplace)' platform was launched to:

options.option_text: Create a unified online marketplace for government procurement of goods and services — ensuring transparency, efficiency, and reduced costs in public purchasing
Sell government surplus assets and old equipment to private buyers
Allow government employees to purchase personal goods at subsidised prices
Create a marketplace for state governments to exchange resources

explanation: GeM (Government e-Marketplace): launched August 2016 under DPIIT (Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade). Enables central and state government buyers to purchase goods and services directly from sellers online — like Amazon but for government. Features: reverse auctions, price comparison, transparency, MSME and startup seller promotion. Mandatory for government procurement above certain thresholds. GMV crossed ₹4 lakh crore (FY24). Eliminates corruption in government buying.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile (JAM Trinity)' as a policy framework enables:

options.option_text: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) — linking bank accounts (Jan Dhan) + unique identity (Aadhaar) + mobile phone to deliver subsidies/benefits directly to beneficiaries, eliminating leakages
Three-factor authentication for income tax filing
Digital payment system for rural traders using mobile phones
A universal credit scoring system using bank and identity data

explanation: JAM Trinity (coined by Arvind Subramanian, Economic Survey 2015-16): Jan Dhan accounts (500mn+ zero-balance accounts) + Aadhaar (biometric identity for 1.3bn people) + Mobile (telecom penetration). Together enable: DBT for LPG subsidies (PAHAL saved ₹1.1 lakh crore in 3 years), MGNREGA wages, scholarship, PM-KISAN. Eliminated ghost beneficiaries, fake accounts, middleman leakages. Estimated savings from DBT: ₹3 lakh crore+ cumulatively.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Startup India' initiative (2016) provides which tax benefit to eligible startups?

options.option_text: 3-year income tax holiday (any 3 years out of first 10 years) for DPIIT-recognised startups meeting eligibility criteria
Complete lifetime income tax exemption for all startups
GST exemption for startups with turnover below ₹40 lakh
Customs duty waiver on all imports by startups

explanation: Startup India (launched January 2016, PM Modi): Key benefit: 3-year income tax holiday (Section 80-IAC) — exemption from paying income tax for ANY 3 years out of first 10 years. DPIIT recognition required: incorporated ≤10 years ago, turnover ≤₹100 crore, working on innovative product/service. Other benefits: Fund of Funds (₹10,000 crore SIDBI), fast-track IPR application, self-certification for 9 labour and environmental laws. India is 3rd largest startup ecosystem globally.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'MSME Classification' in India (revised 2020) classifies a medium enterprise as:

options.option_text: Investment in plant and machinery/equipment: ₹10-50 crore AND annual turnover ₹50-250 crore (both criteria must be met)
Investment: above ₹25 crore; turnover: any amount
Employment: 50-250 workers regardless of investment or turnover
Investment: ₹5-10 crore; turnover: ₹25-100 crore

explanation: Revised MSME Classification (2020, composite investment+turnover criterion): Micro: Investment ≤₹1 crore AND Turnover ≤₹5 crore. Small: Investment ≤₹10 crore AND Turnover ≤₹50 crore. Medium: Investment ≤₹50 crore AND Turnover ≤₹250 crore. Previously: only investment-based, separate for manufacturing vs services. New: composite (both criteria), unified for manufacturing and services. MSME sector: 6+ crore enterprises, 11+ crore employment, ~30% of GDP, ~48% of exports.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Performance Grading Index (PGI)' for school education is released by:

options.option_text: Ministry of Education — ranks States/UTs on 70 indicators across 5 domains: learning outcomes, access, infrastructure, governance, and equity
NITI Aayog — as part of SDG India Index
NCERT — the curriculum body evaluating state textbook quality
World Bank — as part of Human Capital Index assessment

explanation: PGI (Performance Grading Index): Ministry of Education (MoE), released annually since 2017-18. Grades States/UTs on 1000-point scale across 5 domains: (1) Outcomes (Learning/Access outcomes). (2) Effective Classroom Transaction. (3) Infrastructure/Facilities. (4) Equity. (5) Governance Processes. Grades: Level 1++ (top) to Level X. Kerela, Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Chandigarh typically score highest. Encourages competitive federalism in education. PGI 2.0: expanded to 73 indicators.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Faceless Assessment Scheme' in income tax (2020) aims to:

options.option_text: Eliminate face-to-face contact between taxpayers and tax officers — all assessments done digitally and randomly assigned across different jurisdictions to reduce corruption and harassment
Exempt taxpayers with annual income below ₹5 lakh from tax assessment
Allow AI to automatically compute tax liability without human review
Remove the requirement for taxpayers to show their face (identity) when filing online

explanation: Faceless Assessment (PM Modi, August 2020 — 'Transparent Taxation' platform): Tax notices, hearings, and orders issued through centralized IT system. Taxpayer doesn't know which officer is handling their case; officer doesn't know whose case they're reviewing. Random assignment prevents building of corrupt relationships. Team-based assessments (not individual officer). Faceless Appeals also launched. Reduced taxpayer harassment significantly. Part of broader digitization of income tax including pre-filled ITR forms.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Production Linked Incentive (PLI) for Pharmaceuticals' primarily targets:

options.option_text: Reducing import dependence for Key Starting Materials (KSMs), Drug Intermediates, and Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients (APIs) — and promoting high-value pharmaceutical products
Making all medicines free for Below Poverty Line population
Building government pharmaceutical factories to reduce private sector dependence
Regulating maximum retail prices of all medicines

explanation: PLI Pharmaceuticals (₹15,000 crore, 2020): Two schemes — (1) PLI for KSMs/Drug Intermediates/APIs: incentivise domestic production of 53 critical APIs (penicillin, paracetamol, vitamin C, etc.) where India is 80-100% import dependent on China. (2) PLI for Pharmaceuticals: high-value complex generics, biopharmaceuticals, cell/gene therapy, orphan drugs. Lessons from COVID: API shortage (China supply disruption) exposed vulnerability. Aligned with 'Pharma Vision 2047' to make India a global pharmaceutical innovation hub.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code 2016' changed the creditor-debtor power balance by:

options.option_text: Shifting from 'Debtor-in-Possession' (debtor controls during proceedings) to 'Creditor-in-Control' (creditors decide through CoC with RP managing day-to-day) — time-bound resolution
Giving debtors more time to repay by extending court proceedings
Making all loans collateral-free so creditors bear full risk
Nationalising defaulting companies and compensating creditors from government funds

explanation: Pre-IBC: Promoter/debtor retained control during BIFR/DRT proceedings, leading to value destruction and delays (average resolution: 4+ years). IBC: Creditor-in-Control — existing management suspended, Resolution Professional (RP) manages operations, Committee of Creditors (CoC, primarily financial creditors) decides on resolution plan. 180+90 day limit prevents delay tactics by promoters. Cultural shift: 'exit is not failure.' India rose to 52nd in World Bank's Resolving Insolvency indicator.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Bad Bank' concept in India (National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited — NARCL) was set up to:

options.option_text: Purchase stressed (NPA) assets from banks at agreed prices — freeing bank balance sheets to lend fresh; NARCL sells/resolves the bad loans over time
Shut down banks that fail to meet capital adequacy requirements
Provide loans to borrowers rejected by commercial banks
Collect tax arrears from defaulting large taxpayers

explanation: NARCL (Bad Bank, approved 2021): Acquires NPA accounts (>₹500 crore) from banks. 15% paid in cash; 85% in government-guaranteed Security Receipts (SRs). IDRCL (India Debt Resolution Company Ltd) — 'India's first bad bank' — manages resolution. Backed by ₹30,600 crore government guarantee on SRs. Allows banks to clean balance sheets quickly. Global precedents: KAMCO (South Korea), AMC (China) post-Asian Crisis. NARCL has been slow to achieve scale as of 2024-25.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Quantitative Easing (QE) as used by central banks post-2008 GFC involves:

options.option_text: Large-scale asset purchases (government bonds, MBS) by the central bank to inject liquidity when conventional policy rates are at the zero lower bound
Increasing bank reserve requirements to reduce money supply
Distributing cash directly to households (helicopter money)
Fixing exchange rates to stimulate export-led growth

explanation: QE: Used when policy rate hits zero (ZLB) and further cuts are impossible. Fed, ECB, Bank of Japan, Bank of England all used QE post-2008. Mechanism: Central bank creates money → buys long-term bonds → bond yields fall → mortgage rates fall → wealth effect (asset prices rise) → stimulates spending. Risks: asset price bubbles, inflation when unwinding ('taper tantrum' 2013). India used a modified version (GSAP — Government Securities Acquisition Programme) during COVID.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: RBI's 'Standing Deposit Facility (SDF)' replaced the Reverse Repo Rate as the floor of the LAF corridor in April 2022. The key advantage of SDF over Reverse Repo is:

options.option_text: SDF absorbs excess liquidity WITHOUT providing collateral to banks — RBI simply accepts deposits; Reverse Repo required RBI to provide G-secs as collateral to banks
SDF pays higher interest than Reverse Repo making it more attractive
SDF is available 24×7 while Reverse Repo only operated during market hours
SDF allows RBI to absorb foreign currency deposits not just rupees

explanation: Reverse Repo: RBI borrows from banks by providing G-secs as collateral. Problem: as RBI absorbed massive COVID-era liquidity, its G-sec portfolio depleted — RBI had no more collateral to offer for Reverse Repo. SDF (Section 17(1)(a) of RBI Act, amended 2018): RBI accepts deposits WITHOUT providing collateral. Uncollateralised facility. Allows unlimited absorption. Set at Repo − 25 bps (same spread as old Reverse Repo). The SDF rate became the new effective floor of the LAF corridor from April 2022.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'G-Sec Acquisition Programme (GSAP)' introduced by RBI in 2021 was:

options.option_text: A commitment to purchase a predetermined quantum of government securities from the open market — providing advance guidance on OMO quantum to anchor long-term bond yields
A scheme to sell government securities to foreign investors at fixed prices
