A programme to issue new government securities to fund COVID stimulus
A system to exchange old government securities for new digital bonds

explanation: GSAP (April 2021): RBI announced it would purchase G-secs of specified quantum on specified dates — unlike traditional OMOs (which were discretionary). Pre-announced purchase calendar gave markets certainty → bond yields fell → 10-year yield dropped from 6.2% to 5.9%. Similar to QE's 'calendar guidance.' Discontinued as liquidity normalised and yields needed to rise. GSAP showed RBI could use yield curve control tools similar to developed market central banks.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'SWIFT GPI (Global Payments Innovation)' initiative improves cross-border payments by:

options.option_text: Providing end-to-end tracking, same-day settlement, and transparency of fees for international wire transfers — like a tracking number for money transfers
Replacing SWIFT messaging with blockchain for all international transfers
Creating a new currency for global transactions eliminating forex risk
Allowing individuals to bypass banks for direct cross-border transfers

explanation: SWIFT GPI (launched 2017): addressed main pain points of traditional SWIFT transfers: (1) Slow (days). (2) Opaque fees. (3) No tracking. GPI adds: Unique End-to-End Transaction Reference (UETR) for tracking. Same-day settlement. Fee transparency. 75%+ of GPI payments settle within 30 minutes. Covers 4,000+ financial institutions. GPI is evolving toward ISO 20022 standard — richer data, better compliance screening. Complements but doesn't replace national systems like NEFT/UPI for domestic transfers.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'FPI (Foreign Portfolio Investment)' flows affect the rupee because:

options.option_text: FPI inflows → foreign currency enters India → rupee demand rises → rupee APPRECIATES; FPI outflows → foreign currency leaves → rupee DEPRECIATES
FPI flows don't affect rupee — only FDI matters for exchange rate
FPI inflows → rupee depreciates as India owes returns to foreign investors
FPI flows affect only stock prices, not the currency market

explanation: FPI (portfolio investment — stocks, bonds): 'hot money.' Highly sensitive to global risk sentiment and interest rate differentials. Inflows: investors sell USD/EUR → buy INR → buy Indian stocks/bonds → INR appreciates. Outflows (sudden): sell Indian stocks → sell INR → buy USD → 'sudden stop' → sharp INR depreciation. 2013 'taper tantrum': FPI outflows caused INR to fall from 55 to 68/USD. RBI sterilises excessive FPI inflows via OMO/MSS to prevent excessive appreciation.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Union Budget 2024-25 continued the practice of significantly increasing 'Capital Expenditure.' The economic rationale for prioritising capex over revenue expenditure is:

options.option_text: Higher fiscal multiplier for capex (creates assets → long-term growth) vs revenue expenditure (mostly consumption, less multiplier); also 'crowding in' private investment via better infrastructure
Capital expenditure is not subject to FRBM limits so it can be increased freely
Revenue expenditure is fully funded by tax revenue so capex needs extra borrowing anyway
Capex reduces the revenue deficit while keeping fiscal deficit unchanged

explanation: Capex multiplier > Revex multiplier (empirically): IMF estimates capex multiplier ~1.5x in emerging markets. Capex on highways, railways, ports → logistics cost reduction → private sector productivity gains ('crowding in'). Revenue expenditure (salaries, subsidies) has lower multiplier as significant portion is saved or leaked. India's capex push: FY21 ₹4.4 lakh crore → FY25 ₹11.1 lakh crore (2.5× increase). This drove construction sector revival and supported post-COVID growth recovery.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Voluntary Retention Route (VRR)' for FPIs in India refers to:

options.option_text: An investment channel where FPIs voluntarily commit to retain at least 75% of their investment for 3 years — in return they get relaxed investment limits and exemptions from certain macro-prudential limits
A scheme where foreign companies voluntarily retain their Indian profits without repatriation
An RBI directive for banks to retain a portion of FPI deposits on their books
A SEBI requirement for FPIs to hold shares for minimum 3 years to avail long-term capital gains rate

explanation: VRR (RBI, 2019): Addresses 'hot money' problem of FPIs. Traditional FPIs are volatile — can exit instantly during global risk-off. VRR: FPIs commit minimum 75% investment retention for minimum 3 years → reduces volatility risk. Reward: Exempt from investment limits that apply to normal FPIs under G-sec/corporate bond route; no macro-prudential measures (short-term cap). Helps India attract 'stickier' long-term debt capital from pension funds, insurance companies that suit VRR's lock-in.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Expenditure Management Commission' set up by the Government of India in 2014 was tasked with:

options.option_text: Reviewing Central Government expenditure to identify savings, rationalise subsidies, and improve expenditure efficiency — recommending reforms to reduce revenue expenditure and revenue deficit
Managing the day-to-day expenditure of all Union ministries
Regulating state government expenditure to ensure fiscal discipline
Auditing government spending on behalf of CAG

explanation: Expenditure Management Commission (EMC, 2014, chaired by Bimal Jalan): Reviewed Central Government expenditure structure. Key recommendations: Direct Benefit Transfer for subsidies (fertilizer, food, kerosene), rationalise CSS (Centrally Sponsored Schemes — reduce from 66 to 30), end plan/non-plan distinction (implemented in 2017), plug leakages in welfare spending. EMC was part of the BJP government's fiscal consolidation agenda post 2014. Many recommendations were implemented incrementally.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Revised Estimates (RE)' presented in the Budget differ from 'Budget Estimates (BE)' in that RE:

options.option_text: Are mid-year revised projections based on first 6-9 months of actual performance, correcting original BE for changed economic conditions, revised revenue forecasts, or new spending requirements
Are the final audited accounts of the completed financial year
Are prepared by state governments to revise their budget allocations
Are the Parliamentary Committee's revised recommendations on budget allocations

explanation: Budget document timeline: BE (February): Forward estimate for April-March year. RE (presented with next year's BE in February, or sometimes separately in monsoon/winter Parliament session): Mid-year revision. Corrects for: Higher/lower tax revenues, additional expenditure needs, scheme reallocation. RE is more accurate than BE since 8-9 months of actuals are available. Actual (May-June following year): CAG-audited final accounts. RE > BE for fiscal deficit: usually means government spent more or collected less than planned.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Consolidated Fund of India' (Article 266) is the government's main account where all revenues, loans received, and repayments are made. Which of the following does NOT go into the Consolidated Fund?

options.option_text: Amounts received by government for specific purposes (court deposits, escrow amounts) — these go to the 'Public Account of India'
Income tax collected by the Central Government
Market borrowings (dated government securities issued)
Repayments of loans given by Centre to States

explanation: Three Government Accounts: (1) Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 266): All revenues (taxes, non-tax), all borrowings, all loan repayments. All expenditure must be authorised from CFI by Parliament (Appropriation Act). (2) Contingency Fund (Art. 267): Emergency corpus (₹500 crore) — President can draw without Parliament's prior approval; ratified later. (3) Public Account (Art. 266): Moneys received for specific purposes — provident funds, deposits, court deposits, small savings, escrow. Parliament's supervision lighter for Public Account.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'Interest Payment to Revenue Receipts Ratio' being very HIGH (around 30-40%) indicates:

options.option_text: A significant portion of every rupee collected in taxes goes to servicing past debt — compressing fiscal space for development and social spending ('debt trap' risk)
Government is earning high interest on loans given to states
Interest rates are low, making borrowing cheap for the government
Revenue receipts are higher than expenditure — the government has surplus

explanation: Interest-Revenue ratio (IIPR): India's central government interest payments ~₹11 lakh crore/year (FY25). Revenue receipts ~₹28-30 lakh crore. IIPR ≈ 37-40%. Meaning: for every ₹100 in tax/non-tax revenue, ₹38 goes to interest alone before any development spending. This is the 'fiscal compression' problem — leaves little room for capex, health, education. States with high IIPR (UP, Bihar) have less development spending capacity. IMF considers IIPR > 25% as a warning sign of debt unsustainability risk.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team)' issued controversial directions in 2022 requiring:

options.option_text: All VPN providers, cloud providers, and data centres to maintain detailed logs of users for 5 years and report cybersecurity incidents within 6 hours — raising privacy concerns
All Indian users to register their devices with CERT-In annually
Government approval before any new cybersecurity product can be sold in India
All websites to encrypt data using only government-approved algorithms

explanation: CERT-In Directions (April 2022, under IT Act Section 70B): Required VPN service providers, cloud companies, data centres to: (1) Maintain logs of users (5 years). (2) Collect and store verified subscriber data. (3) Report cybersecurity incidents within 6 HOURS (vs 72 hours in EU GDPR). Led to several major VPN providers (NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark) exiting India or moving servers offshore. Rationale: improve threat investigation capability. Critics: privacy violation, surveillance concern, chilling effect on dissent.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Open Credit Enablement Network (OCEN)' framework is designed to:

options.option_text: Democratise credit access by allowing any digital platform to act as a Loan Service Provider (LSP) connecting borrowers with multiple lenders — enabling small/gig economy workers to get credit using their digital transaction history
Provide government-subsidised credit to below-poverty-line households through Aadhaar
Create an open-source credit scoring algorithm for banks to use
Enable banks to share customer credit data across institutions without consent

explanation: OCEN (iSPIRT, 2020): Part of India's open credit infrastructure. LSPs (e-commerce platforms, gig worker apps, FMCG distributors) connect borrowers with lenders via standardised APIs. Borrower's cash-flow data (GST returns, bank statements via AA, UPI transactions) serves as credit assessment basis. Use case: Kirana store owner gets ₹50,000 credit based on GST filing history via their B2B ordering app. Fills the credit gap for 6 crore+ MSMEs lacking collateral. Complements Account Aggregator (data) + GSTN (tax data).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Narasimham Committee I (1991) recommended a 3-tier banking structure. Its key structural recommendation was:

options.option_text: 3–4 large banks with international presence, 8–10 national banks, and local banks for specific regions — replacing the 'one-size-fits-all' nationalised bank model
Nationalisation of all private banks to create a unified public sector banking system
Merging all public sector banks into a single National Bank of India
Allowing foreign banks to operate without any restrictions in India

explanation: Narasimham Committee I (1991, M. Narasimham): Recommended phased deregulation of banking. Key: 3-tier structure — 3-4 large banks with international presence + 8-10 national banks + local/rural banks. Also: reduce CRR and SLR (which were at peak 25%+15%), introduce capital adequacy norms, NPA provisioning norms, interest rate deregulation. Was the foundation of banking sector liberalisation in 1991 reforms. Most recommendations implemented by 1994-95.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Narasimham Committee II (1998) was specifically set up in the context of:

options.option_text: Strengthening the financial system AFTER the first round of banking reforms and preparing for next-generation challenges — including NPA resolution, bank mergers, and banking sector stability
Responding to the 1991 Balance of Payments crisis
Designing the regulatory framework for payment banks
Creating the blueprint for GST and indirect tax reform

explanation: Narasimham II (1998): Second-generation reforms. Key recommendations: (1) Weak bank merger with stronger bank (not SBI/large bank). (2) Capital adequacy — increase from 8% to 9% (already ahead of Basel I). (3) NPA target: reduce gross NPAs to 5% by 2000, 3% by 2002. (4) Narrow banking for weak banks (restrict to G-sec investment). (5) Introduced concept of 'bridge banks.' (6) Recommended independent Banking Supervision Board. Context: post-East Asian Crisis (1997) — ensuring India's banks were crisis-resistant.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Small Finance Banks (SFBs) in India were given bank licenses in 2016 with a specific mandate. Their PRIMARY requirement is:

options.option_text: At least 75% of net bank credit must go to Priority Sector — and 50% of their loan portfolio must consist of loans of size ≤ ₹25 lakh
100% of deposits must be invested in government securities only
Operate exclusively in rural areas without branches in metros
Lend only to women self-help groups and microfinance borrowers

explanation: SFBs (RBI license, 2016): Primarily serve unserved/underserved sections — small farmers, micro industries, unorganised sector. Mandates: (1) PSL target 75% of Net Bank Credit (vs 40% for SCBs). (2) 50% of loan portfolio: loans ≤ ₹25 lakh. (3) Minimum capital: ₹200 crore. (4) 25% branches in unbanked rural centres (Tier 5-6). First batch (2017): Equitas, Ujjivan, Jana, AU, ESAF, etc. Can accept all deposits and issue debit cards — unlike Payment Banks. Key difference from Payment Banks: SFBs can lend.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following money market instruments can ONLY be issued by corporates (not banks or government)?

options.option_text: Commercial Paper (CP) — unsecured short-term promissory note issued by corporates, primary dealers, and all-India FIs; minimum ₹5 lakh face value, maturity 7 days to 1 year
Treasury Bills — issued by Government of India through RBI
Certificate of Deposit (CD) — issued by scheduled commercial banks and select FIs
Call Money — interbank overnight lending without collateral

explanation: Money Market Instruments: Treasury Bills (T-Bills): Government of India — 91/182/364 day. Certificate of Deposit (CD): Scheduled commercial banks — 7 days to 1 year; select FIs 1-3 years. Commercial Paper (CP): Corporates, primary dealers, all-India FIs — minimum net worth ₹100 crore, credit rating A2/P2 required. Call Money: Interbank overnight — only scheduled commercial banks participate. CMBs (Cash Management Bills): T-bill variant for < 91 days. Repo: Collateralised overnight — between banks and with RBI.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Call Money Market' in India operates as:

options.option_text: An UNCOLLATERALISED overnight/short-term lending market exclusively between scheduled commercial banks — where surplus banks lend to deficit banks at the 'call rate'
A market where RBI lends directly to corporate borrowers for working capital
A platform where the public can make one-day deposits with banks at special rates
A telephone-based market where brokers buy and sell corporate bonds

explanation: Call Money Market: Participants — only scheduled commercial banks (interbank segment). Notice Money: 2-14 days (slightly longer than 1 day). Term Money: 15 days to 1 year. Rate = Call Rate, fluctuates daily based on liquidity conditions. Bounded by LAF corridor: SDF rate (floor) and MSF rate (ceiling) — call rate cannot persistently stay below SDF or above MSF. When RBI injects liquidity via LAF, call rates fall; when RBI absorbs, rates rise. Key liquidity indicator for RBI's monetary operations.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Treasury Bills (T-Bills) of 91 days, 182 days, and 364 days are issued by:

options.option_text: Government of India through RBI — sold at DISCOUNT, redeemed at face value; difference = yield; no coupon payment
Reserve Bank of India from its own account to fund its operations
SEBI-registered mutual funds as short-term debt instruments
State governments to fund short-term expenditure gaps

explanation: T-Bills: Zero coupon (discount) instruments. Face value ₹100, sold at ₹98 → yield = ₹2/₹98 × 365/91. GoI issues through RBI via weekly auctions. 91-day T-Bills: most liquid, closest to risk-free rate. Uses: (1) Government's short-term borrowing. (2) Banks park surplus funds. (3) Benchmark for money market pricing. CMBs (Cash Management Bills): ad-hoc, maturity < 91 days. State governments issue 'Ways and Means Advances' from RBI (not T-Bills) for short-term cash needs. T-Bills are Central Government-only.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) 2002, 'money laundering' is defined as:

options.option_text: Concealment, possession, acquisition, or use of proceeds of a 'scheduled offence' — projecting them as untainted property; three stages: Placement → Layering → Integration
Printing of counterfeit currency notes by non-government entities
Tax evasion through offshore accounts in foreign countries
Import of gold without paying customs duty to avoid detection

explanation: PMLA 2002 (enforced 2005): Three stages of money laundering: (1) Placement — illegal money enters financial system (cash deposits, smurfing). (2) Layering — series of transactions to hide trail (wire transfers, shell companies, crypto). (3) Integration — cleaned money re-enters economy as 'legitimate' (real estate, luxury goods). PMLA: reporting entity (banks, FIs, NBFCs) must file Suspicious Transaction Report (STR) with FIU-IND within 7 days. Enforcement Directorate (ED) — key investigating agency. Proceeds of crime: attachable, confiscatable.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Financial Intelligence Unit — India (FIU-IND) under PMLA 2002 collects and processes:

options.option_text: Cash Transaction Reports (CTR) for ₹10 lakh+ cash transactions, Suspicious Transaction Reports (STR), and Cross Border Wire Transfer Reports — to detect money laundering and terror financing
Foreign exchange reserves data reported by RBI
Income tax returns filed by NRIs and foreign companies
Government procurement tender irregularities reported by CAG

explanation: FIU-IND (Financial Intelligence Unit – India, Ministry of Finance): Receives, processes, analyses financial intelligence. Key reports: (1) CTR: all cash transactions ≥ ₹10 lakh (fortnightly). (2) STR: suspicious transactions (no threshold, within 7 days). (3) CIBTR: Cross Border Incoming/Outgoing transfers ≥ ₹5 lakh. (4) NTR: Non-profit organisation transactions. FIU shares intelligence with CBI, ED, IT, Customs. India's FATF mutual evaluation (2022-24): found deficiencies in monitoring; follow-up action ongoing. FIU is the nodal agency for FATF reporting.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) 'Grey List' (Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring) designation means:

options.option_text: The country has committed to resolving identified deficiencies in anti-money laundering/counter-terrorist financing (AML/CFT) within agreed timelines — increased monitoring but NOT blacklisted
The country is facing economic sanctions from the UN Security Council
The country's banks are banned from using SWIFT messaging
Foreign investors must get government approval before investing in the grey-listed country

explanation: FATF (Financial Action Task Force, est. 1989, Paris): Sets global AML/CFT standards. Three lists: (1) Black List (Call for Action): High-risk countries — North Korea, Iran, Myanmar. Enhanced due diligence required. (2) Grey List (Increased Monitoring): Country acknowledges weaknesses, commits to action plan. Examples: Pakistan (2018-2022), Turkey, UAE (both removed after reforms). (3) Clean: All others. India is a FATF member (since 2010). Grey list affects: correspondent banking, IMF lending terms, investment flows. India's last mutual evaluation (2010): partially compliant.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: KYC (Know Your Customer) norms for banks in India are mandated by RBI primarily to:

options.option_text: Verify customer identity and address, understand the nature of the customer's business, and prevent banks from being used for money laundering or terrorist financing
Calculate the credit score of customers before loan disbursement
Enable the bank to cross-sell insurance and investment products to customers
Ensure customers pay income tax on their bank interest income

explanation: KYC: RBI mandated under PMLA 2002 and Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules. Documents: Proof of Identity (Aadhaar/Passport/Voter ID/Driving License) + Proof of Address. Video KYC (V-CIP): RBI allowed in 2020 — customers can complete KYC via video call. eKYC via Aadhaar: OTP-based verification. Periodic updation: every 10 years (low risk), 8 years (medium risk), 2 years (high risk). Central KYC Registry (CKYCR): customer registers once, KYC shared across financial institutions. C-KYC number assigned.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: MCLR (Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate), introduced by RBI in April 2016, improved upon the earlier Base Rate system by:

options.option_text: Using MARGINAL cost of funds (not average cost) as the basis — ensuring interest rate changes by RBI are transmitted more quickly to loan rates; includes negative carry on CRR, operating cost, and tenure premium
Allowing banks to charge any rate above zero percent without any RBI-set floor
Creating a single universal lending rate for all banks to eliminate competition
Linking loan rates directly to the inflation rate (CPI) instead of bank costs

explanation: Lending rate evolution: PLR (Prime Lending Rate, pre-2010) → Base Rate (2010-16, average cost) → MCLR (2016-19, marginal cost) → EBLR (External Benchmark, Oct 2019, current). MCLR improvement: used marginal cost (new deposits) not average cost → faster transmission. Components: marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating cost + tenure premium. Problem with MCLR: banks still had discretion in computing marginal cost. EBLR (repo/T-bill linked) solved this by linking to RBI's policy rate directly — automatic, transparent transmission.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: TReDS (Trade Receivables Discounting System) was established in India to solve:

options.option_text: The delayed payment problem faced by MSMEs — they supply to large companies but wait months for payment; TReDS lets MSMEs discount their invoices immediately through a digital auction among financiers
The problem of trade deficits by promoting export invoice financing
Counterfeiting of trade documents and customs fraud
The problem of banks not lending to the trading community

explanation: TReDS (RBI mandated, 2014; operational 2017): MSME sells goods to large buyer (corporate) → uploads invoice on TReDS platform → financiers (banks, NBFCs) bid to discount the invoice → MSME gets cash immediately at competitive rate → buyer pays TReDS at invoice maturity. Three licensed platforms: Receivables Exchange of India (RXIL, NSE+SIDBI), A.TReDS (Axis Bank+Mjunction), C2FIN (MYND Solutions). Mandated by MSMED Act: companies with ₹500 crore+ turnover MUST register on TReDS. Solves 45-90 day payment delays that cause MSME working capital crunch.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Gold Monetisation Scheme (GMS) launched in 2015 allows individuals and institutions to:

options.option_text: Deposit idle physical gold with banks (minimum 10 grams) and earn interest on it in gold terms — gold is melted and used by jewellers/manufacturers, reducing gold imports
Buy government gold bonds linked to international gold prices
Exchange old jewellery at market prices without capital gains tax
Sell gold to RBI at fixed prices to create official reserves

explanation: GMS 2015 (replaced old Gold Deposit Scheme): Addresses India's estimated 25,000 tonne household gold hoard. Three sub-schemes: (1) Short-term Bank Deposits (STBD): 1-3 years, bank uses gold, interest set by individual bank. (2) Medium-Term Government Deposits (MTGD): 5-7 years. (3) Long-Term Government Deposits (LTGD): 12-15 years. Interest paid in gold terms (e.g., 2.5% per annum, credited in grams). On maturity: gold or equivalent cash. Reduces need for gold imports (India imports ~800 tonnes/year). Complementary to Sovereign Gold Bonds (which replace physical gold purchase).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The key difference between IMF lending and World Bank lending is:

options.option_text: IMF lends for Balance of Payments support (short-to-medium term, with conditionalities); World Bank (IBRD+IDA) lends for long-term development projects (infrastructure, health, education)
IMF lends only to rich countries; World Bank only to poor countries
IMF gives grants; World Bank gives loans
IMF monitors exchange rates; World Bank manages global trade rules

explanation: IMF (International Monetary Fund, 1944 Bretton Woods): Lends for BoP crisis management. Types: Stand-By Arrangement (SBA), Extended Fund Facility (EFF), Rapid Financing Instrument. Conditionality: fiscal adjustment, structural reform. India used IMF in 1991. World Bank Group: IBRD (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development) — middle-income countries. IDA (International Development Association) — poorest countries (concessional/grants). Both: long-term development lending. MIGA: investment insurance. IFC: private sector. India is IBRD borrower. Key: IMF = short-term stabilisation; WB = long-term development.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The IMF's Special Drawing Right (SDR) basket (revised 2022) includes which currencies?

options.option_text: US Dollar (41.73%), Euro (29.81%), Chinese Yuan/Renminbi (12.28%), Japanese Yen (7.59%), British Pound Sterling (8.09%) — 5 currencies total
G7 currencies only: USD, Euro, JPY, GBP, Canadian Dollar, Swiss Franc, Australian Dollar
USD, Euro, Gold, and Oil — representing the major stores of global value
USD and Euro only — the two most widely traded reserve currencies

explanation: SDR (Special Drawing Rights): IMF's international reserve asset. Not a currency — a claim on freely usable currencies held by IMF members. Value is weighted average of 5 currencies. China's Yuan (RMB) added in Oct 2016 (first change since 2000). Revised weights: USD (41.73%) > EUR (29.81%) > GBP (8.09%) > JPY (7.59%) > CNY (12.28%). India's SDR allocation: reflects IMF quota (India has 2.75% quota). SDR interest rate = weighted average of 3-month government rates of 5 currencies. SDR ≠ currency, cannot be used directly by individuals.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: CRISIL (Credit Rating Information Services of India Limited) was established in India in 1987 as the country's first credit rating agency. Credit ratings serve primarily to:

options.option_text: Assess the creditworthiness of debt instruments/issuers — indicating probability of timely payment of interest and principal — enabling investors to price risk and issuers to access capital markets
Determine the credit limit for individual retail borrowers (personal loans)
Certify the quality of products manufactured by Indian companies for export
Grade government ministries on fiscal management performance

explanation: Credit Rating Agencies in India (SEBI registered): CRISIL (1987, S&P subsidiary), ICRA (1991, Moody's affiliate), CARE (1993), Acuité (formerly SMERA), India Ratings (Fitch India), Infomerics. Ratings: AAA → AA → A → BBB (investment grade); BB → B → C → D (speculative/default). Mandated for: public issuance of debentures/bonds, commercial paper, bank loans > ₹5 crore in some contexts. SEBI regulates CRAs via CRA Regulations 1999. Annual surveillance review required. CRISIL also rates sovereigns and mutual funds. Solicited vs unsolicited ratings.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: CGTMSE (Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises) helps MSMEs by:

options.option_text: Providing a government-backed credit guarantee to lenders — so banks can lend to MSMEs WITHOUT collateral; if MSE defaults, CGTMSE reimburses the bank up to 85% of the outstanding amount
Directly lending money to MSEs at subsidised interest rates from government funds
Insuring MSME factory equipment against theft and fire damage
Guaranteeing export payments for MSME exporters against importer default

explanation: CGTMSE (set up 2000, SIDBI + Ministry of MSME): Enables collateral-free lending to micro and small enterprises. Coverage: up to 85% for micro enterprises (loan ≤ ₹5 lakh), 75% for others (loan up to ₹2 crore), 80% for women/NE/SC-ST borrowers. Annual guarantee fee: 0.37-1.35% of loan amount. Since 2000: guaranteed over 50 lakh accounts. Why important: banks normally refuse unsecured MSE loans (no collateral); CGTMSE shifts credit risk to government, unlocking formal credit. Updated 2023: coverage increased to ₹5 crore for select categories.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: AePS (Aadhaar-enabled Payment System) allows financial transactions using:

options.option_text: Aadhaar number + biometric authentication (fingerprint/iris) at a micro-ATM — enabling cash withdrawals, balance enquiry, and fund transfer without a debit card
Aadhaar card physically swiped at a POS terminal like a credit card
QR code scan of Aadhaar barcode to initiate UPI payments
Aadhaar OTP plus bank account PIN for internet banking

explanation: AePS (NPCI platform): Allows banking transactions using Aadhaar + biometric. No debit card, no smartphone, no internet needed. Operated via Business Correspondents (BCs) with micro-ATMs. Transactions: cash withdrawal, cash deposit, mini statement, balance enquiry, Aadhaar-to-Aadhaar fund transfer. Critical for financial inclusion — reaches unbanked rural population where smartphone/card infrastructure is absent. Key in DBT: MGNREGA wages, PM-KISAN, LPG subsidy directly withdrawn via AePS by beneficiaries. Also used by migrant workers to withdraw money near their workplace.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: LIBOR (London Interbank Offered Rate) was phased out by June 2023 and replaced primarily by SOFR (Secured Overnight Financing Rate). The main reason LIBOR was discontinued was:

options.option_text: LIBOR manipulation scandal (2012): banks submitted false rates to benefit their derivative positions — LIBOR was a survey-based rate, not based on actual transactions, making it easy to manipulate
LIBOR was too low during the 2008 financial crisis and caused losses for lenders
Brexit made it impossible to use a London-based rate for global dollar transactions
LIBOR only applied to European banks and was not representative of global lending

explanation: LIBOR manipulation: 2012 scandal — Barclays, UBS, Deutsche Bank, Citigroup traders colluded to submit false survey rates. Since ~US$300 trillion in contracts (loans, bonds, derivatives) referenced LIBOR, even small manipulation = massive profits. FSB (Financial Stability Board) worked on replacement. SOFR (US replacement): based on actual US Treasury repo transactions (secured) → transaction-based, not survey-based, impossible to manipulate. India impact: ECBs and trade finance contracts shifted from LIBOR to SOFR/SONIA (UK). India's MIFOR (Mumbai IBOR) also being replaced by MIBOR-OIS compounded. RBI circular required transition plans.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Priority Sector Lending (PSL) sub-target for 'Weaker Sections' for domestic scheduled commercial banks is:

options.option_text: 10% of ANBC (Adjusted Net Bank Credit) — covering SC/ST borrowers, women borrowers, small/marginal farmers, minorities, differently abled, self-help groups, and distressed persons
40% of ANBC — the overall PSL target
18% of ANBC — specifically for agricultural lending
7.5% of ANBC — target for micro enterprises

explanation: PSL sub-targets for domestic SCBs (RBI Master Direction 2020): Agriculture: 18% (of which 8% to small/marginal farmers). Micro Enterprises: 7.5%. Weaker Sections: 10%. Overall PSL: 40%. Categories: Agriculture, MSME, Export Credit, Education, Housing, Social Infrastructure, Renewable Energy, Others. Shortfall: must deposit in RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund) or equivalent funds at lower interest rate (penalty). Priority Sector Lending Certificates (PSLCs): tradeable certificates — banks with excess PSL can sell to banks with shortfall. Introduced 2016.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Reserve Money (M0), also called 'High-Powered Money' or 'Monetary Base,' includes:

options.option_text: Currency in circulation + Bankers' deposits with RBI (CRR) + 'Other' deposits with RBI — the base on which commercial banks create credit via money multiplier
All bank deposits (savings + current + fixed) across all scheduled commercial banks
Only the currency printed by the government mints (coins)
RBI's total assets including gold reserves and foreign exchange

explanation: Money Supply hierarchy: M0 (Reserve Money) = Currency in Circulation + Bankers' deposits with RBI + Other deposits with RBI. M1 (Narrow Money) = Currency with Public + Demand Deposits with banks + Other deposits with RBI. M2 = M1 + Savings deposits of Post Office. M3 (Broad Money) = M1 + Time Deposits with banks. M4 = M3 + Total Post Office deposits. M0 is 'high-powered' because ₹1 of M0 creates ₹(1/CRR) of M3 via credit multiplier. RBI controls M0 directly; M3 depends on banking system behaviour. Money Multiplier = M3/M0.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Bank Board Bureau (BBB)' set up in 2016 was mandated to:

options.option_text: Recommend appointments to the boards of PSBs, advise on strategy, help banks raise capital, and improve governance of public sector banks — precursor to a proposed Banks Board Bureau with more powers
Regulate the operations of Private Sector banks and set guidelines for corporate governance
Investigate frauds in public sector banks and recommend disciplinary action
Determine the interest rates that public sector banks should charge on priority sector loans

explanation: BBB (set up 2016, part of 'Indradhanush' for PSB reforms): Chaired by retired CAG (M.K. Joshi first, then B.P. Sharma). Members: banking professionals, government nominees. Functions: (1) Select CMDs/EDs of PSBs. (2) Engage with PSB boards on strategy, capital plans. (3) Help banks raise equity through innovative mechanisms. (4) Recommend CEO compensation reforms. Limitation: BBB is advisory, not statutory — limited power. Government's intent was to eventually convert BBB into a statutory holding company for PSBs. As of 2024, BBB rechristened as 'Banks Board Bureau' under more structured governance.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India adopted 'Capital Account Convertibility' partially but not fully. The key distinction is:

options.option_text: Current Account is FULLY convertible (trade in goods/services, remittances — free flow at market rate); Capital Account is PARTIALLY convertible (FDI/FPI/ECB have limits and approval routes)
Both current and capital accounts are fully convertible in India
Capital account is fully convertible but current account requires RBI approval
Neither account is convertible — all forex transactions require prior government approval

explanation: India adopted Current Account Convertibility in 1994 (Article VIII of IMF). Capital Account: still partially controlled. FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973 — liberalised but not fully open. Tarapore Committee I (1997) and II (2006) recommended gradual Capital Account Convertibility (CAC) with preconditions: fiscal deficit < 3.5% GDP, CPI inflation 3-5%, gross NPA < 5%. India hasn't achieved full CAC. FDI: mostly automatic route. FPI in bonds: limited to FPI investment limits. External debt: monitored via ECB policy. Rationale for retaining controls: prevent sudden capital outflows ('sudden stop problem').

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Which of the following items is 'Charged' on the Consolidated Fund of India — meaning Parliament can DISCUSS but NOT vote to reduce or reject it?

options.option_text: Debt charges (interest payments and loan repayments), salary of President, salary of judges of Supreme Court and High Courts, and salary of the Comptroller and Auditor General
Defence capital expenditure, which is too sensitive to be voted upon
Prime Minister's salary and Cabinet Ministers' salaries — as the Executive
Expenditure on national elections — conducted by Election Commission independently

explanation: Charged expenditure (Article 112(3) of Constitution): Parliament can discuss but cannot vote to reduce/reject — automatically appropriated. Includes: (1) President's emoluments and pension. (2) Speaker & Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha. (3) Chairman & Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha. (4) SC judges' salaries. (5) HC judges' salaries. (6) CAG's salary and pension. (7) Debt charges (interest + principal on public debt). (8) Sums required to satisfy Court judgment/decree. (9) Any other sum declared by Constitution. Rationale: independence of judiciary, constitutional authorities, and debt service from political interference.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The distinction between 'Voted Expenditure' and 'Charged Expenditure' is that voted expenditure:

options.option_text: Requires Parliament's approval through Demands for Grants — can be reduced, amended, or rejected by the Lok Sabha; forms the larger part of Union Budget expenditure
Can be spent by the government without any form of Parliamentary oversight
Refers only to subsidies voted for annually by the Cabinet
Includes only capital expenditure items that Parliament reviews each year

explanation: Voted expenditure: majority of budget — presented as Demands for Grants (ministry-wise). Lok Sabha can: approve, reduce, or reject each demand. Cannot increase. Once passed → Appropriation Act authorises withdrawal from CFI. Charged vs Voted: Charged = constitutional mandate, immovable. Voted = political decision, flexible. Important for AAO: Government Accounts are divided between Voted and Charged — CAG audits both but the appropriation mechanism differs. Excess expenditure over voted amount → requires Excess Grant (only Lok Sabha can approve retrospectively after PAC examination).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The National Small Savings Fund (NSSF) in India is:

options.option_text: A fund in the Public Account of India that pools all small savings scheme collections (PPF, NSC, Post Office deposits, KVP, Sukanya Samriddhi) — used to provide loans to Centre and States to fund their deficits
A mutual fund managed by LIC for small retail investors with guaranteed returns
A Social Security Fund to provide pensions to workers in the unorganised sector
A fund that collects fines and penalties from financial sector violations

explanation: NSSF (Public Account of India): Pools PPF, NSC, KVP, SCSS, Post Office MIS, Sukanya Samriddhi, POMIS deposits. These are LOANS to Central/State governments — NSSF lends to them. Centre's net NSSF borrowing = fiscal deficit financing item. States: allocation formula by Finance Ministry. NSSF interest rates (quarterly revision) > G-sec yields → NSSF is expensive debt for government. Why important: NSSF is NOT counted in 'market borrowings' but IS part of fiscal deficit financing. 'Off-budget' concerns: sometimes PSUs borrow from NSSF to avoid fiscal deficit optics.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Article 293 of the Indian Constitution places what restriction on State Government borrowing?

options.option_text: States can borrow ONLY within India, and if the State is indebted to the Centre, it CANNOT raise new loans without Centre's consent — restricts states from bypassing Centre's fiscal oversight
States must approve all borrowings through a two-thirds majority vote in the State Legislature
States can only borrow from RBI and not from commercial banks or capital markets
States must repay all loans within 5 years — no long-term borrowing permitted

explanation: Article 292 (Centre's borrowing): Parliament can authorise borrowing on security of CFI — no limit specified in Constitution (FRBM sets limits). Article 293 (States' borrowing): (1) States can borrow only within India. (2) States cannot raise EXTERNAL commercial borrowings directly (Centre must intermediate — ECBs via Samridhi bonds mechanism). (3) If a State is indebted to Centre (net lender/borrower relationship), Centre's CONSENT is needed for new state loans. In practice: 14th/15th Finance Commission's recommendations and annual state fiscal limits managed via Centres' oversight through CAG-audited state accounts.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Zero-Based Budgeting (ZBB), as distinct from Incremental Budgeting, requires that:

options.option_text: Every activity must justify its ENTIRE budget from scratch each year — starting from 'zero base' with no automatic continuation of previous year's allocation; activities must be ranked by priority
Government must achieve zero deficit — balanced budget — with no borrowing
All new expenditures (zero-based means new) require Parliamentary approval but old ones continue automatically
Expenditure on all government schemes should be increased to zero (eliminated) over 5 years

explanation: Budgeting approaches: Incremental Budgeting (traditional): last year's budget + x% increase. No questioning of base. ZBB (Jimmy Carter used in USA, 1970s): every spending unit justifies full budget from zero. Advantages: eliminates dead programmes, efficient allocation. Disadvantages: time-intensive, difficult for large governments. Outcome Budgeting (India since 2005-06): links expenditure to measurable outcomes (not just inputs/outputs). Performance Budget: relates expenditure to achievement of targets. India: modified ZBB used for CSS (Centrally Sponsored Schemes) review. Sunset provision: automatic discontinuation unless reviewed.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under India's GST, Input Tax Credit (ITC) works on the principle that:

options.option_text: Tax paid on INPUTS (purchases) can be offset against tax liability on OUTPUTS (sales) — eliminating the cascading 'tax on tax' effect; registered taxpayer pays tax only on VALUE ADDED at each stage
Businesses receive cash refunds from the government for GST paid on all purchases
Input materials are tax-exempt so GST is only levied at the final consumer stage
ITC allows exporters to avoid paying GST on export goods entirely

explanation: ITC mechanism: Supplier A sells to Manufacturer B: charges ₹18 GST → B can claim ₹18 ITC. Manufacturer B sells to Retailer C: charges ₹30 GST → net tax payable by B = ₹30 − ₹18 = ₹12. Retailer C sells to Consumer: charges ₹45 → net = ₹45 − ₹30 = ₹15. Consumer pays full ₹45 tax (no ITC). Total government collection = ₹45 (sum of net: ₹18 + ₹12 + ₹15). Pre-GST: CENVAT credit (central taxes) + VAT input credit (state taxes) — but no cross-utilisation; CST had no ITC. GST seamlessly chains ITC across supply chain. ITC NOT available for: personal consumption, blocked credits (Section 17(5)).

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under India's GST, the 'Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM)' means:

options.option_text: The LIABILITY to pay GST shifts from supplier to RECIPIENT — used when supplier is unregistered, or for specified supplies (e.g., legal services, goods transport agency) where tracking supplier compliance is difficult
GST is refunded in reverse when goods are returned by the buyer to the supplier
The last person in the supply chain (retailer) collects GST from all earlier stages in reverse order
Import duties are reversed (refunded) on goods re-exported from India

explanation: RCM (Section 9(3) and 9(4) of CGST Act): Two triggers: (1) Specified categories: goods transport by road (GTA), legal services to business, import of services, advocate services, director fees, etc. (2) Unregistered supplier to registered recipient. Purpose: unregistered suppliers cannot charge GST; registered buyer is accountable and must self-assess and pay GST. ITC of RCM tax is available to recipient (same tax period). Forms: ITC-03 self-declaration. Practical impact: businesses must track RCM applicability for every purchase from unregistered vendors. High compliance burden for small manufacturers.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The GST Composition Scheme allows eligible small taxpayers to:

options.option_text: Pay GST at a FLAT RATE on turnover (1% for traders, 5% for restaurants, 1% for manufacturers) without maintaining detailed invoice-level records — but they CANNOT collect GST from customers or claim ITC
Avoid paying GST entirely if their annual turnover is below ₹5 lakh
Pay GST at reduced rates AND claim full ITC on all purchases
Defer GST payment until the end of the financial year instead of monthly/quarterly

explanation: Composition Scheme (Section 10, CGST Act): Eligibility: Annual turnover ≤ ₹1.5 crore (₹75 lakh for special category states). Rates: 1% for traders/manufacturers, 5% for restaurant sector (no ITC), 6% for service providers. Trade-offs: CANNOT issue tax invoice (only bill of supply) → buyers get NO ITC → composition supplier loses business from B2B buyers who need ITC. Quarterly return (CMP-08 + GSTR-4). Not available: inter-state supplies, e-commerce operators, ice cream/tobacco manufacturers. Benefit: simple compliance, no invoice matching, lower tax. Popular with kirana stores and small manufacturers.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GST e-invoicing (mandatory for businesses above ₹5 crore turnover) means:

options.option_text: Invoices are generated through the taxpayer's ERP/accounting system but must be REGISTERED with the GST Invoice Registration Portal (IRP) which returns a unique IRN (Invoice Reference Number) — auto-populating GSTR-1 and e-Way Bill
All invoices must be physically filed at the GST office within 24 hours of issue
Businesses must use only government-provided software to create all tax invoices
E-invoicing means sending invoices via email instead of post — replacing paper invoices

explanation: E-invoicing (phased from Oct 2020): Invoice generated by supplier → uploaded to IRP (Invoice Registration Portal managed by NIC/GSTN) → IRP validates → assigns IRN (Invoice Reference Number, unique hash) + digitally signed → returns QR Code. Benefits: (1) Auto-populates GSTR-1 (no separate filing needed). (2) Auto-generates e-Way Bill for goods movement. (3) Reduces fake invoice fraud (bogus ITC). (4) Real-time data with tax department. Threshold evolution: ₹500 crore (Oct 2020) → ₹100 crore → ₹50 crore → ₹20 crore → ₹10 crore → ₹5 crore (Aug 2023). Exemptions: banks, insurance, GTA, SEZ units.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 15th Finance Commission (NK Singh, 2020-21 to 2025-26) made the key change of using Census _____ for horizontal devolution (distribution among states), replacing Census 1971:

options.option_text: Census 2011 — recognising demographic reality of current population; also introduced 'demographic performance' as a new criterion rewarding states that reduced fertility rates (10% weight)
Census 2001 — as a compromise between 1971 (southern states' preference) and 2011
Projected 2026 Census data — to future-proof the formula
Rolling 5-year average of census data from 1991-2011

explanation: 15th FC (2020-26) horizontal devolution criteria: (1) Income Distance (from richest state): 45%. (2) Population (2011 Census): 15%. (3) Area: 15%. (4) Forest and Ecology: 10%. (5) Demographic Performance: 12.5% — rewards states with lower TFR (southern states benefit; they feared losing out for controlling population). (6) Tax Effort: 2.5%. Total State Share: 41% (same as 14th FC's 42% minus JAMMU & KASHMIR UT bifurcation adjustment). Southern states (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) argued against 2011 Census as they controlled population better than northern states — demographic performance criterion was the compromise.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In Balance of Payments (BoP) accounting, when India exports software services worth $10 billion:

options.option_text: CREDIT entry in Current Account (under 'Services' → Invisibles) — foreign exchange FLOWS IN; India EARNS; recorded as +$10 billion credit in BoP
DEBIT entry — India is giving away a service so it is a loss
Capital Account entry — software is an intellectual property asset, not a service
Financial Account entry — as it involves cross-border payment flows

explanation: BoP double-entry accounting: Every transaction: one credit (+) + one debit (-). Current Account: Goods (Merchandise) trade + Services (software, tourism, finance) + Primary income (wages, dividends) + Secondary income (remittances, grants). CREDIT: exports of goods/services, remittances received, dividend received FROM abroad. DEBIT: imports, payments to foreigners. India's services surplus (~$100bn/year): software, BPO, finance offsets merchandise trade deficit. IT services export = current account credit. FPI inflow (buying Indian shares) = Financial Account credit. Key rule: CREDIT = foreign exchange inflow; DEBIT = forex outflow.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: In India's GST, HSN code stands for 'Harmonised System of Nomenclature' and is used to:

options.option_text: Classify GOODS into internationally standardised codes (6-digit global, 8-digit India) — determining the correct GST rate applicable to the product based on its category
Track the movement of goods vehicles on national highways
Identify the country of origin for customs duty assessment
Code healthcare and pharma products for drug regulation purposes

explanation: HSN (Goods) and SAC (Services Accounting Code) — used in GST invoices and returns to classify supply. HSN: World Customs Organisation (WCO) system; 21 sections, 99 chapters. India uses 8-digit HSN. Mandatory on invoices: Turnover > ₹5 crore → 6-digit HSN. ₹1.5-5 crore → 4-digit. < ₹1.5 crore (composition): HSN optional. SAC: 6-digit service classification under GST. Why important: different HSN = different GST rate. Example: 'Food preparations' under Chapter 21 may attract 5% or 18% depending on specific HSN sub-heading. Tax authorities use HSN to verify correct rate applied.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD)' concept introduced in India's budget measures:

options.option_text: Revenue Deficit MINUS grants given by Centre to States for creation of capital assets — the REAL consumption shortfall after removing productive grants that states use for asset creation
Revenue Deficit adjusted for inflation using WPI deflator
The total revenue deficit of Centre + all States combined (consolidated)
Revenue Deficit net of revenue earned from disinvestment proceeds

explanation: Effective Revenue Deficit (ERD): Introduced in India post the C. Rangarajan report. Formula: ERD = Revenue Deficit − Grants for creation of Capital Assets (to States/UTs). Rationale: some 'grants' from Centre to States are used by States for capital formation (schools, hospitals) — these are productive. Regular Revenue Deficit counts these as consumption expenditure, understating actual productive spending. FRBM Amendment 2012: ERD target added. Target trajectory: ERD must reach 0% by specific year. NK Singh Committee 2017: kept ERD as a formal FRBM target alongside Fiscal Deficit and Debt/GDP.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's FRBM Act uses a 'Fiscal Deficit to GDP ratio' target. If nominal GDP grows 10% but nominal fiscal deficit grows 12%, what happens to the fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio?

options.option_text: It INCREASES — deficit grows faster than GDP; if last year ratio was 5%, new ratio = 5% × (1.12/1.10) ≈ 5.09%
It stays the same — ratio is maintained regardless of absolute amounts
It decreases — GDP grew so the ratio improves automatically
Cannot be determined without knowing the absolute GDP figures

explanation: Ratio arithmetic: Deficit/GDP ratio = D/Y. If D grows at g_D and Y grows at g_Y: New ratio = D(1+g_D) / Y(1+g_Y) = (D/Y) × (1+g_D)/(1+g_Y). If g_D > g_Y: ratio increases. Here 12% > 10%: ratio increases. Short trick: Ratio improves ONLY IF deficit grows slower than GDP. FRBM discipline: if government wants to reduce fiscal deficit/GDP from 5% to 4.5% while GDP grows 10% nominally, deficit can only grow ≈ (4.5/5.0) × 1.10 − 1 ≈ 0.99% — i.e., fiscal deficit must FALL in absolute terms! This shows why nominal GDP growth helps consolidation without contractionary policy.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: GST subsumed which major Central and State taxes? Which of the following was NOT subsumed into GST?

options.option_text: Basic Customs Duty (BCD) — levied on imports; it was NOT subsumed into GST and continues separately (along with social welfare surcharge)
Service Tax — was subsumed into GST (as an intra-state service supply now under CGST+SGST)
Central Excise Duty — was subsumed into CGST (for most goods)
VAT (Value Added Tax) — was subsumed into SGST

explanation: GST subsumed (Central): Central Excise, Additional Excise, Service Tax, CVD (countervailing duty), SAD, Surcharges. GST subsumed (State): VAT/CST, Luxury Tax, Entertainment Tax (except local bodies), Purchase Tax, Octroi, Entry Tax. NOT subsumed: (1) Basic Customs Duty (BCD) — continues for imports. (2) Stamp Duty — on property/financial instruments. (3) Electricity Duty. (4) Property Tax. (5) Petroleum products (petrol, diesel, ATF, crude) — temporarily outside GST (Article 279A(5)). (6) Alcohol for human consumption — State-controlled. Why petroleum excluded: huge revenue for states; GST Council yet to bring in by consensus.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Outcome Budgeting in India (introduced 2005-06) requires government ministries to:

options.option_text: Present a 'Statement of Outcomes' alongside financial allocations — linking money spent to MEASURABLE OUTCOMES (e.g., km of roads built, children vaccinated) rather than just inputs (amount spent)
Achieve zero fiscal deficit as the required budget outcome
Present budgets in units of 'outcome points' instead of rupees
Allow citizens to vote on budget priorities online before Parliament approval

explanation: Outcome Budget (India, Outcome Monitoring Framework for CSS since 2005-06): Links Outlay → Output → Outcome. Example: Health Ministry — Outlay ₹1000 crore; Output = 10 lakh vaccine doses distributed; Outcome = 5% reduction in child mortality. Traditional budget only reports outlay. Performance Budget (1960s): related expenditure to targets but largely numerical. Output-Outcome Framework (NITI Aayog, 2017): more rigorous, 65 ministries. SDG India Index uses similar logic. CAG audits whether outcomes were actually achieved (Performance Audit = 3E framework: Economy, Efficiency, Effectiveness). Important for AAO: audit role extends beyond compliance to performance outcomes.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: A 'Pigouvian Tax' is imposed to correct for:

options.option_text: Negative externalities — taxing activities that impose costs on third parties (e.g., carbon tax on pollution, excise on cigarettes/alcohol); the tax equals the marginal external cost, internalising the externality
Income inequality — higher tax on wealthy individuals to redistribute income
Government debt — an annual tax on citizens to reduce fiscal deficit
Import surplus — taxing imports to protect domestic industries

explanation: Pigouvian Tax (Arthur Pigou, 1920): Market failure correction through taxation. Negative externality: private cost < social cost (pollution, smoking, alcohol). Pigouvian tax: set at MEC (Marginal External Cost) → brings private decision = social optimum. Example: Carbon tax → firms internalize pollution cost → reduce emissions to optimal level. Pigouvian Subsidy: for positive externalities (R&D, education). Green Budget India: classifies taxes/subsidies by environmental impact — emerging Pigouvian lens. GST Compensation Cess on tobacco/luxury cars has Pigouvian rationale. Limitation: difficult to quantify exact MEC.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Cooperative Federalism' model in India's fiscal management is demonstrated by:

options.option_text: The GST Council — where Centre and States jointly decide tax rates by consensus; Centre has 1/3 voting weight and States have 2/3 — India's first constitutional body with joint Centre-State decision making
The Finance Commission allocating funds only to the richest states for economic growth
States choosing to reject Finance Commission recommendations they disagree with
The Centre directing all state expenditure through centrally sponsored schemes

explanation: Cooperative Federalism in India: GST Council (Article 279A, 101st Constitutional Amendment) — joint decision-making body. Union Finance Minister chairs, State Finance Ministers are members. Decisions by 3/4th majority (not simple majority): Centre's vote = 1/3 of total weightage; States' votes collectively = 2/3. Contrast with Competitive Federalism: states compete to attract investment via ease of doing business, taxation policies. 15th FC introduced 'Demographic Performance' criterion to reward performing states. Centre-State tax relationship: Article 270 (Divisible Pool), Article 275 (Grants), Article 282 (discretionary grants). NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission for cooperative federalism discourse.

subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The concept of 'Tax Expenditure' in public finance refers to:

options.option_text: Revenue FOREGONE by the government due to tax exemptions, deductions, and concessions — treated conceptually as an 'indirect expenditure' that should be disclosed alongside direct budget expenditure
Government expenditure specifically on tax administration (CBDT, CBIC)
Taxes collected by the government and immediately spent in the same financial year
Extra spending permitted by Parliament when tax revenues exceed projections

explanation: Tax Expenditure (Stanley Surrey, 1967): Selective departures from 'benchmark' tax system — exemptions (Section 80C, 80D), deductions, lower rates, deferrals, credits — that function like spending on favoured activities. Examples: 80C deduction (₹1.5 lakh) = government subsidy for saving/insurance. Agricultural income exemption. SEZ tax holidays. India: 'Revenue Impact of Tax Incentives' statement (Statement 15 in Budget documents). Economic Survey regularly estimates tax expenditure. Global practice: UK, USA publish tax expenditure budgets. India's income tax/corporate tax exemptions ≈ ₹5-8 lakh crore/year foregone. Criticism: opaque, often captured by well-organised interest groups.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023 defines a 'Data Fiduciary' as:

options.option_text: Any entity (person/company/government body) that DETERMINES the PURPOSE and MEANS of processing personal data — and is primarily responsible for data protection compliance obligations
A government officer appointed to guard citizens' data from unauthorized access
A bank or financial institution that holds customer financial data under RBI regulation
An independent judicial body that resolves data privacy disputes

explanation: DPDP Act 2023 (India's comprehensive data protection law, replaces Personal Data Protection Bill 2019 draft): Key terms: Data Principal = individual whose data is processed (Rights: access, correction, erasure, grievance, nominate). Data Fiduciary = entity deciding purpose/means (Obligations: notice, consent, data minimisation, accuracy, security, breach notification, grievance officer). Data Processor = processes on behalf of fiduciary. Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF): higher obligations (DPO, DPIA, audit). Data Protection Board = adjudicatory body. Exemptions: national security, research, journalism. Children's data: verifiable consent of parent.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under the DPDP Act 2023, a data breach must be reported to the Data Protection Board:

options.option_text: As SOON AS POSSIBLE — there is no fixed timeline in the Act itself, but the Board may specify timelines via regulations; the Data Fiduciary must also inform affected Data Principals
Within 72 hours exactly — same as EU GDPR requirement
Within 30 days — sufficient time to assess the breach fully
Only when the breach involves more than 10,000 individuals' data

explanation: DPDP Act 2023 breach notification (Section 8(6)): Personal data breach must be intimated to: (1) Data Protection Board. (2) Affected Data Principals. Manner and timeline: as prescribed by the Board (rules not yet notified as of 2024). Compare GDPR: 72 hours to supervisory authority; 'without undue delay' to affected individuals. India's DPDP: more flexible — Board to prescribe timelines. Breach definition: unauthorised access, use, disclosure, alteration, destruction. Data Protection Board can impose penalty up to ₹250 crore per breach. Significant Data Fiduciaries face higher standards and must conduct periodic DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules 2021, 'Significant Social Media Intermediaries' (SSMIs) with > 50 lakh users in India must:

options.option_text: Appoint a Chief Compliance Officer (resident in India), a Nodal Contact Person, a Grievance Officer (resident, respond within 24 hours/resolve within 15 days), and monthly compliance reports — plus enable traceability of 'first originator' of content if required
Censor all content before publishing to prevent misinformation
Share all user data with the government on demand without court order
Delete any content the government flags within 1 hour without appeal mechanism

explanation: IT Rules 2021 (under IT Act 2000 Section 87): Three parts: (1) Intermediary Guidelines (for SM platforms). (2) Digital Media Ethics Code (OTT/news portals). (3) Publisher guidelines. SSMIs (> 50 lakh users): WhatsApp, Twitter/X, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, LinkedIn in India. Key requirements: Chief Compliance Officer (CCO), Nodal Person (24x7 law enforcement coordination), Grievance Officer (named, India-resident, resolve in 15 days). Must enable 'traceability' (first originator of viral message). Must not host prohibited content (nudity, terrorism, sovereignty threat). Challenged in courts on privacy (WhatsApp traceability case). Part II Rules 2023 added fact-checking unit provision (struck down by Bombay HC).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's e-Courts Mission Mode Project (launched 2005, Phase III ongoing) aims to achieve:

options.option_text: End-to-end digitalisation of judicial process — case filing, hearing scheduling, order publication, and service of summons through National Court Management Systems (NCMS), reducing pendency and improving access to justice
Replace all physical courts with virtual AI-based judicial decision systems
Enable citizens to file criminal FIRs online directly with the court bypassing police
Create a single unified court for the entire country accessible from any location

explanation: e-Courts Phase I (2007-15): Computerisation of district/subordinate courts. Phase II (2015-23): Hardware upgrades, video conferencing, online case status (NJDG), e-Filing, e-Payment of court fees, SMS alerts. Phase III (2023-27, ₹7,200 crore): 'Digital, Online, Mobile Courts' — paperless courts, hybrid hearings, AI-based case prioritisation, e-Summons, integrated with police (CCTNS), prisons, forensics. Supreme Court: SupTech initiative. NJDG (National Judicial Data Grid): real-time pendency dashboard (5 crore+ cases tracked). Video conferencing: 36 lakh+ hearings via VC during COVID. Undertrial prisoners: VC from jail, reducing transport costs and security risks.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Jeevan Pramaan (Digital Life Certificate), launched in 2014, was created to solve the problem of:

options.option_text: Pensioners (central government, EPS, defence) having to physically appear at bank/post office annually to prove they are alive — Jeevan Pramaan allows biometric authentication (Aadhaar-linked) from home or Common Service Centre
Fraudulent pension claims by persons impersonating government employees
Pensioners not receiving pension due to incorrect bank account details
Private sector employees proving their work experience for pension eligibility

explanation: Jeevan Pramaan (November 2014, PM Modi): Aadhaar-based Digital Life Certificate. Process: pensioner uses Jeevan Pramaan app on smartphone or visits CSC → biometric authentication (fingerprint/iris) via Aadhaar → certificate generated → shared electronically with pension disbursing authority (bank/post office). Eliminates annual physical visit to bank. Face Authentication launched 2021: pensioners can use face recognition on smartphone (no fingerprint device needed). Doorstep service: India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) postman collects at home. Coverage: 75 lakh+ pensioners enroll annually. Also integrated with UMANG app.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: eSanjeevani, developed by C-DAC and deployed by Ministry of Health, is India's national:

options.option_text: Telemedicine platform — enables online consultation between patients and doctors (doctor-to-doctor for HWC, and patient-to-doctor for OPD) without physical hospital visit
Electronic health insurance claim processing system
Digital drug procurement platform for government hospitals
Medical college admission and seat allocation portal

explanation: eSanjeevani (NTF-based, C-DAC Mohali): Two variants: (1) eSanjeevani AB-HWC: Doctor-to-Doctor teleconsultation for Ayushman Bharat Health and Wellness Centres (sub-health centre to primary health centre to specialist). (2) eSanjeevaniOPD: Patient-to-Doctor; patients register online, get token, wait in virtual queue, get video consultation free. Launched in 2019; scale-up during COVID when hospital visits were restricted. Crossed 10 crore teleconsultations as of 2023 — world's largest government-owned telemedicine platform. Integrated with ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) for health records. Available in 20+ languages. 1.4 lakh+ doctors registered.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: SWAYAM (Study Webs of Active Learning for Young Aspiring Minds) is India's national platform for:

options.option_text: MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) — free online courses for school, undergraduate, postgraduate, and professional learners; courses developed by IITs, IIMs, central universities with video lectures, assignments, and certification
Live streaming of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha proceedings for public viewing
Online scholarships and fellowships management for higher education students
Self-learning AI system for government employees on policy matters

explanation: SWAYAM (2017, Ministry of Education + AICTE): Free MOOCs. Features: 4-quadrant approach: video lectures + e-content + self-assessment + discussion forum. Credit transfer: universities can allow students to earn up to 40% of credits via SWAYAM. Courses: engineering (IIT), management (IIM), arts/science (IGNOU/central universities). SWAYAM Prabha: 32 DTH channels broadcasting educational content 24×7 — reaches areas with poor internet. DIKSHA (Digital Infrastructure for Knowledge Sharing): teacher training and school-level content (Class 1-12). ARPIT (Annual Refresher Programme in Teaching): faculty development via SWAYAM. Over 1 crore enrolments.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: Under GST, an e-Way Bill is mandatory for the movement of goods valued above ₹50,000 and serves as:

options.option_text: An electronic document generated on the GST e-Way Bill portal — accompanying goods during transit to enable tax authorities to check compliance; generated by supplier/recipient/transporter before goods movement begins
A digital road permit issued by the National Highways Authority for toll payments
An insurance certificate covering goods during transit by road or rail
A customs clearance document for goods entering a state from another country

explanation: e-Way Bill (EWB): Introduced with GST from April 2018. Required for: inter-state movement of goods > ₹50,000 and intra-state (threshold varies by state, typically ₹50,000). Generated on ewaybillgst.gov.in. Contains: GSTIN of supplier/recipient, goods details (HSN), value, transport mode, vehicle number, distance. Validity: 100 km per day. Enforcement: checking at checkposts, mobile squads. Benefits: replaced multiple state-level waybills/transit passes; unified market. Integration with e-invoicing: auto-generated from IRP when e-invoice raised. Exemptions: certain goods (fresh vegetables, agriculture under ₹50k, non-motor transport, etc.).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's 'National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC)' is set up under:

options.option_text: Section 70A of the IT Act 2000 — designated agency under the PMO's National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO) to protect Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) in sectors like energy, banking, defence, telecom, transport
The Ministry of Home Affairs under the Intelligence Bureau
Ministry of Electronics and IT as a subsidiary of CERT-In
National Security Council Secretariat under the NSA's direct control

explanation: NCIIPC (Section 70A, IT Act 2000): Designated National Nodal Agency for CII protection. Under NTRO (under PMO). CII = systems whose incapacitation would have debilitating impact on national security, economy, or public health. Designated CII sectors: energy, banking/finance, telecom, transport, government, strategic enterprises. Responsibilities: vulnerability assessment, threat intelligence, cyber security guidelines for CII organisations, coordinate incident response. Distinct from CERT-In (under MeitY): CERT-In handles general cybersecurity incidents across all sectors; NCIIPC focuses specifically on critical infrastructure. CERT-In issues advisories; NCIIPC develops protection policies.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'India Stack' refers to a set of open APIs. The FOUR layers of India Stack in order from most basic to most advanced are:

options.option_text: Presenceless (Aadhaar eKYC) → Paperless (DigiLocker) → Cashless (UPI/IMPS) → Consent (Account Aggregator) — each layer enables more sophisticated digital transactions
Hardware → Software → Network → Application — the standard technology stack
Aadhaar → PAN → Bank Account → Mobile Number — the verification stack
Central Government → State Government → Local Government → Citizen — governance stack

explanation: India Stack (iSPIRT concept): Four layers: (1) Presenceless Layer: Aadhaar eKYC — verify identity without physical presence; biometric authentication; (2) Paperless Layer: DigiLocker, eSign — documents stored/shared digitally; electronic signatures; (3) Cashless Layer: UPI, IMPS, AePS — real-time money movement 24×7; (4) Consent Layer: Account Aggregator (AA) framework — individuals control which financial data to share and for how long (AA Consent Artefact). India Stack has been adapted by other countries (notably Singapore, Australia). OCEN and ONDC are extensions of India Stack logic to credit and commerce respectively.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: India's IT Act 2000, Section 43A (added in 2008 amendment) holds a body corporate liable if it:

options.option_text: Possesses sensitive personal data and is NEGLIGENT in implementing reasonable security practices — causing wrongful loss/gain; can be ordered to pay DAMAGES (no specified maximum under Section 43A)
Publishes objectionable content on its website without prior government approval
Operates a website without registering with the Department of Telecommunication
Fails to report cybersecurity incidents to CERT-In within 6 hours

explanation: Section 43A vs Section 43: S.43 (civil liability): unauthorised access/damage to computer — up to ₹1 crore compensation. S.43A (2008 amendment): data protection for sensitive personal data by body corporates (companies/firms). Requires 'reasonable security practices and procedures' (IS/ISO 27001 standard). If negligent → damages (civil, no upper limit). Sensitive personal data: passwords, financial info, health info, sexual orientation, biometrics. DPDP Act 2023: supersedes/supplements Section 43A with more comprehensive regime. Key difference: DPDP Act = criminal penalties up to ₹250 crore; Section 43A = civil damages. CERT-In 6-hour reporting: separate obligation under CERT-In Directions 2022.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: PM-WANI (PM Wi-Fi Access Network Interface), launched in 2020, aims to:

options.option_text: Create a decentralised public Wi-Fi ecosystem across India — any small shopkeeper can set up a Public Data Office (PDO) without licence, expanding affordable broadband access particularly in rural areas
Provide free government Wi-Fi to only Below Poverty Line households through Aadhaar verification
Build a single government-owned Wi-Fi network across all public institutions
Require all hotels and airports to provide free Wi-Fi to international tourists

explanation: PM-WANI (December 2020, DoT): Decentralised public Wi-Fi model. Three layers: (1) Public Data Office (PDO): Any entity (kirana store, petrol pump) sets up Wi-Fi hotspot — no licence, no fee registration. (2) Public Data Office Aggregator (PDOA): Aggregates multiple PDOs, manages authentication and accounting. (3) App Provider: App through which user discovers and connects to nearest WANI hotspot. Revolutionary: delicensed model (like WiFi Alliance OpenRoaming). Targets: 10 lakh Wi-Fi hotspots. Complements BharatNet (which connects village panchayats to fibre backbone — WANI uses this backhaul for last-mile Wi-Fi).

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM)' creates which core infrastructure for health digitisation?

options.option_text: ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) — a 14-digit unique health ID for every citizen that links all health records (prescriptions, lab reports, discharge summaries) across hospitals, labs, and pharmacies with citizen consent
A centralised national hospital that digitally provides treatment to all citizens online
An AI diagnostic system replacing doctors for routine disease detection
A digital insurance portal for cashless claim processing under PM-JAY

explanation: ABDM (2021, NHA — National Health Authority): Building India's National Digital Health Ecosystem. Components: (1) ABHA ID (Health Account): 14-digit, voluntary, links health records. (2) Health Facility Registry (HFR): Register of all hospitals, labs, pharmacies. (3) Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR): All doctors, nurses. (4) Unified Health Interface (UHI): Open network for health services booking (like ONDC for health). (5) Personal Health Records (PHR): Citizens control who sees their records. As of 2024: 60 crore+ ABHA IDs created. Distinct from PM-JAY (insurance): ABDM = health data infrastructure; PM-JAY = health coverage for 12 crore families.

section: Milestone 10 — IT in Governance & Full Paper Ready (Ch 16)
subject: Economics & Governance
stem: The 'National Data Governance Framework Policy (NDGFP)' proposed for India focuses on:

options.option_text: Creating a framework for sharing NON-PERSONAL government data (anonymised, aggregated datasets from ministries, PSUs) with researchers and businesses to drive innovation, while keeping personal data protected under DPDP Act
Requiring all Indian citizens to register their personal data with a central government repository
Mandating that all data generated in India must be stored only within India (data localisation)
Establishing a government monopoly on cloud computing services

explanation: NDGFP (Draft 2022, MeitY): Addresses non-personal data — the public data generated by government schemes, surveys, satellite imagery, healthcare records (anonymised). Key elements: India Data Management Office (IDMO) to govern. Research/startup access to anonymised government datasets. Data sharing protocols (APIs). Distinction from DPDP Act: DPDP = personal data protection (individual rights). NDGFP = non-personal data sharing (collective value creation). Complement: together they create India's digital data governance architecture. Data as a public good: India's data with India's people. Aligns with India's 'data colonialism' concerns about global tech platforms extracting Indian data value.
